issues.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks
issues.summary: For centuries, lost cargo sparked fierce battles over who had the right to claim treasures washed ashore. The post The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Amelia Soth
issues.content_html:
In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.”

The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns.

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).

More to Explore

Lonely Diarist of the High Seas

April White July 21, 2025 As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story.

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:

The first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.

Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic”:

The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to quickly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.

Their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.

issues.title: Flax Seeds of Revolution
issues.summary: Revolutionary-era women spun flax as resistance against British rule and colonial gender norms. The post Flax Seeds of Revolution appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Jonathan Aprea
issues.content_html:
250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made.

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen, spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

A Brief History of Flax

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum, is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world, with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE. It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil. The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous, appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan—who was usually male—to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century, but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

The (Flax)seeds of Revolution

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports.

The act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins.”

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy.” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins.”

Linen was not the only useful flax product in early America. When clothing, tablecloths, and bedsheets wore out, the material was reused for two other essential colonial industries: bookbinding and papermaking. Flax was the material of choice for bookbinding thread due to its durability and strength. Nearly every book printed in the thirteen colonies was stitched with linen thread.

Before paper came to be made by pulping wood, it was crafted from old linen rags. An advertisement in The Massachusetts Spy from October 18, 1779, sought “all Linen & Cotton and Linen Rags, be they ever so small, as they are equally good for the purpose of making paper.” In fact, in 1776, before later transcribing it onto speciallyprepared vellum, the Declaration of Independence was drafted on flax paper. From textile to text, flax bound and dressed the story of America from the very beginning, making the concept of America itself legible for the first time.

Spinning Freedom

For British rule in North America, however, the writing was on the wall as plainly as it would soon be written on the flax. Growing economic dissatisfaction sowed discontent with mainland England. In 1765, the government of King George III passed the Stamp Act, which required written materials such as legal documents and magazines to be printed on London-milled paper embossed with a special stamp. The act enraged the colonial printing industry and papermaking, spurring the slogan “no taxation without representation.” This legislation was soon deemed unenforceable and repealed.

The Stamp Act was only one of many taxes and trade restrictions implemented by Britain that attempted to force the colonists to import goods at higher prices. In response, Patriots boycotted English goods, leading to shortages of textile products and the rags needed to make paper. Across the colonies, people opted to make their own goods, rejecting English rule in favor of American ingenuity. A wheelwright in Lexington, Massachusetts, reported significantly more business in spinning wheels in the lead-up to the revolution.

Spinning was catapulted into the public eye as a patriotic act. Eighteenth-century newspapers reported dozens of spinning bees where everyone from elderly women to young girls spun yarn and thread to do their part for the Revolution. This work could even take on a competitive edge. In 1769, two Connecticut women went head-to-head in a competition that was covered in several papers:

On the 16th Instant, the Wife of Mr. John Vaughan of Lebanon agreed upon a spinning Match with a neighbouring young woman; they began their work three Quarters of an Hour after Sunrise, and left off at Nine O’Clock in the Evening of the same Day.

After that marathon, they had spun nearly fourteen skeins of fine linen yarn.

Homespun cloth was not only a symbol of rejecting British control, but a religious symbol of piety and humility in the face of European luxuries, which were seen as mere vanity. In the late eighteenth century, spinning one’s own linens was considered a sign of good character, with reference made to the biblical verse (Proverbs 31:10–31) in which the “Wife of Noble Character” “selects wool and flax / and works with eager hands” on behalf of the household.

The respectable sheen of spinning one’s own yarn from flax enabled women to engage with both revolutionary ideology and manual labor without sullying themselves in the eyes of their peers. Newspapers like The Providence Gazette commended their work, describing these women as “Daughters of Liberty” with “good reputation.” These passionate yet respectable young women working for the cause contrasted with the Sons of Liberty, the revolutionary group known for starting riots and initiating the Boston Tea Party. As historians have argued, this negotiation between Revolutionary fervor and female respectability politics revealed a deeper tension between the desire for freedom and fears of unbridled chaos.

More to Explore

How War Revolutionized Ireland’s Linen Industry

Matthew Wills June 7, 2019 During the Napoleonic Wars, Irish women, who had traditionally only spun flax into thread, took over the traditionally male job of weaving linen as well.

As the revolution wore on, linen became a potently political sartorial choice. Remarking on the clothing worn by the ladies at a 1769 spinning bee held on Long Island, a columnist from Massachusetts called them “true Female Patriots,” who, by wearing homespun, demonstrated the intensity of their disdain for British rule. As historian Mathilde Frances Lind writes, “people wearing cloth spun and woven at home were physically enveloped in the fabric of the revolution, bodily experiencing and displaying their allegiance to the colonists’ cause.” Wearing homespun cloth became a desirable characteristic of marriageable elite women. Just as women sought men willing to die for the revolution, so too did men seek wives who were willing to clothe themselves in it.

Flax Fortunes

Long before women held prominent roles in the workforce, their weaving was a tangible, valuable economic production that showed their active role in the early American economy. Spinning flax into linen was a way for women to express their political preferences and participate in revolutionary economic tactics. In 1774, Abigail Adams, known for her sharp intellect, wrote to her husband, future President John Adams, about the increasing political tension in Massachusetts and his proximity to it. “As for me, I will seek wool and flax, and work willingly with my hands; and indeed there is occasion for all our industry and economy.”

With the nineteenth century came the invention of the cotton gin, the exploitation of chattel slavery, and developments in foreign markets that caused the bulk of America’s textile outputs to shift to cotton. As the Civil War boiled over, cotton constituted 61 percent of the value of all US exports. Linen production largely morphed into more specialized markets for industrial products and luxury goods.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

Nonetheless, linen and the “Age of the Homespun” had taken on a mythological valence. Orators and politicians referenced an earlier, simpler age when political change looked like industrious, virtuous women spinning flax yarn together. The Daughters of the American Revolution—a hereditary association founded in 1890 and run by descendants of revolutionaries—adopted an insignia that captured the patriotic spirit of Revolutionary-era women from whom they’d descended. As an homage to the women who supported the boycotts by making their own cloth, they chose a spinning wheel in front of a distaff filled with flax.

The economic and symbolic impact of flax on the American origin story is still visible today, if you know where to look. George Washington’s visage underscores its importance: linen made from flax constitutes 25% of every American dollar bill.

Flax became a product and driver of the American Revolution, enabling women to demonstrate their virulent patriotism within the gender norms of their society. The Plant Humanities Initiative at Dumbarton Oaks seeks to uncover these complexities, revealing the ways that plants tangle with and influence major geopolitical events like the founding of America.

issues.title: Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War
issues.summary: As the nation embraced reconciliation, former Union soldiers questioned whether their sacrifices had been in vain. The post Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Livia Gershon
issues.content_html:
In the decade following the Civil War, many white northerners wanted nothing more than to put the carnage behind them and reunify the country. But, historian Brian Matthew Jordan writes, one group that generally wasn’t ready to forgive and forget was Union veterans.

Jordan writes that the returning soldiers found a society that was happy to hail them as heroes but often offered them little material support. Many employers refused to hire men who they believed were too mentally or physically wounded to function.

“The momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”

And veterans’ efforts to ask for more were frequently dismissed. In the summer of 1865, just months after the war’s end, The New York Times complained that returning military men “prefer to live by begging.”

But Jordan argues that the veterans’ anger was not just about their own needs. Many felt that efforts to move past the conflict insulted their sacrifices. Those who returned with disabilities, painful wounds, and post-traumatic stress were reminded constantly of the war, and some worked to remind their neighbors, staging mock battles on town greens to show the “stay at homes” what the fighting had looked like. One wrote that “the momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”

More to Explore

Capturing the Civil War

Susanna Ashton May 23, 2024 The images, diaries, and ephemera in Grand Valley State University’s Civil War and Slavery Collection reveal the cold realities of Abraham Lincoln’s world.

A prime symbol of this neglect for many was the Confederacy’s president, Jefferson Davis. Soon after the war’s end, one veteran wrote to President Andrew Johnson, saying that he believed he had been “spared to witness the close of this wicked and unjust rebellion” and would be honored to help build a scaffold for Davis’s execution. Instead, despite being accused of treason, Davis was released two years after the war’s end and became a symbol of the Lost Cause. One Union veteran from Massachusetts complained that he had lost an arm “in vain” since “Jefferson Davis is today a hero, and more care is taken of him than the soldiers who fought to preserve the Union.”

Jordan writes that the Grand Army of the Republic (GAR), which was founded in 1866 and quickly became a national organization with 2,000 posts, focused primarily on supporting veterans, widows, and orphans, including by lobbying for benefits. But it also protested the appointment of “rebels and traitors” to government offices that could have gone to former Union soldiers.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

GAR soon became a controversial group, with some northern civilians arguing that its demands and remembrances kept too much bitterness alive and made it difficult for the country to move forward.

In some cases, military service had also introduced northern soldiers to ideas about racial justice that their neighbors back home didn’t embrace. While not every white veteran became a supporter of Black Americans’ rights, Jordan suggests that it wasn’t uncommon. As the planter class attempted to reinstate a system of virtual slavery with the Black Codes and vigilante violence, some wondered if they would end up having to fight the war all over again.

issues.title: What happened to King Harold's children after the battle of Hastings?
issues.summary: William the Conqueror had conquered and launched a new era in England under the Normans, but he had to keep an eye on the heirs of his fallen foe
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
The battle of Hastings was over: from the bloody fighting on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, emerged as King of England while Harold Godwinson, after less than a year on the throne, was dead.

The Norman Conquest had begun, yet the family of the fallen king still posed a threat to William the Conqueror. Yes, three of Harold’s brothers also died that same year: Tostig had allied with Harald Hardrada and been killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge, while Gyrth and Leofwine perished alongside Harold at Hastings.

But in the early years of William’s reign Harold’s mother Gytha became a figurehead of rebellion in Exeter, and there were concerns that his seven children may one day seek to restore their line.

Who were Harold Godwinson’s children?

Harold Godwinson had five sons and two daughters. With his first wife, Edith Swanneck, he had three boys, Godwin, Edmund and Magnus, and two girls, Gunhild and Gytha. He had two more boys, Harold and Ulf, possibly with his second wife, Ealdgyth, although the lack of historical records means there remains confusion over who gave birth to Ulf.

  • Read more | What if Harold died at Stamford Bridge, not Hastings?

What happened to Harold’s wives?

Details are scant, but it seems that Edith Swanneck – also called Edith the Fair or the Handfasted Queen as she may have been unofficially married to Harold – survived the immediate aftermath of the battle of Hastings. According to legend, it was she who identified Harold’s body on the battlefield.

Ealdgyth, or Edith of Mercia, was married to Harold in early 1066 as part of a political alliance. After Hastings, her brothers, the earls of Mercia and Northumberland, took her to Chester for safety. It was possibly there that she gave birth to Ulf.

  • Read more | In 1066, King Harold was meant to save England. How did it all go wrong?

What happened to Harold’s sons?

The eldest sons, Godwin and Edmund, were teenagers in 1066 and fled to Ireland, where they lived under the protection of Diarmait, King of Leinster. Twice, they launched a campaign to western England in the hopes of overthrowing the Norman regime.

In 1068, leading a force of Dublin Norse mercenaries, they failed in their initial aim of seizing Bristol before losing a decisive battle in Somerset. They found no support from their father’s former allies, who had made peace with William. The following years, they returned with a fleet of ships and headed for Exeter, but again failed.

Instead, Godwin and Edmund raided parts of Devon and Cornwall, then, with no hopes of success, they fled again, this time to the court of their relative, Sweyn II of Denmark.

It is possible that their younger brother Magnus accompanied them, but only clues remain in the historical sources. He may have died during Godwin and Edmund’s doomed campaigns, or became a monk in Sussex or a count in modern-day Poland.

Accounts suggest that Harold (junior) found his way to the court of Olaf III of Norway, the son of Harald Hardrada. Despite Harold Godwinson defeating and killing Hardrada, he spared Olaf’s life at Stamford Bridge, so Olaf welcomed the young Harold into his service. It appears that he participated in expeditions to the Orkneys, Hebrides, Isle of Man and Anglesey.

Ulf, however, had been immediately captured after Hastings and was imprisoned in Normandy until William’s death in 1087. By then, any thoughts of opposition had been stamped out: in fact, he became a knight of the new Duke of Normandy.

  • Read more | How well did Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror know each other prior to the battle of Hastings?

What happened to Harold’s daughters?

Gunhild was at a nunnery at Wilton Abbey in 1066 and remained in England. She married one of William’s inner circle, Alan the Red, possibly a strategic alliance to help Alan secure his lands, which had belonged to Gunhild’s mother. When he died shortly afterwards, she ended up with his brother, Alan the Black.

Gytha, meanwhile, escaped to Denmark and married Vladimir II Monomakh, ruler of Smolensk and Chernigov and the future Grand Prince of Kiev. They had several children together, with one of them becoming known as Harald; a small way of honouring Gytha’s father, since reclaiming the English crown was out of reach.

issues.title: Speaking more than one language isn’t just about keeping your mind sharp — scientists found it tracks with staying physically healthier too
issues.summary: Holding back the wrong word in conversation feels like a tiny hiccup, but researchers analyzing more than 86,000 European adults linked multilingualism to slower aging across both mind and body. Even more striking, each additional language tracked with a stronger edge — especially in people's late 70s and 80s.
issues.author: PsyPost
issues.content_html:
There’s a split-second pause anyone who speaks more than one language knows well — that fleeting moment when a word from the wrong language tries to jump the line, and you quietly push it aside. Most of us treat extra languages as a practical skill for navigating an airport, ordering dinner abroad, or rounding out a resume.

What rarely crosses anyone’s mind is that this quiet mental juggling act might track with how slowly you age. Yet that’s the striking pattern turning up in new research on multilingualism — the everyday habit of speaking more than one language.

For years, earlier studies comparing bilingual and monolingual adults pulled in conflicting directions, leaving plenty of room for skepticism. Some pointed to clear advantages in later life, while others saw little difference at all.

The quiet juggling act in your head

Nothing about multilingual speech looks strenuous from the outside, yet the brain never puts the unused languages to sleep. Whenever someone who knows multiple languages gets ready to talk, every language they speak stays awake in the background at the same time.

Holding back competing words so the right phrasing comes through keeps attention and mental focus quietly exercised all day. Over a lifetime of ordinary conversation, researchers think that steady mental workout may help shield the brain as it ages.

Why the advantage keeps stacking

To test whether that everyday habit tracks with healthier aging on a much wider scale, researchers analyzed data from more than 86,000 healthy adults across 27 European countries. Using a machine-learning model, they compared each person’s actual age with how old they appeared based on memory, daily functioning, and physical health, then looked at how those patterns lined up with multilingualism across countries.

Monolingual speakers were more likely to appear biologically older than their actual age. People living in countries where speaking multiple languages is common, by contrast, had a lower chance of showing signs of accelerated aging — holding onto both mental sharpness and physical health more reliably.

More striking still, the protective pattern didn’t stop at being bilingual. Knowing even one extra language mattered noticeably, and knowing several tracked with an even stronger buffer — suggesting each added language may layer on further resilience.

That gap wasn’t spread evenly across adulthood, either. The sharpest difference showed up among adults in their late 70s and 80s — right when memory, movement, and everyday tasks tend to face the steepest challenges.

PsyPost’s full coverage of the study unpacks how the computer model built its “biobehavioural age gap” using health factors like heart disease and hearing loss, which European nations ranked highest and lowest for multilingualism, and separate lab findings linking lifelong bilingualism to a physically larger hippocampus.

What wealth and clean air couldn’t explain

Could the whole pattern simply reflect living in a wealthier, more politically stable country? To find out, the team adjusted for a broad range of national conditions, from air quality and political climate to gender inequality and migration patterns.

Even with those differences accounted for, the tie between multilingualism and slower aging stayed steady. Language experience itself seemed to carry something unique that national wealth and environment didn’t explain away.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how everyday language habits relate to healthy aging. However, the researchers did not directly examine brain mechanisms, and the findings reflect broad population-level associations rather than proving that speaking extra languages directly prevents age-related decline — nuance explored alongside the broader brain-health context in the full report.

Speaking multiple languages won’t freeze the clock, and aging well never comes down to one habit. Still, it’s a quiet reminder that some of the steadier workouts for staying sharp and resilient aren’t scheduled at a gym — they may be unfolding invisibly inside ordinary conversation, one chosen word at a time.

issues.title: Evening carbohydrates linked to slightly longer sleep in toddlers
issues.summary: A study of toddlers suggests that eating an evening meal higher in carbohydrates and calories is associated with slightly longer daily sleep durations. However, the observed differences were small, and the findings rely on observational dietary records.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Researchers analyzing the dietary habits of toddlers found that consuming more calories and carbohydrates during the evening meal is associated with slightly longer daily sleep durations. The findings suggest that the types of food young children eat before bed might be related to their sleep patterns. The study was published in the journal Clinical Nutrition.

Sleep is a fundamental requirement for physical and cognitive development in early childhood. Chronic short sleep duration in young children has been linked to a higher risk of developing health conditions later in life, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases. Because average sleep durations in younger children appear to have declined over recent decades, public health experts are exploring lifestyle factors that might promote better sleep.

Past experimental studies in adults have suggested that the nutritional makeup of a meal can influence sleepiness. Macronutrients are the main nutrients that provide the body with energy, categorized primarily as carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Meals rich in carbohydrates are thought to induce drowsiness, while protein-rich meals do not appear to have the same effect.

Carbohydrates that are quickly digested and absorbed cause a rapid rise in blood sugar. These are often referred to as high-glycemic index foods. Some researchers suspect that consuming these types of foods increases the production of insulin, a hormone that helps regulate blood sugar.

High levels of insulin might help an amino acid called tryptophan cross the blood-brain barrier more easily. Amino acids are the basic building blocks of proteins, and the blood-brain barrier is a semi-permeable boundary that protects the brain from circulating blood. Tryptophan competes with other large amino acids to enter the brain.

A spike in insulin helps pull those competing amino acids out of the bloodstream, leaving a higher concentration of tryptophan available to enter the brain. Once inside the brain, tryptophan is used to produce serotonin. Serotonin is a chemical messenger that helps modulate mood and prepare the body for sleep.

Another potential mechanism involves a digestive hormone called cholecystokinin. The intake of food, particularly large amounts of calories or specific macronutrients, stimulates the release of this hormone in the gut. Higher levels of cholecystokinin have been reported to induce sleepiness in previous human studies.

To see if these nutritional dynamics relate to sleep in toddlers in their natural environments, a team of researchers from Germany designed an observational study. Katharina Diethelm and Anette E. Buyken at the Research Institute of Child Nutrition in Dortmund led the investigation. They wanted to know if the absolute amounts and relative proportions of macronutrients in an evening meal were associated with how long children slept during their second year of life.

The researchers analyzed data from the Dortmund Nutritional and Anthropometric Longitudinally Designed Study. This ongoing research project began in 1985 and tracks the diet, growth, and metabolism of participants from infancy into early adulthood. Participants attend regular clinical visits that include medical examinations, lifestyle interviews, and body measurements. The anthropometric measurements included recording the children’s height, weight, and skinfold thickness to assess body fat percentage.

For the current analysis, the investigators focused on 594 toddlers from the larger cohort. They selected children at ages 1.5 and 2 years because at this stage, sleep rhythms are usually established. By this age, toddlers have also mostly transitioned from infant milk to eating standard family meals.

To measure dietary intake, parents completed weighed dietary records over three consecutive days. This required parents to weigh and record every food and beverage their child consumed using a household scale. The research team defined the evening meal as the last food eaten between 5:00 p.m. and 9:00 p.m. that contained at least ten calories.

The team categorized the foods by their glycemic index, which measures how quickly a given food raises blood sugar levels. They also calculated the glycemic load, a metric that accounts for both the glycemic index and the total amount of carbohydrates in a standard serving. Parents reported their children’s average daily sleep duration during regular visits to the study pediatrician.

The researchers first calculated the absolute intake of different nutrients in the evening meal and compared these amounts to total daily sleep. They found that a higher total calorie intake during the evening meal was associated with longer sleep duration. Specifically, for every ten additional calories consumed at dinner, a child slept an average of one extra minute per day.

Carbohydrate intake showed a similar positive relationship with sleep time. Each additional gram of carbohydrate in the evening meal was linked to 0.8 extra minutes of sleep. The association was slightly stronger for carbohydrates from high-glycemic index foods, which corresponded to 1.3 extra minutes of sleep per gram. A higher overall glycemic load was also accompanied by a longer sleeping time.

Next, the investigators examined what happened when they mathematically modeled substituting the energy provided by protein with energy provided by other nutrients. They found that replacing a percentage of protein with carbohydrates from high-glycemic index foods or with fats was associated with longer sleep. However, this specific exchange only showed an effect in the subset of toddlers who did not wake up to eat during the night.

For the children who ate nightly snacks, swapping protein for carbohydrates in the evening meal had no relation to sleep duration. Total daily calorie intake did not differ between children who slept shorter amounts and those who slept longer. This suggests that the differences in evening caloric intake were likely balanced out by the children’s eating habits earlier in the day.

The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot prove that eating more carbohydrates directly causes toddlers to sleep longer. The measured effects were also extremely small. Adding a few minutes of sleep per night is unlikely to be practically relevant for the average healthy toddler. The researchers caution against changing a child’s evening diet solely in an attempt to lengthen their sleep based on these results.

Sleep duration data was based on parent reports rather than objective measurements like wearable activity trackers. Parents might overestimate how long their children actually sleep, especially if a child spends time lying awake quietly in bed. Assessing sleep over a full 24-hour period without separating daytime naps from nighttime sleep could also obscure specific dietary associations with overnight resting patterns.

The participants in the cohort generally came from families with a high socioeconomic status, leading to a relatively homogenous sample of children who already enjoyed long sleep durations. The researchers could not account for exact family bedtime routines or the physical activity levels of the youngest children. They were also unable to directly measure the amount of tryptophan in the children’s diets.

Future research will need to test these dietary associations in controlled clinical trials. The investigators suggest that while healthy children might not experience major shifts in sleep time from a modified evening meal, adjusting the ratio of carbohydrates to protein could still be relevant for specific vulnerable groups who struggle with sleep disturbances.

The study was initially presented at a scientific nutrition congress in Germany before full publication. The peer-reviewed study, “Associations between the macronutrient composition of the evening meal and average daily sleep duration in early childhood,” was authored by Katharina Diethelm, Thomas Remer, Hannah Jilani, Clemens Kunz, and Anette E. Buyken.

issues.title: Calming kids with screens creates a developmental feedback loop for most families
issues.summary: Handing a toddler a smartphone to calm a tantrum is tied to lower self-control. A new multi-year study reveals that for most children, screen time and cognitive skills influence each other in a continuous developmental loop.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
A new study shows that using digital devices to soothe upset preschoolers is linked to their development of self-control in differing ways depending on the individual child. For most children, screen time and cognitive skills influence each other in a continuous loop, though for a small subset, screen use appears to directly drive developmental changes. These findings were published in the Journal of Communication.

Executive functions act as the brain’s internal air traffic control system. They are higher-order cognitive processes that manage goal-directed behavior. Inhibitory control allows humans to suppress impulsive responses, like stopping oneself from grabbing a toy from another child. Cognitive flexibility allows people to shift their thinking, like adapting to a new rule in a game or looking at a problem from a new perspective.

Handing a child a tablet or smartphone to calm a tantrum is a common parenting strategy known as media emotion regulation. When children rely heavily on a digital device to calm down, they may miss opportunities to practice internal coping strategies. They also miss out on verbalizing their feelings with a caregiver.

Previous research links this specific digital habit to poorer executive function. Yet, the exact sequence of events over time remains uncertain. This chronological sequence is scientifically known as temporal ordering.

Researchers regularly debate whether media use initiates developmental delays, or if children who already struggle with self-regulation prompt their exhausted parents to use screens more frequently. Both scenarios are entirely plausible. Jane Shawcroft at The Ohio State University led a team to investigate this timeline. Researchers from several institutions, including Brigham Young University and Georgetown University, contributed to the project.

The research team drew data from a longitudinal project tracking child development in the United States. They analyzed a cohort of 87 children spanning the ages of two and a half to seven and a half. Through yearly surveys, parents reported how frequently they offered media to their children to handle difficult emotions.

The cognitive testing provides an objective look at brain development during these formative years. To measure inhibitory control, children engaged in a computer-based assessment. A screen displayed a row of arrows, and the children had to indicate the direction of the center arrow. To succeed, they had to suppress the reflex to match the surrounding arrows pointing in opposite directions.

To evaluate cognitive flexibility, researchers used a dimensional card sorting task. Children were asked to match pictures based on a specific rule, such as color. The rule would then unexpectedly switch to a different dimension, such as shape, requiring the child to quickly adapt their matching strategy.

The researchers tracked these behaviors over several years to observe which measures predicted the others in subsequent assessments. To make sense of the individual patterns, the team used a statistical algorithm designed to find hidden subgroups within a data set. This approach allowed them to categorize the children based on their unique developmental timelines rather than assuming a single pattern applied to everyone.

The algorithm identified three distinct groups of temporal ordering. The vast majority of the children, making up slightly more than 87 percent of the cohort, fell into a bidirectional category. In this group, using media to regulate emotions and a child’s executive function skills influenced each other back and forth continuously as the children aged.

A second group, representing 7 percent of the children, showed a one-way directional pattern. For these children, relying on screens to moderate mood strongly predicted later deficits in both cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control. The reverse was not true, meaning early cognitive deficits did not predict increased screen time for this subset.

The third group, comprising 6 percent of the children, displayed a diverging pattern. In this small subset, the time sequence varied depending on the specific cognitive skill in question. For example, screen use might precede changes in cognitive flexibility, but inhibitory control might precede changes in screen use.

The researchers also examined early childhood factors to see if any predicted a child’s placement into these groups. They looked at household income, child temperament, parent stress, and problematic media use. Most of these variables did not reliably predict group membership.

However, parent depression did influence the outcomes. Higher levels of parent depressive symptoms increased the probability of a child belonging to the group where screen use directly drove cognitive deficits. Similarly, parent depression decreased the probability of a child being in the continuous bidirectional group.

The sequence of events over time is a required step for proving causation in science, but it does not prove causation on its own. Entirely different environmental or genetic variables could be driving both the media habits and the cognitive development. The statistical models only establish the order in which these traits appear.

Additionally, the study relied on a relatively small sample of 87 children. Because the study required multiple years of in-person behavioral testing at specific ages, massive sample sizes are difficult to achieve. Even so, findings from smaller cohorts typically require replication in larger populations to confirm widespread applicability.

Future research will need to explore the exact mechanisms that tie screen use to self-control. Clinical interventions might eventually focus on supporting parent mental health rather than simply advising families to reduce screen time. Giving parents alternative tools to handle tantrums and stress could provide a better foundation for early childhood development.

The study, “Media emotion regulation and executive functions: individual differences in temporal ordering among young children,” was authored by Jane Shawcroft, McCall A. Booth, Chris L. Porter, Megan Van Alfen, Megan Gale, Lara A. Maximiano, Elena K. Holmes, Sarah M. Coyne, Hailey G. Holmgren, and Blake L. Jones.
