issues.title: I Let Work Become My Only Hobby
issues.summary: For years I let work double as my hobby. Too much of my life was revolving around the same thing. I had neglected hobbies for years before I changed it. You know that feeling when the thing you do for fun is still work? That was me. I added board games and racket sports so […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
For years I let work double as my hobby. Too much of my life was revolving around the same thing. I had neglected hobbies for years before I changed it.

You know that feeling when the thing you do for fun is still work? That was me. I added board games and racket sports so I would have ways to enjoy time with no business objective. I chose them for enjoyment alone.

Schedule 1 recurring non-work activity purely for fun. Pick it because you enjoy it. An income stream is a separate decision. A productivity project is a separate decision.

Does your week have 1 block that exists only because you enjoy it?

Start from a day you would enjoy

My approach to work-life balance starts with happiness. Describe a day you would genuinely enjoy. Compare it with your current routine. Choose a small change that closes some of the gap. Try that change for the next 30 days.

I see productivity as a way to support the life you want. That philosophy is the core of my lifestyle-design masterclass.

When I check an ideal day I use 4 pillars.

Health

Physical care and mental care both belong in the day.

Wealth

Career and financial stability. A life you want still has to meet the obligations you already have.

Relationships

Quality time with the people who matter. If the people who matter never show up this pillar is empty.

Happiness

Purpose, hobbies, and leisure. Work had been standing in for this whole pillar.

All 4 inform the vision. Implement 1 or 2 at a time. A productive-looking schedule can still be incomplete if it leaves an entire pillar out. I keep this lifestyle framework separate from the time, energy, and attention framework.

Which pillar is thin in the day you just pictured? Add 1 missing element for that pillar to your ideal-day description.

Put both days on paper

Turn a vague wish for better balance into a gap audit. Write your ideal day and your current day with the same prompts.

  1. Wake-up time
  2. Daily activities
  3. Work hours
  4. Self-care
  5. People
  6. Afternoons and evenings

I ask people to write this out. Compare the answers. Look at how each difference affects your energy, your focus, your relationships, or your wellbeing. Specific gaps give you specific problems to solve.

Treat the ideal day as adjustable. Caregiving, shifts, and fixed work hours are real constraints. Name yours. Then mark the part of the schedule you can influence.

Someone who wanted more of the day for meaningful work found that the loved part still took only a short stretch each morning. The surrounding tasks filled much of the rest. That pattern is one person’s experience of their own days. They still felt fulfilled. The ordinary obligations stayed.

A satisfying life can contain ordinary obligations alongside a small protected portion of deeply meaningful work.

Spend roughly 10-20% of your time doing things you genuinely love. Gain more control over your schedule where you have room to move it. I treat 10-20% as a heuristic from my own experience. Have you found the activity that would make an otherwise ordinary workday feel worthwhile? Protect time for it.

Price the life

Before you assume your ideal lifestyle requires dramatically more income put a price on it.

Track a full month of expenses. Build a spreadsheet of what the desired lifestyle would actually cost. Put current spending beside desired spending.

In my coaching the number is often lower than people expect. That is an observation from coaching. Your number may be higher. Meet the obligations you already have while you do the math. Financial stability stays part of the design.

A late morning can stay a late morning

A late start does not have to become a lost day. Someone described oversleeping and feeling behind before work began. Do you know that feeling…the day already feels shot and you have barely started?

Start work with a prioritized to-do list of 5 items or fewer. Take 15 minutes at lunch to regroup. Keep that recovery separate from the sleep pattern that may be contributing to rushed mornings.

I recommend earlier sleep. Insufficient sleep is one possible cause. Oversleeping and persistent fatigue can have other causes too so keep the question open. Park this checklist at your desk.

  • Write a prioritized list of 5 items or fewer.
  • Start there.
  • Take 15 minutes at lunch to regroup.
  • If rushed mornings keep repeating…look at sleep on its own.

Give the habit a way back

A resilient routine needs a recovery plan. Avoid 2 consecutive misses. When an obstacle keeps recurring…investigate it.

Meetings overrun. The workout gets squeezed out. The gym commute takes too long. Both are scheduling friction. Address that friction. An occasional miss is normal.

Decide on a backup slot in advance. If the planned session falls through…when will you resume and where? A reserved Sunday slot can be a way back.

Add an explicit backup to 1 habit. Write the when and the where.

One tweak a week

My rule for lifestyle change is 1 tweak a week. Choose 1 or 2 areas to improve. Break the first change into a manageable action. Schedule it. If weekly changes still feel like too much…practice that 1 action for the next 30 days. The right pace is the one you can follow through on.

Keep the challenge to that single action.

Tonight write the ideal day and the current day side by side with the 6 prompts. Circle 1 gap. Block 1 action on your calendar that closes it.

issues.title: I Looked at a Packed October and Chose 2 Outcomes
issues.summary: In October 2024 I reviewed my month. It was already packed. Personal events. Travel. You know that feeling when the month is full before it starts? A 3-day commitment can consume 5 or 6 days once you include preparation, travel, recovery, and catching up. That’s the estimate I use on my own calendar. Ignore the […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
In October 2024 I reviewed my month. It was already packed. Personal events. Travel.

You know that feeling when the month is full before it starts?

A 3-day commitment can consume 5 or 6 days once you include preparation, travel, recovery, and catching up. That’s the estimate I use on my own calendar. Ignore the surrounding time. The month is already overcommitted.

I allow at most 3 outcomes in a month. The number is a ceiling. I stopped at 2. Launch an online course. Book an overseas trip. The course and the trip were the targets I wrote down. A realistic plan was the result I was after.

The month has 3 boxes

Anchor events. Outcomes. Key tasks. That’s the whole monthly template.

Anchor events go in first. Anything that takes a full day or longer. Travel, conferences, and vacations. Any personal or work commitment that swallows a day goes on that list too. I want those visible before I choose goals. Then the remaining capacity is easy to see.

Outcomes go in second. Only what fits the days you have left. Up to 3. Each outcome needs a yes-or-no finish line. Research filing taxes is a task. Taxes filed is an outcome. You might still collect receipts, organize records, and get professional help. Work, family, and personal results can sit side by side.

Key tasks go in last. These are the actions that produce the outcomes. Those tasks give your weekly plan a place to start.

I put this session on the calendar about a week before the month begins. Same note every time. Plan the month you have.

Someone asked me about a detailed annual plan. I prefer 90 days. You get room for real progress. The deadline still feels close. A year-long target can lose urgency for months and turn into a scramble near the end. Keep a longer direction if you want one. Annual themes can guide the quarter. Turn 1 aspiration into an outcome for the next 90 days. Name the piece this month will carry.

Review before you repeat the week

If you keep overcommitting every week, the missing habit may be the review. Without it, the next plan reuses the same assumptions.

Before you plan next week, write 3 answers. What did I finish? What held me back? What should change? Look at what you intended. Look at what happened. Let that difference shape the workload.

You can review and plan in 1 session. You can also split them. The review still has to inform the plan.

A useful week names outcomes. At most 3. Same yes-or-no test. Then schedule the tasks that deliver them. The cap hits major priorities. Smaller tasks still belong on the list. For the day I pick up to 3 priority tasks. Other work still happens around them.

Course-correct tomorrow

Daily planning checks the weekly plan. Will today’s actions move it forward?

Do it the night before or the morning of. Pull the next steps for today. Resolve any prerequisite those steps still need.

Practice can sit on the calendar and still be impossible. I use a pickleball example for this. No court booked. No partner confirmed. The time is reserved. The session can’t happen. Find that hole. Fix it. Leave the rest of the schedule alone.

If you get distracted or overwhelmed, add an early-afternoon reminder. Where am I, and what needs to change? That check lets you adjust the rest of the day.

Reassess priorities at least once a day. Do it more often when work is moving fast. Capture the new request. Before you start it, compare it with the outcome you already chose. A genuine deadline, a service commitment, or an emergency can move first. Arrival order is a weak way to choose the next task.

I packed a day into 15-minute increments. A short meeting ran long. The rest of the day had to be reworked. That grid created more administrative work than useful structure. The stress spread forward. I still block time. Open pockets give a normal delay somewhere to land. I don’t have to rebuild the whole day. Leave visible margin between commitments when you plan the next workday.

Back to neutral

Feel like quitting the day before you even plan it?

A bigger routine can be the wrong first step when you’re buried. I compare it to money. Someone struggling to pay the next bill has little room to think about investing. Time works the same way. Process your inbox. Organize your projects. Breathing room makes it easier to look past today’s emergencies.

Neutral can include unfinished work. You need the inbox and your active projects clear enough to look ahead.

Start by planning tomorrow. Add weekly planning once that is consistent. Add the monthly template after that. All 3 horizons work together. The month identifies projects and deadlines. The week turns them into commitments you can keep. The day keeps execution on track. You decide what matters, make room for it, and adjust as life happens.

This is how I teach organizing time inside the 25X productivity system.

Tonight, plan tomorrow. Check your weekly plan. Write the next steps. Fix 1 missing prerequisite. Set an early-afternoon reminder: Where am I, and what needs to change?

issues.title: I Said Family Mattered. My Calendar Spent the Year on Work.
issues.summary: I sat down for an annual review in a year when I wanted more time with my family. I looked at where my time, energy, and attention had actually gone. Most of it had gone to work. Stated priority on one side. Actual allocation on the other. The review gave me a concrete direction for […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I sat down for an annual review in a year when I wanted more time with my family. I looked at where my time, energy, and attention had actually gone. Most of it had gone to work.

Stated priority on one side. Actual allocation on the other. The review gave me a concrete direction for the next year: change where those resources went.

You know that feeling when the thing you care about barely shows up in the week? I treat it as an awareness exercise. Taking a vacation belongs on the page. So does sustaining a useful habit. They sit next to the professional milestones. Leave the grading alone.

Answer 5 questions before you set a goal

Set aside a quiet session. Answer these before you set anything new.

What were my biggest accomplishments?

Write the ones that were real. That list can include a useful habit you kept alive all year.

What worked well?

Find the habits and strategies that worked. Decide which ones to continue, repeat, or expand. A better year does not necessarily require adding anything new. Protecting an effective routine can be a better annual-plan decision than replacing it with another ambitious commitment. Write a “keep doing” list before you write new resolutions.

January messaging equates progress with more goals, more tools, or more effort. Start from what already worked.

What did not go as planned?

Name the goal. Write what actually happened.

What obstacles affected my goals?

Notice which obstacles are still in play. Next year’s goals need to account for unexpected caregiving once it becomes an ongoing responsibility. Someone asked me about this in a session. Treat the care as a real planning priority. Explore routines around it. Ask for help. Share responsibilities where you can. A goal that ignores an existing commitment can create a conflict that better scheduling alone cannot solve. Intention does not make caregiving easy. Practical help is not available to everyone. List your ongoing responsibilities before you commit to new goals. Identify 1 source of support to explore.

Where did my time, energy, and attention go, and did that match what mattered most?

This question caught me. I wanted more time with my family. Work is where the year went. Put your answer beside your top priority and see if they match.

Sort last year like a closet

I compare an annual review to cleaning out a closet. Keep the wins and the lessons that still serve you. Remove habits or goals that no longer fit. Identify the strategies that need replacing. Make room for what belongs in your life now. Skip judging the old wardrobe.

Make 3 columns: Keep, Let go, and Replace. Sort the past year’s routines and commitments into them.

Reflect, refocus, recharge

I use the 3 Rs with TEA. Reflect, Refocus, and Recharge. TEA means time, energy, and attention.

Reflect on what happened. You do that with the 5 questions and the closet sort.

Refocus on 3 priorities.

Recharge turns those priorities into measurable goals and supporting habits. The recharge work here is the goals, the habits, and the milestones. I want the daily actions to match what matters.

One move for time, for energy, and for attention

Ask 1 question for each pillar. Then choose 1 action.

Time. Where should I spend more time? Where should I spend less? An action can be as simple as protecting a focus block.

Energy. Which activities fuel you? Which activities drain you? Scheduling 3 weekly workouts showed up as an example in a session I taught. Use it only if it fits your life.

Attention. Which distractions or low-value tasks can you reduce? I put my phone face down and on airplane mode during focused time. I practice this one myself.

Write the plan in 3 rows. Time, energy, attention. One action on each row.

The habit might live next to the goal

The habit that supports a goal may happen somewhere other than the goal itself.

Say you want to protect 2 hours of family time each weekend. Put the hours on the calendar if you want. Then name the recurring behavior that makes room for them. That behavior might be a boundary around checking work messages. It might be a Friday weekly review that helps you close out work. Pick 1 goal and ask what habit would make this easier to follow through on. A supporting habit improves the odds. It does not guarantee the result.

Give it a 90-day finish line

An annual direction gets more actionable when you pair it with a 90-day milestone. I favor this window because the finish line feels close enough to motivate action. You still have room for meaningful progress and a course correction. This is my preferred planning approach. I’m no researcher. I don’t have a study that proves 90 days is the optimum.

Give the milestone a deadline, a specific result, and a way to measure it. Finishing 2 books on a chosen topic within the next 90 days is a clean version.

Use AI once you understand the manual version

AI can help with a hard step in goal planning. Take a desired outcome and turn it into a supporting habit and an action plan. I built a custom GPT that asks questions and generates a plan. I teach the manual process first. Understand your priorities and your constraints. Learn how a goal connects to a habit. Then let AI draft.

Give an assistant 1 goal, your available time, and your constraints. Ask it to propose a supporting habit. Assess what it gives you. I won’t promise that draft is fast or accurate.

Compare the priority with the year

Block a quiet session. Write down your stated top priority. Next to it, write where your calendar and your energy actually went. Change where the time, energy, and attention go if those two lines don’t match.

issues.title: Stop Waiting for a Convenient Moment
issues.summary: I kept waiting for a convenient moment to spend time with people who matter to me. It never arrived…so I booked the trip. I was still working while I was there. Connection belongs in my wellness routine. Meaningful time with family needs a spot on the calendar. Sound familiar? You know the thing that would […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I kept waiting for a convenient moment to spend time with people who matter to me. It never arrived…so I booked the trip.

I was still working while I was there. Connection belongs in my wellness routine. Meaningful time with family needs a spot on the calendar.

Sound familiar? You know the thing that would help. You wait for a clear week anyway.

Trying to improve work-life balance without defining it is like driving through fog. You cannot see clearly enough to choose a direction. Describe the actual day you want. When does work start? When does it end? Who are you working with? What happens afterward? That picture makes boundaries easier to set. Planning a week that supports your life gets easier too.

A clear vision guides your choices. It does not remove external constraints. Sketch the day on a page. Circle 1 boundary that would move your current schedule closer to it.

Keep that boundary for a week.

If you’re retired, write the day around purpose and daily activities. What is the day for? Who is in it? What do you do with the hours?

Resilience means raising your baseline. The valleys still come. Sleep, movement, nutrition, and supportive relationships build the capacity you bring into a difficult day. Setbacks will still happen. The goal is to meet them with more resources. I used to wait until I was depleted to begin taking care of myself. Now I do that work on ordinary days.

A baseline-and-valleys graph is the picture I teach with. Higher line through the week. It is a metaphor. It does not predict recovery speed or severity.

This is the core of my resilience masterclass. Resilience is a productivity skill you can practice. A hard week can still hurt. This practice does not replace mental health care.

Within the time, energy, and attention framework, resilience primarily protects energy and attention. It helps you respond to a setback without letting it consume all your capacity to work.

Practice solving problems

When a problem feels overwhelming I use 3 moves. I break it into smaller parts. I talk to someone who has handled something similar. I write down at least 20 possible solutions.

The point of 20 has no magic in it. The longer list pushes you past the first 1 or 2 obvious answers so more options can show up. Asking is part of being resourceful. It is not evidence that you lack resilience.

I use this exercise with coaching clients. It is a way to explore responses to a challenge. Some painful situations cannot be fixed this way.

In the masterclass I used a family vacation because “plan the trip” hides dozens of decisions. I broke it into choosing a destination, booking travel and accommodation, creating an itinerary, and packing. A participant who had been putting the planning off wrote down a small task to get started. The vacation plan stayed unfinished. What changed was the size of the next action.

Replace 1 oversized to-do with its next concrete action. For the full pass, make space for the smaller subproblems, someone to consult, and 20 possible solutions.

Build a stronger baseline

I attach movement to something I already do. Eating. After a meal I take a 5 to 10 minute walk. When I can’t walk I do something physically active like cleaning the house. I used to rely only on dedicated workouts. Now I look for small openings inside the day I already have.

Try 1 tweak a week. After 1 daily meal, move for 5 to 10 minutes. Walk if you can. Clean the house if you can’t. Do it for a week. My habit. Not a prescribed exercise regimen.

If you add only 1 recovery routine, start with a bedtime wind-down. I prioritize this among my relaxation practices. Begin about 1 hour before bed. Step away from screens. Choose calming activities: journaling, reading, stretching, meditation, or talking with your partner. You give the end of the day a structure. Bedtime stops being whatever work or entertainment is still running.

Schedule a wind-down reminder. Pick a simple sequence for the coming week. This routine will not resolve a sleep disorder.

Before your next busy period, choose 1 baseline-building habit. Sleep. Movement. Nutrition. A supportive relationship. Start with that.

Make self-care a daily routine

This is the walk after a meal, the wind-down, and the person you schedule on purpose.

What if overwhelm has already turned into numbness or lethargy? Skip the dramatic productivity overhaul. Start with professional help and social support. Then pick a manageable action. Make breakfast. Or walk for 5 minutes. Don’t pressure yourself to recover on a deadline.

Small habits can support you. They are not treatment for depression. Identify 1 person you can contact and 1 manageable action for today. Do both today.

A hobby has no commercial outcome

Entrepreneurs, my challenge. Your business does not count as your hobby just because you enjoy it. A hobby gives you something to do for pleasure without a commercial outcome. That is my practical definition of a restorative hobby. I am not writing a universal rule about every paid creative pursuit.

Ask what you enjoyed as a child. Ask what you could do for hours for fun. Ask what you stopped doing when work became busy. Put 1 of those on next week’s calendar. No income goal. No performance goal.

Arrange 1 visit, 1 call, or 1 shared activity with someone important to you. I waited for a convenient moment that never arrived. Put it on the calendar today.

issues.title: My 2019 Annual Review
issues.summary: Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life. As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions. What went well this year? What didn’t go so well this year? What did I learn? Before we begin, it is worth noting that […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life.

As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions.

  1. What went well this year?
  2. What didn’t go so well this year?
  3. What did I learn?

Before we begin, it is worth noting that every Annual Review is a personal process. This is simply an overview of what my year looked like, not advice for how you should live your life. (That said, you are always welcome to use this general format for your own Annual Review.)

1. What went well this year?

I had a lot to celebrate this year.

Book sales.Atomic Habits launched in October 2018, which meant that 2019 was the first full calendar year it had been available. I came in with big aspirations, but I think it’s fair to say that book sales have outpaced my expectations.

As of December 2019:

  • Over 1.3 million copies sold worldwide
  • 12 consecutive months on the New York Times bestseller list
  • 4.8/5 stars on Amazon with over 1,800 reviews
  • 4.8/5 stars on Audible with over 25,000 ratings
  • Over 15 national TV segments in the United States, Canada, and Australia
  • Translated into 40+ languages

This has been a wild ride to say the least.

Of course, the greatest reward has been hearing from readers. It seems like nearly every day someone tells me that Atomic Habits helped them lose weight or start a business or make some positive change in their life. People are finding real value in the ideas and it feels great to produce something useful.

3-2-1 Newsletter. My new project for 2019 was launching the 3-2-1 newsletter, which shares 3 ideas from me, 2 quotes from others, and 1 question to ponder each week. I had been struggling to write consistently during the first half of the year (discussed below) and this new format offered something I knew I could stick with despite a busy schedule. (Sometimes I have to take my own medicine and scale my habits down.)

I didn’t realize it at the time, but it turns out to have been a good idea. I feel good because I’m producing new work each week and the response from subscribers has been quite favorable. Many readers tell me it’s the only newsletter they actually read as soon as it hits their inbox.

Audience growth. I didn’t write many new articles this year, but thanks to the buzz generated by Atomic Habits and the momentum of the 3-2-1 newsletter, audience growth remained strong.

Here’s what the year looked like:

  • 5 new articles published this year (fewest ever; discussed in next section)
  • 353,970 new email subscribers in 2019
  • 586,638 total email subscribers as of December 31, 2019
  • 10,848,250 unique visitors in 2019
  • 47,308,712 total visitors since launching on November 12, 2012

Even after doing this for a few years, the scale of the internet still blows me away. I’m grateful to have the opportunity to share my work with so many people.

Twitter and Instagram. I didn’t put much energy into social media for a long time, but the web has evolved in the last five years and social media plays an important role now. This was the first year I put consistent effort into Twitter and Instagram, and it paid off. My audience doubled on both platforms this year. Feel free to join the fun and follow me on Twitter and on Instagram.

Travel. This was the craziest travel year of my life and, in all likelihood, the craziest I will ever have. I spent a total of 158 nights away from home this year, which means I spent 43% of the year not sleeping in my own bed. It’s a pace I will probably (hopefully?) never match again.

Here’s the rundown…

18 states (0 new) – Arizona, California (5x!), Colorado (2x), Florida (2x), Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois (2x), Indiana (3x), Maryland, Nebraska (2x), Nevada, New York (5x!), Ohio, Pennsylvania (3x), Tennessee (2x), Texas (2x), Utah, and Virginia.

14 countries (7 new) – Australia (2x!), Canada (2x), Croatia, Denmark, Greece, England, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, and the United Arab Emirates.

While I love traveling, I did feel a bit guilty about the number of flights I took this year and the resulting pollution. In response, I decided to buy carbon offsets not only to cover my flights, but also to be entirely carbon neutral for 2019. I bought mine through Project Wren, and it wasn’t nearly as expensive as I expected.

New restaurants. Whenever I travel to a new city, I like to ask for restaurant recommendations on Twitter. Oh man, did you all set me up this year. I had so many great meals thanks to reader suggestions.

I feel compelled to repay you all by sharing some of my favorites (in no order):

  • Los Angeles, CA — fundamental LA
  • Denver, CO — Mercantile Provisions
  • Honolulu, HI — Marukame Udon
  • New York, NY — Manhatta (my meal of the year)
  • Philadelphia, PA — Zahav (runner up)
  • Melbourne, Australia — Chin Chin
  • Sydney, Australia — NOMAD
  • Sydney, Australia — Mr. Wong
  • Toronto, Canada — PAI
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Pantarul
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Taj Mahal
  • London, England — Nopi
  • London, England — Dishoom
  • Athens, Greece — Atitamos
  • Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — Village Park Restaurant
  • Singapore — Artichoke
  • Singapore — Maxwell Food Court
  • Madrid, Spain — El Charrua
  • Madrid, Spain — Ten Con Ten

For more ideas (including specific dishes), check out my full list of recommended restaurants.

Speaking. I delivered 31 paid keynote speeches in 2019. This is far and away the most I’ve ever given in a calendar year. Obviously, this is tied directly to the success of Atomic Habits, but I’ve improved my speaking skills as well. My biggest takeaway is that if you write about a topic for years and are forced to clarify your thinking in a well-structured book, then speaking about that topic for one hour becomes much easier to do. (Note: If you’d like me to speak at your company or event, you can submit a request here.)

2. What didn’t go so well this year?

Many wonderful things happened in 2019, but I suffered plenty of growing pains as well.

Writing. For years, my business was built on the consistency of my writing. I published a new article every Monday and Thursday from 2012 to 2015. From 2016 to 2018, I spent most of my time writing Atomic Habits. Overall, those six years were filled with writing.

Then 2019 arrived and the book began to sell far and wide. My attention shifted to promotion mode: interviews, speeches, book signings. It was all great, but there was very little time left for writing. Honestly, I probably wrote more words on Twitter last year than in new articles.

Thankfully, I began to course correct during the second half of the year by writing the 3-2-1 newsletter (as mentioned previously). We’ll see what things look like in 2020, but if I’m going to write another book at some point, I will need to carve out more time to write.

Weightlifting. Everything has a tradeoff. It turns out that it is hard to maintain consistency in the gym when you are on the road for nearly half the year. In 2019, I completed 91 workouts for an average of 7.6 per month, which is better than nothing, but a steep drop off from previous years.

Workouts per month in 2019:

  • January – 16
  • February – 6
  • March – 4
  • April – 8
  • May – 4
  • June – 2(!)
  • July – 12
  • August – 8
  • September – 9
  • October – 15
  • November – 1(!)
  • December – 6

When looking at these numbers, the thing that sticks out to me is that my worst months were the months I had lots of international travel (March, June, and November). I’ll need a better plan for exercising in foreign locations in the future.

Given how inconsistent things were, I didn’t bother with max lifts this year and just did rep work most days. As a result, my best lifts of the year were:

  • Back Squat – 330 lbs (150 kg) for 5 rep
  • Bench Press – 245 lbs (111 kg) for 5 rep
  • Deadlift – 415 lbs (188 kg) for 5 rep

This marks the second year in a row when I failed to hit an all-time PR in any major lift. Admittedly, it’s unlikely you’re going to reach a personal best every year anyway, but nonetheless I have a lot of catching up to do in the gym in 2020.

Email. I joked earlier this year that my email response time is either 3 minutes or 3 months. Problem is… it’s not really a joke. I’m terrible at answering email. Honestly, this wouldn’t bother me except for one reason: it bothers other people.

My poor email response times came back to burn me multiple times this year. Sometimes it was a missed opportunity due to a delayed reply. Other times people became annoyed or frustrated, or thought I was intentionally ignoring them.

I’m not sure the best way to handle this. I get more email than I can manage and answering emails is certainly not as important as writing the next article or book. And yet, people expect responses within a day or two. One thing is for sure, I’ll probably need a new email approach in 2020.

3. What did I learn this year?

Some of my major lessons from this year include:

Move fast. The importance of moving fast was clarified for me over the last year. The original release date for Atomic Habits was set for March 2019. I pushed to move the date forward six months to October 2018 because I didn’t want to miss out on holiday sales around Christmas. My publishing team agreed, everyone worked their tails off, and we had a fabulous launch in October.

What happened next was even more important: The book was available in January when everyone was thinking about New Year’s Resolutions. As a result, Atomic Habits jumped out to a very strong start during the fall and winter. By the time we arrived at the original launch date in March, we had already sold nearly 500,000 copies.

In this case, the difference between waiting and acting was massive. We all know exactly what would have happened if we had waited: time would have flown by, somehow planning the launch would have expanded to fill all of that time, and six months of sales would have vanished.

Growing up takes time. For the last three years my business has been stuck in that awkward pre-teen stage where one minute it acts like a full-fledged adult and the next minute you realize it’s covered in pimples and doesn’t know how to control all four limbs at the same time.

But in 2019—maybe!—it turned a corner. The to-do list is still endless, but that’s what running a business is like. It does feel like I’m starting to find my footing, however. The strategy is becoming more clear. The products are gaining a foothold. The fog is lifting ever-so-slightly. I have spent nearly a decade as a full-time entrepreneur, but I’m finally uncovering a clear roadmap of what the future of the business looks like.

A life well-lived is a life well-edited. My biggest area of growth this year was prioritization. I had to become much better at saying no— and I’m still not very good at it!

In short: Prune away the inessential. Pour yourself into what remains.

That’s it! As always, thanks for reading. Happy New Year! 1

The Annual Review Archives

This is a complete list of Annual Reviews I have written.

  • My 2019 Annual Review
  • My 2018 Annual Review
  • My 2017 Annual Review
  • My 2016 Annual Review
  • My 2015 Annual Review
  • My 2014 Annual Review
  • My 2013 Annual Review

  1. Thanks to Chris Guillebeau for inspiring my Annual Review format.

issues.title: The Ultimate Productivity Hack is Saying No
issues.summary: The ultimate productivity hack is saying no. Not doing something will always be faster than doing it. This statement reminds me of the old computer programming saying, “Remember that there is no code faster than no code.” The same philosophy applies in other areas of life. For example, there is no meeting that goes faster […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
The ultimate productivity hack is saying no.

Not doing something will always be faster than doing it. This statement reminds me of the old computer programming saying, “Remember that there is no code faster than no code.” 1

The same philosophy applies in other areas of life. For example, there is no meeting that goes faster than not having a meeting at all.

This is not to say you should never attend another meeting, but the truth is that we say yes to many things we don’t actually want to do. There are many meetings held that don’t need to be held. There is a lot of code written that could be deleted.

How often do people ask you to do something and you just reply, “Sure thing.” Three days later, you’re overwhelmed by how much is on your to-do list. We become frustrated by our obligations even though we were the ones who said yes to them in the first place. 2

It’s worth asking if things are necessary. Many of them are not, and a simple “no” will be more productive than whatever work the most efficient person can muster.

But if the benefits of saying no are so obvious, then why do we say yes so often?

Why We Say Yes

We agree to many requests not because we want to do them, but because we don’t want to be seen as rude, arrogant, or unhelpful. Often, you have to consider saying no to someone you will interact with again in the future—your co-worker, your spouse, your family and friends. 3

Saying no to these people can be particularly difficult because we like them and want to support them. (Not to mention, we often need their help too.) Collaborating with others is an important element of life. The thought of straining the relationship outweighs the commitment of our time and energy.

For this reason, it can be helpful to be gracious in your response. Do whatever favors you can, and be warm-hearted and direct when you have to say no.

But even after we have accounted for these social considerations, many of us still seem to do a poor job of managing the tradeoff between yes and no. We find ourselves over-committed to things that don’t meaningfully improve or support those around us, and certainly don’t improve our own lives.

Perhaps one issue is how we think about the meaning of yes and no.

The Difference Between Yes and No

The words “yes” and “no” get used in comparison to each other so often that it feels like they carry equal weight in conversation. In reality, they are not just opposite in meaning, but of entirely different magnitudes in commitment.

When you say no, you are only saying no to one option. When you say yes, you are saying no to every other option.

I like how the economist Tim Harford put it, “Every time we say yes to a request, we are also saying no to anything else we might accomplish with the time.”4 Once you have committed to something, you have already decided how that future block of time will be spent.

In other words, saying no saves you time in the future. Saying yes costs you time in the future. No is a form of time credit. You retain the ability to spend your future time however you want. Yes is a form of time debt. You have to pay back your commitment at some point.

No is a decision. Yes is a responsibility.

The Role of No

Saying no is sometimes seen as a luxury that only those in power can afford. And it is true: turning down opportunities is easier when you can fall back on the safety net provided by power, money, and authority. But it is also true that saying no is not merely a privilege reserved for the successful among us. It is also a strategy that can help you become successful.

Saying no is an important skill to develop at any stage of your career because it retains the most important asset in life: your time. As the investor Pedro Sorrentino put it, “If you don’t guard your time, people will steal it from you.” 5

You need to say no to whatever isn’t leading you toward your goals. You need to say no to distractions. As one reader told me, “If you broaden the definition as to how you apply no, it actually is the only productivity hack (as you ultimately say no to any distraction in order to be productive).”

Nobody embodied this idea better than Steve Jobs, who said, “People think focus means saying yes to the thing you’ve got to focus on. But that’s not what it means at all. It means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. You have to pick carefully.” 6

There is an important balance to strike here. Saying no doesn’t mean you’ll never do anything interesting or innovative or spontaneous. It just means that you say yes in a focused way. Once you have knocked out the distractions, it can make sense to say yes to any opportunity that could potentially move you in the right direction. You may have to try many things to discover what works and what you enjoy. This period of exploration can be particularly important at the beginning of a project, job, or career.

Upgrading Your No

Over time, as you continue to improve and succeed, your strategy needs to change.

The opportunity cost of your time increases as you become more successful. At first, you just eliminate the obvious distractions and explore the rest. As your skills improve and you learn to separate what works from what doesn’t, you have to continually increase your threshold for saying yes.

You still need to say no to distractions, but you also need to learn to say no to opportunities that were previously good uses of time, so you can make space for great uses of time. It’s a good problem to have, but it can be a tough skill to master.

In other words, you have to upgrade your “no’s” over time.

Upgrading your no doesn’t mean you’ll never say yes. It just means you default to saying no and only say yes when it really makes sense. To quote the investor Brent Beshore, “Saying no is so powerful because it preserves the opportunity to say yes.” 7

The general trend seems to be something like this: If you can learn to say no to bad distractions, then eventually you’ll earn the right to say no to good opportunities.

How to Say No

Most of us are probably too quick to say yes and too slow to say no. It’s worth asking yourself where you fall on that spectrum.

If you have trouble saying no, you may find the following strategy proposed by Tim Harford, the British economist I mentioned earlier, to be helpful. He writes, “One trick is to ask, “If I had to do this today, would I agree to it?” It’s not a bad rule of thumb, since any future commitment, no matter how far away it might be, will eventually become an imminent problem.” 8

If an opportunity is exciting enough to drop whatever you’re doing right now, then it’s a yes. If it’s not, then perhaps you should think twice.

This is similar to the well-known “Hell Yeah or No” method from Derek Sivers. If someone asks you to do something and your first reaction is “Hell Yeah!”, then do it. If it doesn’t excite you, then say no. 9

It’s impossible to remember to ask yourself these questions each time you face a decision, but it’s still a useful exercise to revisit from time to time. Saying no can be difficult, but it is often easier than the alternative. As writer Mike Dariano has pointed out, “It’s easier to avoid commitments than get out of commitments. Saying no keeps you toward the easier end of this spectrum.” 10

What is true about health is also true about productivity: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

The Power of No

More effort is wasted doing things that don’t matter than is wasted doing things inefficiently. And if that is the case, elimination is a more useful skill than optimization.

I am reminded of the famous Peter Drucker quote, “There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.”

Footnotes

  1. Taligent’s Guide to Designing Programs. Hat tip to Kevlin Henney

  2. Even worse, people will occasionally fight to do things that waste time. “Why can’t you just come to the meeting? We have it every week.” Just because it is scheduled weekly doesn’t mean it is necessary weekly. You don’t have to agree to something just because it exists.

  3. Saying no to your superiors at work can be particularly difficult. In these situations, I like the approach recommended in Essentialism by Greg McKeown. He writes, “Remind your superiors what you would be neglecting if you said yes and force them to grapple with the trade-off. For example, if your manager comes to you and asks you to do X, you can respond with “Yes, I’m happy to make this the priority. Which of these other projects should I deprioritize to pay attention to this new project?” Hat tip to my friend, Shane Parrish, at Farnam Street who shared this insight from McKeown in the article, “Eight Ways to Say No With Grace and Style.”

  4. Tim Harford, The Power of Saying No

  5. Pedro Sorrentino, [Stoic Capital #21] On productivity, time and wealth

  6. Jobs had another great quote about saying no: “I’m actually as proud of the things we haven’t done as the things I have done. Innovation is saying no to 1,000 things.”

  7. Brent Beshore on Twitter

  8. This is similar to Shane Parrish’s rule of thumb for meetings: “If you wouldn’t do it right now, say no.” A similar philosophy could be extended to many areas of life.

  9. Derek Sivers, No “yes.” Either “HELL YEAH!” or “no.”

  10. Mike Dariano, Start with “no” for a better “yes”

issues.title: 30 One-Sentence Stories From People Who Have Built Better Habits
issues.summary: In this article, I’d like to share 30 “one-sentence stories” about building better habits. (They are not all exactly one sentence, but they are very short.) None of these stories are mine. They were sent to me by readers of Atomic Habits. My hope is that these examples will illustrate how real people are putting […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
In this article, I’d like to share 30 “one-sentence stories” about building better habits. (They are not all exactly one sentence, but they are very short.)

None of these stories are mine. They were sent to me by readers of Atomic Habits. My hope is that these examples will illustrate how real people are putting the book into practice. They will show you what people are actually doing to build good habits and break bad ones. And hopefully, they will spark some ideas for how you can do the same.

I have divided the stories into categories that roughly correspond to different sections or ideas in the book.

Identity-based habits

One of the central ideas in the book is the concept of building “identity-based habits”, which essentially recommends focusing on the type of person you wish to become rather than the outcome you wish to achieve.

One reader named Roland used the idea to improve his eating habits.

“I stopped eating unhealthy food via identity change,” he wrote. “I tried many times in the past, but it became easy — natural — only after I had made the conscious decision that I want to be someone who eats healthy. Instead of aiming for I want to stop eating bad food, I tried changing the mindset to I am someone that eats healthy and lives a healthy life. It changes how you approach things.”

Another reader named Robert employed this idea to help him quit smoking. He wrote, “I recently stopped smoking and the difference between I don’t smoke and I can’t smoke is a powerful trainer of my brain. The positive message of I don’t smoke is that I have not “given up” anything. I am not sacrificing a pleasure. I am investing in my future happiness and wellbeing.”

Like most strategies in the book, the concept of identity-based habits can be combined with other habit building tactics. For instance, one reader used an external reward of $10 to reinforce the desired identity. “I told myself, I am no longer a drinker. Then, after each day of non-drinking, I gave myself $10 to buy something nice rather than poison (like clothes and household items). Today, I no longer need the allowance and I’m six years sober.”

Chapter 2 of Atomic Habits covers these strategies in much greater detail.

Changing the Cues

Another way you can change a habit is by identifying and altering the cues that prompt your behavior. This is precisely what many readers have done.

One woman named Lisa cultivated a reading habit by increasing her exposure to books. “I’ve read more books by continually having 20-30 books on hold at the library,” she said. “It saves time on browsing for books. I always have new things to read with a three-week deadline.”

Heather used a similar strategy to reinforce the simple habit of drinking more water. “I use color and placement for visual reminding and motivation. I poured water in a bright aqua water bottle – my favorite color – and placed it on my nightstand so I couldn’t miss it when I woke up.”

Other readers have done the opposite. They reduced exposure to negative cues. One man named Max managed to eliminate his e-cigarette habit. “I quit e-cigarettes with a combination of determination and also quitting coffee at the same time, which was a trigger for me as I’d smoke and drink coffee together in the morning.”

Habit Stacking

Another popular tactic in the book is something I call “habit stacking.” It’s strategy I first learned from Stanford professor B.J. Fogg. He refers to it as “anchoring” because you anchor—or stack—your new habit onto a current habit.

One reader used habit stacking to create a simple rule for learning a new language.

“When I first moved to China and started to learn Mandarin, I committed to strike up a conversation with the taxi driver whenever I went into a cab (I took a lot of cab rides, 5+ daily). I did it for 2 years no matter the time of day or how tired I was. I now speak fluent Chinese.”

Similarly, a reader named David told me, “I meditate for 20 minutes after brushing my teeth in the morning. Linking new habits onto a keystone one seems to work.”

You’ll find all sorts of habit stacking examples in Chapter 5 of Atomic Habits.

Environment Design, Part I

I have written about the power of the environment and the importance of choice architecture in the past. The simple truth is our environment often shapes our behavior. Many readers are using this fact to their benefit by installing some of the environment design strategies I share in the book.

For starters, you can break a bad habit by increasing the friction in your environment.

One woman named Cyd curtailed her snacking habit with the following strategy. “My husband still loves his Pringles, as do I, but they’re now kept in a locked car that’s parked in the cold. It works!”

Multiple readers are learning to wake up earlier.

One reader named Daniel told me, “I jump out of bed every morning without any hesitation. The reason? The only way to turn off my alarm is to scan a QR Code I keep in the bathroom. This worked wonders for me.”

Chris utilized both environment design and habit stacking to stop sleeping in. He wrote, “I have a bad habit: Hitting snooze. To eliminate it, I “made it hard” and put phone in the bathroom. The phone then became a habit stack. The first thing I do when I wake up: turn off alarm, go to bathroom, brush teeth, etc.”

One of my favorite examples was sent to me by J. Money, the personal finance blogger. He wrote, “I brush my teeth right after putting my kids to bed every night (8pm), which has prevented me from eating or drinking (alcohol) at night for years… ‘Cuz who wants to re-brush them again!”

It’s a great example of creating just enough friction to keep your bad habits at bay.

Environment Design, Part II

Typically, we think of designing physical spaces, but you can use the same principles to shape your digital environment as well. For instance, a reader named Matthew wrote to me and said, “I significantly cut down on mindless Instagram time. Simply logging out of the app makes a big difference.”

Another reader named Viet went even further. “I used my own laziness to my own advantage with my bad habit of browsing Facebook. Deleting Facebook and having to go through the one extra step of going to website and logging in manually was enough barrier for me to not get back on.”

And Rahul did something similar to kill his video game habit. “For gaming addiction, I removed my graphic card,” he wrote. “For excessive net surfing on mobile, I uninstalled apps and removed the Chrome browser.”

Environment Design, Part III

On the flip side, you can foster good habits by reducing the friction in your environment.

Natalie started picking up her cluttered clothes and building better cleaning habits simply by reducing the number of steps between her and the laundry basket. “I quit leaving my socks all over the floor by putting a little basket beside the door to collect them in.”

Similar strategies can be particularly useful for building new exercise habits.

One reader named Justin sent me the following message: “I started going to a gym that was less than a mile from my house. This took away the time and inconvenience excuses. I was never consistent at exercise, but now I work out 8-10x a week. Crossfit, running, and cycling. I’ve been going strong for 2.5 years.”

Another reader wrote, “I’ve been running at 6 A.M. for the past two years. I always put my running gear (Garmin, compression sleeves, shoes, etc.) into a neat pile the night before. When I get up, I just get dressed and go out the door.”

I’ve even heard from readers who go to sleep wearing their running clothes. All they have to do is stumble out the door in the morning.

For more on environment design, see Chapters 6 and 12 of Atomic Habits.

Habit Substitution

In many cases, it can be more effective to replace your bad habit than to merely try to eliminate it.

The beautiful thing about habit substitution is that you can build a good habit and break a bad one at the same time. One reader told me, “At home I would go out to my backyard to smoke, so I put a weight bench out there and every time I wanted to smoke I’d go out and do some reps instead. After that, my craving was reduced.”

I thought the following idea was interesting. One reader replaced biting their nails with cutting their nails. “I stopped biting my fingernails mostly by making sure clippers were always close at hand – especially at work.”

Many readers have substituted a new habit in a “stair step” fashion. They gradually shift from the old habit to something healthier.

Mark, for example, shared the following strategy. “I significantly cut back on beer consumption. I used flavored sparkling water to replace the beer and I asked my wife to stop having beer in the fridge for a while. Once I replaced the habit (it was mostly stress drinking after work), I was able to add beer back into my life.”

And another reader, also named Marc, curtailed his drinking in a similar way. “I replaced drinking beer every day in a succession of replacements, going through fruit juice, then iced tea, then seltzer water. I did it over about nine months by having one less drink a week. Once I finally quit, I got past the cravings in only two weeks. I haven’t had a drink in over a year now.”

Shawn used this approach to stop smoking. “I decided to quit smoking and used a fun-sized Snickers candy bar as a substitute until the major cravings went away. I’m still smoke-free years later.”

Substitution can even be useful in a broader sense. Suraj wrote, “I was addicted to drugs and alcohol. To beat my addiction, I started working out. Now I am planning to compete in powerlifting meets.”

To a certain degree, habit substitution allows you to look for a healthier obsession. Some people are hooked on alcohol. Others are hooked on exercise. Either one can be unhealthy if taken too far, but generally speaking it’s a lot better to spend a few hours exercising each day than to spend a few hours drinking each day.

Mindset Tricks

Sometimes I like to employ clever little mental tricks to stick with a good habit.

One reader named Caelan wrote, “I quit smoking by assigning my cheat days progressively farther in the future. I never quit “for good,” I only quit until my next cheat day. This helped with cravings, because the choice wasn’t between “right now” or “never,” it was “right now” or “later.”

Ken applied a similar strategy to his habit of eating fast food. “I started small when I quit bad habits like eating McDonalds all the time and drinking soda. I told myself I’d take a week off, then said two weeks. That continued. This month, I made it four years without McDonalds and 15 months without soda.”

Another person used the Pointing-and-Calling strategy I discussed in Chapter 4. They wrote, “I quit smoking by saying a mantra out loud every time I wanted a cigarette (“your brain tricks you”) which I think changed my thinking from the subconscious part of my brain to the logical part.”

Qiana used a little math and a clever visual trick. “I stopped drinking soda,” she wrote. “I added up all the sodas I drank for the week and counted how many tablespoons of sugar were in those soda cans and bottles. I began to scoop the amount of sugar into an enormous bowl The visual did it for me. I had to break that habit.”

Habit Tracking

Finally, I’d like to close with one of my favorite strategies: habit tracking.

Here’s how a few readers are using it…

Cindy sent me an email saying, “I purchased a large wall calendar and started building the chains. This really works for me. I like to build that chain. There are 6 months of red X’s on my calendar. I am healthier, have lost 30 pounds, feel stronger, exercise more, garden, read more, work on my small business, and practice my French.”

The easiest way to start tracking your habits is to use the templates provided in the Habit Journal. It will make the whole process a breeze.

My favorite approach is to pick a very tiny version of your habit and track that. For example, I have been tracking the habit of “reading 1 page” for the last month. One reader named Günter did something similar. “I’ve done a simple workout every day for over half a year now. I managed to stick to it by changing the scope: when I don’t have time for a full set or don’t feel like it, instead of skipping altogether, I do an abbreviated session. I also mark it in my calendar.”

Hopefully, these short stories give you some ideas on how to build better habits in your own life. If you’d like to learn more about the strategies discussed above, check out Atomic Habits. And if you’re interested in a notebook that makes it easier to build better habits, try the Habit Journal.

But no matter what, keep taking action in small ways each day. It is so gratifying for me to see people making real changes in their life because of these ideas. As always, thanks for reading.

issues.title: The best credit cards with airline fee credits
issues.summary: Compare credit cards that reimburse airline fees or airfare, including baggage, seat selection and inflight purchases, and learn how each credit works.
issues.author: Becky Pokora
issues.content_html:
Call it a la carte pricing or just nickel-and-diming. Either way, it's not in your head.

U.S. airlines collected about $7.4 billion in baggage fees in 2025, and that's before you pay to pick a seat or buy a snack onboard. As a benefit to cardholders, a handful of credit cards will cover some of those fees for you. However, each credit works differently, and restrictions can make some much easier to use than others.

Here's a closer look at the best credit cards with airline fee credits and how to use them.

Comparison of the top cards with airline fee credits

Card nameAirline creditsAnnual feeAmerican Express Platinum Card® Up to $200 in statement credits every calendar year with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment is required) $895 (see rates and fees) The Business Platinum Card® from American Express Up to $200 in statement credits every calendar year with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment is required) $895 (see rates and fees) Citi Strata Elite® Card (see rates and fees) Up to $200 in statement credits each calendar year with American Airlines when it is selected as a Splurge Credit merchant; exclusions apply $595 Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card Up to $200 in statement credits each calendar year (up to $50 in statement credits each quarter) $550 (see rates and fees) Bank of America® Premium Rewards® Elite Credit Card* Up to $300 annually $550 Bank of America® Premium Rewards® credit card Up to $100 annually $95 Wells Fargo Autograph Journey® Card (see rates and fees) $50 after making an airline purchase of at least $50 each annual credit period $95 The Ritz-Carlton™ Credit Card* Up to $300 annually $450

*The information for these cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Details on the best cards with airline fee credits

The Platinum Card from American Express

The Amex Platinum's annual fee definitely raises some eyebrows, but if you use the card's benefits, you can easily justify its cost.

Annual fee: $895

How the airline fee statement credit works: Every calendar year, Amex Platinum cardmembers can receive up to $200 in statement credits toward airline incidental fees charged by one qualifying airline selected in advance from the following list:

  • Alaska Airlines
  • American Airlines
  • Delta Air Lines
  • JetBlue
  • Southwest Airlines
  • United Airlines

The easiest way to think about this benefit is as a cushion for the extras that come with a trip, not the ticket itself. Common qualifying expenses include checked or overweight baggage fees, change fees, seat-selection charges, airline lounge passes and inflight food or beverages.

Airfare, seat upgrades, award tickets, gift cards and mileage purchases or transfer fees do not qualify. Also, bundling a fee into a single transaction with your airfare purchase may not trigger the statement credit.

Other key perks: The Amex Platinum card offers access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection for eligible cardmembers, including Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass™ lounges. It also earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through American Express Travel®, on up to $500,000 in these purchases per calendar year, which pairs nicely with airline fee statement credits.

Enrollment is required in advance for some benefits.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum card.

Apply here: American Express Platinum Card

The Business Platinum Card from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum is best suited to business owners who travel frequently enough to use its airline, lounge and Pay with Points benefits.

Annual fee: $895

How the airline fee statement credit works: The Amex Business Platinum's airline incidental statement credit works like the Amex Platinum statement credit mentioned above. Each calendar year, you'll get up to $200 in statement credits for eligible spending with your selected, qualifying airline. Enrollment is required.

Other key perks: The Business Platinum card includes other perks for frequent flyers, including a Clear+ membership statement credit of up to $219 every calendar year after enrollment (subject to auto-renewal). The card also offers exceptional airport lounge access and hotel elite status benefits.

Plus, when you use Pay with Points for an eligible flight booked through American Express Travel® with the same selected qualifying airline, you can get 35% of those points back, up to 1 million points back per calendar year. For some benefits, enrollment is required in advance.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Business Platinum Card.

Apply here: The Business Platinum Card from American Express

Citi Strata Elite Card

The Citi Strata Elite Card is most compelling for travelers who regularly fly American Airlines.

Annual fee: $595

How the airline fee credit works: Each calendar year, cardholders can receive up to $200 in statement credits across up to two selected Splurge Credit merchants. American Airlines is one of the eligible choices. The credit applies to airfare as well as fees and incidentals for greater flexibility. Just keep in mind you'll need to select American Airlines as one of your Splurge credit merchants before making a purchase (exclusions apply).

Other key perks: Frequent American flyers can also use four Admirals Club passes each calendar year, while a Priority Pass Select membership adds broader lounge access. The card also offers up to $300 off one prepaid hotel stay of at least two nights booked through Citi Travel each calendar year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Strata Elite.

Apply here: Citi Strata Elite

Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

The Hilton Aspire is best for Hilton loyalists who can use both its hotel benefits and a flight statement credit spread throughout the year.

Annual fee: $550

How the airline statement credit works: The Hilton Honors Aspire provides up to $200 in statement credits every calendar year (up to $50 each quarter). The statement credits apply to flight purchases made directly with an airline, through AmexTravel.com or in the Amex Travel App™. Because the statement credit comes in $50 quarterly installments, though, you'll need an airline purchase each quarter to get the full $200.

Other key perks: The hotel benefits do most of the work in justifying this card's annual fee. Cardmembers receive Hilton Diamond status, a free night reward each account anniversary and up to $400 in Hilton Resort statement credits each calendar year, provided as up to $200 semiannually.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Aspire.

Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite Credit Card

If transfer partners aren't a necessity for you and you're in the market for a premium travel card, consider the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite.

Annual fee: $550

How the airline fee credit works: The Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite card offers up to $300 in airline incidental statement credits each calendar year. While you don't need to choose just one airline, the benefit works only with U.S. airlines and only on flights originating in the U.S.

Unfortunately, you can't use this credit with Allegiant Air or Sun Country Airlines.

Other key perks: On top of the airline fee credits, you'll receive up to $150 annually in lifestyle credits for streaming services, food delivery, fitness subscriptions and ride-hailing services, plus up to $120 in statement credits toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years.

And, no other card offers the same Priority Pass flexibility: Cardholders can enroll up to four people in their own memberships with guest access, even if they aren't authorized users or traveling with you.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite.

Bank of America Premium Rewards Credit Card

If high annual fees aren't for you, the Bank of America Premium Rewards card is right up your alley. In fact, its airline credit is worth more than its annual fee.

Annual fee: $95

How the airline fee credit works: Receive up to $100 annually in airline incidental statement credits, subject to the same coverage and airline restrictions as the Premium Rewards Elite card above.

Other key perks: The Bank of America Premium Rewards card also provides up to $100 in statement credits every four years for your Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee, plus travel insurance protections. That gives travelers a practical set of benefits without forcing you to commit to more expensive cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards card.

Apply here: Bank of America Premium Rewards credit card

Wells Fargo Autograph Journey Card

The Autograph Journey Card has the smallest airline credit here, but also one of the lowest annual fees.

Annual fee: $95

How the airline credit works: You'll receive a one-time $50 statement credit after making your first airline purchase of at least $50 during each annual credit period. Any airline-coded charge counts as long as it's $50 or more, including airfare or fees. That means purchases from international carriers can count, too.

Other key perks: This card is also popular because it earns 5 points per dollar spent at hotels and 4 points per dollar spent with airlines without requiring you to make your purchase through a card booking portal.

To learn more, read our full review of the Wells Fargo Autograph Journey.

Apply here: Wells Fargo Autograph Journey Card

The Ritz-Carlton Credit Card

The Ritz-Carlton card is a special case: it isn't open to new applicants, but eligible Chase Marriott cardholders may be able to product change into it.

Annual fee: $450

How the airline fee credit works: You can receive up to $300 in airline fee credits per calendar year. Unlike other cards, where the credits are applied to your account automatically, you'll need to manually request the credit within four billing cycles of an eligible purchase.

Eligible fees include checked bags, inflight purchases (including Wi-Fi), airline lounge passes or memberships and seat upgrades.

Other key perks: You'll enjoy a Priority Pass Select membership along with unlimited complimentary access to Chase Sapphire Lounges, each with up to two guests per visit. Authorized user cards can be added at no additional fee and also receive their own Priority Pass membership.

This card also provides a free night award worth up to 85,000 points, given on each account anniversary (certain hotels have resort fees).

To learn more, read about how you can still get the Ritz-Carlton card.

Mistakes that can cost you the credit

These credits reset on a schedule, so one slip can mean losing the full value. Here's what to watch out for, with a couple of examples for each:

  • Forgetting to enroll or pick your airline: The Amex Platinum statement credits require enrollment and an airline selection, and you're limited on how often you can switch airlines. The Citi Strata Elite's Splurge Credit requires you to choose American Airlines as your splurge partner.
  • Bundling fees with airfare: On some cards, a seat or bag fee paid in the same transaction as your ticket may not trigger the credit.
  • Booking through the wrong channel: The Strata Elite's credit requires you to book directly with American, and the Hilton Aspire requires you to book through the airline or Amex Travel.
  • Flying the wrong airline: The Bank of America credits don't work with Allegiant, Sun Country or non-U.S. airlines.
  • Missing deadlines: The Ritz-Carlton card requires you to request your credit on a timeline and the Hilton Aspire credit resets quarterly without carrying over.

Cards with general travel credits

If the restrictions above put you off, several of the top travel rewards credit cards offer broader travel credits that may be easier to use.

Chase Sapphire Reserve and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business

Both the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) come with $300 in travel credits every year. These credits apply automatically to airfare, hotels, public transit and other qualifying expenses paid for with the card.

Both cards carry a $795 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve and the Sapphire Reserve for Business.

Capital One Venture Cards

With the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, you'll receive a $300 annual travel credit. The caveat is that the credit only applies to bookings made with Capital One Travel, but you can use it toward flights, hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars. The card's annual fee is $395.

The Capital One Venture X Business also offers an annual $300 travel credit valid on flights and other travel bookings, though with this card you'll need to book through Capital One Business Travel.

The Capital One Venture Business has a lower $95 annual fee and offers a smaller $50 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture X card, Venture X Business and Venture Business.

Bottom line

Holding a credit card with an airline fee credit is a great way to avoid paying for things like checked bags, flight changes and inflight purchases. But how much value you get depends on how easy the credit is to use.

If you want an airline credit that's easy to use, start with the cards that cover airfare: the Citi Strata Elite (if you fly American), Hilton Aspire and Autograph Journey.

If you're willing to do more homework, you might get more value through American Express, Bank of America or the Ritz-Carlton cards. They only cover incidental fees, though in today's market most travelers pay for these often enough to maximize that type of credit.

For anyone who thinks tracking rules is a chore, a broader travel credit like that of the Chase Sapphire Reserve is a better bet.
