issues.title: Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program: Complete guide to earning and redeeming miles
issues.summary: Here's everything you need to know about earning Turkish Airlines miles and redeeming them through the carrier's Miles&Smiles program.
issues.author: Ben Smithson
issues.content_html:
Turkish Airlines' Miles&Smiles program is known for being a hidden gem of a loyalty program that offers an award chart with some attractive redemption rates for economy and business-class travel.

Although rates increased significantly in 2024, useful options remain, including domestic partner awards within the U.S. Miles&Smiles is also a direct transfer partner of four U.S.-accessible rewards currencies.

Here's everything to know about Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles, including how to book a one-way business-class ticket between North America and Istanbul for just 65,000 miles.

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles elite status

The Miles&Smiles program has three elite membership tiers (aside from its basic membership, Classic):

  • Classic Plus: Earned after accruing 25,000 status miles or taking 40 flights in 12 months. Benefits include domestic business-class check-in and lounge access, 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of extra baggage and 25% more status miles on eligible Turkish business-class flights.
  • Elite: Earned after accruing 40,000 status miles in 12 months. Benefits include all of the Classic Plus perks, plus Star Alliance Gold status, lounge access with family or one guest for domestic and international flights, priority services, complimentary eligible seat selection and 20 kilograms (44 pounds) or one extra bag.
  • Elite Plus: Earned after accruing 80,000 status miles in 12 months. Benefits include all of the Classic Plus and Elite benefits, as well as two cabin upgrade vouchers per year, the ability to gift Elite status, guaranteed seats in select fare classes and 25 kilograms (55 pounds) or one extra bag.

Status generally lasts until the end of the month two years after it begins. Status miles only count toward qualification; regular miles can be redeemed for awards.

Renewal thresholds are lower. Classic Plus requires 17,000 status miles or 30 flights in the first year, or 35,000 miles or 60 flights over two years. Outside of Turkey, Elite requires 25,000 miles in year No. 1 or 37,500 miles over two years; Elite Plus requires 40,000 or 60,000 miles in the first or second year, respectively.

How to earn Turkish Miles&Smiles

There are plenty of ways to boost your Miles&Smiles balance.

Earn with the U.S. Miles&Smiles credit card

The Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles Premier Visa Signature® Credit Card has a $99 annual fee. New cardholders can earn up to 40,000 bonus miles: 25,000 after spending $2,000 on eligible purchases in the first 90 days of account opening and 15,000 additional bonus miles after spending another $6,000 (for $8,000 total) in the first 12 months. The second bonus posts after the first anniversary if the account remains open and in good standing.

It earns 3 miles per dollar spent on eligible Turkish Airlines purchases through Turkish-owned channels; 2 miles per dollar spent on eligible dining, grocery, entertainment and lodging purchases; and 1 mile per dollar spent on all other purchases. Eligible benefits include cardholder access to Turkish Airlines lounges worldwide, priority check-in and boarding on Turkish flights to and from the U.S. and 125 status miles per $500 spent each statement cycle, up to 5,000 miles per calendar year.

The information for the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles Premier card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Transfer points from credit card programs

You can also transfer rewards directly to Miles&Smiles at a 1:1 rate from four programs with transferable currencies: Bilt, Capital One, Citi ThankYou Rewards and Rove.

Here are some of the best welcome bonuses available that you could transfer to Miles&Smiles:

  • Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card ($95 annual fee): Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year.
  • Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card ($395 annual fee): Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.
  • Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (no annual fee): Earn 20,000 bonus miles after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.
  • Capital One Venture X Business ($395 annual fee): Earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit: 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening, plus an additional 150,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit (to use in the first cardholder year) after spending $120,000 total on purchases in the first four months from account opening.
  • Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees; $95 annual fee): Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening.

Transfer points from hotel programs

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer at a 3:1 ratio, with 5,000 bonus Miles&Smiles miles earned for every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred. You can also convert 5,000 Choice Privileges points to 1,000 Miles&Smiles miles.

Hotel transfers generally offer less value and are best saved for topping up a specific award.

Related: Your complete guide to earning Marriott Bonvoy points

Earn miles for flying

You can fly Turkish Airlines-operated flights to earn reward miles based on your fare class, Miles&Smiles elite status level and flight distance.

As a Star Alliance member, Turkish lets you earn Miles&Smiles miles on partner flights, including Lufthansa, United Airlines, Air Canada and Swiss.

Members can also earn miles and status miles on eligible AJet flights, though AJet awards are unavailable. Outside of Star Alliance, eligible Azul Brazilian Airlines and Olympic Air flights earn both, while Gol Airlines and Oman Air only earn redeemable miles. Awards are available on Azul, Gol and Olympic Air.

There are different earning charts for each partner airline. So, check whether your fare class earns miles and see how many miles you'll earn before entering your Turkish frequent flyer number on a partner reservation.

Earn miles through other partners

The Miles&Smiles program has a comprehensive list of other earning partners available here. It includes (but is not limited to):

  • Hotels: Hilton Honors, Marriott Bonvoy, Choice Privileges and Wyndham Rewards
  • Rental cars: Avis Preferred, Budget Fastbreak, Enterprise Plus, Europcar Privilege For You, Hertz Gold+, National Emerald Club and Sixt One
  • Shopping and booking: The Bicester Collection and Turkish Airlines Holidays

Keep Miles&Smiles miles from expiring

Miles expire at the end of the third full calendar year after they are processed; activity does not reset the clock. Before expiration, you can pay $20 per 1,000 miles to extend them by three years. Expired miles cannot be restored.

Related: How to keep your points and miles from expiring

How Miles&Smiles prices award flights

Miles&Smiles uses fixed one-way charts. Turkish-operated flights have capacity-controlled Promotion Award Tickets and more expensive Award Tickets with broader availability. Partners use a separate region-based chart with special rates for direct same-country flights and mainland U.S.-Hawaii awards.

Below are some current one-way examples, excluding taxes, fees and surcharges:

Example awardEconomyBusiness class Turkish Airlines Promotion Award Ticket between North America and Turkey 40,000 miles 65,000 miles Turkish Airlines Promotion Award Ticket between Turkey and Europe 1 10,000 miles 20,000 miles Direct partner flight within the same country 15,000 miles 22,500 miles Direct partner flight between the mainland U.S. and Hawaii 25,000 miles 40,000 miles Partner flight between the U.S. and Mexico or Canada 30,000 miles 40,000 miles

Connecting Turkish itineraries are charged per segment. For example, a New York-to-Istanbul-to-London itinerary in promotional business class costs 65,000 miles plus 25,000 miles for the Europe 2 segment for a total of 90,000 miles one-way when both segments have promotional space available.

Check the current Turkish Airlines award charts before transferring because prices can change without notice.

How to redeem Turkish Miles&Smiles

How to book a Turkish Airlines-operated award flight

If you want to book an award ticket only operated by Turkish Airlines, you can get to the award booking engine from the Turkish homepage by clicking the "Award Ticket" checkbox.

This will require logging in to your Miles&Smiles account and then going to the award ticket booking engine. There, you can enter your origin, destination, dates, class of service and number of passengers.

After selecting a flight, you'll see the flight details, the aircraft type and the award space labeled as promotional or regular pricing, which will match the published award charts.

The following page will give you the total flight cost, including taxes and fees, even if you don't have the required miles in your account. Expect to pay around $300 in taxes, fees and surcharges for a one-way business-class ticket to Istanbul.

How to book a Star Alliance partner award flight

Partner awards are harder to book. Follow these steps:

  1. Find saver-level space through United MileagePlus, Air Canada Aeroplan or Seats.aero.
  2. In your Miles&Smiles account, open "Miles Transactions," select "Star Award Ticket" and search the exact route, date and cabin.
  3. If it appears, verify the mileage, taxes and surcharges before transferring rewards to Miles&Smiles.
  4. If it does not, call Turkish or visit a sales office. Azul, Gol and Olympic Air awards must be booked through one of those channels.
  5. Have your membership number, passenger details, dates, flight numbers and cabin ready. If an agent cannot see the seat, try again.

Other ways to use Miles&Smiles miles

You can also use miles for upgrades on eligible Turkish Airlines tickets, Cash&Miles bookings, seat assignments, extra baggage, selected lounge access, taxes through Tax&Smiles and purchases through Shop&Miles.

Cash&Miles is a paid-ticket option rather than an award ticket, which are much easier to find. It lets you cover up to 50% of the fare, excluding taxes, with miles on eligible Turkish-operated tickets booked through the Turkish website or app, and you will still earn miles according to the paid fare rules. It is not available on codeshare or partner flights.

Things to know about the program

The best way to redeem Turkish miles is for award flights. While other options may be available in the program, booking Turkish Airlines- or Star Alliance-operated flights will usually give you the most value.

Website and booking quirks

  • The Miles&Smiles website is glitchy, complicated and frustrating. You'll need plenty of patience and persistence to navigate it. For example, when choosing a login password, it can only be numeric, must be exactly six digits, cannot have the same number more than twice (whether consecutive or not) and will not be remembered by your Google password manager. You must then receive a text message code to log in, which may or may not arrive, especially if you have a non-Turkish cellphone number. Turkish added smart-notification login approvals in November 2026, but you must first register a device through the mobile app using a one-time code.
  • If your membership number fails, try removing the first two "TK" letters.
  • You can book for others, but online restrictions may require saved passenger details, the call center or a sales office.

Award rules, fees and surcharges

  • Published prices are one-way; round trips generally cost twice as much.
  • United awards have no fuel surcharges. Turkish surcharges are fairly modest, but Lufthansa and Swiss can be expensive.
  • International award changes or refunds before departure cost $70 per transaction; no-shows cost $170.

Stopovers, open jaws and Istanbul connection perks

  • One open jaw is allowed, but it cannot be booked online.
  • A stopover over 24 hours is allowed on the outbound or return of a round-trip Turkish-operated award, but it cannot be booked online.
  • Eligible international travelers connecting for six to 24 hours at Istanbul Airport (IST) on one reservation and a ticket starting with "235" can use Touristanbul, which includes a city tour, transportation and specified meals or admissions. Entry requirements remain the traveler's responsibility.
  • For eligible international round-trip itineraries with a connection of at least 20 hours and no more than seven days, the Stopover in Istanbul program provides hotel accommodation. The standard benefit is one night in a four-star hotel for economy passengers and two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel for business-class passengers. Eligible trips originating in the U.S. receive up to two nights in economy or three nights in business class. Applications must be made at least 72 hours before travel.
  • These benefits are separate from an award-ticket stopover and cannot be combined into a single layover.

Best uses of Turkish Miles&Smiles

Miles&Smiles uses two different award charts, one for Turkish Airlines-operated flights and the other for Star Alliance and other partner-operated flights. Here are some of the best ways to redeem Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles:

  • Turkish Airlines flights between North America and Istanbul: Tickets start at 65,000 miles one-way in business class or 40,000 miles one-way in economy. Connections beyond Turkey add another segment, so compare the total with Air Canada Aeroplan, Avianca Lifemiles and United MileagePlus.
  • Direct partner flights within one country: Tickets start at 15,000 miles in economy, 22,500 miles in business class and 30,000 miles in first class each way. This can still be useful for an expensive nonstop United transcontinental flight or a long domestic flight on another partner, provided saver-level space is available. Mainland U.S.-Hawaii awards now cost 25,000 miles in economy or 40,000 miles in business class, so other programs are often better.
  • Partner flights between the U.S. and Mexico or Canada: Tickets start at 30,000 miles in economy or 40,000 miles in business class one-way. Business class can be useful on expensive United flights, but compare other programs.

Related: A review of Turkish Airlines' 787 in business class from Cancun to Istanbul

Note that while you can book Turkish Airlines-operated flights and most partner-operated flights online, it is difficult to find the cheapest promotional award tickets operated by Turkish Airlines without clicking through day to day. You may wish to use an external tool like Seats.aero to easily find the cheapest rates across 12 months.

Bottom line

Miles&Smiles is worth considering if you can tolerate its frustrating website. No program is best at everything, but Turkish still has useful fixed-price awards.

Logging in to your account on the website can be challenging, especially if you have a non-Turkish phone number registered. However, if you can get past that quirk, you can take advantage of solid redemption opportunities like 65,000-mile Turkish business-class awards between North America and Istanbul and 15,000-mile domestic partner economy awards.

A U.S. branded credit card and partners like Rove now also make it even easier to earn miles, but no-notice devaluations reinforce the rule to transfer only when you're ready to book.

issues.title: 10 easy-to-earn credit card welcome bonuses
issues.summary: Here are 10 top cards that are offering easy-to-earn welcome bonuses right now. Analyze their benefits, and decide which credit card is best for you.
issues.author: Augusta Stone and Stephanie Stevens
issues.content_html:
When considering which rewards credit card deserves your next application, its welcome offer should be a top factor.

Many bonuses are worth hundreds of dollars (or even more than $1,000) in the form of cash back or travel rewards. However, these offers sometimes carry steep spending requirements, requiring you to spend anywhere from $4,000 to $10,000 within the first few months of having the card.

It doesn't have to be that way. Here, we dive into high-value card bonuses that are easier to earn. Each of the offers we've listed here comes with a minimum spending requirement of $2,000 or less.

While this isn't an exhaustive list, these are 10 of the best cards you can add to your wallet with an easy-to-earn welcome bonus.

Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards credit card

If flexibility is what you want, the Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card may appeal to you.

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 online cash rewards bonus after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 90 days of account opening.

Annual fee: $0.

Why we chose it: The Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards credit card lets you customize your rewards structure, allowing flexibility in your cash-back rewards strategy.

Being a member of the BofA Rewards™ program means you'll earn even more cash back on every purchase.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards.

Apply here: Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards credit card

Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card is an all-around winner when it comes to earning cash-back rewards in popular bonus categories.

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Annual fee: $0.

Why we chose it: It's easy to stack up cash-back rewards with the Capital One Savor. It earns bonus rewards across popular categories like dining, entertainment, grocery stores (excluding superstores like Walmart® and Target®) and select streaming services.

Plus, the card is a solid one to bring abroad, as it charges no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Savor.

Learn more: Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card

Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card — Miles Boost

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card — Miles Boost is a solid option for travelers looking to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, this offer is worth $740.

Annual fee: $0

Why we chose it: The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card — Miles Boost offers an accessible way to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

With just $1,000 in spending required to earn 40,000 bonus miles, this offer could be a solid match for those looking to get started with points and miles. Plus, cardholders have access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners.

Keep in mind that this version of the VentureOne doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period, unlike the standard Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card*, which has a smaller welcome bonus and lower spending requirement.

*0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74%.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card and our guide to the two VentureOne offers.

Learn more: Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card - Miles Boost

Chase Freedom Unlimited

One of the best no-annual-fee cards on the market is the Chase Freedom Unlimited® (see rates and fees).

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

Annual fee: $0.

Why we chose it: The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a great card for nonbonus spending since it earns at least 1.5% cash back on all purchases.

If you also have a card that earns Chase Ultimate Rewards points, you can pair them with the Freedom Unlimited to convert your cash back into valuable, transferable Ultimate Rewards points. You can then transfer them to airline and hotel partners for potentially even more value.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Apply here: Chase Freedom Unlimited

Citi Double Cash Card

The Citi Double Cash® Card (see rates and fees) makes it easy to earn solid cash-back rewards on every purchase.

Welcome bonus: Earn $200 cash back after spending $1,500 on purchases in the first six months of account opening.

Annual fee: $0.

Why we chose it: The best perk of the Citi Double Cash is its simple rewards structure. Cardholders earn 2% cash back on all purchases (1% when you make a purchase and another 1% when you pay it off).

Plus, the card is a fantastic choice if you want to fit it into a larger Citi-oriented strategy. That's because cash back is earned in the form of Citi ThankYou Rewards points, and you can unlock higher-value redemption options if you hold certain ThankYou Rewards cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Double Cash.

Apply here: Citi Double Cash Card

Citi Strata Card

The Citi Strata® Card (see rates and fees) provides a valuable bonus and great earning rates, especially when you consider it charges no annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, this welcome offer is worth $390.

Annual fee: $0.

Why we chose it: The Citi Strata earns ThankYou Rewards points at a high rate across multiple categories. Plus, you can make your rewards flexible thanks to its bonus category on quarterly self-select categories.

As with the Double Cash, you can receive more value from your rewards if you pair this card with certain ThankYou Rewards-earning cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata.

Apply here: Citi Strata Card

Hilton Honors American Express Card

The Hilton Honors American Express Card comes with solid perks and earning rates for those who occasionally stay with Hilton.

Welcome bonus: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027.

TPG's November 2026 valuations value this offer at $280, not including the value of the free night reward.

Annualfee: $0 (see rates and fees).

Why we chose it: The Hilton Honors Amex is an entry-level card in the Hilton Honors hotel program. You'll earn bonus Hilton points in multiple bonus categories and receive complimentary Hilton Silver elite status.

These are decent perks for a card with no annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Amex.

issues.title: Brian Kelly's wallet: My go-to card for earning miles on business expenses
issues.summary: Here's why the Capital One Venture X Business is one of my go-to cards for business expenses, from earning bonus miles on purchases to valuable travel perks.
issues.author: Brian Kelly
issues.content_html:
I get asked a lot about credit cards and how to maximize points and miles. One of the simplest strategies I always recommend is to never settle for earning just 1 point or mile per dollar on your purchases.

That strategy is especially valuable when you're running a business and want to maximize expenses.

I have plenty of credit cards that earn bonus rewards in specific spending categories, but not every business expense fits neatly into one of them.

This is why the Capital One Venture X Business is a regular part of my card rotation. It earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase, helping me turn everyday business expenses into valuable travel rewards.

And because Capital One miles are transferable to airline and hotel partners, I can put all those miles earned through business spending toward my next big trip.

Here's why the Venture X Business continues to earn its place in my wallet.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

Why I carry the Venture X Business

When you're running a business, you have enough decisions to make without having to think about which credit card to pull out for every expense. That's what I appreciate about the Venture X Business: Its straightforward earning structure makes it easy to rack up miles without keeping track of bonus categories.

Here's how the card earns rewards:

  • 10 miles per dollar on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel
  • 5 miles per dollar on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Business Travel
  • 2 miles per dollar on all other purchases

Think about how much your business spends on things like equipment, professional services, insurance and other expenses that may not fall into traditional credit card bonus categories.

Depending on your business, those purchases alone could add up to thousands of dollars each month.

And those miles can add up surprisingly quickly.

For example, if your business spends $10,000 a month on purchases earning 2 miles per dollar, that's 240,000 Capital One miles in a year — before factoring in any welcome or anniversary bonuses.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that's $4,440 in potential travel value from expenses your business was already going to incur.

Turn big business expenses into a big welcome bonus

Right now, the Venture X Business also has a huge welcome offer.

New cardholders can earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit. Here's how it breaks down:

  • Earn 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening.
  • Earn an additional 150,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit (to use in the first cardholder year) after spending $120,000 total on purchases in the first four months from account opening.

Don't get me wrong, that's a hefty spending requirement. But if your business spends that kind of money, or you have big expenses coming up, consider for a moment the enormous value you can get from that bonus.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, the full offer is worth up to $6,550, including the $1,000 travel credit.

The $395 annual fee is also easier to justify thanks to a $300 annual Capital One Business Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary bonus miles (worth $185, per TPG's valuations). Throw in unlimited access to Capital One Lounges, and I have no trouble getting my money's worth.

Related: Brian Kelly's wallet: Why the United Club Card still earns a spot

How I use my Capital One miles

My favorite use of Capital One miles is transferring to one of the issuer's 15-plus airline and hotel partners. By moving miles to these loyalty programs, often at a 1:1 ratio, you can book flights and hotel stays using their rewards currencies, often getting more value than you would by redeeming miles directly through Capital One.

I have often been able to get at least 2 cents in value per mile when I leverage my miles with airline partners, particularly for international business-class flights.

Anyone who knows me knows how much I love flying Air France, particularly its La Première first-class experience. I recently traveled to Paris to see Céline Dion, and France is a destination I never get tired of visiting.

While only Flying Blue Platinum and Ultimate elite members can redeem miles directly for La Première award tickets, you don't need elite status to score a great redemption in Air France business class.

And one of my favorite ways to stretch my miles even further is by taking advantage of a transfer bonus.

For example, Capital One is currently offering a 20% transfer bonus to Air France-KLM Flying Blue through Nov. 30.

I found business-class awards to Europe for as little as 45,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, meaning you could book one of these flights by transferring just 38,000 Capital One miles with the bonus (subject to award availability and applicable taxes and fees).

That same flight would cost more than $2,000 in cash. Even after accounting for award taxes and fees, you'd get about 4 cents in value per Capital One mile, more than double TPG's valuation.

Of course, you don't have to transfer your miles to get value from the card. Capital One also lets you redeem miles to cover eligible travel purchases at 1 cent apiece, which is a straightforward option if you don't want to deal with award availability.

Related: Capital One vs. Chase: Which is better for business travel?

Who should get the Venture X Business (and who shouldn't)

The Venture X Business isn't for everyone, but I think it's a great option for business owners who have significant expenses and want to earn valuable, transferable miles.

I'd consider it if you:

  • Have a lot of business expenses that don't fall into traditional bonus categories, where earning at least 2 miles per dollar on everything can really add up.
  • Spend enough to comfortably meet the full welcome offer without making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make.
  • Travel regularly and can use the $300 annual Capital One Business Travel credit to help offset the annual fee.
  • Prefer earning transferable miles rather than being tied to a single airline or hotel program.

However, if most of your business spending falls into categories like advertising, shipping or office supplies, you may get more value from a card that earns higher rewards in those categories.

Related: The best business cards of the month

Bottom line

I have a wallet full of credit cards, but the Venture X Business is one I keep coming back to. Earning at least 2 miles per dollar on business expenses is a no-brainer for me, especially when I can transfer those miles to airline and hotel partners to get even more value.

Between the $300 annual travel credit, 10,000 anniversary miles and lounge access, I get more than enough value to justify the $395 annual fee.

And if your business meets the spending requirements, the current welcome offer is one I'd seriously consider.

For more details, check out our full review of the Capital One Venture X Business.

issues.content_html:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

issues.content_html:
Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

Beyond its stone walls stretch the waters of the Bay of Biscay, with the tiny island of Le Pilier visible on the horizon. issues.content_html:
On the northwestern tip of France's Noirmoutier Island, behind the 19th-century Church of the Sacred Heart, a small cemetery overlooks the Atlantic Ocean. Beyond its stone walls stretch the waters of the Bay of Biscay, with the tiny island of Le Pilier visible on the horizon. Many of those buried here were sailors and fishermen whose lives were intimately connected to the sea.

Among the traditional graves stands a striking row of white Commonwealth headstones, commemorating the victims of a largely forgotten maritime tragedy.

On June 17, 1940, as British troops and civilians were being evacuated from France, German aircraft bombed the British troopship HMT Lancastria off the coast of Saint-Nazaire. The ship sank within minutes, taking thousands of lives in one of the deadliest maritime disasters of World War II.

In the following days, the Atlantic currents carried the bodies of victims onto the French coastline, including the shores of Noirmoutier.

Today, the cemetery contains 40 Commonwealth war burials, 22 of them unidentified. Most were victims of the Lancastria disaster.

Overlooking the very ocean that claimed so many lives, L'Herbaudière's marine cemetery remains a peaceful yet poignant reminder of the island's maritime heritage and the tragedies of war.

issues.title: Beguinage of Anderlecht in Anderlecht, Belgium

issues.content_html:
Tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht. Founded in 1252, it is considered the smallest beguinage in Belgium and once provided a home to a community of just eight women.

Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opportunity to live in a religious community without taking permanent monastic vows. The beguines were typically unmarried women or widows who chose a life of prayer, work and mutual support. They followed rules of chastity and obedience but remained free to leave the community whenever they wished. This offered women a degree of independence that was relatively unusual in medieval society.

The Anderlecht beguinage consists of two modest buildings surrounding an enclosed courtyard garden with an old well. The buildings date from different periods, with sections originating in the 16th and 18th centuries. From the garden, visitors can enjoy a view of the neighbouring Gothic collegiate church.

Interestingly, the beguinage was locally nicknamed the Klaphuis, meaning 'chatterbox' in Dutch, a playful reference to the conversations that supposedly took place among its residents.

Following the French Revolution, the religious community disappeared and the buildings were converted into a hospice for disadvantaged women. They continued serving this purpose until 1928. In 1930, the complex became a local history museum, displaying archaeological finds, religious art and objects illustrating Anderlecht's past.

After decades of use as a museum, the buildings underwent an extensive restoration, completed in 2022. The restoration aimed to recover the original appearance of the complex, allowing visitors to appreciate its historic architecture. Today, the beguinage offers a rare glimpse into the everyday lives of medieval women and the history of one of Brussels' oldest communities.

Despite being surrounded by the busy streets of Anderlecht, stepping through its entrance feels like discovering a little pocket of tranquillity that has survived for almost eight centuries.

issues.title: A UK macro and wildlife specialist makes the case for protecting native species
issues.summary: From kingfishers at Barnwell to slime moulds on the woodland floor, this photographer pairs an OM-1 Mark II and a Canon R5 for close-up and distant subjects. What's your favorite local patch to photograph?
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
From kingfishers at Barnwell to slime molds on the woodland floor, this photographer pairs an OM-1 Mark II and a Canon R5 for close-up and distant subjects. What’s your favorite local patch to photograph?

Meet WildlifeInFocusUK

Home base: Peterborough, United Kingdom

This week, we head to the United Kingdom to chat with forum member WildlifeInFocusUK, a photographer who splits his time between the hides of his local patch at Barnwell Country Park and the cliffs of Bempton. His subjects range from kingfishers and puffins to fungi and slime molds.

“Ever since I was a kid, I have been completely fascinated by the natural world. I used to spend hours out at the bottom of my garden, quietly watching frogs by the pond or peering under damp logs and stones just to catch a glimpse of things like the not-so-common UK earwig. Most people walk straight past those tiny creatures without giving them a second thought, whereas I was always captivated by the intricate details of how they lived.”

Our What’s in your bag? community spotlight series features readers sharing their favorite gear and photography, including from past DReview collaborators. See below for what today’s guest has to share.

Have your photography featured on the DPReview homepage! Find out how.

What’s in WildlifeInFocusUK’s bag

Favorite camera(s): “For macro and close-up work, I use the OM System OM-1 Mark II paired with the M.Zuiko Digital ED 90mm F3.5 Macro IS PRO lens.

The Micro Four Thirds sensor gives me that extra bit of depth of field, which is worth its weight in gold when working at high magnifications, and the in-body focus bracketing and computational features make capturing intricate arthropods, fungi, and tiny slime molds an absolute dream.

When I am heading out for wildlife, birds, or anything further afield, I reach for my full-frame system: the Canon EOS R5 Mark I with the Canon RF 100-500mm F4.5-7.1 L IS USM. It is sharp as a tack, balances brilliantly in the hand for tracking fast-moving birds in flight, and gives me plenty of reach whether I am in a hide at Barnwell or standing on the cliffs at Bempton.”

What makes photographing wildlife a different experience?

“When I eventually started taking photographs in 2010, it felt like a natural extension of that childhood curiosity – a way to freeze those fleeting moments and share the hidden beauty of nature with others.

Over the last decade and a half, my relationship with photography has deepened significantly. Whilst I still love the technical challenge and the thrill of getting a great image, it has evolved into something much more personal for me.

The moment I am out in the field, tracking a bird through the viewfinder or kneeling on the woodland floor looking for tiny subjects, all of life’s everyday woes just seem to melt away. That sense of calm and connection is really what keeps me coming back.”

How has your photography changed since you started?

“Alongside early attempts at wildlife, I spent a lot of time shooting sweeping landscapes and grand architectural buildings, particularly cathedrals. Narrowing my focus down to wildlife and macro was a huge turning point. Henri Cartier-Bresson famously said, “Your first 10,000 photographs are your worst,” and honestly, that quote could not be more true.

What has improved most over the years isn’t just my technical grasp of exposure or composition – it is having a clear sense of direction and purpose in what I shoot. I no longer just spray and pray hoping for a lucky frame.

I still happily take and keep plenty of photographs purely for my own memories, because that keeps the hobby fun and pressure-free. At the same time, however, I push myself to capture that “perfect” action shot or intricate macro stack for competitions and to build a strong, cohesive portfolio as I work towards my photography qualification.”

How do you adapt your setup to fast macro scenes?

“Because wildlife and macro photography often require split-second reactions, I rely heavily on pre-programmed custom shooting modes.

On my OM System OM-1 Mark II, I have all four custom modes dialed in specifically for different macro lighting and focus scenarios. Custom Mode 1 is set up for focus stacking with flash, which is my go-to for static subjects like fungi or cooperative insects where I want maximum depth of field and crisp, frozen detail.

Custom Mode 2 is configured for single-shot macro with flash, ideal for lively arthropods that won’t sit still long enough for a full stack.

Custom Mode 3 switches over to macro stacking using constant light rather than flash, which works brilliantly when I am using my tripod and SmallRig lights on slime molds.

Custom Mode 4 is set up for single-shot macro with continuous autofocus and no artificial light at all, giving me flexibility in bright, natural conditions.

On my Canon R5, I use all three custom modes to adapt to changing wildlife and travel situations. C1 is my generic wildlife-and-birding mode. C2 is dedicated to wildlife photography. Finally, C3 is my flexible, everyday mode that I tweak on the fly whenever I swap over to the RF 24-240mm lens for landscapes, architecture or general walkaround shots.”

What areas of the UK are perfect for bird photography?

“One of my favorite trips is heading up to Buxton in Derbyshire specifically to photograph Dippers bobbing along the fast-flowing rivers – they have so much character.

When I fancy coastal wildlife, RSPB Bempton Cliffs is unbeatable for Puffins, Northern Gannets, and dramatic cliffside seabird action.

Closer to home, though, my absolute go-to is my local patch, Barnwell Country Park in Northamptonshire. Sitting quietly inside, you can have over twenty different species of small garden birds perching no more than three meters away from your lens. You get stunning, intimate views of Nuthatches, Blue Tits, and even a resident pair of Blackbirds going about their daily routines.

And trips to places like Bempton Cliffs put you out in the elements on towering chalk cliffs battered by sea winds, shooting dynamic flight scenes against the crashing waves of the North Sea below, or down on the rocky, fast-flowing riverbanks of Derbyshire tracking Dippers amidst rushing white water.”

How important is your gear to getting a great wildlife shot?

“If I could pass on one key piece of advice to other photographers, it would be to invest your time in learning your equipment inside out until operating it becomes pure muscle memory, and then pair that with genuine patience in the field.

Early on, it is very easy to get caught up in chasing the newest camera body or copying someone else’s exact settings, thinking that will magically produce great images. In reality, light and nature change constantly. Being able to adjust your shutter speed, exposure compensation, or focus modes instinctively, without taking your eye off the viewfinder, is what allows you to react when a split-second moment unfolds in front of you.

More importantly, I think we, as nature photographers, have a collective responsibility to shine a spotlight on our native species. The reality is that wildlife populations across the UK are quietly declining. If more of us don’t take the time to observe, photograph, and care about the creatures living in our local parks, woodlands, and hedgerows, we risk losing them altogether.

Get out into your local patch, support your local reserves, and fall in love with the wildlife right in front of you.”

WildlifeInFocusUK really enjoyed participating in this spotlight article and would love to hear what you think of his photography and to answer any of your questions in the comments below.

You can check out WildlifeInFocusUK’s other work and photography discussions right here on DPReview in the community forums, or visit his Instagram channel.

issues.title: Share your instant camera photos to celebrate the first Polaroid camera sold in 1948
issues.summary: We're celebrating the launch of the Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 on November 26, 1948, by sharing your instant camera photos!
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
We’re celebrating the launch of the Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 on November 26, 1948, by showcasing your instant camera photos.

Attention photographers: Thursday, Nov. 26, marks the anniversary of the first Polaroid camera going on sale!

On Nov. 26, 1948, inventor Edwin Land’s Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 debuted at the Jordan Marsh department store in Boston. It cost $89.75 (in 1948 dollars), and it did something no camera had done for the public before: it produced a finished print in about a minute (as opposed to days or even weeks). The cameras reportedly sold out on the first day.

Land got the idea after his young daughter asked why she couldn’t see a photo he had just taken of her right away. Instant photography has been an epic win for photographers ever since, from the earliest sepia prints to today’s remarkably small instant cameras.

Share your instant cameras and photos

We’re marking the anniversary by rediscovering or shooting new instant cameras and photos, and we’re challenging you to do the same. Dust off that Polaroid, Instax or any other instant photo and camera.

  • Rediscover an old camera and photo and share it with a story about it and the era it was taken in. Or, take a new instant photo.
  • Any subject is welcome: your family, your pet, a favorite spot around town or whatever you have in front of you.
  • Submit your photo in a comment reply below (take a photo of the hard copy if necessary). Tell us something about it (preferably at least 25 words), along with the camera and film you used.
  • Please submit by 12 p.m. PT / 3 p.m. ET / 8 p.m. UTC on Monday, Dec. 7, to be considered for inclusion in our honorary article. New posts after that are welcome for general discussion.
  • Please only submit up to two photos.

That’s it! We’ll pick our favorites and publish a set of them in an exclusive article on the DPReview homepage on Dec. 8. The article will also be mentioned in an upcoming newsletter.

Any instant camera counts, but if you manage to shoot with an original Model 95 between now and then, we can pretty much guarantee your submission will be highlighted in a special section.

Bring on the instant photos!

issues.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale, Report Details Limited Damage to Bayeux Tapestry Following Transport to the British Museum, and More: Morning Links for November 27, 2026
issues.summary: Here's what we're reading this morning.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale.
  • In a report, France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum.
  • A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for $1.97 million.

The Headlines

THE PRINCESS AND THE VENICE BIENNALE. Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s largest recurring art exhibition, which runs from April 8 to November 26, 2028, ARTnews reports. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority. She will be the first Arab curator of the Venice Biennale, and was selected upon the recommendation of its president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. In a statement, Al Qasimi said: “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco and the board for their confidence and trust.”

DAMAGE REPORT. A report made public yesterday by France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, Le Figaro reports. While the overall state of the 950-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened before the voyage. The loan of the fragile tapestry was heavily criticized for risking damage to the artifact, but was ultimately made possible in part thanks to carefully controlled ground transport that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations. The artifact has since become the hottest museum show in London, attracting long lines and selling out tickets within minutes.

The Digest

A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for £1.5 million ($1.97 million), and it is among several rediscovered paintings in an exhibition titled Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, open until December 18. [The Art Newspaper]

Two illuminated manuscripts and three crosses from the 15th century were returned from the American collection of Robert McCarthy to Ethiopia, as part of a unique new partnership between the Ethiopian Heritage Authority (EHA), the Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) and McCarthy. [The Voice]

Veruschka, the German supermodel, who became an iconic muse to the fashion, arts and cultural world of the 1960s and 70s, has died at 87. [WWD]

Neil Simmons, a sculptor whose famous marble piece depicting Margaret Thatcher was decapitated by a protester, has died at 73. [The Times of London]

A rare “Breast Bowl,” or “jatte-téton,” that belonged to French Queen Marie Antoinette and was used in her royal “pleasure dairy,” hammered in Paris for $3.23 million with fees, beating its high estimate of $2.19 million. [ARTnews]

The Princess of Wales, spent time at the Hugo Burge Foundation in Berwickshire, which supports the arts in the UK, and she spoke about the healing qualities of art-making with painter Siobhan McLaughlin, who makes her own pigment and works with stone and earth. [Times of London]

The Kicker

KANALIZING. On Saturday, Kanal or Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels’ nearly 10-acre “city-museum,” opens to the public, heralding the Belgian capital’s first major modern and contemporary art museum organized in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou. As ARTnews reported in September, the mega-project of free and ticketed spaces has been met with controversy over the course of its decade in the making, notably because of ongoing uncertainty about its financial survival, its cost, as well as its dependence on the Pompidou in Paris. Unless there is a political turnabout, Kanal’s publicly funded budget allocated by the Brussels-Capital Region is expected to drop from its current €28 million to €10 million by 2029, which is not enough to keep the project running, according to its leaders. This week, at a large press conference attended by ARTnews, Boris Dilliès, the minister-president of the Brussels region, was on the defensive about the initiative, he said he has faith, while admitting to heavy criticism. The story of Kanal’s rocky road to becoming reality has been widely reported in stories pegged to this week’s opening, but few have offered their thoughts on the 10 exhibitions debuting with it, and what it’s like to wander the vast halls of this new cultural phenomenon. ARTnews stayed on to more fully experience the myriad of shows open to previewing guests, which, over the course of two days, included artists and about 5,000 local schoolchildren. Watch this space to hear our take on Europe’s latest, highly ambitious cultural endeavor, including where it already shines, and where there is room – literally, a whole lot of space – for much more still to come.

issues.title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History
issues.summary: Since 2022, at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims have disappeared.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

issues.title: ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry

issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
Deadline: January 9, 2027.

Foundation for Contemporary ArtsEmergency Grants(U.S.)
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
Deadline: Rolling.

National Lottery Project Grants(U.K.)
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
Deadline: Rolling.

Black Artists Grant(U.K.)
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
Deadline: Rolling.

The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
Deadline: Rolling.

Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
Deadline: Rolling.

Residencies, Fellowships, & More

Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency (U.S.)
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.

Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence (International)
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.

2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists (Minnesota)
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Open AIR Residencies (International)
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28 (International)
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on a rolling basis.)
Deadline: December 11, 2026.

An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency (International)
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
Deadline: December 14, 2026.

Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28 (International)
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.

ren AiR (International)
ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.
Deadline: December 31, 2026.

Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship (International)
The Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship offers twelve weeks to slow down and deepen your practice within a creative community. The program will welcome 18 fellows and is open to senior BFA students, MFA students, postgraduates, and artists with comparable professional experience.
Deadline: January 7, 2027.

Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency (International)
The Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown grants 10 annual fellowships each to visual artists and writers for a seven-month residency that runs from October 1 to April 30. Visual arts fellows are provided with a private furnished apartment and a separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend, plus a $1,000 exit stipend to support relocation at the end of the fellowship. There is a $55 application fee until midday on December 1, then $65 until the opportunity closes.
Deadline: February 6, 2027.

Smithereen Farm Winter Residency (International)
Smithereen Farm offers affordable, shared, winter housing to farmers and agrarian-adjacent people and creatives. In the winter, its studio spaces and rooms in shared houses are generally rented for $350 per month, which includes access to common rooms, space for studio work or desks, utilities, fast Wi-Fi at Reversing Hall, a carpenter shop, sewing machines, video projection space, and access to the farm’s agricultural library.
Deadline: Rolling.

Jackrabbit Studios Residency (International)
Jackrabbit Studios is a creative sanctuary and retreat space in the Southern California High Desert that welcomes creatives, healing arts practitioners, and facilitators at any stage of practice to our five acres of secluded and sublime desert expanse to craft a residency tailored to your season of practice. Fees range from $450 per week to $2,000 per week, and pets are welcome for an additional fee.
Deadline: Rolling.

issues.title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
issues.summary: In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? The article Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos appeared first on Colossal
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is now available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

issues.summary: Jump onto Wade and Leta's sculptural design in Shanghai. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

issues.summary: British artist Rachel Whiteread has been commissioned to design the trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards, the annual awards for British and international music. The artist’s design will be presented to winners at the annual music awards ceremony, which will take place at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on February 27, 2027. Whiteread follows a succession of prominent artists and designers who have reimag
issues.author: Arun Kakar
issues.content_html:
British artist Rachel Whiteread has been commissioned to design the trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards, the annual awards for British and international music. The artist’s design will be presented to winners at the annual music awards ceremony, which will take place at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on February 27, 2027.

Whiteread follows a succession of prominent artists and designers who have reimagined the trophy, which takes its form from Britannia, the female personification of Britain. Previous designers include Tracey Emin, Peter Blake, Vivienne Westwood, Zaha Hadid, Rachel Jones, and Slawn.

For her design, Whiteread has drawn on her signature artistic approach of making negative space visible. Throughout her career, the artist has used materials such as plaster, resin, and concrete to cast the spaces within and around everyday objects, from furniture to entire buildings.

“I used the moti of the BRIT Award and tried to change it in some way,” Whiteread said in a statement. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music.”

In 1993, Whiteread became the first woman to win the Turner Prize, the same year she unveiled House (1993), a life-sized concrete cast of the interior of a Victorian terraced house in East London. In 1997, she became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale in a solo presentation.

Among her most significant public commissions is the Judenplatz Holocaust Memorial (2000) in Vienna, a concrete sculpture resembling an inverted library that commemorates the 65,000 Austrian Jews murdered in the Holocaust. She was awarded a damehood in 2019 for her services to art.

“Art and culture are under very real threat, so I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists—whether from music or the visual arts,” Whiteread added.

Last year’s trophy was designed by British fashion designer Matthew Williamson, and awards were won by musicians including Olivia Dean, Wolf Alice, and Sam Fender. The 2027 ceremony will be broadcast on ITV1 and ITVX in the U.K.

The board had appointed her on November 20 as director of the Visual Arts Department, after the biennale’s president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco recommended her. The 62nd International Art Exhibition will run from April 8 to November 26, 2028, with pr
issues.author: Josie Thaddeus-Johns
issues.content_html:
Hoor Al Qasimi, president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, will curate the 2028 Venice Biennale, La Biennale di Venezia announced on Thursday. The board had appointed her on November 20 as director of the Visual Arts Department, after the biennale’s president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco recommended her.

The 62nd International Art Exhibition will run from April 8 to November 26, 2028, with pre-opening days on April 5, 6, and 7. The title and theme of the exhibition are not yet announced.

Al Qasimi will take on the show two years after the 2026 edition, whose curator, Koyo Kouoh, was announced in December 2024. Kouoh died in May 2025, and the exhibition, "In Minor Keys," went ahead as planned under the team she had assembled.

Buttafuoco praised Al Qasimi's “rare ability to listen to places and their people.” He linked her “balance and composure” to mīzān, or inner harmony. “We entrust her with the 62nd International Art Exhibition with great confidence,” he said.

Al Qasimi said she first visited the Biennale's 50th edition in 2003, soon after she began curating the Sharjah Biennial, and called Venice “a critical space” for engaging with artists and curators. “I am honoured to have been invited to curate this exhibition,” she said, and thanked the board and Buttafuoco for their trust.

She has run the Sharjah Biennial since 2003 and founded the Sharjah Art Foundation in 2009. In 2023, she curated the biennial’s 15th edition, a show Okwui Enwezor conceived before his death in 2019. She was artistic director of the 2025 Aichi Triennale in Japan, the first curator from outside the country to lead it, and curated the 2026 Biennale of Sydney. She also curated the United Arab Emirates pavilion at the 2015 Venice Biennale.

ArtReview named her the most influential person in the art world on its 2024 Power 100 list, up from 36th place the year before. In 2025, she ranked third.
