issues.title: Why School Improvement Fails So Often
issues.summary: Meaningful change takes more than a good program or process. Here’s what helps educators solve problems together and make real progress. The post Why School Improvement Fails So Often first appeared on Cult of Pedagogy .
issues.author: Jennifer Gonzalez
issues.content_html:
Listen to the interview with Max Yurkofsky and Jal Mehta (transcript):

Sponsored by Brilliant and Listenwise

This page contains Bookshop.org links. When you make a purchase through these links, Cult of Pedagogy gets a small percentage of the sale at no extra cost to you. What’s the difference between Amazon and Bookshop.org?

Imagine this: You go to your first faculty meeting of the school year, and after a few welcoming remarks, your principal says, “This year, I just want you to keep doing what you’re doing. No changes.”

If that has ever happened anywhere, at any time, I’d love to hear about it, because as far as I can tell, every school for all of eternity has been trying to improve in some way. It’s part of our nature as humans to keep looking for ways to make things better. And schools are such complex ecosystems that there’s always going to be room for improvement.

These efforts vary in size and scope. Sometimes we’re just fine-tuning, on our own or with a group of colleagues, reflecting on our practice and making things a little better by degree. This kind of improvement tends to be pretty organic; we identify a need, make an adjustment, see how it goes, and keep refining.

Then there are the big, school-wide or district-wide efforts: a new curriculum, a branded leadership program, a whole new set of practices everyone is expected to start using. These often follow a familiar pattern. The initiative rolls out, everyone invests time and energy into it, and a few years later it’s replaced by something else. The churn can be exhausting.

Some of that is inevitable. We’re working with complex problems, the solutions aren’t always obvious, and there’s bound to be some trial and error. But a big reason these initiatives keep getting replaced is that they often don’t get the results people hoped for.

In recent years, schools have turned to improvement models that work differently. Rather than bringing in a prepackaged solution and asking teachers to just implement it, these frameworks give the people closest to the problem a process for studying it, trying possible solutions, seeing what happens, and adjusting from there. In theory, these approaches should get better results: The people doing the work have a hand in figuring out what needs to change, and the solution develops through a process of learning and adjustment.

But they don’t always work that way in practice. Sometimes the framework itself becomes just another thing handed down from above, another set of steps people are trained to follow, with more attention paid to following the process than to creating the conditions that make real problem-solving possible.

And yet, in some places, they really do work the way they should, leading to the kinds of improvements people were hoping for.

So what’s happening in the places where it’s working? What allows this kind of improvement work to actually become a way for people in schools to solve problems together, rather than just another program that eventually gets replaced?

Jal Mehta and Max Yurkofsky have an answer to that question. In their new book, A Chance to Solve Their Own Problems, they take a close look at how these kinds of problem-solving approaches play out in real schools and districts, examining why they succeed in some places and falter in others. Through that research, Mehta and Yurkofsky identified a set of conditions that seem to make the difference.

On the podcast, they explained what those conditions are, why so many well-intentioned improvement efforts fail to create those conditions, and what schools can do differently if they want improvement to become something people actually do, rather than another initiative they’re asked to implement. You can listen to the full interview above, read the full transcript here, or get the highlights below.

Why School Improvement Efforts Go Wrong

In their research, Mehta and Yurkofsky saw a few patterns that repeatedly got in the way of successful improvement efforts. Here are four of the most common.

The People Closest to the Problem Are Left Out

In many school improvement efforts, the problems to be solved are identified by people at the top, then handed down to educators to work on. Mehta argues that this leaves out the people who are in the best position to see what needs attention in the first place. “We’re not actually trusting the people who are closest to the ground to sort of say, ‘Hey, I have an inquiry question.’”

That trust matters because people are far more likely to engage in improvement work when it addresses a problem they actually experience. “Are you addressing a problem that teachers think that they have,” Mehta says, “or are you addressing a problem that you think teachers have? Because if ultimately this is a process that’s going to be taken up by educators, educators need to feel really connected to the problem.”

We Focus on People Instead of Systems

Schools often use data to identify which teachers, students, or teams are struggling, then focus their attention there. Yurkofsky argues that it’s more useful to look beyond the individual and examine the system around them.

“What’s more helpful is to go one layer deeper and think about, why is this particular teacher struggling with those standards? What part of the system is contributing to that outcome continuing to happen? . . . How is our instruction set up to support this teacher? How are we coaching and onboarding? What kinds of curriculum are we using? Where might that be falling short? When you address that, you’re not just helping that one teacher, but you’re trying to make an improvement for anyone who’s impacted by that system.”

Shifting our focus to systems can also make it safer for people to be honest about what isn’t working. “It kind of liberates folks to share where they’re having trouble, to say, hey, I’m struggling with this, our curriculum is actually not that strong here, the activities we’re using could be improved here.”

We Focus on Fidelity Instead of Learning

When schools adopt a new curriculum, program, or initiative, a lot of attention can go toward whether people are implementing it the way it was designed. Yurkofsky says this emphasis on fidelity can get in the way of something more important: learning from what happens when we actually put it into practice.

A program that wasn’t written for a specific context will never be perfect, he says, so making it work requires iteration. “The only way we’re going to make [it] better is by trying to do what we can, hollering when something’s not working, … and then adjusting and revising it so that it can be better tailored to our system.”

That means making a real commitment to trying something, but continuing to share where it falls short and adjusting it along the way. “Fidelity is never the point,” Yurkofsky says. “Fidelity means we’re not learning.” Instead, he prefers the term adaptive integration: “You’re integrating something adaptively into your system to make it work for your system. And that’s a continuous process.”

We Jump to Solutions Before Fully Understanding the Problem

Sometimes schools commit to a program, curriculum, or improvement method before they’ve fully defined the problem they’re trying to solve. Once that investment has been made, it’s easy to start shaping the problem around the solution instead of asking whether that solution is actually the right fit.

Mehta illustrates this with an example from a design thinking exercise he did with his students. Their task was to look for ways to improve the physical space in their education school, so they interviewed people who used different parts of the building to find out what was and wasn’t working. When they came back, one group reported that the school needed phone booths or small rooms where people could take Zoom calls. Mehta pointed out that they had already jumped from the problem to a solution: The actual problem was that people needed private spaces for Zoom calls.

Once the problem was framed that way, many more solutions became possible. “You want to define the problem in a way that opens up enough space that there are different solutions,” Mehta says, “ then see which one actually helps you move forward.”

The Building Blocks of Effective Improvement

So when school improvement initiatives do work, what does it look like? Across the different approaches they studied, Mehta and Yurkofsky found that three elements need to work together: mindsets, routines, and practices. Having one or two isn’t enough; successful improvement efforts depend on all three.

Mindsets

Mindsets are the beliefs and assumptions people bring to improvement work, and they can have a big impact on whether that work goes anywhere. Yurkofsky gives the example of a school trying to improve literacy: Even with a strong curriculum and good supports in place, progress will be difficult if teachers believe that teaching literacy isn’t part of their job.

“You might have secondary teachers who say, ‘It’s not my job to teach literacy. They should have learned this in elementary school,’” he says. If that mindset stays in place, simply giving teachers new practices or routines won’t be enough. For the work to be successful, the people involved need to believe in the problem they’re working on and see themselves as capable of helping to solve it.

Routines

Routines are the structures that allow educators to work together on a regular basis. These might include regularly looking at student work or other data together, observing one another’s classrooms, or meeting to decide how students should be grouped and regrouped.

Without these routines, improvement can become something people pursue on their own rather than something they learn about together. In one district Mehta studied, people were encouraged to experiment and innovate, but without clear routines, “people who were innovating felt like they were a little bit on an island and that they weren’t in common conversation with other people in the system.”

Practices

Practices are the actual strategies, methods, and resources educators use to make the improvement happen. If a school is working on literacy, for example, teachers need a clear picture of what good literacy instruction looks like, along with strong instructional materials and people with the expertise to help them use those materials well.

This piece can easily be overlooked when a school is focused on getting the improvement process right. Mehta points out that if you’re trying to make a significant change in instruction, “you’re not gonna, like, PDSA cycle your way” from one kind of teaching to another. At some point, he says, you need “some infusion of . . . disciplinary expertise.”

That expertise might already exist within the school, or it might need to come from somewhere else. The important thing is that educators have access to knowledge and practices that can actually help them solve the problem they’ve identified. As Mehta puts it, “the ideas have to come from somewhere.”

Cultivating the Right Environment for the Work

Having the right mindsets, routines, and practices isn’t enough on its own. For those pieces to actually work together, they need to exist in an environment that supports them. That means school and district leaders need to create and protect the conditions that allow people to take risks, learn from one another, and stay focused on meaningful improvement over time. Mehta and Yurkofsky point to three ways they can make that happen.

Protect Time and Space

“The first thing to recognize is that teachers are time-starved,” Mehta says. “There is no greater scarcity in our system than time for teachers.” Real improvement work requires time to step back from the immediate demands of getting ready for tomorrow and look for larger patterns in what’s happening. “Somebody with some authority has to protect the space and time to really do this kind of work.”

Make It Safe to Learn

Improvement also requires people to feel safe admitting when something isn’t working. “Learning requires trying things and sometimes failing,” Mehta says, but in some of the schools they studied, people felt that “it’s just not safe to fail here.”

If teachers are expected to have everything working perfectly, they can’t openly examine mistakes, experiment with new approaches, and learn from the results. As Mehta puts it, “That’s not the kind of environment that will produce learning.”

Make Improvement Part of a Larger Strategy

Finally, improvement methods shouldn’t become ends in themselves. Mehta says the most successful efforts are part of a larger strategy with “some direction and purpose” and the resources needed to achieve it. Instead of deciding, for example, “we’re gonna do rounds,” schools should start with a clear goal, then use improvement processes as one part of a larger plan for reaching it.

If all of this feels like a lot, that’s because it is. None of these changes can be made overnight, and trying to tackle all of them at once would probably be overwhelming. So where can a school leader start?

Yurkofsky suggested reframing the way we think about problems.

“We can’t learn if we’re not raising problems,” he says. “That’s what drives improvement.” In fact, he encourages leaders to “view problems as a gift.” When teachers are willing to say what isn’t working, it’s a sign of trust. And how leaders respond in those moments, with curiosity rather than defensiveness, can determine whether people will keep bringing problems forward.

Maybe that’s the simplest place to start: Make it safer for people to tell the truth about what isn’t working, listen carefully when they do, and give them a real chance to help solve the problems they see.

You can read more of Max Yurkofsky‘s writing about education on his Substack and explore Jal Mehta‘s work through Harvard’s Deeper Learning Institute, including its annual Deeper Learning Educator Camp.

issues.title: The Perfect Attendance Paradox: When Showing Up Isn’t Enough
issues.summary: Perfect attendance in school is often seen as the ultimate prize. You show up every single day, and you may get your name on the morning announcements or a perfect attendance award certificate at the end of the year assembly. It’s viewed as proof that a student is responsible and dedicated. But here is the... The post The Perfect Attendance Paradox: When Showing Up Isn’t Enough appeared first on T
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Perfect attendance in school is often seen as the ultimate prize. You show up every single day, and you may get your name on the morning announcements or a perfect attendance award certificate at the end of the year assembly. It’s viewed as proof that a student is responsible and dedicated.

But here is the problem: what if that message doesn’t tell the whole story? Some kids may push themselves to come to school even when they are sick for fear of losing this coveted award. Others may miss because of family issues or chronic health problems. Then there are the students who never miss a day but are not engaged at all.

The perfect attendance paradox challenges the belief that showing up to school is enough. Here we’ll take a look at why serving students is more than just tracking the days they show up.

The Pressure to Power Through

One of the most obvious downsides of perfect attendance is the pressure a student or their parent may put on them to power through not feeling well and coming to school. By staying home, a student may feel like they are being left out or may lose recognition as the kid with perfect attendance.

Think about the risks a student is taking by coming to school when they are sick. It also teaches them the wrong lesson. Instead of listening to their bodies and resting up, they think that their worth is tied to never missing a day of school. This mindset can follow them into adulthood and lead to unhealthy habits.

Overlooking Students with Chronic Health Needs

Imagine being a student with a chronic health condition, a disability, or a medical condition that makes it hard to attend school every day. Perfect attendance programs can unintentionally leave these students behind. These students may feel less valued than their classmates who don’t face the same obstacles as they do.

Let’s take the example of a student who has diabetes. They may do everything they can to stay engaged when they are in the classroom, but their efforts may go unnoticed because they don’t have a perfect attendance record. Instead of noticing their resilience, the focus lands on the days they are missing. This creates a space that feels unfair. The focus moves away from supporting a student and instead lands on enforcing a rule.

Family Realities That Interfere

Health issues are not the only thing that affects attendance. Family circumstances can also play a big role in whether a student attends school or not. Students who may have a death in the family, a crisis at home, unstable housing, or family responsibilities may miss school and be completely outside of their control. Perfect attendance awards and certificates rarely take these realities into account.

A child who may be late to school every day or misses class due to taking care of their siblings or because they have to work may be less committed to learning than other classmates. Yet the system values perfect attendance over responsibilities that may be out of a child’s control. Instead of making these students feel excluded, schools could support families in ways that address the root cause of their absences.

Missed Opportunities for Root Causes

If schools are focusing on perfect attendance records, they risk ignoring the root causes of why some students are not attending classes. Is a student getting bullied? Do they have a ride to school? Is their mental health keeping them from coming to class? Oftentimes, these issues get ignored, leaving larger issues unaddressed.

Instead of tallying absences, schools should consider looking at attendance patterns. Patterns can reveal a lot of information and can be a starting point for deeper conversations. Looking at the root causes of absences can help educators find meaningful solutions.

Attendance Does Not Equal Engagement

Perfect attendance programs focus on whether a student is in attendance, not how engaged they are when they are in the classroom. Being in the classroom doesn’t guarantee a child is engaged or motivated to learn. Some students may show up but struggle silently, while others may lack the support they need to thrive academically.

Awarding attendance based solely on whether a student is present overlooks building a sense of belonging or sparking curiosity. Attendance is just the starting point. The real question we should be asking is, are students connected and participating while they are here?

Rethinking How We Celebrate Attendance

Being in school regularly is important. It helps kids build routines and supports learning. But trying to get perfect attendance shouldn’t be the ultimate goal, and it doesn’t always send the right message. Consider celebrating effort, growth, and resilience. Students who have made progress in coming to school may receive the “improved attendance certificate.”

Students who have missed school because of an illness or struggle but stayed connected and kept learning may get the “resilience award.” When schools pair attendance with also taking care of themselves, it will show students that being present matters, but so does taking care of their well-being.

Practical Shifts Schools Can Make

Here are a few shifts schools can make to rethink the perfect attendance paradox.

  • Create recognition awards that move away from “perfect attendance” and towards growth and persistence.
  • Teach students that staying home when they are sick is a responsible choice.
  • Create flexible policies for students with chronic illness or unique challenges.
  • Look at attendance patterns as ways to get to the root cause of absences.
  • Partner with parents and guardians to address barriers to student absences.

Attendance is important, but it’s not the most important thing. By shifting focus from perfection to progress, schools are sending the message that effort and growth are more important than perfect attendance.

issues.title: Using Technology Tools for the Classroom to Build Equity
issues.summary: Classrooms today are heavily reliant on technology. From Chromebooks and iPads to interactive whiteboards, technology has become a part of everyday teaching and learning. As classrooms become more and more dependent on devices, the question many are asking is whether the shift is equitable for all students. Equity in a tech-driven classroom isn’t just about... The post Using Technology Tools for t
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Classrooms today are heavily reliant on technology. From Chromebooks and iPads to interactive whiteboards, technology has become a part of everyday teaching and learning. As classrooms become more and more dependent on devices, the question many are asking is whether the shift is equitable for all students.

Equity in a tech-driven classroom isn’t just about making sure that every child has a laptop; it’s ensuring that all students, regardless of their race, gender, ability, or circumstance, have access to technology. It also means being aware of the challenges that come with digital tools and finding ways to tackle those challenges.

Here are some key areas to focus on when creating a tech-driven classroom that supports all learners.

Addressing the Digital Divide

When you hear the term “digital divide,” you’re probably thinking about students who have access to technology and those who don’t. While this is mostly true, it’s actually a bit more complicated than that. A student may have a school-issued device, but may lack the internet, or some students may share a computer with their siblings or not have a quiet place to use it. The divide isn’t just about having the technology; it’s about whether the student can use it in a meaningful way to learn.

To address these challenges, school districts can partner with local internet providers to offer low-cost or even free internet services. Keep school libraries or student services open later to help students who need access to the internet. Or allow students to utilize WIFI hotspots on their school-issued devices.

To truly address the gap, consider sending out a survey to parents to find out what technology and internet services their child has access to. This can help you identify families that need extra support.

Training for Both Students and Teachers

It’s easy to assume that today’s students know how to use all digital devices and online tools. However, while most students are comfortable navigating social media, they may need more support with digital literacy and evaluating and formatting resources.

Teachers also may feel confident with some programs or trying new platforms, but others may need more support. Providing professional development that is specific to classroom needs, as well as giving teachers time to practice, is essential.

When both students and teachers receive training, technology becomes less of a challenge and more of a tool to support learning.

Meeting Diverse Learning Needs

One of the greatest uses of technology in the classroom is that it can support different learning styles and abilities. With the right digital tool, technology can meet the needs of all students. For example, students struggling with reading can use the Natural Reader tool that turns text to audio, while visual learners can use the Canva app to help organize and present information.

English Language Learners can be supported through apps like Google Translate, while students who learn better through hands-on learning can utilize apps like Kahoot. Technology can be a powerful tool that can help every student learn in a way that is best for them.

Watching Out for Algorithmic Bias

Many of the digital tools schools use rely on algorithms. These are systems that decide on what content a student sees or how their work is scored. While it’s a great time-saver for teachers, it can also create problems.

For example, predictive text may not recognize certain names or phrases, which can leave some students feeling left out, or some programs may grade one student more harshly than another based on a certain preferred writing style. Even some facial recognition software used for student attendance or security has been shown to be biased against darker skin tones.

This is why it’s so important not to solely rely on technology for all decision-making regarding students. Educators need to look closely at how these programs affect students and use the data along with their own personal judgment.

Ensuring All Students are Heard

One of the great things about technology is that it gives all students a platform to be heard. In traditional classrooms, students raise their hands when they have something to say, and the teacher takes turns allowing students to talk. Technology changes that. Collaborative tools like Google Docs make it easy for all students to contribute.

Podcasts and videos allow students to share their voices in creative ways that teachers would never see if they were to just raise their hands or write it down. When tools like these are intentionally used, they do more than just increase participation; they give students a voice and allow everyone to be part of the conversation.

Practical Steps for Teachers

Making technology work for every student can be a challenge, so here are a few practical steps that can help make a difference.

Review Student Resources

Survey students and parents to see what technology resources are accessible at home. Once you know the situation, you can connect families to after-school lab hours or internet hotspots.

Offer Student Choice

Not all students learn the same way. Offer students choices on how they learn best, using different formats, such as creating videos, using apps, etc. This flexibility levels the playing field for students.

Rotate Tools

Offer students different tools and platforms throughout the year so they can see what works best for their specific learning style.

Check for Bias

Think critically about the tools that you use and ask yourself if the program works well for all groups of students. Use the data from your apps as well as your own observations.

Encourage Student Feedback

Ask students for feedback on the tech they are using. Use this information to help guide your choices and adapt your instruction to meet the needs of all students.

Prioritize Balance

Equity means using technology in a meaningful way. Pair technology with offline activities to give all students the chance to shine.

Equity in a tech-driven classroom is not just about ensuring all students have access to technology, but also can use these tools in a way that supports learning. It’s about making sure that all students can thrive in a digital world.

issues.title: Memory Games for Kids in the Classroom
issues.summary: Memory plays an essential role in almost everything students do in the classroom. Whether it’s recalling math facts or following directions, having a strong memory makes learning easier. While rote memorization and traditional worksheets have their place, incorporating memory games for kids is a great way to help students strengthen their memory. Adding memory games... The post Memory Games for Ki
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Memory plays an essential role in almost everything students do in the classroom. Whether it’s recalling math facts or following directions, having a strong memory makes learning easier. While rote memorization and traditional worksheets have their place, incorporating memory games for kids is a great way to help students strengthen their memory.

Adding memory games for kids to your classroom routine can help students’ working memory in a fun and engaging way. The great thing about adding these games to your routine is that they not only help students build recall, but they also can be adjusted to fit any grade level.

The Games: Practical Activities to Strengthen Student Recall

  1. What’s on the Tray?

  • Best for: Grade 1-5
  • Activity: This classic memory game is a great warm-up activity. Place 10-15 objects on a tray (pencil, eraser, piece of candy, small toy, a block). Give students about one minute to study the tray, then cover it up with a cloth. Challenge students to write down as many objects as they can remember.
  • Variation: For younger students, you can have a printout of the objects they can circle, and for older students, you can add more objects to the tray.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens recall and attention to detail. Supports reading comprehension and observation skills.

  1. Memory Story Chain

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: This is a verbal game; one student begins a sentence such as, “I went to the park and saw a bird.” The next student repeats the sentence and adds on to it, “I went to the park and saw a bird and tripped over a rock.” This chain continues around the room until everyone has a turn, or someone messes up, and it starts again.
  • Tip: Instruct students to keep sentences short so it doesn’t become overwhelming.
  • Learning Outcome: Builds auditory memory, sequencing, and language skills. Also great for strengthening listening comprehension.

  1. Number Pattern Recall

  • Best for: Grades 3-8
  • Activity: Write a sequence of numbers on the board, then give students about 30 seconds to look at it, and then erase it. Ask students to write down the sequence of numbers from memory. Gradually increase the number of digits as students get better at it.
  • Variation: For older students or an extra challenge, include patterns (2,4,6,8…) and ask students to extend the sequence.
  • Learning Outcome: Builds memory, mental math, and pattern recognition.

  1. Sound Match Recall

  • Best for: Grades K-3
  • Activity: Challenge students to listen to simple sounds (bells, chimes, clapping), then have them match the sound that they hear.
  • Variation: Use instruments for younger students or create sound cards with written cues for older students.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens auditory memory.

  1. What’s Changed?

  • Best for: Grades K-4
  • Activity: Select a student volunteer and have them stand in front of the classroom for about 30 seconds. Instruct the student to leave the classroom and have them take off one thing (glasses, bracelets, or switch shoes). When they return, have the classmates try and figure out what has changed.
  • Learning Outcome: Sharpens observation skills and memory of visual details, which is essential to focus and attention.

  1. Recall Words

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Write 5-10 words on the board and give students one minute to study them. Erase the list and challenge students to write down as many words as they can remember. Connect words to topics you are studying or vocabulary words.
  • Variation: Challenge students to use the words in a sentence for a bonus.
  • Learning Outcome: Improves short-term memory and reinforces vocabulary.

  1. Memory Match-Up

  • Best for: Grades 1-6
  • Activity: This game may remind you of the classic concentration matching game. Create cards with vocabulary words on one side and their meaning on the back, or math facts on one side and the answers on the back. Instruct students to flip two cards at one time, trying to match a pair.
  • Variation: Have students create the cards.
  • Learning Outcome: Reinforces content while strengthening memory.

  1. Memory Map

  • Best for: Grades 6-12
  • Activity: Show students a simple map (neighborhood labeled, state with cities labeled). Give them a few minutes to study it. Take it away and challenge them to recreate it from memory by filling in as many details as possible.
  • Variation: Use diagrams (water cycle, plants, etc.)
  • Learning Outcome: Enhances spatial memory and visual recall.

  1. Picture Recall

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Display a picture for about 30 seconds. This can be a photograph, a poster, or even a classroom photo. After 30 seconds, cover it and challenge students to list everything they can remember.
  • Variation: Split students into teams and have them race to see which group can write down the most things in the picture.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens visual memory, attention to detail, and teamwork.

  1. The Name Game

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Start with one student and have them say their name along with an adjective that starts with the same letter as their name (Brave Brady, Joyful Jenny, Funny Frankie). The next student repeats the name before them, adding their own. By the end of the game, the class knows everyone’s name.
  • Learning Outcome: Boosts memory while encouraging peer bonding.

Why Memory Games are Important

A strong working memory helps students retain key concepts. It also helps them to follow directions and apply knowledge to new situations. Not to mention, they are fun! Who doesn’t like to play games?

By adding memory games for kids to your routine, you are helping students build the cognitive skills they need to focus and retain information.

issues.title: 5 Benefits of Science Journaling for Student Learning
issues.summary: Journaling has been around for decades and can be a powerful tool to enhance learning. Science journaling is more than just a place to jot down terms or lab results. It gives students the chance to express their understanding of key concepts in ways that worksheets or tests cannot. It also encourages them to explore... The post 5 Benefits of Science Journaling for Student Learning appeared first o
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Journaling has been around for decades and can be a powerful tool to enhance learning. Science journaling is more than just a place to jot down terms or lab results. It gives students the chance to express their understanding of key concepts in ways that worksheets or tests cannot. It also encourages them to explore ideas, sharpen observation skills, and think critically.

Here’s a closer look at the benefits that make science journaling worth your time.

Fosters Critical Thinking

Science is based on curiosity, such as asking questions, testing ideas, and making sense of evidence. Journaling allows students to think more deeply about what they are observing. Rather than simply writing down answers, they can use their journals to explain their observations, make connections, and reflect on what they’re learning.

For example, during a unit on plants, students might predict what happens during different stages of growth, record their observations of the changes, and then compare their predictions to what actually happens. They even use their journals to sketch, add diagrams, or add new information. By engaging with questions, students develop and use their problem-solving skills, which not only benefits them in science class but also throughout their lives.

Enhances Observation Skills

Observation skills are the foundation of science class. They help students notice details and gather the information and evidence needed to understand what they are learning. Journaling helps students pay attention and notice the small details they may not have seen if they weren’t writing them down.

Take the lesson mentioned earlier on plants. Instead of just writing down that the plant has sprouted, a science journal ensures students measure the height of the plant, the number of leaves it has, or how it changes over time. Writing down these details helps to sharpen their ability to notice patterns.

Improves Scientific Communication and Literacy

Having the ability to communicate clearly is another key component of science class. Journaling helps students practice using scientific vocabulary, writing explanations, and supporting data. This helps students with their scientific terminology as well as prepares them to write any formal reports or presentations.

For example, when upper elementary students are experimenting with different soils to help their plants grow, they can include key terms like “nutrients” and “retention” instead of saying the soil is “good” or “bad.” For middle and high school students, journaling can be paired with peer reviews to help with feedback and accuracy. This helps to build solid communication skills.

Promotes Creativity and Curiosity

Science journaling is not just about writing key terms and data. When students are encouraged to draw, sketch diagrams, and ask questions, it gives them a space to be curious and use their imagination. An elementary student may sketch a plant and label it, while a high school student may use their journal to draw the life cycle of a plant and explain the process. These approaches are creative and personal. They provide a place for students to imagine and explore without the fear of being graded or having the right answer.

Serving as an Authentic Form of Assessment

One of the best benefits of a science journal is using it as a means of assessment. While science journals typically are not graded, they can be a great resource for teachers to show a student’s learning process. Teachers can use the journal to see how students’ understanding has evolved. By tracking entries, teachers can see not only the students’ progress, but also the effectiveness of their own instruction.

Older students can also use their journals as portfolios. They can look back at them to reflect or use them as a study tool, reminding them of key terms they’ve forgotten about or previous experiments.

How to Bring Science Journaling into Your Classroom

To start integrating science journaling into your classroom, start small with just a few minutes at the end of each lesson. Be flexible and allow students to choose whether they want to record observations, write questions they may have, or sketch diagrams. Over time, students will begin to see that their journals are a valuable tool.

To get students into science journaling, consider using simple prompts like “What surprised you the most during the experiment?” or “What are you still curious about?” This will help students think beyond the data and facts and dive more into their curiosity.

It’s also important to note that students need to be aware that there is no “correct” way to use their journals. Based on their own learning style and preferences, each student’s journal will look different. Some students may have their notebooks filled with sketches and diagrams, while others may just have key terms and explanations.

Science journaling can be so much more than just recording information in a notebook; it can be a place where students can explore their creativity, sharpen their observation skills, and deepen their learning. By using this strategy in your classroom, you’re allowing students to learn ways to wonder, question, and explain concepts.

issues.title: 8 years after a deadly wildfire, young families are returning to this California school district
issues.summary: Rebuilding schools after a natural disaster also requires anticipating academic struggles.
issues.author: Erin Rode
issues.content_html:
Surveying the wreckage in the weeks after the Camp Fire — tens of thousands of people displaced, 85 percent of the town’s buildings destroyed and all but one campus of Paradise Unified School District damaged — it was hard for Jake Timm to imagine when or if the town’s population might recover. It could be 15 or 20 years before enough students returned to fill the schools in the Northern California community, thought Timm, the district’s director of facilities, maintenance and operations.

“I don’t think we knew exactly what we were stepping into,” said Timm. “Especially when we got up here after the fire to assess the damage, when part of the town was still smoldering.”

But after falling precipitously in the years after the 2018 wildfire, California’s deadliest on record, the district’s enrollment began to rebound. Today, it’s up to 1,817 students — still just 53 percent of enrollment pre-fire but enough for the district to speed up the timeline for rebuilding its second elementary school in Paradise to meet demand. This fall the school became the last of the district’s campuses to reopen post-fire, and there are already plans to add new classrooms. An average of just over 80 new students arrive each year.

School districts across the country are dealing with sharp enrollment declines brought about primarily because of falling birthrates, and California’s drop is among the most pronounced. But in Paradise, district officials are seeing an unexpected increase in younger students, as more young families relocate to the area, drawn by its relative affordability and new development.

Still, even as Paradise Unified School District completes the physical rebuilding process, lingering effects on academics show the long tail of post-disaster recovery.

Over a quarter of Paradise Unified’s students are chronically absent, a rate that’s more than 10 percentage points higher than the state average. Graduation rates and state test scores have also suffered.

That aligns with the growing body of research on the impact of wildfires and other disasters on education. In the short term, disasters and extreme weather can lead to increased absences and adverse learning outcomes. Longer term, research has linked experiencing a natural disaster to fewer years of total schooling completed, which in turn can correlate to reduced higher education outcomes and potential lifetime earnings.

And recovering from wildfires and other disasters is becoming an increasingly common challenge for school districts in California and elsewhere, as climate change drives more frequent extreme weather events and more severe disasters. Approximately 25 percent of public schools in the U.S. are located in census tracts designated as very high risk from at least one environmental hazard, including coastal flooding, hurricanes, heat waves, and wildfires, according to research from Brown University’s SustainableED initiative. In the coming years, more of them will face difficult questions about if, and how, to rebuild.

When Southern California’s Pasadena Unified School District — which faced declining enrollment for over a decade before the January 2025 Eaton Fire destroyed more than 9,000 buildings — weighed consolidating its schools earlier this year, families were outraged. Students who lost their homes in the fire said their still-standing schools offered stability and community; in a local editorial, one parent questioned why the district would consider closing schools so soon after the fire, when rebuilding might draw more families.

Read Next In the American West, wildfire comes for the suburbs Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

And after the 110-year-old King Kamehameha III Elementary School was destroyed in the August 2023 Maui wildfires, the majority of community members wanted the historic campus rebuilt in the same location. But state education officials said the campus couldn’t be rebuilt there because of limited space, flood risk and other factors, and instead chose a different site about a half-mile away and outside of the tsunami inundation zone.

Near Paradise, the tiny Golden Feather Union Elementary School District was also affected by the Camp Fire. The water system at the district’s only school, Concow Elementary, was severely damaged, and overall recovery in the more rural and lower-income community of Concow has been slower than in Paradise. The district relocated students to an elementary campus it had closed back in 2010, where they remain today. The new site is about 8 miles from Concow Elementary and closer to the town of Oroville, where many families relocated.

Only two Paradise Unified schools reopened in their original locations shortly after the fire: Pine Ridge Elementary and Cedarwood Elementary, both located in Magalia, which is just northeast of Paradise. Students from other schools spent the months after the fire scattered across Butte County. The junior high operated out of a hardware store, while the two high schools moved to independent study with drop-in hours at a mall. Paradise Elementary and Ponderosa Elementary, which was also destroyed in the fire, both used classrooms provided by other districts, each 20 miles away from Paradise.

Among the town’s boosters, whether Paradise would rebuild wasn’t really a question. The city started on a long-term recovery plan right after the fire and set goals of making the community more fire-resilient and welcoming to new and returning residents.

“My son was a freshman in high school here in town when this all happened, and he said, ‘I won’t go anywhere but Paradise,’” said Timm. “We’re a very strong-headed community, the ones of us that are left here.”

Two days before the fire, residents had passed a $61 million bond to modernize schools and complete a list of maintenance projects. “We passed the bond, we were all, ‘Woo-hoo,’ and then we’re all evacuating,” said Timm.

In April 2020, the school board approved a revised master plan that outlined how the bond money and other funds would rebuild and repair Paradise schools. Initially, that plan didn’t include rebuilding Paradise Elementary — at least not until more students returned.

The district initially combined the two destroyed elementary schools into a single school that opened in 2021. But by the 2024-25 school year, the elementary school population had grown from just over 300 to nearly 500 students — including 100 kindergartners.

Read Next What it takes to regrow a community after wildfire Kylie Mohr

Paradise previously was “more of a senior citizen town,” said Bill Sharrett, a member of the district’s Board of Trustees. But as older residents and others who lost homes in the fire chose not to — or couldn’t — rebuild, lots went up for sale, drawing young families who could buy bigger properties and newer homes for less than in nearby communities.

The city and the Paradise Ridge Chamber of Commerce launched marketingcampaigns focused on attracting new residents, which tout attainable homeownership, fire preparedness and brand-new schools.

And new families are buying in. By 2021, most new homes in Paradise were built for households moving there for the first time. Many new residents feel excited about participating in the recovery process and inhabiting a “blank slate,” according to one survey of over 30 people who moved to Paradise after the fire. They also see the area as less likely to burn after the Camp Fire destroyed so much vegetation, the survey found.

Meanwhile, the community is still visibly marked by the Camp Fire, especially for returning residents, who are quick to point out that rebuilt homes, now clearly visible along the road, used to be shrouded in thick trees. On the Paradise High School campus alone, over 1,000 trees were lost, according to Timm, and more than 97,200 total trees were removed from the burn scar.

Over half of the town’s land area is still vacant, and only about one-third of destroyed homes have been replaced. Still, the pace of rebuilding has ranked Paradise as California’s fastest-growing city in recent years. And school enrollment numbers are recovering even faster than overall population growth.

Nicole Reimer is among these new residents. She grew up in Paradise before moving to Chico, Butte County’s major job center. Last September, she moved back to be closer to family. Her two children now attend transitional kindergarten and first grade at the new Paradise Elementary.

“It was exciting to be able to come and be the first year at the school. It’s kind of a historical moment almost,” said Reimer.

Anna Logan also moved to Paradise from Chico after the fire, in part because her husband works in construction and in recent years his work has been concentrated on rebuilding in Paradise. “It’s a very close, tight-knit community, and we wanted to be part of the growth,” said Logan.

The family moved to town about four years ago, and this year Logan’s third-grade daughter moved to Paradise Elementary when it reopened.

Meanwhile, Paradise students who were in elementary school at the time of the fire are approaching college age — and grappling with how the fire marked their education.

Read Next Wildfire smoke engulfed their cities. Did it make their babies sick? Zoya Teirstein & Jess Davis

Kaydence Mosher, now 18, was a fifth grader at Ponderosa Elementary at the time of the fire, which destroyed both her school and her home. She enrolled in Cedarwood, an elementary school in nearby Magalia still standing after the fire, and struggled socially around classmates from that community who hadn’t lost their homes.

“It was very difficult during, like, a show-and-tell moment where I didn’t have anything that’s of significance to me besides my pets and my family,” she said. “It was something that I kept to myself, that I lost everything.”

Then, about a year later, the coronavirus closed schools again.

By her freshman year in 2022, she felt behind in school, which she “fully blames on my lack of education from the previous years.” She spent her junior and senior years alternating between a semester of in-person instruction at Paradise High School and then a semester from the district’s e-learning option, which she graduated from last year.

The district and other parts of Butte County have struggled overall with attendance and academic outcomes since the fire, although it can be difficult to pinpoint one specific cause, said Michelle Zevely, deputy superintendent of Butte County Office of Education.

In addition to a high rate of chronic absenteeism, graduation rates dipped in the years after the fire but have since crept back up to just above the state average. But the district has fallen further behind the state average on some academic indicators, including math, where Paradise students rank 65.9 points below proficient levels on standardized tests compared to 38.9 points below proficient for the state’s students overall.

“When we think about students losing their schools [in a wildfire], it’s one component of so many pieces of loss in their life at that time, including just the sense of normalcy,” said Lindsey Nenadal, an associate professor of child development at California State University, Chico, and a former Paradise Elementary student in the 1990s. Nenadal worked on a guide for how schools and nonprofit organizations can support youth after a wildfire.

Mosher, meanwhile, is now a student at Butte College and works for the local Boys & Girls Club, whose after-school programming brings her back to Paradise schools. Her own old elementary school was renamed from Ponderosa (an homage to the region’s once tree-filled landscape) to Paradise Ridge when it reopened, which felt like another erasure of the community she remembered.

She often works with students who moved to Paradise after the fire. Others weren’t born yet or are too young to remember — but sometimes they ask questions. “All they know is that it was really big and scary,” said Mosher.

Sign up for theHechinger newsletter.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline 8 years after a deadly wildfire, young families are returning to this California school district on Nov 28, 2026.

issues.title: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline
issues.summary: Outgoing Governor Gretchen Whitmer froze state permits for a proposal to replace an underwater segment of the aging pipeline.
issues.author: Vivian La
issues.content_html:
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer said Tuesday that she’s pausing both pending and issued state permits for the plan to replace a segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline beneath the Straits of Mackinac.

Whitmer said regulators at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE, need to answer questions about the full scope of the plan’s threats to the environment.

Those questions, according to Whitmer, were raised by a Michigan Supreme Court ruling this summer on a related Line 5 tunnel permit. Justices tossed out a permit issued by a separate state agency, saying their review of environmental harms was too narrow.

Line 5 has been transporting oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles between Ontario and Wisconsin since 1954. A 4-mile segment passes through the Straits of Mackinac, the narrow waterways that connect Lake Michigan to Lake Huron, separating Michigan’s Lower and Upper peninsulas. Sensitive coastal and wetlands habitats are found in the straits, and the area is sacred to Anishinaabe peoples, featuring prominently in their creation story and serving as burial grounds for their ancestors.

“I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water,” Whitmer, whose second and final term will end January 1, said in the announcement. “Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life.” The permit pause comes weeks after regulators in Wisconsin had been dealing with a spill on the portion of Line 5 that crosses that state.

It’s the latest setback for pipeline owner Enbridge Energy, which first proposed the plan to replace an aging portion of the pipeline with a new one, buried in a tunnel beneath the straits, almost a decade ago.

Enbridge maintains that the pipeline is safe. In a statement, spokesperson Ryan Duffy pointed to the company’s record of permit approvals — including the pending EGLE permit, which would have been a renewal of one it received in 2021.

Line 5 delivers the energy people depend on every day, Duffy said. “At Enbridge, we remain committed to that purpose and equally committed to safeguarding the Great Lakes,” he said.

The permit freeze is a win for Line 5 opponents who have protested for years against the tunnel project and have fought to shut down the entire pipeline.

“I think this is a really, really excellent step in the right direction,” said Ashley Rudzinski, climate and environment program director for the nonprofit Groundwork Center for Resilient Communities. “We’re seeing the Whitmer administration, finally, putting some real strength behind the words that she had already spoken.”

The Line 5 tunnel project has received federal approval, but with the remaining state permits in question, it’s unclear what its future looks like. Separately, Line 5 faces legal challenges from groups that have fought to shut down the entire pipeline for years, including the Whitmer administration.

Lawyers representing Michigan tribes in their fight to shut down Line 5 said they hope this momentum continues into the administration of Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, who, like Whitmer, is a Democrat. All 12 federally recognized tribes in Michigan oppose the pipeline.

“No matter who the governor is, it’s in all of our interests to keep the Great Lakes free of oil and to transition away from Line 5,” said Laura Berglan, senior attorney with the legal nonprofit Earthjustice, which represents the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. “We need to protect our shared resources and our tribal resources for the future.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.title: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
issues.summary: Consumer spending drives the U.S. economy, but voting with your dollars has its limits.
issues.author: Frida Garza
issues.content_html:
The headlines say what people already know: Food is getting more expensive. Consumers have been feeling an uptick in the overall price of both dining out and preparing meals at home this year, according to numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

And just in time for the holidays, things seem to be getting worse. The American Farm Bureau Federation found that the price of goods usually found in a Thanksgiving dinner increased this year for the first time since 2022. One economist told Bloomberg that Americans should expect food prices to keep creeping up into next year.

The high price of fuel, driven by the war in Iran, has contributed to the sticker shock Americans are feeling at the grocery store. Farmers need diesel to harvest, process, store, and transport produce and other crops from the field to retailers. Climate change, as well as El Niño spurring extreme weather globally, is also at play.

And yet, however flummoxed U.S. consumers may be about the high costs of living — a major driver of the midterms’ “blue wave” — consumer spending has only gone up. In fact, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of the U.S. gross domestic product, or GDP, and has driven the economy for some time, increased by 3.8 percent in the third quarter of this year.

At the same time, food systems are still responsible for somewhere between a quarter and a third of global greenhouse gas emissions. With food prices creeping up, it’s worth asking whatever happened to the idea of consumers as climate or environmental activists. The concept of “voting with your dollars” is often described as a meaningful tool for combating carbon-intensive practices in the food supply chain, such as deforestation. But do today’s shoppers still care about where their food comes from and how it’s grown when they’re worried about their supermarket bill (and all the other ones)?

The research is mixed. Some studies suggest that shoppers are comfortable springing for the more eco-friendly option, such as climate-proof wine, even if it costs a premium. But buyer motivations are complex: When it comes to food, even when consumers are paying for more sustainable options, some research shows that they’re more likely to have made that choice for other reasons, such as its taste or health claims.

If the question is whether consumers are motivated by sustainability or by price, the answer may be both, said Sandra Goldmark, a professor at the Columbia Climate School focused on circular economies. “People want a sustainable option. They want it to be healthy for their body and the planet,” said Goldmark. “And they have a price factor,” she added.

The practice of voting with your dollar “has limits,” said David Ortega, an agricultural economist and professor at Michigan State University. Such a practice works when “the sustainable option costs about the same [as the standard option] — less so when there’s a real premium and budgets are tight.”

Eggs, Ortega said, are a good example. When the price of eggs ballooned last year, higher-income households were more likely to be able to afford the more expensive, more sustainable options like cage-free eggs. “Most shoppers can’t, so they reach for the cheapest eggs or conventional products at the supermarket,” he said.

Additionally, the share of GDP that comes from consumer spending may overstate shoppers’ leverage in the food sector, said Ortega, as the bulk of that spending currently goes toward housing costs. What’s more, Ortega noted that the way cage-free eggs have become the industry standard had more to do with shifting state laws and retailer commitments than just “shoppers choosing to pay more.”

Read Next The American Dream wasn’t built for climate change Kate Yoder

Still, history shows that public pressure campaigns can still push companies to flip their supply chains. This works best when the campaigns are targeted and sustained — like when the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, a worker-led human rights group, led boycotts of Taco Bell across the U.S. over its supply chain agreements with tomato farms that mistreated workers. After four years, Taco Bell’s parent company agreed to only work with suppliers that are compliant with a code of conduct developed by farmworkers.

Companies gain something when they respond to consumer demands for change — they avoid reputational harm. In the early 2000s, outrage over a Greenpeace report on deforestation in the Amazon led to soy traders agreeing not to purchase soy from newly deforested lands. Although it fell apart earlier this year, that agreement lasted for nearly two decades — and it was considered widely successful.

The end of the Amazon soy moratorium presented a major blow to conservation efforts in Brazil — but that doesn’t mean consumers today have no say in where their food comes from. The growing influence of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement shows that these concerns matter more than ever to many households.

Real change may come when policy changes and public investment in sustainable food systems matches consumer desires, said Jody Kirchner, director of market insights at Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on the alternative protein economy. When the option that’s better for the environment and the planet costs more than the status quo, “shoppers can’t break that loop on their own,” Kirchner added. But maybe they can do it together.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability? on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.title: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
issues.summary: He’s the first Democrat elected to the Texas Railroad Commission since 1990. What can Jon Rosenthal accomplish?
issues.author: Celeste Guajardo
issues.content_html:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and KERA, a public media organization serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

This month’s midterm elections featured a previously unthinkable result in Texas: Democrats won every single statewide race in the Lone Star State. Some of those newly elected Democrats have become household names, like Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. But the list of Democratic victors also includes a centrist set to occupy a little-known office with outsize influence over the country’s oil and gas industry.

Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission against Republican Bo French, whose racist social media posts drew national bipartisan backlash. Rosenthal, the first Democrat elected to the commission since 1990, isn’t trying to usher in radical change, and his influence will be limited by the two Republicans already sitting on the commission. But he’s aiming to bring transparency, accountability, and a bigger budget to the regulatory board.

“Voters have delivered a mandate for a change,” said Rosenthal at a post-election press conference. “My top priority … is doubling the Railroad Commission’s budget. I believe the commission needs more resources to do the work they are [tasked] to do.”

The Railroad Commission was established in 1891 to regulate the rail industry. Over the years, the agency’s focus shifted to overseeing the state’s booming oil and gas industry. In 2024, Texas accounted for almost half of the country’s crude oil production. This fact makes the Railroad Commission one of the most powerful state-level regulatory agencies in the country. The commission generally takes a deregulatory approach and is widely considered friendly to the industry it regulates, especially with oil companies donating generously to the campaigns of commissioners they support.

Rosenthal describes himself as a “drill, baby, drill” Democrat, arguing a clean environment and good jobs can coexist. He worked in the oil and gas industry for over 25 years as a mechanical engineer. In 2018, he was elected to the Texas House of Representatives, representing parts of Houston, and was reelected three times before running for the Railroad Commission.

His victory likely has much to do with the unpopularity of his opponent. French, a former local Republican Party chair, prompted widespread criticism when he made a racist social media post in September about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. The race also drew attention to French’s previous offensive remarks, like posting a since-deleted online poll in 2025 asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose a bigger threat to the United States. Several prominent Republican politicians denounced French’s bigoted comments, which led to a fundraising boost for Rosenthal.

Rosenthal will join Republicans Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick on a commission that has recently attempted to shield itself from public scrutiny. In August, the agency adopted a new public participation policy that does not guarantee public comments at its monthly meetings. A public comment period is now included only if a commissioner requests it on the agenda.

Christian, a far-right conservative, championed the new policy, while the more moderate Craddick voted against it. Christian faced criticism from Democratic state lawmakers for not showing up to a legislative hearing that would have included discussion of that decision, and he used profanity when defending the vote from Commission Shift, a nonprofit watchdog group.

In a social media post, Rosenthal called the new policy “shameful.” He campaigned on making hearings more accessible. Virginia Palacios, the executive director of Commission Shift, expressed optimism that the new commissioner can help increase transparency.

“It’s a possibility that if we have someone like Jon Rosenthal who ran his campaign on the idea that open meetings should be open, you could potentially have two commissioners that would vote for open public meeting policy,” she said.

Rosenthal could occasionally team up with Craddick to neutralize Christian on other policy questions as well. “There are times when [Craddick and Christian] vote differently on some of these permit … or policy approvals, even though the vast majority of their votes tend to be the same,” Palacios explained.

Palacios does not expect “drastic changes” with Rosenthal’s election, but she does believe there will be greater opportunity for public engagement. According to his campaign website, Rosenthal wants the commission to hire regional community liaisons to make it easier for Texans to offer input.

“We’ve recently heard of communities that requested the Railroad Commission to go out and visit them in person … and the Railroad Commission denied those requests,” said Palacios. “We would hope to see that this new sitting commissioner would be more responsive to the public and try to show up in person where others haven’t.”

Apart from improving transparency and community relations, Rosenthal’s biggest ambition is to double the agency’s biennial budget from approximately $500 million to $1 billion. He argues this will help “turbo-charge” the plugging of orphaned oil wells, those that have been inactive for at least 12 months, and zombie wells, those whose plugs are failing.

Thousands of these wells across Texas are leaking methane , a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to trapping heat in the atmosphere. The Railroad Commission plugged over 2,000 orphaned wells during its last fiscal year — a record number — but still ended up with more of them at the end of the year than they started off with. That’s because a large number of low-producing and inactive wells become orphaned.

“We want to enable this agency to further ramp up well-plugging operations … but also get proactive in helping to prevent future wells from being orphaned,” said Rosenthal at his post-election press conference. “If we don’t go after what causes this … we’re going to be chasing our tail forever.”

Notably, Rosenthal’s ambition to double the commission’s budget is not something the board can accomplish on its own. The Texas Legislature would have to approve such a budget increase, and Governor-elect Hinojosa would have to sign it. Democrats will have a majority in the Texas House come January, and although the Texas Senate remains in Republican hands, the Democratic lieutenant governor-elect will wield significant power in the upper chamber.

Hinojosa and the new class of Democratic state lawmakers haven’t spoken publicly on whether they’ll prioritize the Railroad Commission’s budget, but Rosenthal expressed confidence that his history as a state representative will come in handy as he seeks more money for the agency’s operations.

“In this new environment, I might be one of the Railroad Commission’s more valuable players,” said Rosenthal at the press conference. “Because some … lobbyists or agency personnel are not used to walking into a Legislature controlled by the Democrats.” Meanwhile, “I know how to talk to Democrats because I am one. And it will be my job to help educate my former colleagues about how important this is.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.summary: In mid-October, Lander Van Tricht received a message from a woman. Instances of public engagement like these were exactly what […]
issues.author: Abhishyant Kidangoor
issues.content_html: In mid-October, Lander Van Tricht received a message from a woman. She had visited a glacier when she was 10 years old and, according to a tool that Van Tricht had developed, that same glacier was now expected to go extinct in less than 40 years. Instances of public engagement like these were exactly what Van Tricht says he wished for while developing the tool. “What I really hoped was that scientific results are shared beyond the academic world,” Van Tricht, a postdoctoral researcher at ETH Zürich and Vrije Universiteit in Brussels, told Mongabay in a video interview. The Global Glacier Extinction Explorer is an interactive platform that allows people to zoom in on glaciers on a map and find out how they’re faring in the face of global warming. The tool is based on the findings from a 2026 study, published in the journal Nature, that looked at the disappearance of individual glaciers. The findings from the study, on which Van Tricht was the lead author, are dire. They show that even in a world where warming is limited to 1.5° Celsius (2.7° Fahrenheit) above the pre-industrial baseline, half of Earth’s glaciers will be lost. “I was surprised by how fast everything is happening,” Van Tricht says. He adds he hopes the tool will help translate the science to the general public, and also help communities around the world prepare for scenarios where glaciers go extinct. “Communities, cities and people have to prepare themselves for a future without glaciers,…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.summary: International Jaguar Day has been marked every Nov. 29 since 2018, to raise awareness of the threats faced by the Americas’ biggest cats and the efforts to protect them. issues.author: Mongabay.com
issues.content_html: International Jaguar Day has been marked every Nov. 29 since 2018, to raise awareness of the threats faced by the Americas’ biggest cats and the efforts to protect them. Jaguars (Panthera onca) were once found across some 19 million square kilometers (7.3 million square miles), from what is today the southwestern U.S. to central Argentina. But their range has shrunk by more than half, and today spans about 9 million km² (3.5 million mi²). Most jaguars live in a stronghold ranging from the Amazon Rainforest and stretching into the Pantanal wetlands, the Chaco dry forest and the Llanos grasslands of Colombia and Venezuela. However, recent sightings and reports from outside these core areas highlight that many jaguars are still holding on at the edges of their historical territory. For example, in Brazil’s eastern Atlantic Forest and dry Caatinga, fewer than 250 adult jaguars survive, and researchers have begun banking their genes in an effort to save them through cloning. At the northern edge of the species’ range, a male nicknamed Cinco showed up on camera footage in southern Arizona state in late 2025, becoming the fifth jaguar recorded there in 15 years. Meanwhile, in Honduras’s Sierra del Merendón, a mountain range in the country’s northwest, camera traps recorded a young male at an altitude of about 2,200 meters (7,200 feet) for the first time in a decade. “The fact that they’re able to travel through these high elevation areas also shows how resilient they are,” Allison Devlin, who directs the…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.summary: KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled […]
issues.author: Ata Ullah
issues.content_html: KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled persecution eight years ago. Here, amid the world’s largest refugee settlement with over 1.1 million refugees, space is tight and evergreen forests have paid the price. But families are combining NGO-funded farming projects with traditional Rohingya agroecology techniques to create agroforestry plots that are restoring land while helping refugees become self-sufficient in response to deep cuts in international food aid. “I feel so bad here as I have no land, but I am keeping my ancestors’ heritage alive. Growing these crops reminds me of the life we had in Myanmar. Here, life is difficult,” said Amina Khatun, a 58-year-old refugee living in Camp 1W, a sector of the sprawling settlement. Before the 2017 influx, Kutupalong refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar was a tropical evergreen forest, dominated by Dipterocarpus species, and sanctuary for endangered Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). To make way for the massive refugee settlements, the Bangladeshi government allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of protected forest land, and refugees and aid agencies cleared the vegetation to build shelters and provide firewood. Over 1,500 hectares of forest were cleared in total. The rain, with nowhere to soak in, ran straight down the slopes. Landslides became…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.summary: Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry. “We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents […]
issues.author: Elodie Toto
issues.content_html: Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry. “We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents people living in the working-class neighborhood, told Mongabay on the phone. The civil case, filed in October, is the latest in a series of actions taken against Metssa Congo, a foundry that opened in the neighborhood in 2013.The facility recycled, among other things, car batteries, extracting lead and turning it into lead bars for export. The plant is part of the Metssa Group, an industrial metals trading company based in the United Arab Emirates. The battery recycling process can pose serious health risks. According to the WHO, lead can be released in the form of fumes, particles and dust at every stage of the process, from draining and dismantling to smelting and refining. Environmental contamination from recycling can be substantial, exposing workers and nearby communities to significant levels of lead, the health agency says on its website. According to Traore Ndembi, residents of Vindoulou soon experienced this reality first-hand, complaining about toxic fumes coming from the plant. issues.title: Rose Bowl officials warn fans to arrive early for UCLA-USC showdown
issues.summary: The UCLA Bruins take on the USC Trojans in what should be a packed Rose Bowl on Saturday in Pasadena.
issues.content_html:
When the UCLA Bruins take on the USC Trojans in the 2026 edition of the Victory Bell, the Rose Bowl, the rivalry's host venue this season, will be filled to near capacity. Emphasizing the importance of this contest, the fans will be out in full force for what should be one of the most anticipated games in program history.

The crowd is expected to be so massive that stadium officials are asking fans to show up early to avoid issues as they enter the iconic venue.

"PSA: With a massive, near-sellout crowd expected for UCLA-USC on Saturday at the Rose Bowl, stadium officials are encouraging fans to arrive extra early to avoid congestion and maximize their game-day experience," wrote the California Post's Ben Bolch.

The Rose Bowl will remove all tarps on the north side of the stadium, with fans expected to fill out those seats, which could see attendance numbers hit 70,000 fans.

If UCLA wins, they punch a ticket to the Big Ten title game and have one foot in the door for a College Football Playoff spot. If USC wins, their playoff dreams remain alive. This game is a likely playoff eliminator for the Bruins, while a loss for USC will end their playoff ambitions and could see the team part ways with head coach Lincoln Riley.

This article originally appeared on UCLA Wire: Rose Bowl officials warn fans to arrive early for UCLA-USC showdown

issues.title: UCLA's Wayne Knight close to securing rushing touchdown crown
issues.summary: The UCLA Bruins running back could go down as one of the best ever if he continues to score touchdowns
issues.content_html:
The UCLA Bruins enter the final game of the 2026 regular season with everything on the line, as a win over the USC Trojans will get them into the Big Ten Championship Game and would place them on the verge of qualification for the College Football Playoffs.

One of the biggest reasons for their success is running back Wayne Knight. The All-American running back transferred to Westwood from James Madison, helping Bob Chesney and company maintain their success through their transition from program to program. Entering the final week of the regular season, Knight leads the country in rushing touchdowns.

Scoring touchdowns left, right, and Knight 😤 pic.twitter.com/otug2GKd2o

— PFF College (@PFF_College) November 26, 2026

The senior will lead the offensive charge on Saturday as the Bruins look to retake the Liberty Bell. Knight has 875 rushing yards so far this season and remains an underrated threat in the passing game, especially in the red zone, with 195 receiving yards and two touchdowns.

If UCLA wins, Knight will have led the program to their first-ever 11-win season.
