issues.content_html:
Marketers need to know how to track brand visibility in AI search because search has changed. AI-generated answers now show up earlier in the discovery journey, often before a traditional search result. In 2025, nearly a third of Gen Z consumers (31%) defaulted to chatbots or AI to find information online, according to HubSpot’s 2025 AI Trends for Marketers report, and it’s clear that AI search is growing — rapidly. In 2026, Google reported that AI Mode has over one billion monthly users, and queries have doubled every quarter since launch.

Failure to place brands in AI Overviews (AIO) or within AI search tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Claude is a failure to meet prospective buyers where they’re searching. That’s harmful to audience connection, conversion, and ultimately, revenue. Brands that show up in AI search are the ones that audiences consider. The ones that don’t simply disappear from the conversation, with no ranking position, no impression count, and no obvious way to tell.

This article breaks down what brand visibility is, how to track brand visibility in AI search, the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that marketers need to pay attention to, and the best tools to support AI visibility tracking.

Table of Contents

  • What is AI search and brand visibility?
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search Right Now.
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with the Right KPIs and Cadence
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with a Repeatable System
  • How to Improve AI Search Visibility and Fix Inaccurate Answers
  • Best Tools to Track Brand Visibility In AI Search
  • How To Connect AI Visibility To Content And Pipeline
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Tracking AI Search Visibility
  • Tracking AI visibility isn’t optional anymore — search changed.

What is AI search and brand visibility?

AI search refers to search that takes place on AI platforms, like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Google’s AI Overviews. There are many more, and AI search platforms are growing. Unlike Google or other search engines, which return a list of links to click through, AI search engines answer questions directly. Those answers are lifted or paraphrased from trusted sources.

Brand visibility in AI search relates to the impressions that brands get within AI platforms. A brand mentioned or cited in AI in an answer has visibility. Brand visibility in AI search includes mentions, citations, sentiment, and accuracy. The goal is for brands to increase their visibility. They want to be cited and mentioned often, accurately, and favorably.

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search Right Now

The most basic way to check AI brand visibility is manually: Open ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Copilot. Ask the same set of questions across each one. Then, record whether the brand appears, how it’s described, and whether competitors show up instead. This is an easy starting point. But, it breaks down quickly.

A single spot check only captures one moment in time. That result reflects one user’s search history and personalization, not any broader trend. When multiplied across several platforms and hundreds to thousands of prompt variations, manual tracking becomes a task that nobody has time to maintain.

HubSpot ran an experiment testing hundreds of queries across AI chatbots, search engines, and social platforms. The experiment found that AI tools were noticeably weaker at handling specific, niche information, like details about a particular local business, than they were at answering broad or general questions. This is why prompts need to be tracked consistently — and ideally automatically. No one can infer how a platform or brand performs across the board just because it performs well in one prompt, particularly if that prompt is broad and general.

This is where dedicated tools come in.

Rather than replaying the same prompts by hand, tools built for AI brand tracking run them automatically, on a schedule, across multiple engines at once, then organize the results into a usable format, such as:

  • Which prompts triggered a mention.
  • Which sources got cited.
  • How sentiment trended over time.

Different tools approach brand visibility measurement in different ways; some focus narrowly on mention frequency, others build out fuller scoring models across multiple dimensions.

HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader is one example. The grader gives marketers a baseline read on AI visibility, and what it provides for free is pretty amazing. Here’s what the start of the report looks like.

While tools like AI Search Grader are excellent, there are limitations.

AI Search Grader captures a baseline read; it doesn’t track improvements or declines in trends. Ideally, most marketing teams will move from a one-time snapshot to ongoing tracking, so that they can adapt marketing strategy based on data.

Tools like HubSpot AEO provide ongoing tracking and data related to performance in AI search tools. It monitors brand mentions, citations, and sentiment across AI platforms continuously. With continuous tracking, marketing teams can see how efforts and campaigns have impacted visibility.

Here’s a look at a citations report, showing a brand’s domain performance versus competitors:

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with the Right KPIs and Cadence

Switching between tools or KPIs will only provide inconsistent and confusing results. No two tools report the same numbers. All a tool can provide is a third-party overview of what’s happening with a brand’s visibility, and none of them are completely accurate.

Feedback from a tool should be treated as a directive, not absolute truth. What marketers are looking for are trends in the data, and that comes from consistent tracking using the same tool and the same metrics.

Now that caveat is out there, let’s look at KPIs:

Brand Mention Rate

Brand mention rate measures how often a brand appears in AI-generated answers. It’s a foundational metric; it’s calculated by dividing the number of AI answers that mention the brand by the total number of answers analyzed across a set of tracked prompts. A low mention rate indicates that AI platforms rarely surface the brand at all.

Here’s an example of a brand mention in ChatGPT. The mention of the brand is there, but there’s no clickable link:

Mentions and citations are not the same thing: an AI platform might mention a brand by name without linking to anything it owns, or it might cite a third-party review site instead of the brand’s own content.

Citation Rate

Citation rate measures how often AI answers link to or reference brand-owned sources. Tracking citation rates separately shows which domains and pages are actually earning a reference inside AI answers, which points directly to the content that needs to be built or strengthened.

Here’s an example of a brand citation in AIO. There’s an actual link, and if clicked, the user will visit the website of the cited source (in this case, HubSpot):

Source

Pro tip: To support citation rates, marketers can track actual clicks to the website from AI sources. I include this metric on all of my client reports. It reports to stakeholders that we’re getting cited, but also that these citations are turning into valuable actions for the business. Kyle Rushton-McGregor has a guide on how to track AI visits in GA4.

Sentiment and Accuracy

Sentiment measures how AI platforms describe a brand. It’s typically scored on a scale from negative to positive.

Accuracy is related to sentiment.

Marketers want their brands to appear accurately in AI.

A negative sentiment might not be a bad thing if it’s accurate. For example, if an AI platform describes a brand as ‘expensive compared to competitors’ and that brand has a premium price point, the sentiment reads as negative, but the description is accurate, and the brand probably wants to defer searchers looking for a cheap solution.

That said, marketers must manage brand sentiment and ensure that sentiment is overall positive. Brand sentiment can teach marketers about things customers are unhappy about. If marketing comes across a repeated negative sentiment, then they can share information with customer success or product development to try to change that narrative.

Share of Voice

Share of voice measures how often AI search platforms mention a brand compared to competitors across the same set of prompts. It’s important because if marketers look at their brand in isolation, the mention rate might look great, but comparing share of voice against competitors reveals the wider opportunities and potential.

A low share of voice relative to competitors shows where the gaps are and what brands need to do to close the gap.

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with a Repeatable System

A repeatable system turns AI brand tracking from ad hoc checks into a data-driven marketing approach. With this approach, marketing teams can make strategic decisions based on data and trends, leading them to meaningful solutions that improve a brand’s visibility in AI search.

The following five steps give marketing and AEO (also called GEO) teams a framework to set up once and run on an ongoing basis.

1. Run a baseline visibility check.

Before setting up ongoing tracking, it helps to research and establish a starting point. Otherwise, marketing is creating a tracking system based mostly on feeling.

AI Search Grader helps measure brand visibility in AI search, scoring how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity currently describe a brand across sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position.

Marketers can use tools like AI Search Grader to get a big-picture overview of how their brand performs. They’ll start to build a picture of how the brand sentiment looks and where there might be opportunities.

And it’s free. So, marketing can run AI Search Grader for competitors to build a mental map of the wider AI search landscape. The beauty of AI Search Grader is that there are no limits, so marketing teams can use this free tool as much as they like. Every search in AI Search Grader builds research, curiosity, and insights that can be carried into the final plan.

2. Write consistent, structured prompts.

AI search tracking requires consistent prompts across multiple AI platforms. Like switching tools or KPIs, switching prompt wording between checks makes it impossible to tell whether a shift in results reflects a change in visibility or just a different question.

Marketing teams should write out the exact prompt list in advance, document it, and reuse the same wording every time a check runs. This is a lot easier when working with a tool, because the tools will categorize prompts and maintain the exact prompt over time, but if working manually, marketers need to manage it.

Tools like AI Search Grader can inspire prompt selection, but marketers don’t have to stop there. Existing keyword research is a great starting point, especially long-tail keywords in Google Search Console (GSC). Specifically, keywords that include problems and solutions for certain audiences, for example, “How do I solve [problem] in my [company]” or “how to fix [problem] in your forties.” Many keywords are already phrased as questions, or close enough that it’s not a leap to see how they’d translate into a query on an AI platform.

Talking directly to customers helps, too. Sales and customer success teams often have a good sense of the exact language prospects use when researching a purchase. If sales or customer support have a good relationship, they could even ask customers if they’d share their own AI chat history, which will surface real prompts marketing teams would not have thought to write themselves.

Important note: Asking for chat history could be invasive. This ask can only work if there’s a customer relationship that’s already been built.

Once marketing has the prompts locked down, it’s time to decide where to track them and how to manage them.

3. Map the core AI platforms and build a prompt taxonomy.

Core AI platforms include ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, and Google AI Overviews. However, most brands don’t need to track every single platform, which is good news for brands working with tighter budgets. Some tools charge a base fee for ChatGPT tracking, with add-on costs for each additional AI platform.

How to Decide Which Platforms to Track

For one of my clients, who had a limited budget, we focused solely on ChatGPT. We used a marketing report to decide which platforms to pay the most attention to. I tracked clicks from all the core platforms, as well as a few others. Clicks from ChatGPT far exceeded all other core AI platforms, with over 87.18% of total AI visits coming from ChatGPT. Claude and Gemini were next with 4.49% each, then Copilot at 2.56% and Perplexity at 1.28%.

Important note: Some AEO tools don’t charge to track data from additional AI tools, so check what the tools allow users to track as part of a free or paid package, and what costs extra.

HubSpot’s AEO tracks brand visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity as part of the same $50-a-month package, with no extra charge to add the second or third platform once a prompt allowance is purchased. Other tools, like Profound.ai, charge $99/month to track ChatGPT, then $399/month to track three platforms.

For my client, HubSpot AEO is ideal because it’s affordable and tracks the major AI platform they need — ChatGPT.

Once marketing has the platforms to track, marketers need a prompt taxonomy (a way of organizing prompts). The prompt taxonomy should include brand, competitor, category, task-based, and comparison prompts.

Check out the example below.

4. Set a tracking cadence and automate ongoing monitoring.

With prompts written, categorized, and platforms selected, the last piece is deciding how often to check them.

Cadence matters as much as the metrics themselves. Weekly reviews support baseline AI brand monitoring, giving marketing and SEO teams a steady read on trends without demanding daily attention. Daily checks make sense during active optimization sprints — testing content changes, responding to a citation gap, or catching a sentiment issue that needs a fast fix.

Tools like HubSpot AEO automate this cadence, running the same prompt set across engines on a schedule and organizing the results so nobody has to manually replay the same questions week after week.

5. Route visibility data into CRM and content workflows.

If marketing can route visibility data into CRM and content workflows, AI visibility can turn from a vanity metric into a revenue input. With this, AI reporting becomes highly engaging to stakeholders, who ultimately care about revenue because it shows how AI search performance and pipeline are integrated.

This ‌routing is where most standalone AEO tools fall short entirely. The fact that HubSpot AEO is built on a CRM gives it an incredible advantage.

With an integrated CRM and AI tool, visibility data becomes a system where it gets routed to the people and workflows that can respond to it.

Here’s how:

  • HubSpot Smart CRM stores AI visibility properties, prompt clusters, and dashboard data, keeping visibility metrics in the same system as the rest of a brand’s customer and campaign data instead of siloed in a separate tool.
  • HubSpot Content Hub turns visibility gaps into content briefs and refreshes, so a low mention rate on a topic becomes an assignment rather than a stat that nobody acts on.
  • HubSpot Marketing Hub connects AI visibility efforts to campaign reporting and attribution, closing the loop between AI search visibility and the pipeline and revenue outcomes leadership actually cares about.

How to Improve AI Search Visibility and Fix Inaccurate Answers

Once marketing tracks prompts and performance, it will reveal gaps, and once gaps are identified, marketing can construct a data-driven plan to close them.

The next section details some best practices to address common visibility and accuracy issues.

Strengthen entity consistency across the web.

AI platforms build their understanding of a brand from many sources at once, such as:

  • The company website.
  • Review sites.
  • Social profiles.
  • Directories.
  • Press mentions.

AI platforms pull information from across the web to create one synthesized answer. The best thing marketing can do is control the controllable, and, where possible, ensure that information is consistent and accurate.

For example, be consistent with the brand’s name, description, location, and core offering. Naturally, marketing can’t control everything, like a bad or incorrect review, but marketing combats negative sentiments with the truth. Plus, marketing can work with product teams or customer success to identify issues and prompt resolution.

Ultimately, AI platforms have a hard time confirming what’s correct if multiple versions of a narrative exist. That increases the odds of an inaccurate or inconsistent mention.

Build content that earns citations.

Page structure has been a topic in the world of search for many years. We all know that structuring pages well, with titles, headings, and body text, is good, but it’s possible to take things a step further for AI search.

For example, marketing can get super-specific about audiences and problems, creating pages around the exact problems buyers are having.

Answering questions directly, providing solutions, and backing them with claims with concrete details and data all make a page easier for AI platforms to lift from and cite.

For more information about writing for AI engines, read: How to Write Content that Generative AI Search Engines Will Cite, According to Experts

Correct inaccurate AI answers.

Inaccurate AI answers should trigger content updates, correction requests, and follow-up monitoring, especially if the inaccuracy is on owned media, like the brand’s website or Google Business Profile.

Tip: If you’re not sure where a piece of information has come from, because AI hasn’t cited anything, try searching for the information in Google and see what ranks. Look at your own website for inaccuracies. Let’s say an AI platform has cited your brand’s package as costing $69, but this price is over two years old, search in Google “site:yourwebsite.com $69.” This search would look for mentions of “$69” on your website. It’s possible the price is listed somewhere, like an old blog.

Expand presence across multiple channels.

AI platforms draw on a wide mix of sources, so a brand’s visibility is rarely built from its website alone. Active participation in industry discussions, consistent responses to reviews and feedback, and a presence across the platforms where a brand’s category gets discussed all contribute to how AI models perceive and describe a brand. The broader and more consistent that footprint, the more material AI platforms have to draw an accurate, favorable picture from.

Monitor for recurring issues.

A single inaccurate answer might be a one-off. The same issue appearing across multiple prompts or platforms is a pattern worth escalating. When negative sentiment or a factual error keeps showing up, it is worth routing that finding beyond marketing — into product, customer success, or support — since the underlying cause is often something those teams are better positioned to fix.

Best Tools to Track Brand Visibility In AI Search

The four tools below cover the full range of what a marketing team needs, from foundational SEO work to dedicated AEO tracking.

Marketing Hub SEO Marketing Software

This article focuses a lot on AEO and AI visibility, but AEO is not separate from SEO. Regardless of how many people search in AI, traditional SEO is still critical, more popular than AI search tools, and impactful on the sources that are mentioned and cited in AI tools.

Therefore, SEO tools are still a must.

Marketing Hub’s SEO tools lay the groundwork on which AI visibility depends‌.

Source

HubSpot’s SEO tools include an audit that surfaces prioritized fixes for on-site issues like broken links, missing meta descriptions, and thin content, then groups related content into topic clusters designed to build topical authority around core subjects rather than isolated keywords. It also pulls keyword data directly from Google Search Console, so marketing teams can see which queries are already driving organic traffic and which ones represent gaps worth closing.

What I like: Having data in one place is efficient. HubSpot allows integrations with Google Search Console, so data can be managed and checked from one place. The SEO recommendations are easy to use, written in plain English, and even have impact scores (high, medium, and low). The system names the person responsible for the fix, meaning tasks that keep SEO flowing are easily delegated.

HubSpot AEO

Source

HubSpot AEO is undoubtedly the core tool for ongoing AI visibility tracking. It provides marketers with four key capabilities:

  • A brand visibility score that tracks how often a brand appears across a set of tracked prompts.
  • Prompt-level tracking that shows the exact response each engine gave for each question.
  • Citation analysis that breaks down which domains and content types are earning references.
  • Competitor share of voice that shows how a brand’s mention rate stacks up against named competitors on the same prompts.

HubSpot AEO suggests a starting prompt set based on a brand’s industry, competitors, and business context, which can then be edited or expanded by the marketing humans in the team. Everything is trackable across major AI platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and results roll up into a dashboard that tracks visibility over time rather than showing a single static score.

Finally, recommendations turn the data into specific next actions:

  • Create a new page or update an existing one
  • Publish a LinkedIn post
  • Reach out to a third-party site for a mention.

One limitation worth flagging: Claude and Copilot are not currently tracked. For brands where either platform sends a meaningful share of AI referral traffic, that’s a real coverage gap to weigh before committing.

What I like: The recommendations and AI visibility tracking within HubSpot are absolutely useful and critical to marketing, but the real differentiator, in my opinion, is the CRM. Most AEO tools operate as a standalone dashboard, disconnected from what actually happens after a brand shows up in an AI answer.

HubSpot AEO doesn’t have that problem because it’s built on top of HubSpot CRM. The connection between marketing performance and sales matters more than ever. A visibility score sitting in isolation is just a vanity metric. What pays bills is knowing whether a mention, a citation, or a jump in share of voice actually turned into a contact, a deal, or revenue.

HubSpot AI Search Grader (free)

AI Search Grader is the place to start if marketing is new to AI brand visibility or tracking AI in any form.

AI Search Grader runs a one-time scored assessment of how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity currently characterize a brand, scoring five dimensions out of a 100-point total:

  • Sentiment (40 points): The overall tone AI models use when describing a brand, evaluated across three layers: general tone, how that tone shifts across different topics and use cases, and the credibility of the sources shaping that characterization.
  • Presence Quality (20 points): How substantively AI platforms discuss the brand (“mention depth”), the quality of the sources feeding that understanding, and the overall richness of data available about the brand.
  • Brand Recognition (20 points): How widely the brand is recognized within AI training data itself.
  • Share of Voice (10 points): How often the brand is mentioned relative to competitors within the same set of responses.
  • Market Position (10 points): How the brand is positioned competitively compared to others in its category, based on how AI platforms describe its standing in the market.

The scoring is weighted toward sentiment because how a brand is described tends to matter more to buyers (and therefore marketing and sales) than simply whether it’s mentioned at all.

AI Search Grader runs against pre-set queries automatically, without requiring the marketer to write any prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini responses draw on model training data, while Perplexity’s results come from live web search, since Perplexity works differently under the hood. The tool also benchmarks a brand’s score against competitors, so the output reads more like a competitive snapshot than an isolated report card.

The trade-off is exactly what its name suggests: it’s a grader, not a tracker.

AI Search Grader captures one moment and doesn’t retain history or show trend lines, so running it repeatedly over time won’t build the kind of longitudinal data a brand needs to prove whether a strategy is working.

What I like: I always start with AI Search Grader for a benchmark, and I use it in pitches to show a brand exactly where it stands before any investment is made. It’s also my go-to when I want a read on competitors, but I can’t justify paying to track brand mentions in AI, like a secondary competitor that I’m curious about but don’t need tracked with full accuracy over time.

HubSpot AI Search Sensor

Source

HubSpot AI Search Sensor takes a different angle from the other three tools on this list.

It doesn’t track a specific brand at all.

It’s a free public dashboard built from anonymized HubSpot customer data, tracking industry-wide shifts in AI search behavior through three views:

  • AI-Referred Traffic Trends shows aggregate weekly traffic from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, useful for checking whether a brand’s own traffic dip reflects something brand-specific or a broader industry pattern.
  • AI Visibility Benchmarks by Industry shows visibility and citation share for a handful of representative brands across ten industries, giving a sense of what a “good” score looks like in a given category.
  • Citation Share Trends breaks down which content types (blog posts, product pages, listicles, and more) and which source channels (owned, earned, review sites, affiliate, and more) are earning citations, and how that mix is shifting week over week.

There’s also a daily Answer Engine Volatility Tracker, scoring how much answer engine behavior is shifting on a given day, from Calm through Extreme.

What I like: Marketing teams can use this broad data alongside their own AEO data: if a brand’s visibility score drops on a day when the volatility tracker also spikes, that points to a model update or algorithm shift rather than a brand-specific problem.

How to Connect AI Visibility to Content And Pipeline

AI visibility data should shape the content calendar directly. A low mention rate on a category prompt signals a content gap worth filling. A low citation rate on an existing page suggests the page needs restructuring, not replacing. A competitor winning share of voice on a comparison prompt means there’s a comparison page worth building.

This shifts content strategy from “what ranks” to “what gets cited and recommended.” The two overlap but aren’t identical — a page can rank well in Google and still get ignored by an AI platform if it doesn’t answer the question directly enough to lift and cite.

Connecting that data to pipeline is what makes the work defensible.

When visibility metrics sit in HubSpot’s CRM and marketing tools rather than a standalone dashboard, a content brief generated from a visibility gap can be tracked through to the campaign it supported and the deals that followed. That’s the difference between reporting a visibility score and reporting what the score was worth.

Frequently Asked Questions About Tracking AI Search Visibility

Tracking AI visibility isn’t optional anymore — search changed.

Failing to track AI visibility in 2026 and beyond is a failure to keep up with search, serve clients, and keep your brand at the top of prospective buyers’ minds.

For anyone starting from zero, HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader remains the fastest way to get a baseline read on where a brand currently stands, and HubSpot AEO is the natural next step once that baseline is set and marketing are ready to track mentions, citations, and sentiment across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, all while feeding directly into the same CRM already running a brand’s marketing and sales data.

In my own client work, I’ve been tracking AI visibility for a year or two, and things are trending up for every single client, even those in niche B2B. For me, the major benefit of starting now is that brands have a benchmark and can see clearly how the search landscape is changing and how it’s impacting brand and visibility.

This is an experimental serie
issues.author: Fabricio Teixeira
issues.content_html:
Essays from designers in the middle of the AI storm.

Most conversations about AI in design are about how. How other teams are prototyping with it, how AI is making them more productive, what it’s doing to user research, and what’s happening to the much-chased “design process.” Humankind goes the other way, and looks at what’s shifting inside the people doing the work.

This is an experimental series written by designers who are living through this like everyone else, struggling, learning, and unlearning along the way. In a way, it’s also an evolution of the State of UX we used to publish here on the UX Collective at the end of every year. But now, looking inward.

We don’t have answers. What we have is a growing list of questions, and they’re probably the best summary of what the series is about:

  • Who are we becoming while the tools make us faster and more sure of ourselves?
  • What do we want to keep doing slowly, even when we don’t have to?
  • What do we owe each other, and the things we make?
  • What do we lose when nothing is hard anymore, and would we notice?
  • Where do we still go to not know?

We’re still figuring most of this out.

Humankind

issues.title: The end of the interface is the beginning of design
issues.summary: AI already builds interfaces without a designer pushing a single pixel. Soon, users will not even see the interfaces we design: their agents will. Our brains are being rewired. Our ways of working are reinvented every day. Lik
issues.author: Patrizia Bertini
issues.content_html:
AI already builds interfaces without a designer pushing a single pixel. Soon, users will not even see the interfaces we design: their agents will. Design can burn out like a meteor, or go back to what it was always meant to be: solving problems.

Design is changing. DesignOps is changing.
Our role as humans is changing. Our brains are being rewired.

Our ways of working are reinvented every day. Like modern-day Penelopes, we weave during the day, and at night the speed of technology unpicks our work. And we start again.

We hang on to what we know, to our familiar ways of thinking and doing. We read books. We search for answers in the wisdom of the past, in what we learnt and in what we have been taught.

We live, not rhetorically but factually, in unprecedented times.

What we knew about the world has collapsed.
For around 300,000 years, our species lived by hunting and gathering. Farming arrived about 12,000 years ago. The factory, about 250 years ago.

Then the timeline collapsed. ARPANET sent its first message in 1969. The web reached the public in the early 1990s. Generative AI reached everyone’s desk in the 2020s. Today we talk about agents, and about recursive self-improvement: AI that helps build better AI. Since 2020, the computing power used to train frontier language models has grown about five times every year ( Epoch AI).

We have compressed into decades, and now into years, a change that once took millennia. The world as we know it is already an old model.

And yet many of us still believe that a profession and a specialised education will save us. That they will grant us a social and economic position, as they did for centuries. This is one of the biggest mistakes professionals can make today. Closer to home, it is the mistake designers, DesignOps professionals and digital product workers are making right now.

Design is going to be transformed in ways we are not preparing for.

How did design lose its thinking?

To understand where design is headed, we need to take a look back.

In 2008, Tim Brown of IDEO brought design thinking to a business audience in Harvard Business Review, and a year later Roger Martin made its business case: design as the art of solving problems, centred on people and driven by experiments. Boutique agencies boomed, large corporations bought them, and J ohn Maeda tracked the wave in his first Design in Tech Report in 2015. I was part of that wave myself.

And this is how we moved from design thinking into design doing: the focus on outputs, pixels, layouts, expression. Shape more than substance.

It did not happen overnight. In my view, design doing took hold in the late 2010s and early 2020s, when three things happened at the same time.

  • The tool became the studio. Figma launched in 2016, in the browser, built for teams, and within a few years design lived inside it. In 2022, Adobe agreed to buy it for $20 billion, a deal later abandoned under regulatory pressure. When one tool becomes the place where design happens, the work starts to look like … the tool.
  • Value got a number. In 2018, McKinsey’s The Business Value of Design found that the top design performers had 32 percentage points higher revenue growth than their peers over five years. The report argued for design as a leadership practice. Many organisations heard something simpler: more design, more growth. So they scaled what was easiest to count: the output.
  • Design joined the sprint. Designers moved into product squads and agile delivery. Design became a lane in the backlog, measured by tickets closed and screens shipped.

Then came the correction. From 2022, waves of tech layoffs, and design teams were not spared. In November 2022, ChatGPT arrived. The craft we had spent a decade optimising for was about to become the cheapest thing in the room.

Meanwhile, delivery had grown complex. In the 1990s, a webmaster could build an HTML page alone. Today, a digital experience needs many moving parts: content writing, video editing, visual design, branding, user experience, front-end coding, content management systems, back ends, repositories, design systems. Design had moved from thinking to doing, so it needed an operational layer to enable and orchestrate all of it.
This is where DesignOps entered the scene.

But when the output seems so easy to replicate, design that has lost its thinking becomes a “ pixel pusher.” And a “ pixel pusher” allows non-designers to question the value of design: if product managers know the problem (once core to design thinking) and can do “pixels”, where does design stand?

If someone learnt design for delivery, they may struggle to see the complexity and the beauty of design thinking. It had little to do with pixels and Figma. It was a mindset.

Some of us (older) design thinkers, who learnt design from those early papers and experiments, can see the direction. I, for one, see it clearly.

What did a stylesheet teach me twenty years ago?

When I was working in accessibility in the early 2000s, one thing excited me more than anything else.

A person with a visual impairment could simply override all the beautification of the UI with a simple stylesheet of their own. It forced the site to render the way they needed it: more contrast, larger fonts.

It was limited, of course. But it was an option.

The designer gave the content and its structure. The user decided the form. Hold on to that image, because it is coming back.

What happens when nobody sees the interface?

Fast forward to today. AI tools are building interfaces on demand, via prompts, with designers not pushing a single pixel. But the tools are not focusing on the problem as much as design did at the beginning.

Meanwhile, design systems have organised our assets, components, patterns and libraries. The next step is an ontological layer, where each element carries meaning, relationships and intention. Simply put, an ontology is a map of what things are and how they relate to each other.

In an ontology, a button stops being a blue rectangle. It becomes “the action that confirms a payment”, with rules about when it appears, for whom, and what it must never hide.

Think of it as three steps in what designers define:

  • Pixels: how each screen looks.
  • Components: the reusable parts, and how they fit together.
  • Meaning: what each element is, what it relates to, and why it exists.

At the same time, devices keep multiplying: phones, laptops, smartwatches, glasses. We access information through sound, images, visuals and text, in very different contexts.

This is where the stylesheet comes back. In the same spirit as that user’s stylesheet, agentic assistants will use the layer of meaning to give each of us a personal, dynamic experience, based on incredibly detailed context: the device, the situation, our preferences, the specific need of the moment.

We won’t have any control over the interface. It may be conversational, graphical, agentic, or something we have no name for yet.

What does this mean in practice? Users won’t necessarily see and experience what designers do and see. They will have agents doing the interface for them.

John Maeda, whose reports once tracked design’s rise in tech, now says it himself. His 2026 Design in Tech Report is titled “From UX to AX”: from user experience to agentic experience. In his view, designers move from building screens to judging what AI produces.

I would go one step deeper. Before we judge what machines make, we need to shape what machines know.

Designers will not define interfaces. They will define relationships and variations, and work on ontologies and semantics, so experiences can be executed in the most fluid and personal way possible. Returning, again, to solving problems instead of focusing on pixels.

In one sentence: design is going to move into a space that is new and old at the same time. Its job is to define the information structures that will enable users to create their own experiences.

What does this mean for DesignOps?

While layoffs are growing, we are watching and wondering how to stay relevant. And we are not focusing on the direction of the change.

At the frontier of AI, the work is moving from surface to structure. Yann LeCun left Meta to build world models: AI that learns how the world works, not only how words follow each other. World models are not ontologies, but they point the same way, and ontologies are design’s version of that step, as I see it. Meanwhile, many designers still talk about Figma and pixels, and ignore the direction.

That, of course, impacts design operations. We have lost ground and traction because we look backwards and expect to solve problems that are fading away. We fail to be ahead of the curve, and to tell our partners, leaders and designers the hard truth: much of what we know may be outdated within months.

And there is one more force pulling design back towards meaning, one that few designers have noticed yet: the law. That adds another layer of complexity and urgency and whoich is the subject of my next article.

DesignOps can be a meteor: bright for a moment, then gone.

Or we can embrace ambiguity and uncertainty, and use our design mindset, our process focus and our problem-solving skills to enable and empower this transformation.

There is an incredible role to be played. But it requires acknowledging that what we have been doing cannot simply be scaled, or done better. The context around us has shifted so much.

There is one detail of Penelope’s story we often forget. She was weaving a burial shroud, and she was the one who unpicked it every night. She did it by choice, to buy time, because she knew exactly what she was waiting for.

We are not unpicking our own work. Technology does it for us, in an era where machines realise the product without any human hand on the loom. And the world we are waiting for, the one where a profession and a title kept us safe, is not coming home.

Our value is not in what we have done in the past, but in what we can do today and tomorrow, which is radically different and extremely necessary.

Penelope knew what she was waiting for.

Do we?

Thank you for reading. I write about design, systems and the human side of AI, and I work with organisations that want to get it right. You’ll find more of my work at PatriziaBertini.com.

Author’s Note: The ideas, the research and the arguments in this piece are human — mine. I used AI to help shape the form and structure, then went through every line myself. The images are AI-generated.

issues.title: The Pain in You and the God in You: Carl Jung on the Relationship Between Psychological Suffering and Creativity

issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
When AI first began colonizing language — which is still our best instrument for bridging the abyss between us, a container for thought and feeling that shapes the contents — I asked chatGPT to compose a poem about a solar eclipse in the style of Walt Whitman. It returned a ledger of cliches in rhymed couplets. Getting the form wrong — Whitman did not rhyme — seemed like an easy correction by a line of code. Getting poetry itself wrong was the interesting question, the question that gets at the heart of why we make poems (or paintings or novels or songs) — a question fundamentally about what it means to be human.

I asked an elder poet friend why she thought chatGPT rang hollow where Whitman could compact infinities of feeling in a single image, could unseat the soul in a word.

She paused, then said: “Because AI hasn’t suffered.”

On the one hand, this echoes a dangerous myth: the archetype of the tortured genius handed down to us by the Romantics, who, cornered in their time and place, in a century of bloody revolutions, deadly epidemics, and punitive Puritanical norms, must have needed to believe that their suffering — those lives of poverty and privation, those ill-fated exercises in projection mistaken for love, all those premature deaths — was a fair price to pay for such creative volcanicity.

On the other hand, this is reality: Art is the music we make from the bewildered cry of being alive — sometimes a cry of exultant astonishment, but often a cry of devastation at the collision between our wishes and the will of the world. Every artist’s art is their coping mechanism for what they are living through — the longings, the heartbreaks, the triumphs, the wars within and without. It is these painful convolutions of the psyche — which used to be termed neurosis at the dawn of modern psychotherapy, and which we may simply call suffering — that reveal us to ourselves, and it is out of these revelations that we create anything capable of touching other lives, that contact we call art.

Our power and our freedom lie in learning to neither negate our suffering nor romanticize it but to harness its catalytic power as a current passing through us to jolt us alive, then passing on and down into the ground of being.

No one has refuted the myth of the tortured genius without negating the fact and fertility of suffering more pointedly than Carl Jung (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who thought deeply about the nature of creativity.

In 1943, a scholar of Kierkegaard asked Jung’s opinion of the relationship between “psychological problems” and creative genius. With an eye to Kierkegaard’s gift for letting his anxiety fuel rather than hinder his creativity, Jung declares him a “whole” person and not “a jangling hither and dither of displeasing fragmentary souls,” and writes:

True creative genius does not let itself be spoilt by analysis, but is freed from the impediments and distortions of a neurosis. Neurosis does not produce art. It is uncreative and inimical to life. It is failure and bungling. But the moderns mistake morbidity for creative birth — part of the general lunacy of our time.

It is, of course, an unanswerable question what an artist would have created if he had not been neurotic. Nietzsche’s syphilitic infection undoubtedly exerted a strongly neuroticizing influence on his life. But one could imagine a sound Nietzsche possessed of creative power without hypertension — something like Goethe. He would have written much the same as he did, but less strident, less shrill — i.e., less German — more restrained, more responsible, more reasonable and reverent.

A century before Alain de Botton offered his assuring perspective on the importance of breakdowns, Jung weighs what makes suffering generative or degenerative:

Neurosis is a justified doubt in oneself and continually poses the ultimate question of trust in man and in God. Doubt is creative if it is answered by deeds, and so is neurosis if it exonerates itself as having been a phase — a crisis which is pathological only when chronic. Neurosis is a protracted crisis degenerated into a habit, the daily catastrophe ready for use.

Jung considers the advice he would have given Kierkegaard about how to orient to his suffering, which was the raw material of his philosophical writings:

It doesn’t matter what you say, but what it says in you. To it you must address your answers. God is straightaway with you and is the voice within you. You have to have it out with that voice.

Couple with a forgotten young poet’s extraordinary letter to Emily Dickinson about how to bear your suffering, then revisit Kierkegaard himself on the value of despair.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. issues.title: Nobel-Winning Biochemist Gerty Cori on the Single Most Important Element of a Meaningful Life
issues.summary: We call it “the long run,” life, and spend it trying to understand what keeps us running, trying to run toward, to see the true goal through all the false trophies promised us by the merchants of approval and acclaim. What keeps the body running is glycogen — the essential fuel of muscles. What keeps the soul running is a substance we must each synthesize out of the mystery we are. There are two k
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
We call it “the long run,” life, and spend it trying to understand what keeps us running, trying to run toward, to see the true goal through all the false trophies promised us by the merchants of approval and acclaim.

What keeps the body running is glycogen — the essential fuel of muscles. What keeps the soul running is a substance we must each synthesize out of the mystery we are. There are two kinds of running the soul does: running away from — our fears, our past, our mistakes — and running toward. The first kind is easier, for it is reflexive. The second kind is life’s most difficult, most rewarding work — to discover the track on which to run and its most authentic destination, to synthesize out of our dreams and desires the glycogen of a strong animating spirit to fuel the long run of a purposeful, substantive, meaningful life.

Czech biochemist Gerty Cori (August 15, 1896–October 26, 1957) — the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in science, for her discovery of how glycogen works in the body — articulated with poetic precision the animating spirit of a purposeful life when she appeared on Edward R. Murrow’s popular radio series This I Believe in the late summer of 1952:

The love for and dedication to one’s work seems to me the basis for happiness… For a [scientist], the unforgotten moments of life are those rare ones, which come after years of plodding work, when the veil over nature’s secret seems suddenly to lift and when what was dark and chaotic appears in a clear and beautiful light and pattern.

This clarity of vision is not singular to science. Pulsating beneath Cori’s words is the insistence that a meaningful life — one that makes the long run worthy of running — springs from devotion to work, any work, that parts the veil of meaninglessness to reveal a glimpse of some greater truth. The most alive people I know, whether they make postulates or poems, furniture or film, are animated by such devotion. It is the best antidote to the existential catatonia of cynicism and despair that leaves people too petrified to live up to and into their gifts. Cori observes:

I believe that art and science are the glories of the human mind… Contemplation of the great human achievements through the ages is helpful to me in moments of despair and doubt. Human folly then seems less important… I believe that cynicism and despair and the straitjacket into which totalitarian systems try to force the human mind are inimical to first rate achievements in art and science.

Complement with pioneering astrophysicist Maria Mitchell on the art of knowing what to do with your life, then revisit psychologist Carl R. Rogers on the three elements of the good life and Victor Frankl on the secret to success.

issues.title: Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader
issues.summary: "A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H.P. Lovecraft advised aspiring writers. We’ve already seen that reading is a learned skill and an optimizable technique, and that non-reading is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a good reader?

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life. He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected Lectures on Literature (public library), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:

  1. The reader should belong to a book club.
  2. The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
  3. The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
  4. The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
  5. The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
  6. The reader should be a budding author.
  7. The reader should have imagination.
  8. The reader should have memory.
  9. The reader should have a dictionary.
  10. The reader should have some artistic sense.

The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Complement with Mark Twain’s humorous list of the fourteen types of readers and Nabokov on the three qualities a great storyteller must have.

issues.title: US roads have a ‘big’ problem
issues.summary: Bigger vehicles tend to produce more emissions, contribute to road deterioration, and limit street parking capacity.
issues.author: Brendan Cosgrove
issues.content_html:
The vehicles on the road in the US today are much bigger than they used to be. While that’s great for hauling mulch on the weekends, it’s contributing to gridlock during the week.

Size-mic shift: According to Bloomberg, SUVs and pickup trucks accounted for less than 25% of new car sales in the 1970s. By 2025, it was closer to 80%. Physically, they tend to take up a lot more room on the road than sedans. Plus, they’re heavier, so drivers need more space to brake.

More is less: From 1995 to 2019, SUVs in Minnesota’s Twin Cities were responsible for a 9.5% decrease in the maximum number of vehicles that could move through a lane in an hour, according to research published in the journal Transportmetrica A: Transport Science.

It’s more than traffic, though

Bigger vehicles tend to produce more emissions, contribute to road deterioration, and limit street parking capacity. They’re also the leading cause of thinking you’re about to hit your roof on the ceiling of the parking garage.

The safety factor: Bigger cars are a little safer for the people inside them, but they’re much less safe for everyone else. According to a New York Times analysis this year, bigger cars caused about 200 to 400 more pedestrian deaths per year than would have occurred if cars had not grown larger over the past 25 years, because larger vehicles can have bigger blind spots and higher hoods that can worsen injuries.—BC

issues.title: The most obvious fix for traffic doesn’t actually work
issues.summary: Traffic typically ends up just as bad, or worse, after highways are expanded.
issues.author: Molly Liebergall
issues.content_html:
On paper, it seems like a straightforward solution: If a main road gets too busy, widen it or add another street nearby. It sounds great, kind of like how printing more money to plug the national debt sounds great. But the problem is, it often doesn’t curb traffic.

Spending billions of dollars on new lanes…or connector roads can reduce traffic on busy roadways in the short term. But in the long term, research shows that congestion (and the air pollution it causes) typically ends up just as bad, or worse, than it was before the expansions:

  • For every 1% increase in road capacity, the number of cars on the road will also increase by 1% in metropolitan areas, according to a 2009 study by economists from the University of Toronto.
  • Case in point: Rush-hour traffic briefly subsided but ultimately rebounded after Los Angeles spent $1 billion to widen I-405, one of the most bottlenecked corridors in the US.
  • Sometimes, an expansion backfires. Peak travel times increased on one of the world’s widest highways, Houston’s 26-lane Katy Freeway, within five years of the throughway’s last expansion in 2008.

This is called “induced demand,” a phenomenon where adding more road capacity encourages people to drive more. Yogi Berra might call it everybody going to that street because it’s so empty. Some transportation officials reject this idea, claiming instead that widening roads helps “manage new travel demand,” as Texas officials characterized the Katy expansion.

It’s not the only downside

Road expansions over the past 30 years have pushed more than 200,000 people from their homes, with Black and Latino areas disproportionately impacted, the LA Times reported in 2021.

If not more roads, then what? As your friend who bikes everywhere would probably tell you, other ways to reduce road congestion include investing in more public transit and pedestrian infrastructure. To pay for more of those projects, New York City is using revenue generated by another type of traffic fix—congestion pricing. In its first year, the toll made $550+ million and shortened commute times, according to the NY governor’s office.—ML

issues.title: Some cities show traffic isn’t an inescapable fate
issues.summary: Tolls are just one solution.
issues.author: Sam Klebanov
issues.content_html:
Cities worldwide are demonstrating that the bane of your dad’s existence and your favorite excuse for being 20 minutes late can be solved. They’re doing this by embracing proven measures to fight traffic effectively.

(Lane) Change is possible

Aside from banning cars, the highest-impact anti-traffic measure is charging drivers to enter designated zones in the city, aka enacting congestion pricing. The toll is meant to spur some people to consider alternative routes or take public transit instead, reducing traffic and pollution in central areas:

  • After New York City imposed congestion pricing in 2025 in the zone below Central Park in Manhattan, traffic fell 12% in the first year, according to state data.
  • London implemented congestion pricing in 2003 and Stockholm, in 2007. Public opposition to both programs waned after people saw how it made driving less nightmarish.

This may seem expensive, but research firm INRIX estimates that traffic itself costs an average US driver 97 hours annually, or $1,348 in lost productivity.

But tolls are just one solution. For instance, NYC is testing so-called “low traffic zones,” using design elements like plastic bollards, speed bumps, and expanded sidewalks to steer drivers away from using certain residential neighborhoods as shortcuts. While meant to reduce congestion and pedestrian deaths, the measures have led some New Yorkers to complain that traffic now flows into their previously quiet streets instead.

Meanwhile…many cities are taking a simpler road to zero traffic: banning cars from select streets. This lets walkers saunter while letting their guard down, and local businesses benefit from the window-shopping.—SK

issues.title: Zeppelins might be making a comeback
issues.summary: A constellation of startups is betting that next-gen blimps are the future of cargo delivery.
issues.author: Sam Klebanov
issues.content_html:
Almost 90 years after the Hindenburg disaster gave blimps the worst reputation imaginable, gas-filled levitating ships might be returning to ferry your Temu orders. A constellation of startups is betting that next-gen blimps are the future of cargo delivery, pitching them as a cleaner and cheaper (albeit slower) alternative to freight planes:

  • Sergey Brin-backed LTA Research has been testing the 406.5-foot-long rigid airship Pathfinder 1—the world’s biggest aircraft—in the Bay Area skies. The company says that the prototype hybrid-electric blimp is a step toward building a fuel-efficient cargo vessel that can land in otherwise inaccessible areas.
  • French startup Flying Whales aspires to produce blimps for remote shipments of up to 66 tons at its Quebec factory.
  • Airship company Hybrid Air Vehicles, backed by the UK government, has $2.2 billion worth of orders for its anticipated gas-buoyed aircraft intended for civilian and defense purposes.

For those worried about Hindenburg 2.0: Modern safety advancements make a big difference. For one, these next-gen blimps use inflammable helium for buoyancy (instead of flammable hydrogen), and they’re built with more durable modern materials, like carbon fiber. Plus, digital controls allow for precise navigation, while improved wind prediction can help avoid storms.

But it’s a turbulent liftoff: Airship engineers have spent years tinkering with the unwieldy floating beasts, contending with the fact that they’re still more prone to weather disruptions than planes.—SK

Build Durable AI Agents & Workflows in TypeScript — Trigger.dev runs AI agents as tasks inside your codebase, in plain TypeScript with full control of runtime. Dominik Dorfmeister

Your Tools are Hiding npm Audits From You — npm audit on a new create-next-app app shows '0 vulnerabilities' but Next vendors over 100 packages and the audit doesn't notice those. Zach Leatherman

React Forms Beyond onSubmit — See the differences between a form built three ways (with onSubmit, React 19's action prop, and onSubmit plus useTransition). Each has pros and cons, shown in a comparison table.

Giorgi Moniava

Kasturi Khanke

Josh W. Comeau

Carl Vitullo

Hayder

#​496 — November 6, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile keeping native UI over Rust code shared with the desktop client.

Tom Warren (The Verge)

▶️ Just prior to this reveal, Software Mansion interviewed Discord's Chas Jhin about how React Native development works at Discord's scale, in the ominously titled 'Maybe React Native Is Impossible'.

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

A Roadmap for Redux Toolkit v2.x and 3.0 — Mark Erikson has laid out the roadmap for Redux (complete with a neat history lesson) with RTK 3.0 expected in six to eight months, going ESM-only with 'React 19-scale' breaking changes. But a run of 2.x releases will ship the groundwork first, starting with 2.14 this week.

Mark Erikson

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Update to Next.js 16.4.5 or 15.5.29, as appropriate: the November security release fixes seven advisories. Most are Cache Components bugs, so the post is worth reading.

  • 🤖 TanStack Query maintainer Dominik Dorfmeister says work on Query v6 can start once 'slop PRs' stop coming in and taking up his time, leading to a thread on the effects of AI-made contributions on maintainers.

  • Vercel is folding Next.js's Data Cache into Runtime Cache with bigger allocations but… new per-read and per-write pricing. Hobby teams migrate on November 29, but check the dates and prices for your use case.

  • Vercel builds also now block known-malicious npm package versions before and during install, on all plans and with no configuration needed.

Next.js is Prototyping Go(lang) Route Handlers — A merged experimental PR lets an App Router route be a route.go file exporting GET and friends, compiled by Turbopack and run in supervised Go-powered workers. Tim says Rust could follow along the same path.

Tim Neutkens (Vercel)

Understanding React Internals: A Deep Dive — A seven-part, source-grounded tour of React's internals that, unusually, starts from the server end before getting to fibers, lanes and the commit phase.

Alexandre Trotel

Amazon's React Native-Based Vega OS Hits 2.0 — Vega, the React Native-based OS behind newer Fire TV devices, is out of beta. SDK 2.0 takes apps from RN 0.72 to 0.83, bringing the React Compiler and Hermes v1 into play. The release notes go into more detail than the post.

Barak Schlosser (Amazon)

📄 Why We Finally Left Next.js for TanStack Start – Production memory leaks in two Next.js 16.3 releases were the last straw. Harrison Milbradt

📄 Writable Derived State: Stop Synchronizing State – Using clientData ?? serverData instead of a useEffect that wipes user edits on refetch. Corbin Crutchley

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Skullet: Skeleton Loading States Measured from Your Components — Hand it sample data and it renders your real component invisibly, measures everything, and draws a matching skeleton to reduce layout shifts when data arrives. The docs have a neat How it Works section explaining the technique.

Lochie Axon

Parcel 3 Alpha: A Rust Rewrite with React Compiler, Tailwind and RSC — Parcel's core is now a Rust binary with no Node dependency, and the team reports cold builds up to 100x faster than v2. React Compiler (opt-in), Tailwind and MDX are built in, with RSC support in beta.

Devon Govett (Parcel)

🤖 Reticle: Let Coding Agents Verify Their Changes Against Your Running App — A dev-only SDK and MCP server so coding agents can drive your running app, inspect network requests, application state, and console activity, and return a pass, fail or 'can't tell' verdict with what needs fixing.

Reticle Labs

react-resizable-panels Gets a VS Code-Style Workspace Component — Brian Vaughn's popular panel library now does dockable tabs you can drag to split or merge panes, and moved tabs keep their state rather than remounting. There's a live demo here.

Brian Vaughn

  • Preact 11.2 – Now has a runtime for React Compiler output via preact/compat, plus scoped custom element registries in shadow roots.

  • XState 6.0 Beta – "No further breaking changes are planned" for public APIs, and @xstate/react 7 is in beta alongside.

  • TanStack Redact 0.3 – The lightweight, synchronous-only React / React DOM replacement adds browser SPA plugins for Webpack and Rspack.

  • React Native 0.89 RC – Faster text layout and native module calls, legacy bridge APIs gone. Stable expected in December.

  • Storybook 11.0 Beta

📰 Classifieds

🤖 Fimo gives your marketers a visual editor and AI agents for SEO and GEO. No more tickets for your React devs. By the Strapi team.

QVAC allows you to run any AI capabilities for free, on your phone or laptop, privately. Try the QVAC SDK now on GitHub.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • James Long has been reviving Prepack, Facebook's abandoned JavaScript partial evaluator. There's a React demo where a pretend site is server rendered three ways, by React, by Prepack's output (which essentially 'compiles' React away), and a hybrid, with the render times to compare.

  • Node.js 27 Alpha has landed, the first version using Node's new release process (where a release will spend six months in 'alpha' before going Current), while Node 26 is now the new LTS line.

  • Chrome 157 rolled out this week with HTML-in-Canvas now stable. It provides a way to draw real DOM elements into 2D, WebGL and WebGPU canvases. The demos are striking.

  • Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new serif font that shares metrics with Geist Sans so the two can mix cleanly. It's not on Google Fonts yet, but the geist npm package includes it.

issues.title: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance
issues.summary: Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny’s Podcast Network
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer)

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • Parallel—Web search built for AI scale

  • GiveDirectly—Send cash to the world’s poorest

Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of Innovaccer and the creator of a personal AI chief of staff he runs through OpenClaw on a Mac Mini. In this episode, he shows how his Jarvis handles work approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers who miss Slack messages, books restaurants, and controls his smart home. He also explains how he uses soul files, specialist subagents, and strict guardrails to make the system trustworthy, and why he is testing local models against a $500 to $600 monthly Anthropic bill.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best reason to stick with an agent platform is control, not habit. Ankit remains on OpenClaw because it can use his credentials, act on his behalf, and complete tasks without requesting permission at every step. That autonomy is an architectural advantage, not brand loyalty.

  2. Start with the bottleneck, not the grand vision. Ankit’s first automation was a cron job that runs every four hours and briefs him on every resume awaiting approval, including candidate pedigree and GitHub history. Once it worked, he began spotting similar bottlenecks throughout his day.

  3. Specialized agents outperform generalist ones once the workload becomes complex. Ankit’s master agent struggled to maintain the right persona across restaurant bookings and coworker check-ins. Moving voice calls to a dedicated agent improved consistency and clarified the split between orchestration and execution.

  4. Configuring soul files requires more work than integrations. The hardest part was defining each agent’s personality, boundaries, permissions, and routing logic through files such as soul.md. Getting those instructions right required more iteration than connecting the underlying tools.

  5. Guardrails should cover the worst case before it happens. OpenClaw once approved expiring travel requests while Ankit was in transit, using the same budget and customer-impact criteria he would have applied. The decisions were sound, but the experience exposed other actions, such as job-role approvals, that needed explicit limits.

  6. The model bill is worth optimizing before the system becomes indispensable. Jarvis costs Ankit roughly $500 to $600 per month on Opus 5.5. Early tests suggest a nearly free local model can handle summaries, email, cron checks, and call orchestration, while complex browser work still requires a frontier model.

  7. The “1% annoyance” rule is an effective way to discover automations. If a task is even slightly frustrating and repeats a few times, Ankit automates it. That approach led to agents for lunch ordering, unanswered Slack messages, home automation, and potentially even calling the elevator.

  8. A terminal-first approach can keep agent building surprisingly simple. Ankit set up OpenClaw by opening its terminal interface and speaking to it like a new employee. When coding was required, OpenClaw launched Claude Code and managed the implementation itself.

  9. Teach agents the messy details, then let them keep learning. Ankit’s lunch agent confirms his order at 9:30 a.m. and acts independently if he does not respond. After one correction about ordering curry without bread, it learned both when to add bread and when a meal already includes it.

issues.title: 2026.47: Down in DC
issues.summary: The best Stratechery content from the week of November 16, 2026, including obituaries and exceptionalism, arguments about agents, and Ben gets a Duo.
issues.author: Ben Thompson
issues.content_html:
Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings.

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

  1. Obituaries and Exceptionalism. After several days to mull the shocking departure of Jensen Huang, Ben’s article on Monday delivered an omnibus obituary for a variety of American eras that may now be ending. Tracing the decisions that made Huang great, the strategies that made him a target, the implications of his demise for the rest of the tech ecosystem, and a shift in the U.S. government’s perspective on tech companies — and specifically AI companies — to which Huang never quite adapted, Monday’s piece was both comprehensive and poignant. —Andrew Sharp
  1. Arguments About Agents.Recurring Stratechery guest and advertising expert Eric Seufert is often aligned with Ben in his view of the digital advertising landscape, which is why this week’s Stratechery Interview was fun: Ben is a big believer in the potential upside in agentic commerce, while Eric has been (correctly) calling BS on a variety of hyped agentic commerce stories and trends over the past year. Both of them made their case Thursday, and it was sandwiched between thoughts on how Muse plans to monetize, why the market have misread Google’s recent earnings report, and ChatGPT’s progress building an ads business. — AS

  2. Ben Gets a Duo. In the middle of a heavy week of Nvidia takes and ominous infrastructure failures, I was delighted to find out that Ben not only purchased an iPhone Duo, but loved it. Come for his review at the end of Tuesday’s Update, and then stay for his discussion with John Gruber on Tuesday’s Dithering. We doubled back (Duo’d back?) to discuss all of it at the end of this week’s Sharp Tech , including some hands-on testing, comparisons to the iPhone Air, and a variety of shots fired at the iPhone Pro. —AS

Presented by

As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story.

Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year, from three to six.

Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents.

The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity.

OpenRouter, which recently joined Stripe, allows businesses to access and govern hundreds of models with the flexibility to optimize for cost, performance, and reliability as the market evolves.

Learn more at openrouter.ai.

Stratechery Articles and Updates

  • Obituaries — The demise of Jensen Huang was the end of a great many things, including Nvidia’s long-term prospects, the AI bubble, and the exceptional way in which the U.S. viewed itself in the world.
  • Apple Permissions Update, The New App Paradigm, My iPhone Duo Review— Apple doesn’t ruin the Mac, but they don’t fix the agent problem, raising questions if they can think outside the app paradigm. Then, my iPhone Duo review.
  • Nvidia Earnings; Office Convergence; OS Wars, AI Edition— Nvidia’s earnings were boring, and also a statement as to why Jensen Huang probably isn’t coming back; then, Microsoft and Anthropic ship dueling operating system updates.
  • An Interview With Eric Seufert About Agentic Commerce— An interview with Eric Seufert about agentic commerce, including why he thinks ads will be the answer, and why I want retailers who cater to agents.

Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp

  • Wizards Groundhog Day — Four more years of winter for basketball fans in Washington.

Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber

  • Ben Gets a Duo
  • GTA and Windows Apps

Asianometry with Jon Yu

  • The Rise and Fall of the Soviet Union’s Workhorse Computer

issues.title: 🎁 Azeem’s holiday gift guide
issues.summary: My favorite stationery, long flight must-haves, books, records & the best phone since the Nokia 6110
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Readers have been emailing me to find out which paper and pen I use as I return to handwriting. So, that gave me an excuse to put together a gift guide for you all. Everything from my favorite stationery, tech and boozy ice cream. 20 items. Here you go:

For the person who thinks on paper

  1. Kolo Tino fountain pen. I use AI a lot, and handwriting is how I protect my thinking. I sometimes take the cartridge out of my fountain pen and dip the nib in ink. Every ten or fifteen words I have to stop, which gives me a moment to look at what I’ve just written.

  2. Paper Republic le trifold. I keep three inserts in my leather journal. One is for to-dos, and the other two are for thinking.

  3. An unlined Moleskine. You can’t go wrong with this one.

  4. Wispr Flow or Otter. Once I’ve worked through something by hand, I read it aloud into Wispr Flow. I tend to edit as I speak. Sometimes that’s when I hear that I’ve put two ideas in the wrong order. Otter is an older transcriber I’ve used for nearly a decade. It doesn’t have some of the fancy frills of Wispr Flow or Granola. But sometimes you just want good, old-fashioned transcription.

For music lovers

  1. The Saturday Night Fever soundtrack on vinyl. My first record, at seven, and still one of my favorite albums. I’ve had it on cassette, CD, MP3, and streaming. Eventually I bought it on vinyl again.

  1. DJ.Studio. This is how I got into making house mixes. It helped me work out where to bring in the vocals and how to get from one track to the next. I’ve since bought a pair of decks, but I still make mixes on my laptop during long flights.

  2. Roon. I use Roon to play music around the house.

  3. T+A Solitaire T headphones. These are the noise-canceling headphones I use at home when I’m listening and want to wander about. They have a built-in DAC, which gives a much higher-quality sound. A few tracks I use to try out headphones are Dire Straits’ “Sultans of Swing,” Bach’s Goldberg Variations, Yosi Horikawa’s “Letter,” and Energy 52’s “Café del Mar.”

For the person who spends too much time on planes

  1. Beats Fit Pro earbuds. These are the ones I use day to day, especially for music, workouts, and long flights. I’ve had less luck with the mic on calls. The Fit Pro is an older model, so check the listing. I love headphones and have about seven other pairs, including a couple of Apple wired Earpods in different bags as backups.

  2. Pzizz. I’ve used this sleep-audio app for about a decade. I put it on for naps, overnight flights, and jet lag. Paired with the Beats Fit Pros, it can almost give you a half-night’s sleep on a flight.

issues.summary: El Niño and climate change don't fully explain it
issues.author: Hannah Petrovic
issues.content_html:
Hello, here. I was on a long-haul red-eye flight last week that hit turbulence so bad it was hard to sleep. Being a scientist, I started looking into turbulence data to understand what it is and how it’s changed over time.

What surprised me was where conditions favored clear-air turbulence, the kind of turbulence that often forms near jet streams and that ordinary onboard weather radar can’t detect. It accounted for 29% of turbulence-related accidents on US airlines between 2009 and 20181. From August through October this year, the pattern departed further from the long-term trend than in any other year I examined.
