issues.title: 🔮 Certified human, twin primes, Anthropic++ #611
issues.summary: Your Sunday briefing on AI and exponential technologies
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
A must-read for asset allocators who are not tech specialists. – SHK, a paying member

Subscribe now

A big issue this weekend. Settle in with a cup of coffee.

The handmade’s tale

The year’s biggest launch is a testament to manual labor. Rockstar’s 5,000 staff built Grand Theft Auto VI without generative AI. Reports say that 30,000 unique characters in the game were made by hand. Proof of humanity paid handsomely – the game made $3.79 billion in sales by the end of the first day, including preorders.

Back in 2017, I argued that, in a world of AI, we should look for lessons from artisanal cheesemakers. AI would make perfection cheap, and what would be scarce is human imperfection. We do seem to love the human touch. In one study, people rated AI-generated paintings more favorably when they were labeled human-made.

William Morris and the British Arts and Crafts movement of the 19th century resisted industrial mechanization, only to find that manual labor couldn’t compete on price. In the end, only the well-heeled could afford the premium. He raged that he spent his “life ministering to the swinish luxury of the rich.”

Digital culture might escape the trap that held Morris. Created carefully by hand once, the costs can be spread across millions of buyers, as a mass-market phenomenon, not the plaything of the rich. But the specter of Morris (and the artisanal cheesemakers) still looms over a world flooded by generative content. An ocean of synthetic digital drivel (what my Instagram feed has become) might drown out a scarcer “certified human” tier.

👉 I’d love to hear how you are thinking about this. Leave your thoughts in the comments below.

Leave a comment

See also:

  • The team at Substack profiled my work and how we try to balance human thinking with AI’s capabilities:

On Substack Model Behavior: Azeem Azhar has a team of AI agents. He starts nearly every piece by hand anyway Welcome to Model Behavior, our interview series featuring writers and creators on AI’s frontier. In previous editions, we spoke to author George Saunders and music producer Rick Rubin about AI and the creative process. Today we’re chatting with British entrepreneur and technology writer… Read more 7 days ago · 506 likes · Azeem Azhar and Arielle Swedback

Anthropic’s big week

Wall Street got a piece of Anthropic this week. What exactly did it buy?

  • The Exponential View view. Could Anthropic take a cut of the value its AI creates across the intangible economy? I shared my early analysis of what Anthropic is really listing.

  • From our AI Investment Brief desk.We model three futures for Anthropic, from licensing models that run on your devices to becoming an AI utility.

  • published a reflection on a year of conversations with people inside Anthropic. The firm has hallmarks of a religion: the only way to save humanity from an existentially dangerous technology is to race as fast as possible to build it first, and they are the only ones virtuous enough to wield that power.

Twin primes

You wait 167 years for a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and then two come in the same day. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, says he and Claude may have proved the Riemann hypothesis. That same day, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil rushed out a proof of the same conjecture by Alessandro Masullo: “all human, with no AI.”

I’ve not read either proof. Alpöge says his runs to 17.4m lines of Lean, a formal language used to prove logical arguments. Masullo’s proof was still being checked by a third party, but a team is now translating his argument into Lean, where it can be verified more quickly.

Scott Aaronson makes the case that no AI result that has been verified in Lean has ever been retracted. But it’s also a sign of the times that the human team wants to lean on Lean to prove Masullo’s work.

See also: Why the Riemann hypothesis is so important. (Lovely video.)

Wright of way

More than 2,000 gigawatts of new power plants and batteries are waiting to connect to the US grid. For perspective, that’s more than every power plant running in the country right now. About 85% of the queue is for solar, wind, and storage.

Meanwhile, solar modules keep getting 24% cheaper with every doubling of capacity — we have long believed this will open new markets that were previously unavailable (see our solar supercycle model). Well, since Wright’s law continues to deliver, the queue is pushing AI off the grid.

While an AI chip rents for about $3 an hour, a month spent waiting for power costs more than the power itself. In Friday’s edition, our Investment Brief showed how on-site solar and batteries are the cheapest option to power data centers in half of the United States.

issues.title: 🔮 What Anthropic is really listing
issues.summary: Tithes, not tokens
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

It’s Anthropic’s big week. It will become the first real AI company in the West to list on a public market.

Anthropic has an extraordinary market opportunity. The battle hangs on the sustainability of its business model – whether falling token costs or competition from open-weight models won’t simply erode its margins. These forces, no doubt, exist. The bear case claims the company is merely a peddler of progressively devalued tokens. This misses the point.

Anthropic is building an ever-improving system that produces machine intelligence. That machine intelligence is valuable because of the nature of modern economies. Most value in our economies now comes from intangibles, scientific knowledge, patents, software, brand, and data. If Anthropic’s machine intelligence can create intangibles like these – breakthrough science, information, or software – then it should be able to create extraordinary value.

Over the past fifty years, value in the S&P 500 has shifted from tangibles, things you can count in warehouses or can stub your toe on. Most value now resides in that ethereal flim-flam of the intangible: brand, customer lists, patents, and software.

Put another way, Anthropic’s machine intelligence lets it compete for 92% of the value of the S&P 500 before it needs to deploy a single robot.

That is the big macro-level survey that paints the opportunity. But I’ve been digging deeper. My conclusion is that AI companies in general, and Anthropic, are in a unique position. Look at the chart below. Each time Anthropic announced a new product feature that encroached on a given sector, the stock prices of firms in that sector responded as you’d expect.

AI companies might be able to extract a permanent tithe on the economy. Anthropic, as the leading player, is best positioned to do that.

The following are my sketches. They’ll give you a sense of the direction that I think merits further exploration.

Capturing the intangible

Anthropic has three approaches to capturing value in an intangible economy:

  1. It can ask companies to pay to defend their assets. As I wrote in The Internet’s Wuhan moment, AI has laid bare the software’s non-existent security model. Anthropic’s Mythos is the world’s most powerful security-oriented AI.

issues.title: Zillow says mortgage rates will stay above 7% until at least mid-2027
issues.summary: "However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner,"
issues.author: Jason Ma
issues.content_html:
For would-be homebuyers hoping for a reprieve in mortgage rates next year, the outlook isn’t good as borrowing costs are expected to remain high.

According to Freddie Mac, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.21% as of Wednesday, down from last week’s average of 7.28% as the stock market selloff pushed investors to safe haven Treasuries, lowering bond yields. But at this same time last year, the 30-year rate was 6.23%.

The rate spike in recent months has frozen the housing market. Sales of existing homes plunged 5.5% in October from the prior month and 8.8% from a year ago to an annualized pace of just 3.75 million units, the lowest in 16 years. Pending sales, an indicator of future closings, hit a second consecutive record low in October, down 4.7% month over month and 16.7% year over year.

Americans are also physically stuck. The housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, is just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate before the financial crisis. And the rate at which people move from region to region has been falling for two years.

Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of this year and through mid-2027 with sales falling 3.5%, potentially dampening the spring selling season and weighing further on the housing market next year.

The problem is that inflation is accelerating, so the Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep hiking rates, which will push up borrowing costs across the economy.

To be sure, oil prices have eased as the Iran war continues to simmer without re-escalating, but the latest consumer price index came in hotter than expected with inflationary pressure spreading beyond energy categories.

Ironically, the frozen housing market is also stoking inflation, keeping the Fed hawkish, as discouraged buyers turn to the rental market and push up rents.

“New-lease rents are growing at their fastest pace in 2025-2026, so they’re no longer pulling down housing inflation measures, and forecasts for on-market rents have been revised upward in recent months,” Zillow Senior Economist Kara Ng wrote earlier this month. “In other words, while oil-related developments could ease some inflation pressure, firmer rent growth means the Fed may get less help from shelter in 2027.”

The U.S. economy is also booming as AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and other infrastructure. Their capital expenditures are expected to top $1 trillion in 2027. Third-quarter GDP jumped 4.3%, and the fourth quarter is on pace to see still-robust growth of 2.9%.

That continues to support strong wages and resilient consumer demand, allowing businesses to pass on higher costs and add further to inflation.

“However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner,” Ng pointed out. “With inventory forecast to rise about 11% next year, there should be enough supply to meet demand if buyers return.”

For now, the housing market is still reeling from the mortgage rate shock. The 30-year fixed mortgage had been around 6.60% in July, then soared to 7.61% by the start of October, and has stayed above 7% since then.

Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman told CNBC earlier this month that the full-percentage-point surge was one of the fastest three-month increases seen in decades. That has sent the purchase mortgage market down 4% year over year, and he expects it to be down 10%-15% in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, rents in the third quarter were up nearly 20%.

“That is buyers just not being able to afford the homes they were looking at,” Wacksman explained. “They were thinking about a mortgage and then they couldn’t pull the trigger, and so now they’re renting longer.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Inside Anthropic’s culture clash: Effective Altruists, IPO hopefuls, and an acrimonious breakup with the AI safety movement that helped create it
issues.summary: Anthropic built itself around the fear that AI could end humanity. Now a $1 trillion public company, it's struggling to hold on to its safety-first culture—and losing allies in the movement that helped create it.
issues.author: Beatrice Nolan
issues.content_html:
“Anthropic is an unusual company. Some might say weird—and in fact, many have,” Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and president, joked from the stage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square, just hours before the company’s blockbuster IPO earlier this month. In her speech, Amodei stressed that the company was not like other technology companies, largely because of its “safety-first” culture.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the most responsible AI lab. The company had an AI safety team before it even had a product. Its founders and employees have been vocal about AI risk, and even its IPO prospectus warned investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

For this reason, over the majority of its five-year history, Anthropic has counted the community of people focused on AI safety—both technical researchers and policy experts—among its closest allies. But in the run-up to the company’s IPO, some prominent figures in that once-sympathetic field openly broke with the company and now see it as a threat instead of an ally.

“Anthropic is absolutely not the voice of the AI safety community,” said Steven Adler, a former OpenAI safety researcher who co-founded Guidelight AI Standards, which sets safety benchmarks for AI companies. “Many researchers I know believe that Anthropic is the most likely company to get everyone killed.”

These divisions were on full display the day Anthropic made its market debut. Outside the company’s headquarters in San Francisco, more than 100 protesters gathered to demand a ban on “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, a term for using AI systems to autonomously build yet more powerful AI. Among them was Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher who made headlines around the globe when he quit in September over safety concerns.

Inside the company, Anthropic has, at times, struggled to keep hold of its safety-conscious culture as it has grown, according to three former employees and two people familiar with the company who spoke to Fortune. From its origins as a group of researchers primarily concerned with AI safety, Anthropic’s headcount has swelled to more than 5,000 employees, and its market value closed its first day of trading at about $1.76 trillion. (Since then, it has slipped closer to a $1 trillion market cap.) Now some are questioning whether Anthropic’s safety-first culture can survive life as a public company, and whether the company has already betrayed its founding principles.

“Anthropic has sought to create a race to the top on safety: to show that it’s possible to build AI carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “We remain true to our vision to build AI systems that put safety and humans at the center, while maximizing the benefits for humanity.”

“A close second”

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, led by the siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. The group split off primarily because they felt OpenAI’s leadership was not taking AI safety seriously enough and was not trustworthy enough to control such a powerful technology, several former employees said. (Personal conflicts between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei also played a role, some said.)

Because of that founding mission, most of the company’s early employees came from the AI safety community. Many also hailed from the world of effective altruism—a philanthropic movement that uses evidence and reason to try to do the most good and whose adherents came to rank AI as one of humanity’s most neglected risks. To this day, Anthropic has more people who are adherents of effective altruism, or share many of its values, than rival labs, two former employees who spoke to Fortune said.

Much of Anthropic’s early money also came from EA-aligned investors. Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn, who has backed a number of EA-affiliated organizations, led Anthropic’s $124 million Series A in May 2021, with Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz, another major funder of EA-related philanthropies, and the Center for Emerging Risk Research also investing. A year later, Anthropic’s $580 million Series B was led by the disgraced crypto kingpin Sam Bankman-Fried, then the movement’s best-known donor.

In the early days, one of Anthropic’s principles was that it would not push the frontier of AI research, according to one former Anthropic engineer, who asked for anonymity to discuss sensitive information about their former employer. Leadership said explicitly that it did not want to start or worsen an AI arms race, and described the lab’s aim as being “a close second,” the person said. Most employees also believed strongly that advanced AI posed an existential risk to humanity.

The company continues to weigh safety concerns heavily, funds its safety teams generously, and holds onto its safety talent, former employees say. But some in Anthropic’s organization also have deep qualms about what the world looks like following the development of the kind of superintelligent AI Anthropic wants to build.

David Duvenaud, a University of Toronto professor who led Anthropic’s Alignment Evaluations team from 2023 to 2024, says many early Anthropic employees believed AI presented a chance of destroying or enslaving humanity. (Duvenaud himself has put the odds of AI destroying much of what humanity values at 70% to 80% by the year 2100).

As a result, Anthropic initially didn’t want to release a product, former employees said. In the summer of 2022, months before OpenAI debuted ChatGPT, launching the AI boom, Anthropic had developed a working chatbot but chose not to release it. Dario Amodei later called that incident a “one-time overhang.”

As Anthropic has grown, its commitment to some of these early principles seems to have eroded. In March 2024, Anthropic released Claude 3, which by some measures beat OpenAI’s GPT-4. It no longer seemed to be playing just for second place.

Then came Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, released in 2025. The tool’s wild popularity kicked off a race between the leading AI labs to perfect AI’s coding abilities. But because AI models are themselves code, advancing AI’s coding capabilities inherently pushes the entire field toward recursive self-improvement. Most AI safety advocates see RSI as inherently dangerous, since an AI model that can autonomously improve itself with little to no human oversight could quickly evolve beyond human control.

Some of Anthropic’s critics argue that the lab pushed the rest of the industry toward that dangerous threshold by loudly demonstrating how good Claude Code was. One former employee pointed to Google DeepMind’s recent increased investment in developing AI coding abilities, in part to keep pace with Anthropic, and OpenAI’s retreat from side projects like video generator Sora, in part in order to free up resources to work on its coding agent Codex, as examples of Anthropic pushing rival labs to the frontier.

For years, the former employee said, colleagues at Anthropic would argue that their competitors were already racing as hard as they could, so Anthropic’s choices didn’t matter. In truth, they said, the rest of the industry was racing harder every year because of Anthropic.

“We’ve been clear that Anthropic may at times go slower than we could to make our systems safer, even at a competitive disadvantage,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “As our founders have written, we are committed to standing up for our values at critical points, even when it is costly for us commercially.”

Holding back the tide

Anthropic’s leaders have made culture a priority to a level that former employees say is unusual even by standards of Silicon Valley, which frequently pays lip service to the importance of “mission-driven” companies. Dario Amodei has said publicly he spends “a third, maybe 40%” of his time attending to Anthropic’s culture. In interviews, candidates have been asked unusual culture questions, such as how they would feel if Anthropic abandoned its business ambitions for safety reasons and the stock went to zero.

Anthropic famously went to mat with the Pentagon over its “red lines,” refusing to give in to demands that its models be used by the government for “any lawful use.” The company also takes seriously the philosophical position that very powerful AI models might deserve moral consideration, two former employees said.

Anthropic apparently sees the possibility of a shift in this culture as a potential financial risk. In the company’s IPO prospectus, Anthropic warns investors that employees who joined for its safety commitments “may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity” if they believe the company is not living up to its values. But keeping that highly-prized culture intact got harder as the company scaled, multiple former employees told Fortune.

For the past 12 months, it’s been clear that an IPO was looming—a liquidity event that might attract people more interested in a financial payoff than in saving the world from dangerous AI.

Coxon, the 27-year-old researcher who resigned in September, has since criticized Anthropic’s broader workforce, claiming many of its employees were just in it for the money. “There were so many non-EA guys at Anthropic who snuck through the interview,” he said. “Just silently praying for the IPO of a lifetime while their whole company crashes out and declares imminent apocalypse.”

Duvenaud said the company “spend[s] a ton of time worrying about culture and who they’re bringing in. But I think it’s almost like trying to hold back the tide.”

“If you build this thing that’s super powerful and going to make everyone rich … you’re in an awkward position if you want to only select for people with really good motivations,” he added.

Anthropic has so far been successful in keeping talent from leaving. The company’s IPO filing reports “regrettable attrition” of just 1% in the 12 months through September, amid a talent war where rivals offer individual researchers hundreds of millions of dollars. The company says its culture is a big reason why.

A clash with the safety community

By the time Anthropic’s cofounders rang the Nasdaq bell, prominent AI safety figures were calling the company a danger.

On the day Anthropic priced its shares, the Center for AI Safety and a coalition of scientists, legal scholars, and tech figures published the “MisAnthropic Statement.” It declared that “Anthropic is not a safe AI company” and launched with 89 signatories, including cognitive psychologist Steven Pinker, president of the Future of Life Institute, Max Tegmark, and xAI cofounder Igor Babuschkin.

“People in this coalition disagree on almost everything, yet we all recognize the danger of a company that convinces itself its own dominance is the greater good,” said Dan Hendrycks, CAIS’s executive director, in the announcement.

According to Adler, Coxon’s resignation was a missed opportunity for Anthropic and the start of its rift with the wider safety community. “Jacob Coxon’s resignation could have been a moment for Dario to speak candidly,” he said. “He ought to have said in no uncertain terms that he is concerned about human extinction, as I know him to be. Instead, Dario mostly dodges questions like these now that Anthropic is in the spotlight.”

Amodei has pushed back on some of this criticism. In October, after Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer of the AI safety advocacy group Encode AI, published a long post accusing Anthropic of racing toward superintelligence, Amodei replied on X with a roughly 2,000-word defense. “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry,” he wrote. “The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier.”

“Anthropic’s leadership is open and candid about the risks of powerful AI, including those of AI-automated research, and has led the call for pacing with governments and the industry,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control.“

But a recent report from METR, an outside evaluator, widened the growing rift between the company and AI safety advocates. From August to October this year, METR had unprecedented access to Anthropic’s internal data and was tasked with assessing whether AI was speeding up Anthropic’s own research—an important safety concern.

The evaluators concluded that the pace of AI research at Anthropic had almost doubled in the past year and that use of AI to automate research was a key reason. However, Anthropic eventually “redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions,” METR wrote in a blog post about the report. METR’s disclosure about the redactions, and other comments METR made about how Anthropic had limited the scope of its evaluation, earned Anthropic derision from AI safety experts.

“We determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” Anthropic co-founder Sam McCandlish said in an X post responding to the criticism. “We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work.”

Public pressure

The company has tried to build in protections against market pressure and to guard the culture it values so highly. For example, it remains a public benefit corporation, legally required to weigh its mission alongside shareholder returns, and its Long-Term Benefit Trust helps choose its board. Its prospectus warns investors that this structure could lead to decisions that “may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests.” But governance experts have questioned whether those safeguards will hold when profits are on the line.

While some say Anthropic’s life as a public company will make it more difficult to prioritize safety, two former employees said the IPO itself doesn’t change much. The company has always been conflicted, Duvenaud said: building a technology while telling everyone it is “so insanely dangerous” that it could kill everyone.

“I’m not sure being public actually changes the calculus all that much,” he added.

For a long time, the AI safety community was willing to believe that Anthropic cared more about making the world safe than making money. They believed the company could avoid the “god complex” that has driven other AI labs to keep pushing the frontier. But now, many in the AI safety community have come to doubt that is true. Indeed, some now think Anthropic has become exactly the kind of company it was founded to stop.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Lauren C. Templeton’s 3 rules for ‘maximum pessimism’ investing
issues.summary: The hedge fund manager treats a market crash as an opportunity for a “shopping spree.”
issues.author: Jeff John Roberts
issues.content_html:
The investor Lauren C. Templeton is not a pessimist—though she’s happiest when everyone around her is.

The Tennessee-based author and fund manager has taken up the creed of “maximum pessimism” espoused by her legendary great-uncle, Sir John Templeton, whom many view as the greatest stock picker of the 20th century. Sir John famously said that every bull market is born in pessimism, which creates an environment where bargains abound—if you know where to look for them.

Templeton, who began her career working alongside her renowned great-uncle, has likewise made a name for herself by placing bets in bad times. Those bets have included buying airline stocks after 9/11 and scooping up Amazon shares at the outset of the pandemic. She and her husband run the hedge fund Templeton and Phillips Capital Management, with $325 million in assets.

Templeton inherited her contrarian investment style from her great-uncle, but also from her stockbroker father. She recalls the time he returned home from work on Black Monday in 1987—a day when the Dow Jones plunged 23%—and told her mother he was the only broker in his branch to put in a buy order.

As a child, Templeton says, she was passionate about stocks because purchasing even a single share made her feel like a part owner of the company. She once even wrote a letter of disappointment to Walmart founder Sam Walton about a filthy restroom she encountered at a store. (Walton wrote back promising to tighten things up.)

Today, Templeton’s investment thesis reflects Warren Buffett’s famous maxim to “be greedy when others are fearful.” It’s a sound strategy, but that doesn’t mean it’s easy. Here are three rules she follows.

1. Know how to play the waiting game

“There are only three sources of alpha available in the markets: You can have a better model; you can have better information; or you can have better behavior,” says Templeton.

“Behavior” in this case means discipline, which can be hard to maintain in times of volatility. The undoing of many retail investors, says Templeton, comes from selling when the market is diving—a decision that can lead to unloading good assets and, even worse, missing out on the big bounce backs that often follow selloffs. Indeed, there is sobering research that shows that, over the past 30 years, 78% of the stock market’s best days occurred during bear markets and in the first two months of a bull market—and that missing the market’s 10 best days during that period would have reduced your portfolio by half.

Templeton stresses that it’s crucial for investors to know how to wait. She says her fund’s approach can be unsettling for younger employees, who may be itching to trade. “I always tell them, ‘We’re just sitting around reading. It’s not going to be an eventful day-to-day environment, because we don’t overtrade.’”

This premium on patience is something Templeton also conveys to potential investors. While they may appreciate her “maximum pessimism” philosophy, not all have the stomach for it. “If clients hire and fire managers based on their own personal cycles of fear and greed, the strategy breaks,” she says. “A major part of our responsibility isn’t just managing the asset allocation, but actively managing our investors’ emotions.”

2. Keep a wish list at the ready

The investing success of Sir John Templeton, who as a student at Yale paid for his tuition in part by playing poker, was based on a clever trick of psychology: He kept a wish list of stocks at the ready for the next downturn, which helped anchor his thinking when opportunity arose. His grandniece uses the same strategy.

“The psychological pressure of a market crash is immense. When prices tank, human nature forces you to obsess over your losses and fear opening your financial statements,” she says. “But if you can actively shift your mindset by pulling out a preapproved list of elite companies that you’ve always wanted to own but found too expensive, the script completely flips. Suddenly, a market crash becomes an exciting shopping spree.”

She and her partner and spouse, Scott Phillips, use this strategy not only to buy quality stocks on the cheap when the market dives, but also to turn their portfolio over. To do this, they typically use a dollar-cost averaging approach to take large positions in new stocks while divesting other ones they hold.

The couple employed this strategy during the financial crisis of late 2008 and early 2009. Templeton recalls this period, which brought about the collapse of numerous major banks, with happy nostalgia. “At that point, asset prices were so detached from reality that it felt like shooting fish in a barrel,” she says.

3. There’s always a bargain—somewhere in the world

It’s easy enough to understand the idea of waiting to buy at the bottom of the market. The problem, of course, is that no one—including Templeton—can be sure exactly when the bottom is in.

“The simple answer is that you don’t ever truly know,” she says. “We might be getting a little uncomfortable or excited as prices plummet, but we don’t have a crystal ball. You simply observe that a massive cluster of high-quality bargains has emerged, and you want to get your hands on them.”

Such moments don’t come along all the time. Indeed, the current bull market in U.S. equities recently entered its fifth year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t opportunities to find elsewhere.

Templeton recalls that her great-uncle realized this in the late 1950s and 1960s when he looked at publicly traded companies in Japan. He understood that investors had significantly undervalued these firms because of lingering anti-Japanese sentiment from World War II as well as quirks in the companies’ accounting that didn’t properly account for subsidiary profits. Sir John bought shares—and profited handsomely.

Lauren Templeton says she has never forgotten this lesson, and that it leads her to scour the globe for regions where investors are undervaluing the shares of companies that are performing well. It’s a playbook she has run repeatedly—and is ready to do so again.

“Right now, we have our eyes firmly on India,” she says. “It all goes back to that global perspective: Why wouldn’t you look across the globe for the absolute best bargains available? We believe some of the greatest bargains today are in India.”

This aritcle appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

issues.title: For banks, a breach is now a matter of when, not if, says OCBC’s tech head—and reaction time matters as much as prevention
issues.summary: For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster.
issues.author: Angelica Ang
issues.content_html:
Since September, South Korea’s financial sector has been hit by a rolling wave of cyberattacks, with regulators counting 40 incidents at 37 financial firms, including banks, brokerages, insurers and crypto exchanges. Researchers traced the September attacks to Artex, an AI-powered tool that automated the intrusions.

“With the velocity that cyberattacks are happening, it is a matter of when rather than if,” Praveen Raina, head of group operations and technology at Singapore’s Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. (OCBC), tells Fortune.

For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster. “I wish I could prevent them—and we’ll try—but what we can control is having the right processes so that we can react quickly to whatever happens,” Raina says.

His strategy consists of two elements: cybersecurity and resilience. “We’re leveraging AI for cybersecurity,” he explains. “With agentic AI attacking organizations, humans cannot keep up with it… it’s the nature of the beast. So, we’re building a defensive AI wrapper around the bank to protect it.”

His team also regularly conducts red-teaming exercises: structured simulations in which a group acts like a real-world attacker to improve their ability to react in the event of a hack. “We practice a lot among ourselves and with other industry players,” Raina says. “We also have a bug bounty program for white hackers to identify [security] issues in exchange for a reward.”

Building in-house

Raina joined OCBC in 2008 as its SVP in group operations and technology, after spending the early years of his career as an IT consultant to telcos and enterprise software firms in Canada. (OCBC was founded in 1932; Today, it is Singapore’s second-largest bank, and ranks No. 13 on Fortune’s Southeast Asia 500 list.)

In his first year at OCBC, while spending the holidays away from home, Raina amassed a small team to build an iPhone-native banking app. “The tech team was a lot smaller then,” he says. “We didn’t have a deep expertise in building things, and instead mostly bought [our tech solutions] from vendors and implemented them. As the world changed around us, we made it a point [to develop in-house expertise].” (The final product, launched in 2008, was the first digital banking app debuted by one of Singapore’s three local banks: OCBC, DBS and UOB.)

From then on, Raina’s team—which today consists of roughly 600 to 700 employees—started building almost everything in-house. “It gives us better control of things, and we can do more and faster releases,” he explains, adding that failing “over and over again” adds to the joy of creation.

In July, OCBC launched its Avatar Banking app, which allows clients round-the-clock access to AI-enabled virtual relationship managers. The entire process from ideation to release took four to six weeks, Raina says. “It was an unplanned pregnancy,” he says. “We just happily stumbled upon the idea, and worked every day to generate ideas to see what we could do [to bring it to life].”

The new app was initially launched as a beta version to just fifty customers, but Raina says he’s preparing to onboard all the bank’s private wealth clients onto the platform by the first quarter of 2027. (On the app, users can pick between two virtual wealth managers: a man named Wayne and a woman named Wendy.)

“The white glove service is always important, and we are not taking that away,” says Raina, who also heads up the tech division at the Bank of Singapore, OCBC’s private banking subsidiary. “The point is, if I wake up at 3 a.m. and want to look at what’s happening with my portfolio, who do I go to? At that time, even if you call your relationship manager, they will likely not pick up.”

The quantum frontier

Experts estimate that “Q-Day”, the day quantum computers will be able to crack traditional encryption, will happen around the year 2030. Raina expects a Y2K-style crunch, with every institution competing for the same vendors at the last minute. OCBC is trying to get ahead by training over 100 quantum-literate staff, and running pilots with universities and ST Engineering.

“When we go into our mobile banking app, our phone sends a signal to the OCBC data center, and there’s a handshake happening and a key is exchanged to verify our identity,” Raina explains. “The issue with quantum computing is that it’s so powerful that it can break those keys… so the security layer is gone.”

Raina compares quantum technology today to AI in the pre-ChatGPT era. “It’s a theoretical field, which we aren’t experts in, so we partner with universities to get a better understanding of the technology stack,” he says. “We are building [quantum security] for the future; we don’t need it today, but when the technology comes to life on Q-Day, we will be ready.”

Ultimately, banking is a trust-based business, and Raina sees it as his role to upkeep the faith that users have in OCBC. “People work and they put their life savings with the organization—there’s no bigger trust than that,” he concludes. “We as an organization have to do our part to ensure that everything is protected.”

issues.title: Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
issues.summary: Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our … Continue reading "Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Uk
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

issues.title: Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc
issues.summary: While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends … Continue reading
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A large 3,200-year-old Mycenaean tomb has been discovered in Psachna on the Greek island of Euboea. It is a tholos tomb, a type characterized by a circular burial chamber vaulted by a distinctive beehive-shaped dome. The excavation has uncovered its long entrance passage (the dromos) and monumental doorway (the stomion), but has not yet accessed the burial chamber.

They were reserved for people of high social and political status, and this example is exceptional for its size. Out of the 126 Mycenaean tholos tombs identified so far in Greece, this is among the 20 largest.

Like tumuli from many cultures, tholos tombs were typically covered by earth and stone to create a visible mound on the landscape. Some of them were used over generations by one family or social group. Further excavations are needed to clarify if this tomb was built for a single occupant or multiple people and over what span of time.

Archaeological evidence of occupation dating back to prehistory has been found before in the Psachna area, but this is the first monumental burial. At the time of its construction, Euboea was ruled by the Avantes tribe, fearsome warriors who according to Homer took part in the Trojan War. Such an impressive tomb strongly suggests the deceased was someone at the top of the Aventes power structure.

The discovery brings new insight to how Mycenaean burial traditions, well-established on the Greek mainland, developed on islands with their own power centers, and how they may have interacted with the cultural and commercial networks of Late Bronze Age Aegean communities.

The tomb was found during construction of a new highway bypass, so now the question is how to protect it. Proposals include building a bridge over the site to accommodate the new bypass without disrupting the archaeological remains and redirecting the roadway.

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
Sections of chain mail of exceptional quality have been recovered from the15th century Danish royal flagship Gribshunden. The main is made of copper-alloy and is very finely wrought. It is not traceable to a single individual of high status on the ship. Although certainly it was originally worn by someone who could afford the cost of such high-quality armor, chain mail of this level of craftsmanship was repaired and reused for decades.

Gribshunden was the flagship of King Hans of Denmark. It caught fire and sank while anchored off the coast of Ronneby in southeastern Sweden in 1495. It is the oldest armed warship ever found in Nordic waters, and one of the best-preserved ships from the 15th century. Archaeologists have been exploring the wreck since 2001, recovering important artifacts like nine oak carriages for iron breech-loading guns and the sea monster figurehead.

Maritime archaeologists discovered the fine chain mail during this year’s fieldwork documenting the wreck site using advanced robotic survey technology and 3D photogrammetric imaging. The team was recording an ammunition tool chest on the forecastle of the ship when they discovered the armor.

“The remains of the armour were just below the forecastle, in a section that may have served as a storage area for military gear on the ship. It was a truly amazing find!,” says Dr Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, Visiting Fellow at the Centre for Maritime Archaeology (CMA), University of Southampton, and co-investigator on the Griffin project.

“Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495. This part of the ship may therefore have been used to stow equipment associated with these soldiers, including their armour, although we’ve yet to establish a precise function for the space.”

issues.title: Gallic cast coins found in northeastern France
issues.summary: A small hoard of coins has been discovered in a late Iron Age structure in Bure, northeastern France. They are Gallic coins that were cast in a mold rather than struck, and some of them have the casting shank still attached. A team from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (INRAP) found four … Read the full post → "Gallic cast coins found in northeastern France"
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A small hoard of coins has been discovered in a late Iron Age structure in Bure, northeastern France. They are Gallic coins that were cast in a mold rather than struck, and some of them have the casting shank still attached.

A team from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (INRAP) found four holes in the corners of a square: postholes, evidence of a structure built on posts on a rectangular floor plan. Along one of the long side, 28 coins were discovered in a small pit.

They are Gallic potins of a type known as an “Indian head” because it bears the profile of a man wearing a headband on the reverse. This is believed to be a highly stylized modification of a coin of Philip II of Macedon. Most of the coins bear the military standard of the wild boar with stiff back bristles over a small fleur-de-lis on the obverse. The “boar standard” potin is very common in northeastern France.

Archaeologists also found a small bronze wagon wheel 5 cm (two inches) in diameter. It is decorated with swirls. The purpose of these objects is unknown, but they are typically found in a votive context. The wheel points to the possibility that the structure had a religious function. The discovery of human ones in one of the postholes also suggests it may have been a sanctuary.

Despite their fragmentary state, the majority were skull bones (particularly the mandible). It is quite common for Gallic sanctuaries to yield human skulls, although they can also be found in domestic contexts. In the best-known examples, the sanctuaries are usually clearly demarcated by a deep ditch, as at Gournay-sur-Aronde (Oise) or Ribemont-sur-Ancre (Somme). However, perhaps due to erosion, the excavation did not reveal any demarcation system (fence, palisade, etc.). A geophysical survey was carried out a month after the fieldwork, but it failed to uncover any enclosure or other demarcation features.

If this is indeed a Gallic sanctuary, which subsequent research will attempt to verify, associated with a significant coin hoard discovered within its stratigraphic context, this archaeological occupation is unprecedented in the territory of the Leuci and very rare across Belgic Gaul.

issues.title: The Anthropic IPO Concerns Me
issues.summary: Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and ... Read more The post The Anthropic IPO Concerns Me appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for The New York Times, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “​Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game​,” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported (​including myself​), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like Less Wrong and Overcoming Bias, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. ​It’s exactly what they believe​.

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out ​my recent technical article​ for the IEEE Spectrum, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful ​AI Alert newsletter​.)

The post The Anthropic IPO Concerns Me appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: In Search of the Deep Life
issues.summary: Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up ... Read more The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​​more​​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is thekey that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

issues.title: The Good Thing About Hard Things
issues.summary: A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been ... Read more The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been attracting attention.

It explores an obvious question: do AI tools negatively affect your ability to think? It does so with a simple experimental design: participants were divided into two groups tasked with solving a series of math problems involving fractions. One group had to find answers on their own, while the other used ChatGPT to help.

At first, the ChatGPT group performed better, which is not surprising because LLMs are good at solving math problems. But then the researchers turned off the chatbot. Not only did the AI group’s accuracy fall below the control group, but many participants in the AI group gave up and started skipping questions altogether.

The researchers repeated the same experiment several more times, including one instance where math problems were replaced with an SAT reading comprehension prompt. They kept finding the same drop-offs in accuracy and persistence.

Here’s how ​a press release​ about the paper summarized these results:

“The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.”

Brian Christian, one of the paper’s authors, put it plainly: “You almost couldn’t ask for a clearer story.”

I’ve spent the last decade thinking and writing about how technologies might accidentally degrade our ​cognitive fitness​, and how this might in turn degrade not only our economic productivity, but also the quality of the human experience more generally.

In this sense, these LLM findings aren’t revealing something new.

What is new, however, is the jaw-dropping speed of these impacts. We’re accustomed to slow-moving techno-cognition trends such as the negative effects of ubiquitous smartphone usage, which took years to emerge in the data.

With chatbots, the negative impact is immediate. The high generated by side-stepping mental effort using LLMs is so compelling that, with only a short exposure, hard thinking quickly becomes intolerable.

The good news is that we don’t yet know if these effects are permanent. Presumably, the research participants who struggled immediately after ChatGPT was turned off might do much better on the same type of test if they tried again later in a setting where AI help was clearly not an option.

But we cannot ignore the warnings that these early studies are generating. When it comes to our cognitive fitness, we’re playing with a powerful new force that we don’t yet fully understand.

A key theme of my work in the technology critic space is that a life without serious, sustained, intentional thought is impoverished. Thinking is how we make sense of ourselves and the world, and is how we imagine new horizons and create the key elements of our future. It’s at the heart of philosophy, theology, and human empathy; the ability that separates our species from all other animals.

Silicon Valley is good at creating tools, but terrible at figuring out how we should use them. The latter step is still up to us — but it requires us to care.

The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs
issues.summary: Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior. It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ ... Read more The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior.

It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ and reports from OpenAI that try to establish how unnerving and powerful (not to mention ​felonious​) their LLM-powered agent systems have become.

They then handed the baton to Anthropic, whose employees began ​publicly debating​ the exact probability that these technologies would lead to human extinction. They delivered this all with an eerie calmness that conveyed a nihilistic inevitability about their work.

The ground suitably softened, the campaign crescendoed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodi releasing a letter, titled ​“We Must Pace the Frontier,”​ in which he enumerates all the harms his own company’s research might cause, and then, instead of apologizing and promising to stop, concludes that catastrophe can only be avoided if we “build the technology in the right way,” which involves – surprise, surprise – the government slowing down potential competitors and allowing the labs to take the lead in advancing the relevant tech. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly ​tweeted his support​ for this brave plan.

Internally, these labs have long embraced this style of messianic thinking, casting themselves as humanity’s only hope against the defied powers of superintelligent AI. This summer, in some sense, was their attempt to induct the rest of us into this long-held ideology.

It didn’t work.

Instead of inspiring the masses to stand up and applaud these engineers’ heroic rationalism, it made us instead start to ask, “What the hell is going on over in those labs?”

To that end, last Thursday ​I published an op-ed in TheNew York Times​ calling on Congress to begin a public fact-finding mission to uncover what research projects OpenAI and Anthropic are conducting, how they’re conducting them, and for what purposes.

I suggested three key areas to explore with this questioning:

  1. We must move past vague discussions of “AI” and instead isolate the specific types of systems that are creating problems. The frontier labs want us to think of AI as a singular technology on an inevitable, fixed trajectory. In reality, most of the problems in recent months result from a​ narrow band of incautious experiments​, conducted mainly by the frontier labs. They need to justify why they’re running them.
  2. We must examine the internal safety procedures surrounding these research efforts. ​OpenAI revealed​ a long series of unauthorized hacking attacks by their autonomous agents. Why weren’t these efforts stopped after the first such incident was revealed? Why not pursue criminal liability for them running systems they knew would likely commit crimes?
  3. We have to investigate the role of apocalyptic futurist ideologies in the decisions being made by the frontier labs, both about what research to pursue and how fast to pursue it. I’m increasingly concerned that OpenAI and Anthropic, in particular, are becoming increasingly reckless because they believe collateral damage is justified in a race to redeem humanity. (For more on these beliefs and their connections to the labs, see: ​this​ and ​this​ and ​this​, all published in the Times in just the last several weeks.)

“We need to stop letting a small number of private companies, acting and talking in increasingly erratic ways, dictate how we’re supposed to feel about A.I.,” I concluded. “We’ve heard what they want to say; now it’s Congress’s turn to step in on our behalf to find out what’s really going on.”

The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

What are Holafly Plans?


Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas. You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic eSIMs vs Plans


Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Here’s how it compares:

depending on monthly, quarterly, or annual payment plan $100–$300 / month ($10/day add-ons) $60–$120 / month (varies by region) Data Allowance Unlimited Capped at high speeds, then throttled Varies (usually 5GB–10GB packages) Hassle FactorZero. What about the Ultra Plan?

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

  • Luggage protection – If the airline loses or delays your checked bag, you get €150 within 24 hours of filing your claim. No receipts needed for what was in the bag. They’ll also help you recover up to €1,900 from the airline. (Amounts are also available in USD. Check the plan terms for the details.)
  • Flight claims – If your flight is delayed, cancelled or overbooked, they’ll review your case and handle the claim for you. You keep 100% of what’s recovered. No commission. (Heads up: this mainly applies to flights covered by EU and UK passenger rights rules, plus Brazil, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Most flights within the Americas and Asia aren’t covered.)
  • 24/7 doctor and pedriatics chat – You can chat with a real doctor or pediatrics (for those traveling with children) in English any time, day or night. This is great for figuring out whether that fever or stomach bug needs a hospital or just rest and water.
  • Unlimited video sessions with psychologists, nutritionists and personal trainers – Usually booked within 48 hours. If you’ve been on the road for months, you know loneliness and burnout are real. This is a nice thing to have in your back pocket.
  • Virtual Locations and an ad blocker (coming soon) – Safer browsing on hostel and café Wi-Fi.
  • Always On – Like the other Plans, you still get 1GB of free backup data every month for emergencies.

    • How much does it cost?
    Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly.
    For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

    So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

    If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

    Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

    How Plans Work and How to Subscribe

    Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

    1. Check compatibility – Most modern smartphones support eSIM, but it’s worth confirming yours does before you buy.
    2. Choose your plan – Head to the Holafly Plans page, pick Unlimited or Light, choose monthly, quarterly, or yearly billing, and complete your purchase. Heads up: your billing cycle starts the moment you pay, not the moment you land somewhere, so if you’re buying ahead of a trip, time it close to departure.
    3. Install the eSIM – You’ll get a QR code and an email guide, or you can install it directly through the Holafly app, which walks you through the whole thing in about two minutes.
    4. Turn on data roaming – when you land, activate the eSIM, and you’re connected. No local SIM shop, no border-crossing scramble.

    If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

    Who are Holafly Plans Actually For

    Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

    Pros and Cons

    Pros:

    • One eSIM covers 160+ destinations, no swapping at borders
    • True unlimited data and hotspot on the top tier, no throttling
    • Always On gives you free backup data for life, even after you cancel
    • Cancel anytime, no lock-in contract
    • Monthly, quarterly, or yearly billing, with real savings if you go yearly
    • No hidden fees, a 6-month refund policy, and real humans answering support
    • Setup takes about two minutes

    Cons:

    • Not the cheapest option if you’re staying in one country for a long stretch

issues.title: Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs
issues.summary: If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a...
