issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

So what do you do?

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

What is Nomad Citizen?

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Who can sign up?

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

How much does it cost?

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

What’s Included?

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage : Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance, you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support : You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

Making claims

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

***

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

issues.content_html:
We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

It’s available in all 50 states.

One Plan, Done Right

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

  • Trip cancellation and trip interruption
  • Emergency medical for non-U.S. travel (up to $250,000)
  • Emergency m edical evacuation (up to $500,000)
  • Trip cancellation (up to 100% of non-refundable trip costs)
  • Trip interruption (up to 150% of non-refundable trip costs)
  • Trip delay (up to $2,100/trip ($300/day) after a 6+ hour delay)
  • Missed connection (up to $200, after a 3+ hour covered delay)
  • Non-medical emergency evacuation (up to $100,000)
  • Lost, stolen, or damaged belongings (up to $2,000/trip (capped at $150/item))

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

  • Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) – up to 75% of nonrefundable trip costs reimbursed, if you buy it within 14 days of your initial trip deposit and cancel up to 48 hours prior to your departure date
  • Rental car damage – covers collision, theft, vandalism, natural disasters
  • Adventure and extreme sports – for the bungee jumpers, free divers, and skydivers
  • Vacation rental damage – for the inevitable spilled wine on someone’s Airbnb couch
  • Pet care – vet expenses up to $2K if your pet is traveling with you, kennel costs if you get delayed coming home

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

All About the App

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Filing a Claim

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

What It Costs

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

****

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

issues.title: Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life
issues.summary: Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand... The post Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture,
issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Day 1: Immersion in the Art Walk


This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

Day 2: The Grandeur of the Historic Center


The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Day 3: Culinary Discovery


Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Day 4: UNESCO World Heritage Wonders


Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

Day 5: Off-the-Beaten-Path Treasures


On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

***

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

issues.summary: The post OBSBOT Tail Air 2 Advances Professional Video Production with 1-Inch 4K Imaging – Announced appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . Combining 1-inch 4K imaging, AI-powered shooting and flexible production capabilities, the compact PTZR camera makes professional-quality production simpler and more adaptable. OBSBOT, an industry leader in smart videography t
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post OBSBOT Tail Air 2 Advances Professional Video Production with 1-Inch 4K Imaging – Announced appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Combining 1-inch 4K imaging, AI-powered shooting and flexible production capabilities, the compact PTZR camera makes professional-quality production simpler and more adaptable.

OBSBOT, an industry leader in smart videography technology, has officially unveiled their OBSBOT Tail Air 2, an AI-powered PTZR camera designed for flexible video production. Combining a 1-inch CMOS sensor, 4K/60 imaging, OBSBOT Log, and Custom 3D LUTs, Tail Air 2 delivers professional-quality imaging with greater control over color and detail. AI Tracking 2.0, upgraded AI Director Grids, and automated camera movements reduce manual operation, while motorized PTZR, uncropped vertical 4K/60 recording, and native IP connectivity allow creators to adapt to different shooting setups, content formats, and multi-camera workflows.

Why would a traditional photography website be talking about this camera?

As well as being a very well-specced unit, based on my experience using the baby version of this new PTZR camera over the last year, I reckon this is going to be a beast!

But what could you actually do with it for your photography business clients?

Think about all the content you’re probably already creating, or should be creating. As a solo operator, you could use it to capture behind-the-scenes content, record workshops, produce tutorials, create social media videos, document client shoots or even livestream an event. And you can do all of that without needing another person behind the camera.

For photographers running workshops or teaching online, there’s another interesting angle. Imagine having a camera that can follow you around a room, automatically frame the action and capture multiple perspectives while you concentrate on actually teaching. It’s another pair of hands, without having to put someone on the payroll.

And that’s really why I think this sort of technology deserves a place in a photography conversation. The business of photography has changed. We’re not just making photographs anymore; we’re building brands, creating content and finding new ways to connect with clients. Tools that help us do more, without necessarily needing more people or equipment, are worth paying attention to.

“Creators shouldn’t have to choose between image quality, creative control, and production efficiency,” said Liu Bo, CEO of OBSBOT. “With Tail Air 2, we’re bringing these capabilities together, making professional-quality video production simpler and giving creators more freedom to focus on their content.”

A 1-Inch Sensor That Brings More to Every Frame

Tail Air 2 features a 1-inch CMOS sensor with 3.2 ?m pixels, an f/1.9 aperture, and an eight-element optical lens. It captures detailed 4K footage at up to 60fps and 1080p video at up to 120fps, enabling creators to shoot crisp talking-head videos, capture fast-moving action, and produce smooth slow-motion footage in post-production.

A dedicated AI imaging chip achieves superior low-light performance by reducing noise while preserving fine details in low light. LOFIC HDR technology supports up to 13 stops of dynamic range at frame rates up to 30fps, helping retain detail in bright highlights and dark shadows. For fast-changing scenes, All-Pixel Phase Detection Autofocus (PDAF) offers Global Focus, Foreground Focus and Face Focus modes for everything from group conversations to product close-ups. Sensitivity reaches ISO 25,600 when HDR is disabled.

More Professional Control Over the Final Look with OBSBOT Log

Tail Air 2 introduces OBSBOT Log, the company’s proprietary 8-bit Log recording profile and the first of its kind in an OBSBOT camera. By retaining tonal information across highlights and shadows, it provides greater latitude for color grading and post-production adjustments, giving creators more control over how their footage looks.

Custom 3D LUT support lets creators preview different color treatments through OBSBOT Center, Obsbot Start and Obsbot Live. They can explore a preferred look while filming or streaming, then make their final color adjustments in the edit. These previews help them decide on the visual direction before applying their final color grade in post-production.

AI Tracking That Follows Your Story

Whether a creator is teaching, demonstrating a product or presenting alone, Tail Air 2 is designed to keep the camera focused on the action with less manual intervention. AI Tracking 2.0 recognizes people, more than 30 animal species, and over 200 object categories. Users can simply double-click a subject or draw a selection box on the control interface to tell the camera what to track.

Beyond recognizing and following a subject, AI Tracking 2.0 also adjusts framing to suit different shooting scenarios. Single-Person Tracking maintains focus on the selected subject, even when they are briefly obscured, and reacquires them when they return. Group Tracking adjusts the camera angle and framing as people move or enter and leave the shot, maintaining a balanced composition. Face Framing leaves sufficient space in the direction a subject faces, while Auto Zoom maintains the selected full-body, medium or close-up framing as the distance changes.

Creators can further tailor how the camera responds by adjusting tracking speed, selecting a single movement axis, setting active tracking zones and customizing subject positioning within the frame. Upgraded AI Director Grids bring these controls together, allowing creators to switch between AI Tracking, Preset, and Launchpad together in one intuitive interface. Gesture Control adds another layer of hands-free operation, allowing users to control tracking, zoom and recording from up to five meters away.

Together, these capabilities help creators manage subject tracking, framing and camera movements within a single workflow, making it easier to produce multi-shot content without a dedicated camera operator.

More Than PTZ: Creative Movement and Native Vertical 4K

Tail Air 2 expands traditional PTZ camera movement by introducing a dedicated Roll axis, adding rotation to its Pan, Tilt, and Zoom capabilities. This PTZR architecture gives creators more ways to control camera orientation, movement, and framing.

Launchpad 2.0 makes these creative camera movements easier to execute and repeat, with eight preset camera movements and two customizable modes that allow creators to tailor camera motion to their production needs. The Roll axis also enables an Auto Leveling System that automatically corrects camera orientation to keep the horizon level, even when the camera is mounted on an uneven surface.

For vertical content, Tail Air 2 physically rotates its lens module 90 degrees to capture native vertical 4K video at up to 60fps, without cropping the sensor’s full imaging area. This allows creators to switch between landscape and vertical formats while retaining the full resolution of each shot.

Together, PTZR movement and native vertical imaging give creators more control over camera movement and framing across different production formats, from livestreams and long-form videos to vertical social content.

Designed for Modern Production Workflows and Multi-Camera Setups

Built around a native IP architecture, Tail Air 2 integrates into a wide range of production environments. It supports SRT, RTSP and RTMP protocols, along with NDI®|HX3 through the NDI-enabled version or a separately purchased license, with Wi-Fi 6 and wired Ethernet connectivity for network-based video transmission. VISCA, OSC, Stream Deck integration and an Open SDK further support camera control and customized workflows.

For more direct production setups, Tail Air 2 offers a 3.5mm audio input, Micro HDMI output and two USB-C ports for power and data. It also supports local recording to microSD cards up to 1TB, alongside its built-in microphone and Bluetooth connectivity with OBSBOT wireless microphone Vox SE.

Tail Air 2 also features a built-in 2,630mAh battery, delivering up to 205 minutes of operation at 1080P/30fps, with USB PD 3.0 fast charging support.

For multi-camera productions, Tail Air 2 supports Timecode and Precision Time Protocol (PTP) synchronization. With compatible external timecode equipment, recordings from multiple cameras can be aligned more easily in post-production, while PTP helps maintain synchronized timing across networked devices.

Full Details: https://www.obsbot.com/obsbot-tail-air-2-streaming-camera

We will have a review coming on the new gear from OBSBOT, stay tuned!

A new locking filter system from Freewell and

issues.content_html:
The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!)

A new locking filter system from Freewell and photographer and filmmaker Dunna Did It combines magnetic attachment with a mechanical locking mechanism, allowing photographers to share filters across lenses with different thread sizes.

Freewell has teamed up with photographer, filmmaker and YouTube creator Dunna Did It to launch a new modular camera filter system designed to make switching filters between lenses quicker and easier.

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System uses a combination of magnetic attachment and a mechanical locking mechanism. Rather than needing a separate set of filters for every lens, photographers can use a single collection of filters across lenses with thread sizes ranging from 49mm to 95mm, simply by changing the base ring.

The system is available in two configurations: a Videography Kit aimed at filmmakers and hybrid creators, and a Photography Kit designed primarily for still photographers.

One filter system for multiple lenses

Anyone with a growing collection of lenses will know that filter sizes can quickly become a bit of a headache. Even when lenses have similar focal lengths, their filter thread sizes can vary, potentially leaving you with multiple versions of the same ND or polarising filter.

Freewell’s new system aims to address that problem by separating the filter itself from the lens mounting ring.

A dedicated base ring attaches to each lens, with the filters then transferred between compatible rings. Magnets help guide the filter into position, before a short clockwise turn engages the mechanical lock.

The system supports ten filter thread sizes: 49mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm, 82mm, 86mm and 95mm.

There are a few other interesting details worth noting:

  • Ultra-slim design: The fixed ND filters measure just 2.95mm thick and weigh 18.4g, helping minimise additional bulk and weight, particularly useful for handheld and gimbal-based video work.
  • Magnetic attachment with mechanical locking: Magnets help position the filter, while a short clockwise twist locks it in place.
  • Colour accuracy: Freewell says the filters are designed to minimise colour shifts, helping maintain natural-looking skin tones, greens and skies.
  • Stackable filters: Compatible filters can be used individually or stacked to combine different effects, including exposure control, reflection reduction and diffusion.

Two kits for different creative needs

The system launches with two kits, each offering a different selection of filters.

Videography Kit

Designed with filmmakers and hybrid shooters in mind, the Videography Kit includes:

  • ND4 (2-stop)
  • ND8 (3-stop)
  • ND16 (4-stop)
  • ND32 (5-stop)
  • Glow Mist 1/4

The kit also includes a selected base ring, protective caps (including one with built-in reference targets) and a fitted carry case.

The range of ND filters provides exposure control across different lighting conditions, while the Glow Mist filter adds a diffusion option for video and still photography.

Photography Kit

The Photography Kit takes a slightly different approach, with a selection of filters aimed at everyday photography and longer exposures.

It includes:

  • UV filter
  • ND64 (6-stop)
  • ND1000 (10-stop)
  • CPL (circular polariser)
  • Glow Mist 1/8

As with the Videography Kit, it comes with a selected base ring, protective caps and a fitted carry case.

The combination covers lens protection, reflection control, long exposures and a touch of diffusion without requiring multiple filter systems.

Developed in collaboration with Dunna Did It

The system was developed over nearly a year in collaboration with Dunna Did It, a photographer, filmmaker and music producer based on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

With an audience of more than 440,000 YouTube subscribers, Dunna regularly creates photography and video content, including gear reviews and tutorials.

The collaboration focused on refining the physical design and practical workflow of the system, including its locking mechanism, overall profile and ease of use when moving between lenses.

Pricing and availability

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System launched online on 26 August 2026.

Both the Photography Kit and Videography Kit have a launch price of US$299.99, reduced from the regular retail price of US$349.99.

Customers choose a base ring to suit their existing lens, with additional ring sizes available for use across the rest of their lens collection.

For more information, visit the Freewell product page or watch Dunna’s product introduction video on YouTube.

issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

issues.title: ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050
issues.summary: Sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa’s coastal “megacities” to flooding by… The post ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050 appeared first on Carbon Brief .
issues.author: Ayesha Tandon
issues.content_html:
Sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa’s coastal “megacities” to flooding by the middle of the century, according to new research.

The analysis, published in Science Advances, combines satellite data with projections of sea level rise to assess the risk of flooding in 20 of Africa’s most populous coastal cities.

The study finds that, under a moderate warming scenario, an “extreme sea level event” – when sea levels are unusually high due to short-term changes in weather and ocean conditions – could expose a million buildings and $180bn of assets to flooding.

Lagos, the capital of Nigeria, and Alexandria in Egypt are the most vulnerable cities in the analysis.

In these two cities alone, five million people and $150bn in assets could be exposed to flooding and the cities by mid-century.

Human activity, such as pumping groundwater or drilling for fossil fuels, can cause the ground to sink, in a process called “subsidence”.

Seismic or volcanic activity can also drive changes in the height of the land, causing it to either rise or fall. This “vertical land movement” can either alleviate or exacerbate the effects of sea level rise.

The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa’s coastline to determine how quickly different regions are rising or sinking.

Membership

Connect with our community

Join CB+

They identified Lagos and Alexandria as “subsidence hotspots”, finding that the two cities are sinking at rates of 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year, respectively.

This is “comparable to rates reported for south-east Asian megacities such as Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City”, which have recorded “some of the highest subsidence rates yet observed”, according to the study.

The authors combined these estimates with sea level rise projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report under three different emissions scenarios, to assess the regional sea level rise across the African coastline.

They used 2020 population data, building footprints and GDP per capita to estimate how much of each city would be exposed to these flooding events over the 21st century, if the city itself stays the same.

While Lagos and Alexandria are the most vulnerable cities, the research finds that Djibouti City in Djibouti, Mogadishu in Somalia and Tripoli in Libya will face “minimal economic exposure due to their smaller populations and infrastructure bases”.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho, a PhD student at Virginia Tech, tells Carbon Brief that the analysis holds population and city data constant at 2020 levels, so that the authors can isolate the effects of sea level rise and vertical land movement on changing flood exposure.

He notes that if people move away from “threatened areas” over the coming decades, then estimates could be too high. However, if “continued urban growth” causes city populations to increase, the estimates could be too low.

Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing at an average rate of 3.5% every year. By 2050, Africa’s urban population is expected to double from 7m to 1.4bn.

He also notes that “the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, so the estimates are a worst-case physical picture”.

Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored in the past, largely due to a lack of local data, the study explains.

The authors say their method of using satellites to assess subsidence and uplift could be used in other “data-­scarce coastal regions across the global south”.

Dasho, O., et al (2026), Sinking cities: Latent flood risk in Africa’s coastal megacities, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh6538

issues.title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
issues.summary: COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its… The post Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? appeared first on Carbon Brief .
issues.author: Carbon Brief Staff
issues.content_html:
Article Contents Expand menu Close

  • What has the reaction to the presidency been?
  • How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?
  • How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?
  • How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?
  • How has the role of China been portrayed?
  • What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?
  • Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?

COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels.

The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world.

Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “failure”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “divided world”.

COP31 coverage

  • COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes
  • COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
  • Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
  • Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
  • Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
  • Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
  • Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit

There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “oil-rich nations”, while others blame Europe’s “reluctance” to provide more climate finance.

While it is not accurate to say there was “no agreement” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference.

In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.

  • What happened at COP31?

  • What has the reaction to the presidency been?

  • How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?

  • How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?

  • How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?

  • How has the role of China been portrayed?

  • What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?

  • Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?

What happened at COP31?

COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency.

The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days.

An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.

This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.

As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect, the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.

Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”.

Membership

Connect with our community

Join CB+

They noted that there was “progress in a few areas” at COP31, including negotiations on supporting a just transition via a “phased approach” and “improving alignment in climate adaptation”.

For a full overview of what happened at COP31 – both inside and outside the negotiations – see Carbon Brief’s “key outcomes” article.

What has the reaction to the presidency been?

In the aftermath of COP31, commentators have critiqued decisions made by the presidency. An editorial in the Hindu noted that “usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations”, but said the COP31 leadership “thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings”.

Australian “president of negotiations” Chris Bowen has also faced criticism over how he managed competing interests at the summit. An editorial in the climate-sceptic Australian said:

“One thing is clear: Chris Bowen, who presided over Australia’s $150m investment in the conference, has some explaining to do. International reporting has raised questions about Australia and Turkey, the two nations that co-hosted the summit. Some negotiators have criticised their handling of the talks.”

Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.

For Australian news outlet Crikey, journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”.

A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”.

Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.

How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?

In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.

Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”.

After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance. The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said.

A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”.

In the i newspaper, David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process:

“This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.”

Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman:

“At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.”

Writing for the Guardian, University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera, York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”.

(Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.)

In Australian outlet Inside Story, the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28, fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.

Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald, noted:

“The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.”

At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.

The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”.

In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added:

“Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.”

How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?

Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels.

A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times.

Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”.

Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press, wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.)

Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:

“European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.”

Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”.

An editorial in the Hindu stressed:

“It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.”

Writing in US outlet Drilled, reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”.

Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record.

Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded:

“It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.”

How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?

Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31.

A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”.

It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme.

Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31.

Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”.

Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance.

Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”.

Inter Press Service, a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”.

An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding:

“The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.”

Indeed, some developing countries sided with developed countries in blocking the final passage of the Antalya pact.

The Fiji Times reported that Fiji “held the line in the final negotiating rooms”, joining the EU, the UK and several other Pacific countries in “refus[ing] to endorse a weakened compromise that avoided to mention fossil fuels [sic]”. It added:

“Yet standing on principle carries heavy practical consequences…COP31’s breakdown is a sobering reminder that, while Fiji must keep fighting in global arenas, its sharpest shield remains regional solidarity and rapid, resilient action at home.”

How has the role of China been portrayed?

Major Chinese news outlets largely portrayed China as a constructive participant in the COP31 negotiations, a defender of multilateralism and an active advocate for international climate cooperation.

State news agency Xinhua reported that “China acted responsibly and advanced the conference process, earning widespread recognition from all parties”.

State broadcaster CCTV similarly said that the “international community recognised the positive role China played in addressing climate change”.

People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, reported that China played a “constructive role” in building consensus and promoting cooperation. It quoted COP31 president Murat Kurum as saying that China was a “key participant” in the multilateral climate process and that its support was “crucial to the summit”.

State news agency China News Service said that China demonstrated “ability to act” amid divisions at COP31, highlighting China’s participation in negotiations and initiatives on international cooperation in carbon credits and its climate actions in the global south.

Financial newspaper 21st Century Business Herald said that the Chinese delegation “actively participated in negotiations across all agenda items” and highlighted China’s efforts to advance practical cooperation on climate change.

Three of China’s main state media outlets, Xinhua, CCTV and People’s Daily, covered the COP31 outcome.

Xinhua said that climate multilateralism “moves forward under pressure” as COP31 concluded without a deal.

Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper reported that China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were among the parties “willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text”.

CCTV reported that, although COP31 ended without adopting an “outcome document”, this did not mean international climate action had “come to a halt” or that previously agreed climate agreements and international promises would “automatically become invalid”.

State-run newspapers China Daily and the Global Times both published editorials on COP31.

China Daily argued that the COP31 “impasse” underscored the “need to strengthen multilateral cooperation”. It continued that China was “committed to addressing the climate crisis through real action.”

The Global Times editorial, meanwhile, responded to criticism that China was “unwilling to take the lead”. It said:

“With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?”

Regarding China’s role at COP31, several western news outlets’ coverage focused on its approach to climate diplomacy, trade and the proposed final agreement.

Ahead of the summit’s conclusion, Reuters cited diplomats and observers in reporting that China’s envoys to COP31 stuck to the country’s “accustomed low-key playbook”.

The Financial Times reported that China used the climate talks to “complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products”.

On the final day of the summit, the Guardian said that China was among the parties that “did not object to the deal”.

Bloomberg also reported that while Chinese diplomats maintained a “relatively low profile”, its “world-leading” companies featured in China pavilion events.

Bloomberg continued:

“At a United Nations climate conference that was low on delivery and high on dysfunction, China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions.”

What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?

In the aftermath of COP31, many commentators have called for a reform of the COP process.

The European Commission is “drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties”, according to Euronews.

Many other commentators shared the view that the COP process must be reformed.

Marco Lambertini, convenor of the Nature Positive Initiative, said in Reuters:

“We must be clear: reform remains essential. COPs are cumbersome, expensive, bureaucratic, environmentally unfriendly and frustratingly slow. The consensus rule – adopted in the climate and nature conferences – allows a handful of countries to dilute ambition in the main plenary deliberations. Too often, fossil fuel and agrochemical lobbies interfere with negotiations and obstruct progress. This must change.”

Similarly, York University’s Kapoor said in Al Jazeera that the current system results in “an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do”.

The Associated Press’ Prengaman wrote that “reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size”.

The Independent’s climate correspondent, Nick Ferris, said the “collapse” of the talks “represents a shocking nadir in the history of COPs”, adding that “the process requires urgent reform”.

Similarly, Pilita Clark, the Financial Times associate editor and business columnist, said “the disaster that was the climate gathering in Antalya should prompt overdue reform”.

Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time, likened this year’s summit to the 2009 COP in Copenhagen. He added:

“Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement. Today, there’s another opportunity for reinvention.”

(For more on COP reform, see Carbon Brief’s interviews with 16 experts on the topic.)

Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?

While many editorials lamented the failure of COP31 to agree on the Antalya pact, there were various articles that highlighted a more positive view.

In the Guardian, Dr Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, wrote that COP31 was “a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no”.

He continued:

“The [cover decision that parties] rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.”

Others shared the view that numerous countries rejecting the cover decision due to its failure to mention fossil fuels could be seen as a significant moment of pushback.

In an interview in Le Monde, Prof Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, said that it is “better to have this kind of crisis and to do something good with it, rather than having a watered-down agreement”. He added:

“It will have a very positive signal: It means that the world is taking risks seriously. The world is taking science seriously.”

An editorial in Bloomberg stated that COP31 should “serve as a call for action”, pushing like-minded governments to continue working together to make progress. It added:

“The outcome at COP31, discouraging as it was, strongly suggests that much of the world remains committed to fighting climate change. More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration that – amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil-fuel producers – omitted any reference to the transition away from fossil fuels.”

In Reuters, columnist Antony Currie wrote that the failure to adopt the cover decision could in fact be “healthy”. Elsewhere, in Inside Story, the University of Sheffield’s Jacobs argued that “this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed”.

COP31 came to a dramatic conclusion nearly 50 hours after its scheduled close – making it the longest COP in history.

Less than 24 hours later, Carbon Brief published its 21,000-word summary, capturing everything that happened in the negotiations, the cover decision and more.

issues.author: Carbon Brief Staff
issues.content_html:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.

The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.

Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.

COP31 coverage

  • COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
  • CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes
  • COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions

  • Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit

The COP ran nearly 50 hours over time, but did not end with substantive outcomes on several key topics.

For the second year in a row, negotiations on agriculture and food security broke down and will now have to resume next year.

Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened by the explicit inclusion of “agroecology” in a decision within the “just transition work programme”.

Ocean-conservation groups noted an increased focus on ocean-climate links at this year’s COP, but said COP31 did not live up to its promise of being a “blue COP”.

There was also scant new funding for food systems and nature, with just a handful of small pledges to ocean initiatives and two newly announced contributions to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.

Here, Carbon Brief analyses all of the key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at COP31 – both inside and out of the negotiating rooms.
