issues.title: How George Orwell Exposed The Hypocrisy of the British Empire
issues.summary: Years before he used his literary talents to take on totalitarianism, George Orwell initially set his sights on colonialism. From profound first-hand experience in Burma, his political views were shaped, and in his first novel, Burmese Days, he took on the ills of British colonial rule with its brutality and injustice. How British […]
issues.author: Armando Cataldi
issues.content_html:
Years before he used his literary talents to take on totalitarianism, George Orwell initially set his sights on colonialism. From profound first-hand experience in Burma, his political views were shaped, and in his first novel, Burmese Days, he took on the ills of British colonial rule with its brutality and injustice.

How British Rule Devastated Burma Under the Guise of Progress

In 1885, a British army led by Sir Harry Prendergast captured Mandalay, the capital city of Burma’s Konbaung Dynasty. The capture marked the end of the Third Anglo-Burmese War, and the beginning of Burma’s time as a British Colony. By 1886, King Thibaw Min had been exiled, and the country was officially made a province of British India.

British colonialism had catastrophic effects on Burmese society. While colonialism claimed to uplift the natives, in reality it was a highly exploitative undertaking. Traditional Burmese governance was disregarded, and the native people were governed by laws that they had no say in creating. While Burmese rice made British merchants rich, the farmers who cultivated it remained impoverished because they were forced into exploitative labor.

When Indian laborers arrived to work on British agricultural projects, many Burmese farmers lost their farms. This led to destitute Burmese becoming bandits, making the countryside more dangerous than ever. The chaos caused by bandits and holdover rebels led the British army to pursue a scorched-earth policy—all rebels and bandits were to be vigorously pursued. Any village that had given them shelter was destroyed.

George Orwell’s Real-Life Crisis of Conscience in Burma

While Orwell would one day write the greatest dystopian epic in the English language, in 1922 he was still known as Eric Blair and had just joined the Indian Imperial Police

Upon taking an assignment in Burma, Orwell developed a negative opinion of the British Empire’s actions in the country. Many of his countrymen held racist beliefs against the Burmese. This greatly disturbed Orwell, who respected Burmese culture, and he even went on to learn the language.

His relationship with the natives was no better. As an imperial policeman, he held life-and-death power over the Burmese, something that the anti-authoritarian Orwell despised. Furthermore, the natives held considerable contempt for Orwell despite his feelings. They viewed him simply as one of their oppressors, and he would often hear their insults when his back was turned.

The entire colonial system disgusted Orwell. In 1927, he resigned his commission and returned to England, where his thoughts on colonialism and exploitation circulated through his mind. This led to his debut novel, Burmese Days.

How Orwell Channeled His Colonial Guilt Into Burmese Days

The main character of Burmese Days is John Flory, a British teak merchant in 1920s Burma and Orwell’s literary alter ego. Like Orwell, Flory speaks Burmese and has a great appreciation for Burmese culture. However, he is stuck living a miserable existence. His only contact with the Burmese is when he is ordering his servants around, as he is not brave enough to cross racial lines and consort with them as equals. The presence of the few Britons in the country is no consolation either, as they are extremely prejudiced against the natives, and spend most of their time wallowing in drunken misery at the local European club.

His only positive interactions are discussions with his friend, Dr. Veraswami, a naive doctor who believes that British colonialism is beneficial to the natives. Flory, in contrast, sees the racism and exploitation that is endemic to colonialism. Flory spends much time with his Burmese mistress, Ma Hla May. Because he gives her presents, she mistakenly considers herself to be Flory’s wife, a union that Flory can never entertain.

The main villain of the story is U Po Kyin, a corrupt Burmese official who is more than willing to destroy his enemies’ reputations in order to increase his own. As Flory’s European club comes under pressure to admit one native as a member, Dr. Veraswami emerges as the lead candidate. The jealous U Po Kyin desires the honor and sets out to destroy the doctor’s reputation. When Flory does not support his admittance, U Po Kyin sets his sights on the Englishman as well.

U Po Kyin achieves his goal at the end of the novel. After helping to put down an anti-British riot, Flory has impressed a European bride and is preparing to marry. This news devastates the discarded Ma Hla May. She is then approached by U Po Kyin, who instructs her to barge into an English church service and reveal in detail her affair with Flory.

Completely shunned by the European community after the incident, the despondent Englishman commits suicide. U Po Kyin is elected to the European Club and decorated, but he dies of apoplexy before he can build the pagodas meant to balance out his negative karma, leaving his wife to fear that he will return as a frog or a rat.

The novel’s dark ending aptly reflects Orwell’s views on colonialism. Exploitation and racism were tenets of the colonial project in Burma that left many scars on the nation. Not the least of these was the destruction of Burma’s forests, a crisis that continues to this day.

issues.title: 6 Greatest Ancient Mysteries That No One Has Ever Solved
issues.summary: While we like to think we know a lot about history, especially with scientific advances in how we investigate the past, much of the past still refuses to give up its secrets. There are distinct “black holes” in our knowledge where we encounter things that we just can’t make sense of. These are the […]
issues.author: Caleb Howells
issues.content_html:
While we like to think we know a lot about history, especially with scientific advances in how we investigate the past, much of the past still refuses to give up its secrets. There are distinct “black holes” in our knowledge where we encounter things that we just can’t make sense of. These are the world’s oldest unsolved mysteries. Discover six of the world’s greatest mysteries, from lost languages to monolithic structures that should never have been built to technology that should never have existed.

1. The Phaistos Disc: The World’s Most Famous Cipher

There are many undeciphered scripts from the ancient world. However, the Phaistos Disc is probably the single most famous example of a cipher which continues to evade understanding. This is an ancient, Bronze Age object found on Crete, dating to about the 17th century BC. It is a fired clay disc with 242 symbols stamped in a spiral pattern from the outer edge right through to the center.

Why has this posed such a problem for researchers? The key issue is that the symbols on the Phaistos Disc do not correspond to any other known script. Given that it comes from Bronze Age Crete, we might be forgiven for assuming that it was written in Linear A, the script of the Minoans, or Linear B, the script of the Mycenaean Greeks. However, examination of the symbols shows that it fits neither of those scripts. This makes it all the more mysterious.

Beyond the simple fact that we cannot read it, this uniqueness adds to the mystery. Why is this the only artifact archaeologists have uncovered on Crete written in this script? Why was it not used elsewhere?

There are different theories about what the Phaistos Disc is and what it says. One theory is that it contains a prayer to a Minoan mother goddess. Another is that it was a solar calendar. This might explain why we do not see this script anywhere else. Another theory is that it is not a script at all, and that the disc is part of an ancient board game.

2. The Bronze Age Collapse: Why Did Everything Stop?

Undoubtedly one of the most famous mysteries of antiquity is the sudden and dramatic end of the Bronze Age. The Bronze Age Collapse, which occurred from around 1220 to 1170 BC, saw the simultaneous end or severe decline of several major civilizations around the Mediterranean. For example, the Hittite Empire collapsed, as did the Mycenaean Greek civilization. New Kingdom Egypt survived, but the extent of its domain contracted significantly over the next few generations. This widespread, simultaneous societal breakdown involved the end of literacy in ancient Greece, the burning of major power centers across the eastern Mediterranean, and the collapse of international trade.

To this day, no one knows what exactly caused the Bronze Age Collapse. How could there have been such a major societal collapse at the same time across the entire eastern Mediterranean? If it was caused by internal factors, such as rebellions and civil wars, then how could such things have occurred simultaneously in completely separate regions?

Many theories have been put forward to explain this mystery. Commonly, it is thought to have been caused by a perfect storm of multiple different factors. Internal uprisings might have been involved, but these may have been motivated by widespread environmental issues, such as famines, droughts, and even a series of major earthquakes. There is fierce debate over the role of the Sea Peoples in the disaster. These were people recorded by the Egyptians as causing havoc in the eastern Mediterranean at precisely the time of the Bronze Age Collapse. However, were they actually a cause, or just a symptom? Scholars continue to debate this.

3. Linear A: The Silent Language of the Minoans

Another major Bronze Age mystery also involves the Minoans. As mentioned earlier, they used a script which we now call Linear A. This was in use from approximately 1800 BC to about 1450 BC. It ceased to be used when the Mycenaean Greeks conquered Crete, at which point it was replaced by their Linear B script.

The two scripts share significant similarities. In fact, scholars now understand that Linear B was actually an adaptation of Linear A. On the face of it, that might make it seem easy to decipher. After all, linguists have already deciphered Linear B, which was used to write an early form of Greek. Since one was directly based on the other, there are many symbols which are common to both Linear A and Linear B, albeit with stylistic differences. This means that we can read, in terms of identifying the phonetic value, much of Linear A.

Unfortunately, this has not helped very much. For one thing, not all symbols in Minoan Linear A have equivalents in Greek Linear B. However, more significantly, we cannot understand the language of the Minoans. When linguists read Linear A inscriptions using the phonetic values revealed by Linear B, the resultant words and phrases do not correspond to any other known language family.

There are many theories as to what language Linear A was written in. Individual researchers have tried to link it to Egyptian, Tyrrhenian, Hittite, and various other languages, but none of them have proved convincing to the majority of experts. For now, the language of the Minoans is still a complete mystery.

4. Göbekli Tepe: The Temple Before the Farm

Göbekli Tepe is a different kind of mystery. This is a major archaeological site in Turkey, made up of numerous large stone structures. This site has captured the attention of researchers around the globe for the remarkable way in which it seems to contradict the established timeline of humanity. It was long described as the world’s first temple. Based on scientific dating methods, archaeologists believe that it was constructed some 12,000 years ago.

However, its significance goes beyond simply the fact that it is possibly the oldest temple ever discovered. What makes it especially significant is that the date archaeologists have assigned to it, 9000 BC, is earlier than the Neolithic Revolution. This is the name assigned to the period in which agriculture was first developed. Since 2015, however, excavators have found houses, hearths, workshops and rainwater cisterns, which suggests a settled community of hunter-gatherers that lived beside the monumental enclosures. It shows that people built on a monumental scale before farming took hold, though the old “temple before the town” idea is now disputed.

Another reason why this is so intriguing is that it raises the question of how a society of hunter-gatherers was physically able to build Göbekli Tepe. It would have required a high degree of coordination and effort to build. A massive labor force must have been necessary. How did a pre-agricultural society achieve this?

5. The Copper Scroll: A Map to Nowhere?

One of the greatest historical finds of the 20th century was undoubtedly the chance discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls. These ancient scrolls from about 2,000 years ago have significantly increased historians’ understanding of ancient Jewish belief and the development of the Hebrew Scriptures. However, they have also raised a new mystery. One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, found in 1952, was made out of copper. This makes it unique among the scrolls. This Copper Scroll is fascinating not only because it was made from metal rather than parchment, but also because it contains an inventory of buried treasure.

In other words, the Copper Scroll appears to be a treasure map. It describes 64 different locations in which vast amounts of gold, silver, and other valuable items are supposedly hidden. It would be easy to dismiss this as a fictional literary work. However, there is reason for giving it serious consideration.

For one thing, the very fact that it was written on metal means that it would have been expensive, difficult, and time-consuming to produce. Would someone really go to such expensive lengths for a fiction? Perhaps, but it seems unlikely. Furthermore, the treasure itself has a perfectly plausible origin.

The Copper Scroll seems to originate from the first century AD. At that time, the nearby Temple of Jerusalem was immensely wealthy. Some of the specific items mentioned in the Copper Scroll’s inventory point to a priestly origin. This is consistent with the conclusion that the treasure came from the Temple. Additionally, the Romans attacked and ultimately destroyed Jerusalem in that same century, although not without plenty of warning. This provides a plausible historical reason for why the Temple’s riches would have been taken and hidden.

Yet, no one has ever been able to use the directions given in the Copper Scroll to actually find any of the treasure. So, the mystery continues.

6. The Roman Dodecahedrons: The Ancient “What-Is-It?”

One final mystery from the ancient world is the mystery of the Roman Dodecahedrons. These are small metal objects, made from copper, in the shape of a dodecahedron with a small knob at each corner. They are hollow and have holes of varying sizes in their sides. They have mostly been found in Gaul, with others from Britain and the Rhine frontier, often in military or funerary contexts.

These unusual objects have no obvious purpose. They do not appear in any ancient art, nor are they mentioned in any ancient Roman texts. For this reason, it is a complete mystery as to what they were. All sorts of theories have been put forward. One theory is that they were designed to hold candles. Another is that they were used for estimating distances, although the lack of any markings on them argues against this. The suggestion that they were a child’s toy does not seem compatible with the military and funerary contexts in which many of them were found. A popular theory emerged online that they were used for spool knitting. However, the Roman dodecahedrons predate spool knitting by over 1,000 years, and they do not show wear marks around the knobs.

Many scholars believe that they had some kind of religious function. While this does seem like the best guess, this is not very specific. Their exact meaning and purpose are still heavily debated.

Why Some Mysteries Stay Unsolved

The Rosetta Stone facilitated the deciphering of Egyptian hieroglyphs, which revolutionized our understanding of ancient Egyptian history. What made this so singularly effective was that it was a bilingual stone inscription. This essentially provided the “key” to deciphering what was previously a mystery. This is what is missing in the case of mysteries like the Phaistos Disc and Linear A. We lack a Rosetta Stone to provide us the key to the cipher.

However, with the use of artificial intelligence, some undeciphered scripts may soon be demystified. This is because AI can be used to find patterns in scripts where humans might miss them. It remains to be seen just how effective this is.

Of course, history being full of mysteries is by no means a bad thing. An intriguing enigma excites the imagination and motivates further investigation. These mysteries ensure that history remains a living, breathing detective story.

issues.title: How Two Mysterious Green Children Appeared in Medieval Woolpit
issues.summary: Sometime in the 12th century, possibly during the reign of King Stephen, farmers from the village of Woolpit, Suffolk, stumbled upon two truly unusual children. The brother and sister, visibly bewildered, spoke a language unknown to the farmers and, most interestingly, reportedly had green skin. The farmers decided to help the children, and their […]
issues.author: Elmedin Salihagic
issues.content_html:
Sometime in the 12th century, possibly during the reign of King Stephen, farmers from the village of Woolpit, Suffolk, stumbled upon two truly unusual children. The brother and sister, visibly bewildered, spoke a language unknown to the farmers and, most interestingly, reportedly had green skin. The farmers decided to help the children, and their unusual appearance faded as they grew accustomed to the local diet. However, the explanation the children themselves gave regarding their origins was perhaps the most bizarre aspect of all.

The legend of the green children of Woolpit was recorded by two medieval chroniclers, William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall. Although they were not present at the scene, they recounted the event as an absolute fact rather than a folktale.

The Medieval Chroniclers Who Recorded the Mysterious Encounter

We have the story of the green children of Woolpit preserved thanks to two medieval chroniclers, William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall. William of Newburgh was an Augustinian canon from Yorkshire, and Ralph of Coggeshall was a Cistercian monk and later abbot of Coggeshall Abbey in Essex. Therefore, neither of them personally witnessed the events that they wrote down as fact. Their records were based on information that circulated immediately after the event.

William of Newburgh included the story in his work “Historia rerum Anglicarum,” or “History of England.” His record is found in the first book among a series of other unusual events that cannot be confirmed. However, William presents the story with caution but credulity, stating that he received information about the green children from several people. His monastery was quite a distance from Woolpit, and he did not claim to have witnessed the events himself.

Ralph of Coggeshall records the story in his “Chronicon Anglicanum.” Geographically, he was much closer to Suffolk, and he even names the man from whom he learned of the events. It was Richard de Calne, the man who took the two children into his home. Historian John Clark has suggested that Richard de Calne may have been the source for both writers.

The two accounts are very similar in structure. Both describe a green-skinned boy and girl who spoke an unintelligible language and could not eat ordinary food. They also record the boy’s death and the girl’s subsequent fate. However, Ralph’s version contains slightly more details.

The Story About Green Children in Woolpit

The story most likely took place during the reign of King Stephen of Blois (r. 1135–1154). Farmers from the village of Woolpit found two children near one of the wolf-trapping pits from which the village took its name. Their skin was green, they spoke an unknown language, and their clothing was unusual. Ralph of Coggeshall records that the children were subsequently taken into the home of a prominent local man, Richard de Calne.

At first, the children refused to eat until raw broad beans were placed before them at the table. They ate these greedily and then began to consume other foods as well. As they grew accustomed to the local diet, they gradually lost their green skin color. It was decided that the children should be baptized. However, the boy, who appeared to be the younger of the two, was sickly and died either before or shortly after the baptism.

After the surviving girl learned to speak English, she explained that she and her brother came from a land where the sun never shone. She called her home St Martin’s Land. She had no explanation for how she had ended up in Woolpit. William of Newburgh states that she remembered only a loud noise and then being found near the wolf pit. Ralph of Coggeshall, however, claims that the children became lost while following livestock into a cave and that, guided by the sound of bells, they eventually emerged into our world.

According to Ralph, the girl worked as a servant on Richard de Calne’s estate in the years that followed. She behaved in a very wild and insolent manner there. The last piece of information we have is that she married a man from King’s Lynn, a town 64 kilometers from Woolpit. The girl became completely accustomed to life in England.

Were the Green Children Flemish Refugees?

One of the most well-known modern attempts to interpret the legend of the two green children of Woolpit comes from historian Paul Harris. He elaborated on his theory in his 1998 essay, “The Green Children of Woolpit: A 12th Century Mystery and its Possible Solution,” published in Fortean Studies. His thesis was that the children might have been the offspring of Flemish settlers living in East Anglia and that their unusual appearance was the result of displacement, malnutrition, and an unfamiliar language.

The Flemings were the inhabitants of Flanders, a region that included parts of present-day Belgium, France, and the Netherlands. In the Middle Ages, Flanders was famous for producing woolen fabrics. Many Flemings left and settled parts of England because of the economic opportunities.

Harris hypothesized that St. Martin’s Land might refer to Fornham St Martin, where a Flemish community existed. He linked this possibility to the Battle of Fornham, fought on October 17, 1173, during the Great Revolt against Henry II. An army led by Robert de Beaumont, Earl of Leicester, had landed in Suffolk with a large contingent of Flemish mercenaries. The battle ended disastrously for the Flemings, as many were killed or drowned, while others were taken prisoner.

Certain historians have expressed skepticism about Paul Harris’s theory. The biggest argument against it appears to be the small probability that an educated man like Richard de Calne would not recognize the Flemish language if the children really spoke it. Furthermore, the Battle of Fornham took place after the reign of King Stephen, the period to which William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall attributed these events.

Could Malnutrition Have Turned Their Skin Green?

Since both medieval chroniclers recorded that the children had green skin, historians have speculated that the children were severely malnourished and anemic, rather than hailing from another dimension.

One of the proposed diagnoses is chlorosis, historically known as “green sickness.” This condition was described in medical literature for centuries and was eventually recognized as a form of iron-deficiency anemia, specifically hypochromic anemia. Patients were characteristically unusually pale, sometimes exhibiting a greenish or yellowish-green skin tone.

“The likely core of the matter is that these very small children, herding or following flocks, strayed from their forest village, spoke little, and (in modern terms) did not know their own home address. They were probably suffering from chlorosis, a deficiency disease which gives the skin a greenish tint, hence the term ‘green sickness.’ With a better diet it disappears.” (Derek Brewer, A Companion to the Gawain-Poet, 1997, page 182)

Historically, however, chlorosis was associated more with adolescents and women than with young children.

Interestingly, the children were drawn to raw beans, and in large quantities. Beans are rich in iron, a fact that might lend weight to the hypochromic anemia theory. However, the green skin color remains the greatest mystery. While severe malnutrition can cause extreme paleness and a loss of natural pigment, no known disease causes bright green skin. This raises the question of which shade of green the medieval accounts referred to, and whether it was even the kind of green skin we imagine.

Folklore May Have Transformed a Real Medieval Tragedy

The story of the two green children of Woolpit contains elements reminiscent of medieval English tales about journeys to the “otherworld.” Consequently, most historians attribute the details of this story to folklore. But this does not necessarily mean the children did not exist or that their tragedy was not real. Later writers and folklorists such as Charles Oman increasingly linked this story of the green children to fairies and the realm of the fae.

Martin Walsh, a researcher of world folklore, describes the story of the green children as a kind of distorted depiction of an atavistic harvest ritual, during which animals were slaughtered to cull the herd before the winter. Walsh considers references to Saint Martin significant and views the story as evidence that the Feast of Saint Martin has roots in the ancient English past. The children’s green skin could represent the fertility of the land, and broad beans were often considered the food of the dead. The children following the sound of church bells through an underground cavern mirrored ritual pageants where symbolic earth spirits or seasonal mummers were “led out” from darkness into the sunlit harvest field.

Other modern theories link the story of the green children of Woolpit to the traditional English folktale “Babes in the Wood.” This story was first published in the 16th century. It tells of a boy and a girl who were abandoned in a forest, where they wandered, starving and frightened. The children eventually died of cold, and robins covered their bodies with green leaves.

Herbert Read’s “The Green Child” Reimagined the Medieval Legend

The legend of the green children from Woolpit still inspires writers, artists and musicians today. Perhaps the best example is the novel “The Green Child” by Herbert Read, published in 1935. The only novel by the famous English poet, it is directly inspired by the story of the two green children from Woolpit, which he says is “the norm to which all types of fantasy should conform.”

The novel follows the ex-South American dictator Oliviero, who returns to his native England, abandoning his previous life. In England, he meets an unusual green-skinned child and learns that this child is connected to a secret underground world where people live according to principles different from those in the world above.

Throughout the novel, Herbert explores the meaning of life and re-examines established notions of death, nature, and human existence.

issues.title: How Underground Resistance Armies Weakened Axis Forces in World War II
issues.summary: When Axis forces occupied much of Europe during World War II, they did not expect to face formidable enemies that could not be defeated simply by capturing the capital or destroying a conventional army. Resistance movements sprang up across the occupied territories, often called “the underground.” The most effective were the French Maquis, Polish […]
issues.author: Elmedin Salihagic
issues.content_html:
When Axis forces occupied much of Europe during World War II, they did not expect to face formidable enemies that could not be defeated simply by capturing the capital or destroying a conventional army. Resistance movements sprang up across the occupied territories, often called “the underground.” The most effective were the French Maquis, Polish Home Army, and Yugoslav Partisans. These resistance forces gathered intelligence, sabotaged railways, attacked supply lines, and carried out guerrilla operations. Although these groups often lacked the equipment and weaponry possessed by professional armies, their activities created serious headaches for the Axis occupiers.

Why Resistance Movements Emerged Across Occupied Europe

Germany’s rapid military advances during World War II brought most of continental Europe under Nazi occupation, or at least Nazi political dominance. It started with Poland in 1939, and then Denmark, Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and France fell the following year. In 1941, Germany attacked Yugoslavia, Greece and parts of the Soviet Union. In 1942, Germany was at its territorial peak.

The occupation naturally created conditions that encouraged resistance and opposition. The occupiers tried to oppose this with censorship, arrests, requisitions, forced labor, and other methods. In Eastern Europe, such a regime was particularly cruel, and intellectuals, teachers, priests, and other groups that were a potential source of organized resistance were often targeted.

Resistance was difficult to suppress because it did not stem from a single political goal. Some sought to restore national independence after their countries had been conquered. Others opposed the occupation based on ideological convictions, including communism, socialism, nationalism, or opposition to fascism. Religious beliefs and personal experiences of repression also drove people toward resistance.

In the early years of the war, many resistance forces lacked resources, weapons, training, and communication systems. Consequently, resistance activities were initially often limited to publishing underground newspapers, disseminating propaganda, gathering intelligence, forging documents, helping people evade arrest, and maintaining secret communication networks. As the war progressed, some organizations gained better access to weapons, and the resistance became more dangerous.

Forms of Resistance Against the Axis

Armed resistance ranged from individual attacks and assassinations to organized guerrilla warfare. Frequent targets of attacks were German personnel, collaborators, police stations, military facilities, or traffic routes. Resistance groups could raid government offices to obtain food stamps, IDs, or other documents needed by people living illegally. For example, in the Netherlands, population registration offices were often attacked because the Nazis relied on their documents to identify Jews.

Larger forces knew how to conduct ambushes and raids. In Yugoslavia, the Partisans eventually developed into a large, organized fighting force that conducted sustained operations against German and Axis forces.

Sabotage was one of the most important forms of resistance. Railroads, bridges, telephone lines, energy infrastructure, and other facilities important for the German military occupation were sabotaged. Britain’s Special Operations Executive (SOE) supplied European saboteurs with weapons, explosives, and radios.

Another important form of resistance was intelligence gathering. Information about the movement of occupying troops, military installations, fortifications, and other activities was transmitted to the Allied intelligence services. This data proved extremely important before the invasion of Normandy as the French resistance networks had good information about German troop positions, coastal defenses, airfields, bridges, railways, and other military targets. Such information supplemented Allied reconnaissance.

Underground publications in the form of secret newspapers and leaflets spread information that contradicted the media under German control. Publications such as “Combat,” “Libération,” and “Franc-Tireur” were particularly well known in France, and a similar volume of publications existed in Poland. Foreign radio broadcasts such as the BBC became an important source of information in the occupied parts.

Resistance was also provided in other ways, for example by helping people to avoid persecution by assisting Jews, political opponents, or escaped prisoners of war to hide. Escape routes to allied territories were set. This went hand in hand with the forgery of personal documents, ration documents, work permits, and others. From time to time, large strikes against the imposed government were also organized, like the February Strike in the Netherlands, which around 300,000 people joined. Usually, these strikes were suppressed violently.

The French Maquis Disrupted German Reinforcements to Normandy

The Maquis were armed resistance groups that emerged from rural areas of France during World War II. The name originally referred to the scrubland and wooded terrain where many of these groups established camps. They consisted of numerous local groups operating without a unified command. By 1944, many of these groups had joined the French Forces of the Interior (FFI).

The movement expanded after Germany introduced a system of compulsory labor in 1943, requiring hundreds of thousands of young French people to go to Germany for work. Those who refused went into hiding in rural areas and joined resistance groups.

The groups relied heavily on the local population for food, clothing, information, and shelter. They obtained weapons and explosives through theft. Some groups later received support from British SOE and American OSS agents; the Allies dropped weapons, ammunition, radios, and other supplies to them by parachute.

Initially, the Maquis employed guerrilla warfare tactics. They ambushed the enemy, attacked isolated installations, cut telephone lines, damaged railway infrastructure, and disrupted transport. The intensity of the attacks increased during D-Day.

The Maquis caused problems for German troops moving toward the Allied invasion front in Normandy. They managed to slow down the path of one of the strongest Nazi divisions, the 2nd SS Panzer Division Das Reich. The Germans responded with brutal attacks against civilians. They hanged 99 men at Tulle who they suspected of being members of the resistance movement, and the next day they killed 642 people in Oradour-sur-Glane, including women and children.

As German authority weakened, attacks became more open compared to earlier covert acts of sabotage. French resistance movements organized an uprising in Paris in August 1944, and the city was liberated that same month.

The Polish Home Army Built a Vast Underground Network

The Polish Home Army, abbreviated as AK (Armia Krajowa), was the main armed force of the Polish resistance during the German occupation. It was subordinate to the Polish government-in-exile in London. The organization of the AK was far more sophisticated than that of other partisan groups. It featured specialized departments responsible for intelligence, operations, logistics, communications, propaganda, and finance, as well as a civilian branch.

Many members led seemingly ordinary lives while actually having secret identities. That is how they transmitted messages, gathered information, stockpiled weapons, and waited for orders. By the summer of 1944, AK had over 380,000 members. The original goal was a large-scale national uprising, but while waiting for the ideal conditions to be created, smaller operations were conducted against the occupiers.

Kedyw, or the Diversion Directorate, carried out attacks on German transport and communication links, carried out sabotage, freed prisoners, and attacked German officials and collaborators. One of the most important actions was the assassination of the high-ranking SS commander Franz Kutschera, who was nicknamed the Butcher of Warsaw.

Polish secret intelligence was particularly important in uncovering German development of the V-1 and V-2 weapons, secret superweapons of retaliation. Information gathered about the German test facility at Peenemünde contributed to the Allied decision to bomb the site in August 1943, while intelligence later identified the V-2 test area at Blizna.

The Red Army was pushing the German army to the west. As it approached Poland, the conditions for the most important operation of the Armia Krajowa were created. Operation Tempest was launched. The goal was to attack the retreating German forces and take control of Polish cities before the Soviets arrived. In some places, the Soviets and Poles cooperated, but both fought for control.

When the Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising on August 1, 1944, about 50,000 fighters took part. However, they were poorly equipped compared to the German soldiers, so the uprising failed. After that, the Germans destroyed large parts of Warsaw and expelled a large number of inhabitants.

The Polish Home Army was disbanded in 1945, when the Red Army continued its advance. Soviet forces and the Soviet-sponsored Polish communist government took control of the country, while members of the former resistance movement faced arrest and persecution.

The Yugoslav Partisans Waged a Full-Scale Guerrilla War

Led by Josip Broz Tito, the Partisans were Europe’s most effective anti-Axis resistance movement during World War II. Unlike other groups, Yugoslav partisans most often fought in large-scale military operations. After conquering Yugoslavia, the Axis powers divided the country into parts controlled by Germany, Italy, Hungary, and Bulgaria. Germany and Italy established and supported the Independent State of Croatia, which was ruled by the fascist Ustaše movement.

At that time, the Partisans also fought against another resistance group, namely the Chetniks. It was a Serbian nationalist movement led by Draža Mihailović. The Chetniks increasingly avoided conflicts with the Axis powers and even occasionally cooperated against the Partisans.

Despite everything, the Partisans held their ground and increased their numbers. One of the major clashes was the Battle of the Neretva in 1943. German, Italian, Ustaša, and Chetnik forces attempted to encircle and destroy the main body of the Partisan forces. Nevertheless, the Partisans broke through the enemy encirclement and managed to save thousands of wounded soldiers.

Just a few months later, the Germans launched another major offensive in the Battle of Sutjeska. The plan was the same, and the partisans broke through the ring again, this time with heavy losses.

In this period, the Partisans received increasing help from the Western allies, especially in the form of ammunition and medical supplies. After the capitulation of Italy in September 1943, they also confiscated large quantities of Italian weapons and equipment. In the summer of the following year, the Balkan Air Force was founded by the RAF in order to better coordinate air support and supply drops. The Partisans were increasingly becoming a regular army.

Unlike the French Maquis or the Polish Home Army, the Yugoslav Partisans emerged from the war as a victorious military and political force. Tito’s communist movement took power in Yugoslavia and established a new socialist government.

Other Resistance Movements Across Occupied Europe

Soviet partisan units operated primarily in Belarus, Ukraine, and Western Russia after the German invasion. They were mainly composed of soldiers separated from the Red Army, local members of the Communist Party, security personnel, and civilians. Over time, their efforts were increasingly coordinated with the Red Army.

Italy developed a strong armed resistance movement after the fall of Mussolini’s regime in 1943. The Germans began the occupation of Italy and placed Mussolini at the head of the newly formed Italian Social Republic. Thousands of soldiers and other opponents of the occupation organized themselves into resistance movements, including the communist Garibaldi Brigade, Justice and Freedom formations associated with the Action Party, autonomous units, and other groups. Resistance became increasingly important in 1944 and 1945 as the Allied armies advanced north through Italy.

The occupation of Greece also led to the creation of several resistance groups. The largest was the National Liberation Front, or EAM, whose military arm was the Greek National Liberation Army, ELAS. Another important organization was EDES, the National Republican Greek League, which was politically opposed to the communist EAM. One of the most significant sabotage operations was the destruction of the Gorgopotamos railway viaduct in 1942 in cooperation with British units. Resistance activities grew after that until Germany finally ordered the evacuation of mainland Greece in October 1944.

In this way, resistance movements in occupied Europe constituted an additional layer of warfare behind the main battlefronts. They did not replace conventional Allied armies, and their importance varied significantly from country to country. However, their collective impact made the Axis occupation costlier and more difficult.

issues.title: Actress Chloe Bridges and Dr. Charis Chambers on what moms need to know to help protect their baby against RSV infection
issues.summary: In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.
issues.author: Sara Goldstein
issues.content_html:
This episode is sponsored by Pfizer. This article is directed to a U.S. audience and may not be suitable for those outside of the U.S.We partnered with them to bring you this conversation, but everything you hear from me, Chloe, and Dr. Chambers is our own experience and opinion. Not medical advice, just a conversation between moms.

Pregnancy has a way of making you feel responsible for someone before you have ever met them. For actress Chloe Bridges and OBGYN Dr. Charis Chambers, that meant navigating the identity shift of new motherhood while also learning about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a highly contagious respiratory virus that is the number one cause of hospitalization for babies in the United States with nearly 50% of RSV hospitalizations occurring during the first 3 months of life. Both moms built a trusted village of support to help navigate – and have a lot to say about what they wish they had known sooner.

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

Chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

Dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. She is the Chief Medical Officer at the cycle-tracking app Clue and the author of The Period and Puberty Parenting Revolution. She lives with her husband, Zachary, and their son, Joshua.

What was the first lesson that motherhood taught you?

Chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. I’d be like, ‘Oh my gosh, he’s never going to sleep. He’s always going to be a bad sleeper.’ And I just had to learn that a good day today doesn’t necessarily mean a good day tomorrow. A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

Dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. And all of those are really good reasons to ask for help.

How would you describe your mindset heading into motherhood for the first time?

Chloe: I didn’t know what I didn’t know. It was almost like I didn’t want to think about postpartum too much, because I truly didn’t know what to expect. Everyone talks about how it’s just such a big transition, and I did really feel that. What’s that thing that people say? Two people are born that day. The baby is born, but then you are also born as a mother. And I absolutely experienced that. You can try to prepare mentally for what it’s going to feel like, but it’s still so surreal when it actually happens.

Dr. Chambers: I immediately threw up my hands in thanks, and then I looked around like, ‘Wait a second.’ Everything is different. I felt like I didn’t even know which way to move or walk. I didn’t know what to do next. I just sat with that moment. My beliefs, my vision for tomorrow, my to-do list, it all just exploded, all in that moment. And it was immense joy, but a nervousness that I think is in proportion to just the depth and caliber of what this is.

You’ve both described an identity shift. Can you talk a little bit about that?

Dr. Chambers: As someone who spent so long not being a mother, I never thought that motherhood would ever fully define me, and I still don’t feel that way today. I also think when you desire something so much, it’s hard sometimes to verbalize that desire. So knowing that you’re stepping into this role, this space, that has never really been in your control to step into, but that door is opening. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. Once I got that MD, I was going to be a doctor. But this is almost like it’s not an earned thing. It is given. I knew it was a forever shift, but spending so much time desiring to be in that role, and seeing that for myself and not knowing if it was going to happen, that was a real identity shift for me.

Pregnancy can feel like a crash course in invisible responsibility. What decisions felt hardest during your pregnancy journeys?

Chloe: I think a lot of the decisions I was making were just about being so much more cognizant of my own health. Before pregnancy, I don’t know if I was necessarily the healthiest person, but you get pregnant and suddenly it’s not about you, it’s about you and your baby. And your health is intertwined obviously. So it was just a lot of decisions about, you know, obviously I’m going to follow all the advice. I’m going to limit my caffeine intake and I’m going to avoid foods that could give me listeria. And I’m going to, you know, take my prenatal. All of a sudden I was thinking about my health so much more, in a way I hadn’t been before.

Dr. Chambers: So many of the decisions that I knew I had to make, it was almost like I had the answers to the test, just because I’m an OBGYN. But then I started to realize that what I really knew about pregnancy was related to a role that I wasn’t playing this time. I was the actual patient. I had a point in my pregnancy where my cervix was shorter, and they were measuring it, and wondering, are we going to need to do something more invasive, like a cerclage, or can we just do vaginal progesterone. And my very best friend, it was her bachelorette party, but it was in a remote area of Mexico, and I said, ‘How can I reconcile potentially delivering early in this extreme prematurity state that we would be looking at because I just want to be on this girls’ trip?’ I had to just sit with myself, ‘All right, what makes the most sense?’ Of course my friend was amazing and was like, ‘Girl, say less. No one’s going to feel bad. Take care of you and your baby.’ But it just was hard. You want to do so many things, but at the end of the day, you have to stand in your values and stand in your truths and trust that the people around you will be supportive of that.

There’s so much noise around pregnancy, social media, group chats, your mom, your OBGYN. How do you determine whose advice you can really trust?

Dr. Chambers: This day and age, it is just hard, but it depends on the topic. When I was making my registry, for whatever reason, I just couldn’t start it. There’s a billion strollers. What do you mean there’s this many cribs? I was so overwhelmed. So I gave my sister my login and said, ‘Go to town.’ But as it related to my health, being someone who had a high-risk pregnancy, it was a meeting of the minds. I made sure all of my doctors were on the same page, and I wanted a yes. Like when you’re in the emergency row of the flight and they’re like, ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ ‘Nephrologist?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘High-risk doctor?’ ‘Yes.’ OBGYN who’s doing the delivery, yes. I trusted my team.

Chloe: I was also overwhelmed by the whole registry process. But I don’t have a lot of friends who have been pregnant before me, so I was leaning on the internet a lot. Dr. Google, and honestly lots of YouTube videos, all those videos of people being like, ‘This is what’s on my registry,’ or ‘Day in the life.’ And then my OBGYN was so helpful. I would be lost without her. She was truly such a resource, and I really felt like I had built a trust with her, and it really paid off later during birth and everything. I felt like I could ask her anything and trusted her advice.

What is RSV, and why is it such a concern for infants, especially in those first six months of life?

Dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

What are some of the specific signs of RSV in infants, and how do they differ from a cold or flu?

Dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s important to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

If RSV is only vaguely on an expecting mom’s radar, what does she need to know about its potential impact during those early months?

Dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s important to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO ® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

How does maternal immunization for RSV actually work?

Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. She recommended I get ABRYSVO for it, and I remain very happy that I listened to my OBGYN’s recommendation to get ABRYSVO when I was pregnant, and that helped protect him during his first six months of life when he is so vulnerable.

ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components. An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

How can moms care for their own anxiety and fear in new motherhood, especially around their baby’s health?

Chloe: I’m glad we’re talking about this, because sometimes it can feel like so many things are being thrown at you when you’re pregnant, especially if you don’t have a lot of knowledge going into it and then you’re hearing about things from your OBGYN. It can feel sort of rushed, where if I’m hearing about a vaccine in my 32-week appointment, but then they’re like, ‘Oh, by the way, you only have until your 36 weeks to get it.’ So the more you know going in, it can only help to be more informed, to have time to do research.

What about mental preparation for new motherhood, beyond the expected guidance?

Dr. Chambers: The mental shift that was required the most, that I still carry with myself today, is letting go of the whole independent aspect. I would pride myself in being someone who was very self-sufficient. ‘I got it. If you can’t do this, I’ll figure it out.’ And it’s not that I don’t believe in myself, it is that I fully acknowledge the weight of motherhood and all that is required, and I now welcome the help. I had to tell my older sister, ‘I need you to put together my pump,’ and she did. I had to tell my mother-in-law, ‘The only thing I need today is a nap.’ And she’s like, ‘Go nap.’ Until you learn to verbalize those things and truly believe that you’re worthy of it, not as a point of insufficiency, motherhood requires a village. It requires a team. It requires support. Your mental health will be that much better for it.

Chloe: You go from being an individual with all of your independence, and then suddenly you are putting this baby’s needs before your own. My advice would be to try to establish communication with your village early, whoever that is, and have some sort of plan. Learn how to delegate. I don’t think I had done a lot of delegating before becoming a mom, and then suddenly you’re delegating all the time.

When you think about your babies who have grown up already, what do you hope they say about you one day as a mom?

Chloe: I want him to see me as competent and capable, but I also want him to see me as playful and fun. I think that’s been a big part of it. Maybe especially having a little boy, I want to be playful with him, and I want him to be able to have that kind of relationship with me. The nurturing comes so easy, but the playfulness has come a little harder. I hope he looks back and he’s like, ‘You know what? We had fun.’

Dr. Chambers: I hope my son sees me as someone he can trust, as someone who can give him advice, as someone who always makes decisions that are grounded in love and goodness, and someone who’s been making decisions since before he was born to set him up to have the best possible life. I hope that he trusts me with every aspect of who he is, knowing that the love I have is profoundly unconditional, and it has been before I could even picture his face. Before I even knew who he was, he was always worthy of that love and support, and it’s not going anywhere.

This article has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the full episode of The Motherly Podcast on YouTube.

Important Safety Information & Use

  • ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components
  • An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO
  • To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age
  • Fainting can happen after getting injectable vaccines, including ABRYSVO. Precautions should be taken to avoid falling and injury due to fainting
  • Adults with weakened immune systems, including those receiving medicines that suppress the immune system, may have a reduced immune response to ABRYSVO
  • Vaccination with ABRYSVO may not protect all people
  • In pregnant individuals, the most common side effects ( > 10%) were pain at the injection site, headache, muscle pain, and nausea
  • In clinical trials where ABRYSVO was compared to placebo, infants born to pregnant individuals experienced low birth weight (5.1% ABRYSVO versus 4.3% placebo) and jaundice (7.3% ABRYSVO versus 6.9% placebo)

Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

You are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visithttp://www.vaers.hhs.govor call 1-800-822-7967.

Individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

WHAT IS ABRYSVO?

ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO atpfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

The information provided is for educational purposes only and is not intended to replace discussions with a healthcare provider.
