issues.title: The Learning-Visibility Loop: How AI Should Participate in Education
issues.summary: Generic AI is built to hand over answers. The bigger opportunity in education is to make the learning itself visible, for students and for the instructors teaching them. A finished assignment doesn’t show how it was made. It shows what a student turned in, but not how they read the prompt, where they got stuck, […] The post The Learning-Visibility Loop: How AI Should Participate in Education appea
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
Generic AI is built to hand over answers. The bigger opportunity in education is to make the learning itself visible, for students and for the instructors teaching them.

A finished assignment doesn’t show how it was made. It shows what a student turned in, but not how they read the prompt, where they got stuck, which misconceptions surfaced, or what finally helped them move forward. Those moments are where learning actually happens, and they disappear the moment the work is submitted.

AI has widened that gap. The process is even harder to see now, and students, reaching for whatever tool is closest, get generic help that was never built for learning. Retention, integrity, and faculty workload were already compounding pressures on academic leaders. AI is adding to the pressure.

Why AI in higher education makes learning harder to see clearly

The instinct for many in education is to ask whether students used AI. We think the more useful question is, “Can educators tell that students are learning?” Visibility has become a greater challenge since the introduction of AI in education; instructors see the final submission but not the work that led up to it. The learning process itself has become opaque, even to the people responsible for teaching it.

A loop that makes learning visible

There’s a better way to work when AI is in the mix, one that turns that lost process back into something an instructor can see and act on. We call it the learning-visibility loop. Each turn of a student’s work informs the instructor’s next move, and each move shapes stronger work, so every round leaves both sides further along than the last. Here’s how it comes together.

A student works through a problem with an AI agent, a tool that holds a back-and-forth and works alongside them, guiding them rather than handing over the answer. That interaction leaves an honest record of how the student got there. The instructor reads that record, sees where the class is getting stuck, and shapes the next assignment around it. The student works again, now on ground the last round helped shape.

Each turn feeds the next. Instead of ending with a single graded assignment, every round gives an instructor something to act on, and every new assignment is shaped by what students actually struggled with. The loop moves teaching from what happened to what to do next.

One design choice holds the whole thing together: The agent guides the student rather than generating the work. An agent that hands over answers leaves no record of how the student got there. An agent that asks questions and pushes for revision creates that record, because the back-and-forth is itself the trace of how the student worked through the problem. That is what makes the help genuinely educational, and it keeps the instructor’s signal honest. The two sides are one system, and each makes the other stronger.

What faculty told us

The loop is informed by first-party research led by Yolanda Wiggins, a senior researcher at Superhuman: 12 in-depth interviews with US higher education professionals, from professors and adjuncts to academic and technology leaders. The findings are qualitative and directional. The student side draws on separate, prior research with students.

Two things came through clearly.

1. Faculty want to see how learning happens

Again and again, instructors said they wanted to understand where students were struggling and what they could do differently as teachers.

“We have no idea what prompts they used. Most of this is very opaque to me.” — a CIO who also teaches graduate courses

“We need to know what’s in their heads, not what AI can write.” — an MBA program director

“You’re gonna have to give me all of your prompts, and show me the dialogue.” — a social-psychology professor

Some instructors are already rebuilding this visibility by hand, redesigning assignments at real cost to their time. That effort is the clearest sign of the gap.

2. Students want to show their work

This second finding comes from separate, prior qualitative research with undergraduate and graduate students, who documented their real coursework and tool use. Students reached for AI when they were stuck, to interpret a prompt, get started, or check their work, not to do the assignment for them, and they valued tools that supported their thinking while keeping the work their own. Many are already opting into Grammarly Authorship, which documents how a piece of writing actually came together. The desire for greater visibility runs in both directions.

“You can’t just outsource your homework to AI. You can tell, it just creates AI slop. When students instead use it as a tutor or study buddy, we see much better work.” — an MIS professor

What keeps the loop honest

The loop only works if a few things stay true.

First, humans do the work and own the decisions. Students remain the authors of their own learning, so the agent guides while the thinking and the work stay theirs. Instructors stay the decision-makers, so insight informs a teaching decision without ever making one. As one MBA program director put it, “I will never use AI to grade.” We design for exactly that: the instructor stays the decision-maker, and the tools inform decisions rather than make them.

Second, the student-side agent must be built to support learning. When it’s built well, it does four things:

Third, the instructor-side report has to lead with what to do next. It answers three questions a busy instructor rarely has time to answer alone:

The point is to turn otherwise invisible patterns into a teaching decision, while grading, intervention, and course design remain firmly in human hands. Imagine a report that shows most of the class opened with a one-sided thesis, and that once the agent pushed back, the majority revised toward a stronger argument while a smaller group stayed stuck. That gap is the signal, and it points to exactly what to teach next.

What the loop collects, and what it leaves alone

Because the loop is based on how students learn, it collects only what helps teaching: the work process and class-level patterns, not personal or non-academic data. Students should know what’s captured, see what’s inferred, and be able to contest it. And the institution should stay in control of its own data.

Why higher education needs AI built for learning

Generic AI is getting very good at generating answers. Education needs something different: learning support that leaves an instructor with something to teach. That’s a fundamentally different product problem, and general-purpose assistants weren’t designed to solve it.

This is what it looks like when AI is built for education rather than pointed at it. It keeps students doing the doing, gives faculty a path forward instead of more to police, and gives institutions something they can actually measure: whether learning is happening. It complements an institution’s approach to AI rather than competing with it. And it’s built the way the best campus AI is being built right now: with institutions, not just for them.

Keeping learning visible

When an answer is always a click away, the work worth protecting is the learning. The learning-visibility loop is how we think AI can protect it: by keeping students in the work, keeping instructors in the decisions, and making the learning itself visible to both.

Grammarly is now part of Superhuman , and this is the model we’re building toward with Superhuman Go , alongside the institutions putting it into practice. The best campus AI isn’t handed down from a vendor; it’s shaped by the educators who know what learning should look like and built on a foundation higher ed already trusts.

issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
Instructors want to trust the work students hand in. Students want credit for the work they actually did. As AI use in the classroom becomes routine, both are getting harder, and that’s exactly where writing transparency earns its place.

Grammarly Authorship was built to close that gap.

Since Grammarly Authorship launched in beta in Google Docs in October 2024, it has expanded to Grammarly Docs, Microsoft Word, and Word Online, so students can show their writing process wherever they write. It now recognizes AI-generated content both pasted in and generated from within a document, including Copilot in Word and Gemini in Google Docs.

Students have generated more than 5 million Authorship reports to date.

The results show up on campus. After introducing Authorship across its English department, Rowan-Cabarrus Community College reduced academic integrity violations from 27 to 1, a 96% drop, in a single semester.

Authorship delivers value on its own. It goes further when it’s built into the systems an institution already runs. After integrating with Canvas LMS in September 2025, Grammarly Authorship now integrates with Blackboard, giving institutions a scalable way to make student writing transparent while students keep writing in the tools they prefer to use.

What is Grammarly Authorship?

Grammarly Authorship automatically categorizes the sources of text in a document, whether it’s in Google Docs, Microsoft Word, Word Online, or Grammarly Docs. It gives quick signals and detailed reports showing where writing came from: human-typed, AI-generated, copied, or rephrased with Grammarly’s generative AI.

Unlike traditional detection tools, Authorship is built on transparency and attribution, with student consent. Students can show their authentic writing process, and instructors can spend their time guiding rather than second-guessing it with unclear data.

Authorship’s new Blackboard integration

Instructors can require Authorship reports directly within Blackboard assignments. Here’s how it works:

1. Instructor setup

While creating an assignment, instructors simply switch on the new Enable Grammarly Authorship option in the Originality Report section of their Blackboard assignment settings.

2. Students keep writing where they always do

In the tools they already use (Microsoft Word, Word Online, Google Docs, or Grammarly Docs), students can turn on Authorship tracking with a single click and view their Authorship report at any time. It attributes their text sources automatically when they use a gen AI tool or paste from a third-party source. Because Authorship is student-first, students can see their own writing process data but can’t alter it before sharing, which builds two-way visibility into how the work was made.

3. Sharing to Blackboard is easy with a share link

When they’re ready to submit, students select Anyone with the link in their Authorship report access settings.

4. Quick attachment through normal submission workflow

Students attach the Authorship report to their normal Blackboard submission by submitting their report’s share link alongside their assignment document.

5. Instructor insights at scale

Instructors gain a class-level view of the Authorship report and can open any individual student’s full writing process replay when they want to dig in. That makes it easy to focus on outliers while trusting that every submission includes transparent attribution.

Why this matters

Educators want writing to be something students genuinely work through, and institutions need a way to trust in that work as AI use becomes routine. Students want that too: Many are actively looking for ways to use AI they can stand behind .

Here’s what the Blackboard integration gives each group:

  • Students get a low-effort way to show their writing process and get credit for their own thinking, whether or not they used AI, plus protection from false accusations. Over time, attributing their sources builds the AI-literacy habits that matter well beyond any single assignment.
  • I nstructors get assignment-level control with the ability to require students to submit an Authorship report with their assignment. Authorship is visible in Blackboard through a single class view, meaning instructors don’t have to open reports one by one. It also allows them to drill into any student’s process when a conversation is warranted. That gives back hours during grading and turns integrity checks into teaching moments rather than investigations.
  • Institutions get a consistent, scalable way to maintain academic trust across departments, built on tools faculty and students already use, so adoption doesn’t hinge on changing anyone’s habits, plus a defensible answer when leadership asks how AI is being handled.

The Blackboard Authorship integration is now available for Grammarly for Education customers on any institution-wide plan that uses Blackboard. Administrators can install the LTI in a few steps using the setup guide .

We’re glad to partner with Anthology and our school and university customers to make writing transparency a reality for the AI era.

To learn more or get started, visit Grammarly for Education .

issues.content_html:
Writing on your phone is still, somehow, a chore. Between a cramped keyboard, autocorrect that guesses wrong, and the mental load of trying to stay focused while on the move, sending a polished message takes longer than it should.

Voice dictation promised to fix this. But native phone dictation just gives you a raw transcript, full of filler words, false starts, and missing punctuation. Cleaning up your text is just as much work as if you’d typed it manually.

That’s what speech-to-text in the Grammarly Keyboard is built to solve. The Grammarly’ Keyboard now lets you dictate directly into any app and delivers clean, polished text without the cleanup.

Dictate anywhere, get polished text.

Speech-to-text is built directly into the Grammarly Keyboard. Tap the mic icon, speak naturally, and Grammarly returns clean, send-ready text—right in the app you’re using.

Grammarly’s speech-to-text handles a wide range of languages, accents, and speaking cadences. Instead of producing a raw transcript, Grammarly cuts filler words, removes spots where you corrected yourself verbally, and fixes grammar, all while preserving your tone and intent.

If you want to take your dictated text further, Grammarly’s AI assistant is available in the same keyboard. You can switch between speaking and typing at any point, or edit your dictated text with the same Grammarly Keyboard across all your apps.

Built for wherever and however you use your phone

Grammarly’s speech-to-text is for anyone who writes a lot on mobile—knowledge workers drafting between meetings, students capturing ideas mid-walk, or anyone tired of fighting a tiny keyboard.

Grammarly’s mic is designed to cut background noise while also keeping you in control of what is recorded. The mic only activates when you tap it. While it’s on, you’ll see a clear signal in the keyboard, plus the iOS orange indicator light at the top of your screen. After your audio is processed into text, it’s deleted. It isn’t stored, linked to your account, or used to train any models. All that’s left is your polished message, ready to send.

Get started

Speech-to-text lives inside the Grammarly Keyboard. Once it’s set as your default keyboard, the mic is available in any app.

  • Download and install Grammarly for iOS : If you haven’t done so already, download the Grammarly Keyboard from the App Store. Setup takes under a minute.
  • Set Grammarly as your keyboard: Go to Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard, then select Grammarly. Enable full access when prompted. This allows the keyboard to work across all your apps.
  • Tap the mic and start speaking: Open any app, tap into a text field, and you’ll see the Grammarly Keyboard. Hit the mic icon, say what you want to write, then stop. Clean, ready-to-send text appears right where your cursor is.

The definition of unreasonable effort is that people who are willing to work hard think you’re focusing on the wrong thing, or allocating too much time and focus on it. We won’t know if our unreasonable effort is justified until after […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
Breakthroughs don’t come from hard work. Lots of people are willing to work hard.

The definition of unreasonable effort is that people who are willing to work hard think you’re focusing on the wrong thing, or allocating too much time and focus on it.

We won’t know if our unreasonable effort is justified until after it pays off. That’s one more reason why breakthroughs are scarce.

issues.title: Draft your own team
issues.summary: This is the best way to make it onto a basketball team. The league isn’t going to call. But no one can stop you from starting your own league. In fact, the people you draft will be grateful you called. The same is true for an improv troupe, a cadre of co-programmers, a book group, […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
This is the best way to make it onto a basketball team.

The league isn’t going to call. But no one can stop you from starting your own league. In fact, the people you draft will be grateful you called.

The same is true for an improv troupe, a cadre of co-programmers, a book group, a knitting circle, a local political action cadre, and a professional mastermind. Even a group of five that goes for a walk together once a month.

Don’t just pick yourself. Pick the others as well.

issues.title: “That’s on me”
issues.summary: There have always been shortcuts. The small-plot farmer who chooses a crop that’s easier to plant but yields less, or the entry-level bureaucrat who goes along to get along. The person at the gym who avoids the machines that aren’t fun… We’re surrounded by systems that prey on our temptation to try just a bit […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
There have always been shortcuts.

The small-plot farmer who chooses a crop that’s easier to plant but yields less, or the entry-level bureaucrat who goes along to get along. The person at the gym who avoids the machines that aren’t fun…

We’re surrounded by systems that prey on our temptation to try just a bit less. So they create dark patterns and convenient and well-lit paths that end up more like traps than tools.

We’re not under the circumstances, though. We are the circumstances.

There are always going to be systems that work to manipulate us as they offer us shortcuts. And resisting each and every one of them is too much to ask. But when we’re serious about a piece of work, if anyone has figured out the long path, then we can too.

issues.title: 2026 Kindle Paperwhite review: Page-turn buttons are back, for a price
issues.summary: Kindles are getting costlier faster than they're getting better.
issues.author: Andrew Cunningham
issues.content_html:
Supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven't been immune. That's why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago. "New thing, better features, same price" used to be a reliable formula, but now you're lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.

The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year's $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you're choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these new models.

The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.

issues.title: The best Black Friday deals Ars could find
issues.summary: Perhaps some commerce, to help all the Turkey Day leftovers go down easier?
issues.author: Lee Hutchinson
issues.content_html:
Every year has a Prime Day—some years even have two Prime Days!—where we celebrate the life and achievements of the greatest leader the Autobots have ever known: the inimitable Optimus Prime. But just as every dawn is twinned by a dusk that steals its light, so too did Optimus Prime's bright spark fade, extinguished by the foul hand of Megatron during the Great Decepticon Incursion of 2005.

It is a day that lives in infamy forever, and we all know the tale—how the evil Megatron (cursed be the flow of his energon!) commandeered an Autobot shuttle, cruelly murdered its crew, and launched a cowardly surprise attack against Autobot City—a plan utterly bereft of honor, as was so typical of Megatron's schemes. Even as individual Autobots strove to secure Autobot City—heroes, all of them!—hope began to fade under an onslaught that included an attack by the fearsome Devastator, against which there appeared to be no defense.

And then, at the precipice of disaster, Optimus Prime made the fateful declaration whose words still ring out to this day: "Megatron must be stopped, no matter the cost." The fearless Autobot transformed, rolled out, and got the job done—even though that cost was high. Many brave Autobots besides Optimus Prime lost their lives during the fighting. It was truly a dark day, a black day—and so, every year on the Friday after Thanksgiving, we pause to remember the noble sacrifices made by Prime and by so many others. This is why today is known as Black Friday.

issues.title: Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences
issues.summary: Intel faced pressure to surrender a 10% stake to unlock billions in promised grants.
issues.author: Noah Shachtman, wired.com
issues.content_html:
The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

issues.title: Books, bikes, and The Burbs: These are Ars staff’s holiday gift picks for 2026
issues.summary: We polled the Ars staff about their favorite pickups this year; here's the list.
issues.author: Ars Staff
issues.content_html:
The holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we're here with a list of Ars staffers' favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!)

Rather than try to write a definitive "best gifts for your sister or brother" type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they've actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we're into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there's no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it's just a list of stuff we bought that we're happy about. It's heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.

For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.

issues.title: You can get a Pixel 11 Pro for what flagship phones used to cost
issues.summary: Before the RAM crisis, you could get a new, high-end phone for well under $1,000. Those days are gone, and flagship phones now start at a grand or more. Not to mention that you can easily spend double that on a phone that folds in half. But let’s turn back the clock for a moment […]
issues.author: Allison Johnson
issues.content_html:
Before the RAM crisis, you could get a new, high-end phone for well under $1,000. Those days are gone, and flagship phones now start at a grand or more. Not to mention that you can easily spend double that on a phone that folds in half. But let’s turn back the clock for a moment to the heady days of, oh, 2021, when a Pro-level Pixel started at $899.

The Pixel 11 Pro is a few months old at this point, not brand-new, which helps. And with the healthy Black Friday discount available from Amazon, Best Buy, and Google right now, the starting 256GB configuration drops from $1,099 to $749, its lowest price to date. With that kind of money, you can practically party like it’s 2019.

The bigger 11 Pro XL is also receiving a decent discount at Amazon and Best Buy, and the Pixel 10A got a $100 price cut on Amazon (but nowhere else). If affordability is an absolute must, then the latter is the way to go. But if you can spring for the Pro models, you should — and then hold on tight to your phone while we ride out the rest of RAMageddon.

Google Pixel 11 Pro

Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

  • $1099 $749 at Amazon (256GB)
  • $1099 $749 at Google (256GB)
  • $1099 $749 at Best Buy (256GB)

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL

The Pro XL offers the same Tensor G6 processor, triple-camera setup, and seven-year update policy as the standard 11 Pro, but with a larger 6.8-inch display and faster wired charging. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

  • $1299 $899 at Amazon (256GB)
  • $1299 $899 at Google (256GB)
  • $1299 $899 at Best Buy (256GB)

Google Pixel 10A

Google’s new Pixel 10A introduces faster wired charging, Satellite SOS, and new AI tools like Camera Coach and Auto Best Take. Otherwise, it’s basically the Pixel 9A, with the same Tensor G4 chip and a dual-camera system. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

  • $599 $499 at Amazon (128GB)
  • $599 $549 at Best Buy (128GB)
  • $599 $594 at Amazon (256GB)

Price plays a major factor, unsurprisingly, but for the holidays, some people care more about novelty above all else. They just want to gift something cool (or get something nice for […]
issues.author: Cameron Faulkner
issues.content_html:
We’ve covered a lot of deals so far that we think are fantastic during Black Friday, but readers gravitated to some more than others. Price plays a major factor, unsurprisingly, but for the holidays, some people care more about novelty above all else. They just want to gift something cool (or get something nice for themselves).

Deals on streaming services were extremely popular with readers this year because the savings are outstanding, and I think most of us are sick of paying and arm and a leg for monthly access. You can save big on Disney Plus, Hulu, HBO Max, Peacock, and even Apple TV. Streaming aside, Verge readers proved they have good taste in gear as you can see below in our small collection of the most-bought products.

AirPods Pro 3

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

  • $249 $149 at Amazon
  • $249 $149 at Walmart
  • $249 $149.99 at Best Buy

Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

Where to Buy:

  • $12.99 $4.99 at Hulu (ad-supported, monthly)
  • $21.99 $14.99 at Hulu (ad-free, monthly)

Anker Universal Charger (100W)

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

Where to Buy:

  • $79.99 $59.99 at Amazon
  • $79.99 $59.99 at Amazon (silver)
  • $79.99 $59.99 at Anker

Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader

With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering. It also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.

Where to Buy:

  • $109 $54.87 at Amazon (black)
  • $109 $54.87 at Amazon (white)
  • $109 $59 at Xteink

Govee Table Lamp 2

Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

Where to Buy:

  • $79.99 $53.99 at Amazon
  • $79.99 $53.99 at Govee

SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

Where to Buy:

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.

issues.title: Santacon Documentary Takes You Back To ’90s NYC
issues.summary: ‘Santacon’ doc director Seth Porges, who you might also know from “Class Action Park,” stopped by to tell us about his new film which is premiering digitally on VEEPS.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
‘Santacon’ doc director Seth Porges stopped by to tell us about his new documentary. In his own words…

“Santacon.”

Just the word is enough to make most New Yorkers gag.

You know the deal: Fistfights. Projectile vomiting.Thousands of drunk idiots getting sloppy all over NYC, terrorizing law-abiding citizens as well as the bartenders at any establishment brave enough not to ban their presence.

That’s what I thought too. Until a few years ago, when I bumped into my old friend Scott, who let me in on a little secret: He was there when a bunch of friends started the thing in San Francisco in the ‘90s.

He told me that the original creators have all disowned this thing as it transformed from what it was into what it is.

He told me these were the same people who also created (and largely stepped away from) Burning Man.

That they were the real-life inspiration for Fight Club and Project Mayhem, and Chuck Palahniuk was at some of the first Santacons.

The kicker: Scott personally filmed the early Santacon events, basically in their entirety. He had seen some of my prior films (such as Class Action Park), and so offered to show me the footage.

What I saw blew my mind.

I was taken back in time to 1990s NYC. To a version of NYC that barely exists anymore.

There are Santas in Times Square, a Disney Store and a peep show just steps apart.

There they are, literally risking death to climb the cables to the top of the Brooklyn Bridge. The Twin Towers in the background, a reminder that we’re now in a different world.

There they are on 5th Avenue, bumping into Michael Moore for some reason, who merrily leads the crew of Santas in anti-corporate Christmas Carols.

There they are in Astor Place, climbing the cube and turning it into a spinning carnival ride.

There they are in the East Village I remember, partying in the Continental and marching by Odessa.

There they are accusing Chuck Palahniuk of being an undercover cop (he wasn’t).

And there were the faces of countless onlookers, awash in joy and wonder and awe. The faces of people genuinely seeing something for the very first time, before the joke had been beaten into the ground. Before they knew that Santacon was the worst and something to avoid at all costs.

Seeing this footage, I knew I had to make this movie. To bring to life this world of chaos and wonder and possibility.

So with Scott’s help, I tracked down the original Santas, and got them to open up.

Some of the original Santas had kept their role in the event’s creation a closely guarded secret (I mean, wouldn’t you?).

The whole thing felt like a Frankenstein story. What happens when something you create takes on a life of its own, mutates into something monstrous, and becomes something you can no longer control?

And like any Frankenstein story, there was only one way it could end: I had to bring the original Santas back to Santacon, and make them confront their creation for the first time in 25 years.

Santacon happens on Dec 12 in NYC this year. The movie SANTACONwill premiere digitally on VEEPS on December 13, 2026 at 5pm PT/8pm ET. The VEEPS premiere will also feature an exclusive live Q&A.

Can’t make the digital premiere? The movie is playing in select theaters beginning December 2, and comes to VOD on Apple, Amazon, and Google on December 18. All screenings are listed at Santacondoc.com.

Seth Porges is the director of Santacon, which premieres on VEEPS on December 13 and VOD on December 18. His prior films include Class Action Park (HBO Max) and How To Rob A Bank (Netflix).

issues.title: New Godflesh & Jesu with Phoebe too
issues.summary: Some of the many reasons it’s been a great year for post-metal.
issues.author: Jeff Bergstrom
issues.content_html:
The great Jon Wurster (The Mountain Goats, The Bob Mould Band, Superchunk, The Best Show with Tom Scharpling) is a prolific drummer and one of the funniest people on earth. One of my favorite Wursterisms™ is that he utilizes the hashtag #rocknrollweirdness on Instagram when posting images of incongruous moments in rock n’ roll. Whether it’s a picture of The Who holding their Who Are You release party on the Hollywood set of the TV show Battlestar Galactica, Oasis hanging with Wesley Willis, or Motörhead drummer Philthy Animal Taylor and W.A.S.P. guitarist Chris Holmes having ice cream on a nice day, Wurster is a master curator of singular images of #rocknrollweirdness.

It’s rare for an instance of #rocknrollweirdness to land so profoundly with me that it gives me the energy to take finger-to-keyboard for the first time in years. Yet it recently came to my attention that master of heviosity Justin K. Broadrick was recently tapped by mainstream indie icon Phoebe Bridgers to play guitar on two tracks of her August 14, 2026 release Lost Weekend. Justin performs on track #5, “Bobby,” as well as on the ‘hidden’ track “Best Dressed” (track D17 on the vinyl and Track 00 on CD). Broadrick is involved with many different personal projects, each with their own particular signature sonic qualities, so it is important to note that he performs on these tracks under his Jesu moniker. And although I find his contributions to be buried under too many layers of over-production, the Broadrick aficionado can immediately recognize Jesu’s signature guitar sound in the first 15-seconds of “Bobby.” Lost Weekend was the Number 1 album in the UK and debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200. This is almost definitely the first time Justin has been that high in the charts.

But there was more! Phoebe Bridgers then released “On Video,” her song from the new A24 film Primetime. You can listen to it below. Oh and guess what? Justin Broadrick played bass and guitar on that song. As you probably know by now, Phoebe is also in the movie, and has been playing the song on tour.

These aren’t the first instances that Justin and Phoebe’s careers have intersected. Back in 2021, again under the Jesu moniker, Justin remixed Phoebe’s Boygenius bandmate Julien Baker’s track “Favor.” Justin not only executed the remix, but he also played guitars on the track which also features Phoebe Bridgers (and Lucy Dacus) on backing vocals. Check that track out below.

In other Justin K. Broadrick news, we’ve had a few months to let it sink in that the mighty Godflesh has retired from touring due to ongoing health issues plaguing Justin. The good news is that prior to his tour-ending surgery, Justin and Benny had an entire new Godflesh album pretty much already in the can. The album, entitled Decay, dropped on September 25 via Relapse Records and is available in all the formats, including vinyl in all kinds of colors and patterns.

Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.

You can listen to “Living/Ending” below and do some heavy duty ordering of the vinyl.

I interviewed Justin back in 2014 and would love to interview him again someday to discuss all of his projects BUT Godflesh. Until that happens, both Guitar World and The Guardian have published very good interviews with him that do a great job bringing fans up to speed with the current state of Justin’s world.

See also: it’s been a great year for post-metal.

issues.title: 5 Artists We Want to See at Louder Than Life 2026
issues.summary: Louder Than Life’s 2026 edition is coming. Check out who we’re excited to see.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Louder Than Life‘s 2026 edition is this weekend: September 17-20 at Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville, KY. As always, we’re figuring out who we most don’t want to miss. We’ll of course be sticking around for big headliners Tool, Iron Maiden, and My Chemical Romance, but the variety of acts we’re excited about across punk and metal genres this year is vast. Here are five artists that we’re especially looking forward to:

Circa Survive

As Andrew Sacherwrote when the band first announced their return:

Circa Survive went on “indefinite hiatus” in 2022, which came as bummer news considering they had just released some of the best music of their career, and the prospect of a reunion didn’t look very good after singer Anthony Greensaid on HardLore in December that what happened in 2022 was more of a “breakup” than a “hiatus” and added, “I don’t know if the band is ever going to do anything ever again… And even if it did, it wouldn’t be the same. It just wouldn’t.” So, it comes as a nice surprise that Circa Survive just announced their first show in nearly five years! They’ll be playing Louisville’s Louder Than Life festival in September, and Anthony Green will be pulling double duty at that fest, as L.S. Dunes are playing too. (Everyone in L.S. Dunes will be pulling double duty at that fest, as My Chemical Romance, Coheed & Cambria, and Thursday are playing too.

We can’t wait!

Haywire

Boston punks Haywire are one of the most exciting, most fun, and fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, with banger after banger, and with more on the way soon, as they recently announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Their raucous live shows continue to be unmissable, whether in a basement, a boxing ring, a club, or at a fest. See you in the pit.

Missing Link

Staying on the fest’s Friday hardcore stage for a second: playing before Haywire and the recently-announed, no-longer secret guest Knocked Loose, we want to highlight NY heavy hardcore band Missing Link whose intesity blows us away every time we get the chance to catch them (including sometimes with Haywire). Great live show. Don’t mess up and miss them in Louisville.

Hot Mulligan

Louder than Life also brings the pop punk, and the post-hardcore and emo-leaning Lansing, Michigan band Hot Mulligan are doing it better than most right now. Now four full lengths into their career, the band has become a festival staple, somtimes a rare mosh pit-inducing band on a lineup (like when we saw them at Gov Ball and Lolla), and sometimes right where they belong like in between Alkaline Trio and Jimmy Eat World in Louisville in Thursday. Always a super fun time, we can’t get enough of their energy, their humor, and their infectious hooks.

Danzig

The man, the myth, the legend. Danzig on this year’s fest officially brings it over the top for this Danzig-obsesed writer.

Check out the entire lineup HERE, and have fun this weekend.

issues.title: A Former Appliance Store Becomes a Hong Kong Cocktail Bar
issues.summary: Kevin Yiu of Minus Workshop pairs mid-century modern influences with warm wood, metallic finishes, and clever spatial solutions at Mius
issues.author: Anna Zappia
issues.content_html:
Good design is all about transformation and turning the everyday into memorable spaces. Kevin Yiu, principal at Minus Workshop, did just that with his recent conversion of a former appliance store into Mius, a cocktail bar in Hong Kong.

Nestled at 29 Gough Street in the SoHo district, the space reflects owner Shelley Tai’s belief in simple things done right, from libations that honor the classics to comfort food without complication. “Her desire for a genuine neighborhood bar challenged me to translate that specific vibe into spatial design,” Yiu explains.

Photography by Steven Ko

Yiu embraced mid-century modern design, and with only eight months to complete the project, he turned constraints into assets. High ceilings and a curated system of leather blinds capture sunlight by day, then offer layered illumination in the evening. A low structural beam clad in oak now doubles as an element that guides circulation and visually organizes the spaces. Electrical and mechanical systems remain hidden by joinery, which still allows access for maintenance.

Photography by Steven Ko

The material palette blends a range of contrasting textures. Wood veneer adds an organic appeal, while bronze and silver metals cast a subtle sheen, paired with shades of copper and brown. Minimal paint, rather than the artificial brightness of lacquer, keeps the aesthetic grounded.

Photography by Steven Ko

The 14-foot stainless steel bar top is both a statement piece and a functional surface that integrates essential equipment for the staff. Slabs of travertine form high tables where guests enjoy small plates or signature drinks. Reflective accents and strategic voids make the compact interior look more expansive.

Yiu decided to split bar operations across four counters to ease peak-hour congestion, keeping service clean and efficient. The queue flows from the front to the bar, with stools framing the activity in the main area.

Photography by Steven Ko

A floating chandelier by Lee Broom features celestial orbs that cast even light over the crowd. Plush velvet curtains drape over storage room doorways, and accent lamps round out a style that is bespoke but never stuffy.

For Yiu, it is a place that unfolds quietly, meant to be savored like the fare on the menu. “Mius is a sanctuary of simplicity, designed with a contemplative approach, which allows the interior architecture to elevate the hospitality experience,” he says.

issues.title: Friday Five with Nick Doyle: Seeing America Through Shades of Blue
issues.summary: Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, the Brooklyn-based artist shares the inspirations behind his latest exhibition
issues.author: Danine Alati
issues.content_html:
Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps. For Los Angeles-born interdisciplinary artist Nick Doyle, the material of choice is denim. Even when working in other mediums, he often gravitates toward a denim-blue palette, as in his latest exhibition, “Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found.”

Presented at Pace Prints’ New York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man. The gallery will present a selection of these works at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026.

‘Quick Fix’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Now based in Brooklyn, Doyle earned a BFA in interdisciplinary arts from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA in sculpture from Hunter College, in addition to studying at Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. He cites his discovery of denim as an artistic medium as a turning point in his career.

“I had been doing a ton of research on American history and making work exploring our relationship to nostalgia,” he recalls. “One day a fashion designer moved out of the neighboring studio and threw away a ton of stuff. I found a bolt of denim, and my brain flashed across a network of ideas I had already been considering. I intuitively knew I had stumbled across something significant.”

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints

Represented by Perrotin and Brussels-based Stems Gallery, Doyle typically uses denim collage to explore what he calls the “underlying structures in American culture.” His practice encompasses “painting-like wall works as well as interactive installations,” he says.

Doyle’s recent exhibition, Collective Hallucinations, presented at Perrotin New York this past spring, featured wall-mounted collages and an interactive installation called “Mirror Mirror.” The denim-clad structure featured a sign reading “Psychic Readings $10 Special,” while inside, a sassy AI avatar named Ava greeted visitors. The installation marked Doyle’s first foray into AI.

In another unexpected move, he presented his corporate-themed kink bar, Human Resources, at Basel Social Club in Switzerland this June. Built from repurposed cubicles and office furniture, the installation plays with the power dynamics inherent in both corporate and kink culture.

‘The Price of Ascension’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Doyle calls his work “more of a reflection of American culture than an individualist perspective.” Reflecting on being raised Quaker, he says, “It’s a very consensus-driven community that is slow-paced and meditative. It’s culturally very counter to a fast-paced, consumer-driven way of life typical of growing up in a large American city.” The tension between these two ways of life surfaces throughout his work.

In this week’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Nick Doyle ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, where Pace Prints will present selections from Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found, to discuss the inspirations behind his exploration of the contradictions of American life.

‘Empty’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

The Project: Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found

As with much of Doyle’s work, his latest exhibition examines the greed, excess, and toxic masculinity of American culture, this time through bold representations of the minutiae of everyday life: a folded shirt, a necktie, a lottery ticket, a gas gauge on empty, a Coca-Cola machine. Rendered in blue tones reminiscent of denim, the imagery evokes American labor and the archetype of the self-made man.

Together, the works question the country’s deep-rooted belief in self-reliance, drawing parallels between the ideal of the independent American and today’s “America First” mentality, in which individual freedom can come at the expense of collective responsibility. A selection of these works will be on view at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 2–6, 2026.

Here, Doyle discusses his inspirations for the exhibition in his own words.

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints

What Inspired Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found?

The Ken Burns Documentary: Country Music

“This documentary has everything: It traces the origins of country music alongside American history and is a deeply emotional story about the search for salvation and community.

“One of the musical groups featured is The Sons of the Pioneers. The title of this exhibition Lonely but Free I’ll be Found is a lyric in their song ‘Tumbling Tumbleweeds.’ Originally a poem written by Bob Nolan in the 1930s, it describes lonely cowboys adrift on the range.”

The Neon Museum in Las Vegas, Nevada. Photography courtesy of Nick Doyle.

The Neon Museum in Las Vegas

“I take a lot of road trips in the Southwest. Vegas is a great access point, and one of my favorite places is the Neon Museum with a collection of old signage from the last century. There’s something about these retrofuturistic signs rotting away in the desert that I relate to. They exude a sad psychological aura of something that once served a purpose, sitting in functionless rows like a graveyard.

“I think of this body of work functioning similarly to these signs, although different in the sense that what I’m drawing attention to is an idea rather than something that can be purchased.”

‘The Itch’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

The Suicide Belt

“For this show, I was considering the perspective of a man who lived in the ‘suicide belt,’ a term coined by Matt Wray in the early 2000s to describe the high-suicide-rate region of the U.S. Mountain/Intermountain West. The belt includes Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming.

“Wray describes ‘the Intermountain West as a place that is disproportionately populated by middle-aged and aging white men, single, unattached, often unemployed, with access to guns.’ I often think about suicide as a larger social symptom and connect it to broader social issues in the U.S.”

issues.title: The Best Gifts Under $50 for Design Enthusiasts
issues.summary: Clever, colorful, and thoughtfully designed finds that make a big impression on a limited budget
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
There’s something particularly satisfying about finding a great gift at a reasonable price point. And when it comes to design, a smaller price tag doesn’t have to mean settling for something ordinary. Some of the most memorable objects are also the simplest: a cleverly designed kitchen tool, a colorful accessory, or an everyday essential with an unexpected twist.

For this year’s selection, we’re looking for gifts that bring a little more personality to the everyday. Think playful forms, interesting materials, useful details, and objects that reflect the creativity of the people who designed them. Whether you’re shopping for a friend, a coworker, or someone who’s notoriously difficult to buy for, these gifts under $50 offer plenty of reasons to think beyond the usual suspects.

Photography courtesy of Shelton Metal

Shell Espresso Spoon Set by Shelton Metal

Inspired by treasures found along the seafloor, these miniature spoons bring an unexpected sculptural element to everyday rituals. Jewelry and homeware designer Colby Shelton Byrd hand-carves the shell-inspired forms, which are cast in solid brass and designed to develop a natural patina over time. The two-piece set is equally suited to stirring espresso or serving sugar, salt, and other small accompaniments.

The Shell Espresso Spoon Set is available at bloomingdales.com for $42.

Photography courtesy of Original Duckhead

Matisse Duck Umbrella by Original Duckhead

Rainy days get a little more colorful with Original Duckhead’s Matisse-inspired umbrella. Its graphic canopy is made from recycled plastic bottles, while a carved wooden duck-head handle adds an unexpected touch of whimsy. Designed with a wind-resistant frame and automatic opening mechanism, the compact umbrella combines everyday practicality with enough personality to make even a gloomy forecast feel more interesting.

The Matisse Duck Umbrella is available at originalduckhead.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of Goodee

Niwaki Y-Type Tool Box

Who says a toolbox has to live in the garage? Made in Japan from durable steel, Niwaki’s Y-Type Tool Box brings a little personality to everyday organization with its distinctive pitched lid, rounded edges, and compact industrial design. Available in yellow or gray, it’s just as useful for storing art supplies, sewing essentials, or desk accessories as it is for actual tools. At approximately 14 inches long, it’s a practical little storage solution that looks good enough to leave out.

The Niwaki Y-Type Tool Box is available at goodeeworld.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Present & Correct

1Y 52W 365D Planner by Present & Correct

A planner that’s as thoughtfully designed on the outside as it is on the inside. The 1Y 52W 365D Planner pairs a bold, striped cover with textured paper and foil lettering for a graphic take on everyday organization. Inside, 208 pages provide space to map out the year, while the undated format means there’s no pressure to start on January 1. A ribbon bookmark adds a practical finishing touch.

The 1Y 52W 365D Planner is available at presentandcorrect.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of Mark & Graham

Graham Leather Travel Tech Organizer

Tangled charging cables and misplaced earbuds are an inevitable part of traveling, but this sleek leather organizer from Mark & Graham helps keep the chaos under control. Its compact, zippered design keeps everyday tech essentials together, whether tucked into a carry-on, work bag, or backpack. The understated silhouette and leather exterior make it feel more like a thoughtfully designed accessory than a utilitarian storage pouch. Add a monogram for a personal touch that makes it an especially nice gift for frequent travelers.

The Graham Leather Travel Tech Organizer is available at markandgraham.com for $49.

MORE GIFT INSPIRATION

Still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of McGee & Co.

Stoneware Fish Plate by McGee & Co.

A little coastal charm goes a long way with this sculptural stoneware fish plate from McGee & Co. Its softly raised details capture the fish’s distinctive shape, while a white reactive glaze adds subtle variations in color and texture, making each piece slightly different. Measuring just over seven inches long, it’s perfectly sized for serving small bites, holding a few favorite trinkets, or adding a playful touch to an open shelf. Proof that a thoughtful gift doesn’t need a big price tag.

The Stoneware Fish Plate is available at mcgeeandco.com for $26.

Photography courtesy of Galison

Frank Stella Harran II 750-Piece Shaped Puzzle by Galison

Frank Stella’s bold geometric artwork becomes a hands-on experience with this 750-piece puzzle. Featuring Harran II (1967), from the artist’s celebrated Protractor series, the design transforms colorful, overlapping arcs into an unconventional jigsaw with an irregular silhouette. Packaged in a handsome drawer-style box, it’s a thoughtful gift for art enthusiasts who enjoy a creative challenge.

The Frank Stella Harran II 750-Piece Shaped Puzzle is available at galison.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Goodee

Pepin Olla Self-Watering Pot

For the plant lover who occasionally forgets to water, Pepin’s Olla offers a clever solution rooted in centuries-old irrigation techniques. Handcrafted in Portugal’s historic Leiria region, the small clay vessel is designed to be partially buried in a planter, where its porous walls slowly release water directly into the soil. Simply refill it every week or two, and let the plant take what it needs. Finished with a rich burgundy glaze and a natural cork stopper, it’s a charming little object that makes plant care a bit easier.

The Pepin Olla Self-Watering Pot is available at goodeeworld.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Valsa Home

Stainless Steel Egg Cup Set by Valsa Home

A little retro and entirely practical, these stainless steel egg cups bring a sculptural touch to the breakfast table. Made in Portugal, their polished finish and gently flared silhouettes recall midcentury tableware, while the simple design feels right at home in a contemporary kitchen. Sold as a set of four, they’re a charming gift for anyone who appreciates the ritual of a leisurely breakfast.

The Stainless Steel Egg Cup Set is available at valsahome.com for $30.

Photography courtesy of Design Within Reach

Spirale Bowl by Emma Kohlmann for Hay

Artist Emma Kohlmann brings her expressive, painterly style to the table with this charming stoneware bowl. Part of Hay’s La Pittura collection, it draws inspiration from Renaissance apothecary jars and traditional Tuscan pottery. Each piece is hand-painted by artisans in Sri Lanka, making every bowl slightly different. At just under five inches across, it’s perfectly sized for snacks, sauces, or small treats.

The Spirale Bowl is available at dwr.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of Printworks

Yatzy Bazaar by Printworks

Swedish brand Printworks has a knack for turning classic games into objects worth displaying, and its Bazaar edition of Yatzy is no exception. Colorful, graphic packaging gives the traditional dice game a contemporary makeover, making it as at home on a coffee table as it is on game night. It’s a fun gift for anyone who appreciates good design and a little friendly competition.

Yatzy Bazaar is available at printworksmarket.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Toast

Longpi Oil Burner by Toast

Hand-molded from a mixture of ground black stone and locally sourced clay, this oil burner showcases a centuries-old pottery technique unique to two villages in northeastern India. A tea light tucked into the opening below gently heats a mixture of water and essential oils in the bowl above, releasing fragrance throughout the room. Pair it with a favorite essential oil for a gift that engages multiple senses.

The Longpi Oil Burner is available at ⁠us.toa.st for $50.

Photography courtesy of Urban Outfitters

Kodhi Mini Table Lamp by Urban Outfitters

An exercise in playful proportions, the Kodhi Mini Table Lamp pairs a colorful, spherical base with an elongated, tapered woven shade in coordinating hues. The contrast between the rounded base and the angular shade gives the petite lamp an almost cartoonish quality. Sized for a bedside table or bookshelf, it’s an affordable way to introduce both color and ambient lighting into a small space. Just be sure to include the required bulb with your gift, as it’s sold separately.

The Kodhi Mini Table Lamp is available at urbanoutfitters.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Coming Soon

White Elephant Gift from Coming Soon

Take the white elephant gift exchange quite literally this year with a cup that conceals a miniature white elephant inside. The unexpected detail reveals itself as you sip, bringing a little humor to an everyday ritual. It’s a clever choice for a holiday gift swap, but one that’s equally fun to give outside of the party game.

The White Elephant Gift is available at comingsoonnewyork.com.

Photography courtesy of Joon Loloi

Valene Vase by Joon Loloi

With its rounded silhouette and glossy moss-green finish, the Valene Vase makes a small but memorable statement. Handmade in India from EcoMix, a material incorporating upcycled paper, the sculptural vessel offers an unexpected alternative to traditional ceramic. At just 6.5 inches wide, it’s sized for a bookshelf, desk, or bedside table, where it can stand alone or hold a few dried stems. Just note that it’s not watertight, so fresh flowers are off the table.

The Valene Vase is available at joonloloi.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Native Union

Pop Phone by Native Union

Native Union brings the familiar silhouette of a traditional telephone handset into the smartphone era with its Pop Phone. Complete with a coiled cord and oversized receiver, the retro-inspired design offers a more tactile alternative to taking calls on a touchscreen. It’s a fun nod to analog technology for anyone nostalgic for the days of landlines.

The Pop Phone is available at nordstrom.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Wms&Co.

Task Roller by Wms&Co.

An upgrade from the ubiquitous sticky note, the Task Roller pairs a continuous roll of paper with a streamlined stainless steel dispenser. The compact design keeps a fresh writing surface within reach without cluttering a desk or countertop, making it particularly appealing to those who prefer handwritten reminders, grocery lists, and daily to-dos.

The Task Roller is available at wmscoshop.com for $46.

Photography courtesy of Areaware

Everybody Grinder by Dusen Dusen for Areaware

Leave it to Dusen Dusen to give the humble salt and pepper grinder a personality of its own. Designed for Areaware, the Everybody Grinder features a graphic face rendered in the Brooklyn-based studio’s signature playful style. The unexpected design makes a case for leaving your seasonings out on the counter, adding a little character to an otherwise utilitarian corner of the kitchen.

The Everybody Grinder is available at areaware.com for $48.

Photography courtesy of West Elm

Pigeon Glasses Holder by Emma Chamberlain for West Elm

For the friend who’s constantly misplacing their glasses, this unlikely little companion offers a solution. Part of Emma Chamberlain’s collaboration with West Elm, the pigeon-shaped holder brings a dose of absurdist humor to a nightstand or desk. Even when it’s not sporting a pair of spectacles, it makes for an amusing decorative object.

The Pigeon Glasses Holder is available at westelm.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Studio Arhoj

Riso Works 2027 Calendar by Studio Arhoj

Give someone a colorful start to the new year with Studio Arhoj’s Riso Works calendar. Available in orange, pink, and red, the poster celebrates the distinctive aesthetic of risograph printing, turning a practical everyday reference into a piece of graphic art. It’s a particularly fitting gift for design enthusiasts who appreciate the tactile qualities of printed matter in an increasingly digital world.

The Riso Works 2027 Calendar is available at arhoj.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store

Multicolor Glass Jars by Ingo Fremer

For the person who finds as much joy in organizing as they do in decorating, this set of four colorful glass jars makes everyday storage a little more interesting. The transparent glass keeps contents visible while introducing playful pops of color to kitchen counters, bathroom shelves, and desktops.

The Multicolor Glass Jars are available at ⁠store.moma.org for $35.

Photography courtesy of Maharam

Memory Three by Maharam

A childhood favorite gets a design-minded makeover with Maharam’s third edition of its memory game. Featuring 36 distinct patterns drawn from the brand’s archive of classic and contemporary textiles, the game doubles as a miniature lesson in textile design. Even the packaging offers an element of surprise, with one of four cover designs selected at random.

Memory Three is available at ⁠maharam.com for $40.
