issues.title: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist
issues.summary: 4 interior designers share their thoughts on burlwood’s enduring appeal, their favorite material pairings, and how to incorporate it into contemporary spaces
issues.author: Colleen Sullivan
issues.content_html:
Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Why Burlwood Continues to Captivate Designers

“Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

The tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts, while colorful glass candlesticks and art books add color to the display. Photography by Ellen Renee.

For Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he says. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

“The material is timeless,” Brooks says. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”

A honey-toned burlwood table features a richly figured top and tapered legs, standing out against the darker wood cabinetry behind it. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-new piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he says, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Choosing the Right Burlwood

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

A burlwood nightstand introduces warmth and a touch of traditional detail to this otherwise contemporary bedroom, adding a rich wood accent against the sculptural charcoal headboard and modern lines. Photography by Nick Sargent.

Maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he says.

While Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she says. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”

A close-up reveals the distinctive natural markings of a burlwood table, with brass-and-acrylic drawer pulls adding a mix of warm and modern finishes. Photography by Emily Hart.

Pairing Burlwood with Other Materials and Finishes

Because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she says. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

A burlwood tray with a gold-toned rim highlights the wood’s warm coloring and varied markings, with stacked books providing a colorful backdrop. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

For a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

A curved burlwood console showcases the wood’s richly varied grain across its drawer fronts and rounded frame, with pale green stools and white fringe adding a touch of color and texture. Photography by Emily Hart.

How Designers Are Reimagining Burlwood

Burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she says. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.

A burlwood coffee table showcases the wood’s warm tones and naturally irregular markings, while art books and a decorative bowl give the tabletop a relaxed, collected feel. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Contemporary furniture designs also explore the interplay between burlwood, contrasting materials, and simpler silhouettes. Jonathan Adler’s Bond collection, for example, combines burl with acrylic on a dresser and metal on a dining table. Meacham points to Made Goods’ Bradley mirror, which lets the mappa burl frame take center stage. Fenimore recommends looking at brands like Modway and TOV Furniture, particularly for smaller items such as chairs, ottomans, and drink tables with burl accents.

The rich, swirling grain of the half-moon burlwood console complements the delicate branches and floral motifs in the botanical artwork above. Photography by Emily Hart.

Making Room for Burlwood

For anyone hesitant to introduce such a distinctive material, the designers recommend beginning with one piece, such as a side table, mirror, or tray. Brooks suggests starting with something that serves an existing need, even if it’s as small as a drink table next to a chair. Maestri puts it simply: “Pick one piece and let it be the star. Keep what’s around it simpler so the grain can stand out.”

Fenimore encourages mixing burlwood with other wood tones rather than trying to match everything. She also sees the material as a way to ground a room that already has plenty of color and pattern. Meacham recommends giving the grain some breathing room through intentional styling and a variety of finishes. “That doesn’t mean everything else needs to be neutral—I love burl with color—but you want your eye to have somewhere to rest.”

Burlwood’s latest resurgence doesn’t require a revival of any particular decorating style. The same material that characterized Art Deco cabinetry and 1970s furniture feels equally at home alongside contemporary silhouettes, unexpected colors, and contrasting finishes. Its history is part of its appeal, but it needn’t dictate how we use it.

issues.title: DD416 / Adrift in a world of options
issues.summary: Issue 416: Adrift in a world of options – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I left Germany at 20 and, looking back, never quite stopped leaving. A year of travelling around Australia and parts of Asia kicked off two decades of freelancing from wherever I happened to be. I never held a ‘real’ job for more than three months. I wasn’t in a serious relationship until my thirties. Above all, I wanted to keep my options open. Australia became home, but something kept pulling me elsewhere, sometimes for months at a time.

I’m grateful for those years. Few people enjoy that kind of privilege. But I can also see what all that freedom did to me: it turned me into a commitment-phobe. Without really noticing, I’d become uncomfortable with anything that might anchor me to a place. Leases, girlfriends, gym contracts – if it had a whiff of long term obligation, I’d look for a reason to stay clear.

In the last few years, that’s changed. Relationship, mortgage, dog, lovely neighbours. Age surely plays a part, but this work here has also taught me that one of the best responses to the many crises of our time is to stop running from obligations and become a person of place.

Rosie Spinks and Spencer R. Scott, two of my favourite Substackers, verbalised this perfectly in a recent video chat to discuss Scott’s new book As If We Were Staying (see below).

Spinks quotes a line from the book that feels very apt: “One cannot learn to engage in reciprocal partnership with the local environment while planning to flee it at the first inconvenience.” You may swap ‘local environment’ for a person, a city, a child, a pet…

Spinks admits that, like me, not long ago she’d hear the word ‘obligation’ and instinctively file it under ‘bad things’. The goal was always to have as few as possible. Then she became a mother, and suddenly her life was full of them.

I agree with her that our cultural fear of obligation explains a lot of the emptiness people feel. It’s never been easier to live without obligations, and whenever we do need help, there’s a paid service to spare us the inconvenience of relying on other people. But does that add up to a good life?

Scott, who gave up a biotech career to buy a farm in a small US town, went through a similar reckoning. His book argues that capitalism has sealed us into tidy units of individualism. An obligation is the opposite: a draw on your time and energy that you can’t simply outsource. He resisted at first, until it dawned on him that all of his obligations were really relationships. The effort was what made them matter.

And it’s not just about the people closest to us. It’s the local birdlife, that old tree on the corner, the barista who knows our order, the councillor who lives down the road. All those little connections add up to a network of reciprocity.

I guess my generation was the first, though not the last, to be sold this mirage of independence, sometimes for reasons we didn’t choose – insecure work, unaffordable housing, a phone that turns every evening into a sea of options. Other towns, other partners, other careers always look better in the feed, so we never stay long enough to collect what staying gives us. Spinks calls it “floating in the void”.

I’m wary of making obligation a virtue in itself. Plenty of people are stuck in commitments they never chose, and for some of them leaving is the healthiest thing they can do. I also know it was my drifting years that let me put down roots knowing what I was giving up. What matters, I think, is that we pick our obligations with our eyes open, then commit to them. In other words: fuck stick around and find out.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD415 / MBA: school of profit
issues.summary: Issue 415: MBA: school of profit – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
When I finished high school and started exploring my study options back in Germany, I came across the then-new MBA (Master of Business Administration) and found it a bit baffling. I thought you first had to master a craft, then turn it into a business. The MBA seemed to suggest that the craft was not important and you could just learn how to run any business. The course description was thick with English jargon, which didn’t help. I vaguely remember someone describing it as learning how to make more money without producing anything.

That description came back to me while reading a recent opinion piece by Christopher Marquis, who has spent more than 20 years teaching at famous business schools. His verdict on his own industry: business schools can’t be repaired; it’s time to shut them down.

“I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system – they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to ‘fix’ business schools. We need to abolish them.”

Marquis points to research showing that managers with business degrees cut wages, yet didn’t become any more productive. He concludes:

“What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer – value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.”

He also puts into words what I couldn’t as an adolescent:

“A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice – undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they ‘need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.’”

The tension is usually glossed over with the comforting ‘win-win’ story:

“These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of ‘stakeholder capitalism’: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.”

So what should we teach instead? Marquis points to the idea of “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business:

“Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from ‘How do we maximize shareholder value?’ to ‘How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward – and which should we strengthen?’”

“The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.”

To me, this is what rethinking our economic system could look like at its most basic level. An ethics elective won’t do it. The work starts with how we teach people to think about power and capital: how currently both tend to accumulate at the top, while the ecological and social mess gets filed under ‘externalities’ and left for future generations to sort out.

We need people who can read a balance sheet and run a payroll, of course. But we could also teach them to build co-operatives, strengthen communities and organise around shared interests. Extracting value for personal gain is one model of doing business, with a long track record of consequences, but certainly not the only one.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD414 / Organising the discontent
issues.summary: Issue 414: Organising the discontent – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I can still feel it – the collective exhale. Ann Friedman calls it ‘the great unclenching’, and Rebecca Solnit writes that a win for democracy of this size deserves a proper celebration. Fair enough.

But while the rest of us were glued to swing-state maps, something remarkable was unfolding in a corner of Europe that rarely makes our news feeds.

In Serbia, a movement led by students forced snap elections and then won them outright, ending more than a decade of autocratic rule. It started in 2024, when a train station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. To many Serbians, it was corruption made visible. Students blockaded their universities and demanded accountability. Within months, farmers, actors, judges and pensioners had joined them, filling city squares in some of the largest protests the country has ever seen.

What’s amazing is that this ideologically mixed movement hasn’t splintered into rival factions. Instead, it has built a shared identity without a single face on the poster. Its electoral list had no leader. The 250 candidates on the ballot papers were nominated, grilled and voted on by student plenums – open assemblies at each university. This produced something that represents a decent slice of the country: a cardiologist, a grammar school teacher, a coal miner, a social worker, a former central bank governor and, for good measure, a retired basketball star.

I’ve been a fan of citizens’ assemblies for years (see DD220). There is lots of evidence that ordinary people, given time, reliable information and a genuine stake in the outcome, can make remarkably good and fair decisions. Serbia’s plenums aren’t a textbook citizens’ assembly – nobody was picked by lottery – but they share the spirit. The power to choose sat with big, messy rooms full of people. And few people have a bigger stake in the outcome than students, who’ll be living with the results long after today’s power brokers have retired to their holiday homes.

It’s hard not to see echoes of Serbia in the Gen Z protests spreading across the world. Of course, some protests turn ugly, and the looting and vandalism deserve condemnation. But the media is often far more interested in pictures of ghouls smashing shop windows than in understanding why so many people took to the streets in the first place, why so many young people can’t see a future worth studying for. Serbia shows what that frustration can build once it gets organised.

The proof is in the pudding, of course. Leaderless movements can be great at opposing and clumsy at governing. Decision-making by committee isn’t pretty. Consensus takes time, patience and a healthy tolerance for disagreement. But there’s something very inspiring about a political movement that started by asking who should represent it, not who should lead it.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: Top 10 Learnings From Databricks CRO Ron Gabrisko on Scaling Sales From Under $1M to a $200B Company
issues.summary: Ron Gabrisko joined Databricks as CRO when it was doing under $1M in ARR. Databricks is now worth $200 billion and does many billions in ARR, and Ron has run sales the whole way. He joined Sam Blond, co-founder of Monaco and former CRO of Brex, on the SaaStr AI CRO Confidential podcast to talk... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Ron Gabrisko joined Databricks as CRO when it was doing under $1M in ARR. Databricks is now worth $200 billion and does many billions in ARR, and Ron has run sales the whole way.

He joined Sam Blond, co-founder of Monaco and former CRO of Brex, on the SaaStr AI CRO Confidential podcast to talk about how selling has changed since they last recorded in October 2024. Ron’s view is that the fundamentals of great selling are the same: preparation, relationships, account research, grit, EQ and IQ. Almost everything about how Databricks hires, trains, prospects, demos, and prices has changed around them.

Here are the top 10 learnings from Ron.

#1. AE Candidates Build a Working Genie Demo for a Real Account in the Interview

Databricks runs a live test for the skills it wants reps to show customers. Candidates:

  • Pick an account
  • Deliver a CEO-level AI pitch for that company, specific to its industry and how Databricks would change it
  • Get access to Genie, build a demo on the spot, and walk the panel through it and the outcomes it would drive

Back channels and referrals from known networks still count. Every candidate is also met in person.

Ron’s reasoning is simple. His AEs build custom demos for accounts like Pepsi and Rivian as part of the job, so the interview tests whether they can.

#2. Reps Are Certified on the Pitch and the Demo All Year Long

Databricks starts with boot camps that cover the whole product line. Then it certifies reps on the CEO-level pitch and on industry-based Genie demos, and keeps certifying them throughout the year.

Ron says sales has drifted away from big-picture storytelling, and he wants reps who can tell a CEO what’s possible for their business. He played baseball, and he applies the same rule: practice 10x more than you play. He expects his reps to be the best sellers anywhere, and says that takes testing, enablement, training, and mentoring.

Every Databricks rep has to be certified on Genie. The company runs Databricks on Databricks, and reps use Genie on their phones.

#3. 60% of Rep Time Goes to Customers: Prep on Monday and Friday, on the Road Tuesday Through Thursday

Ron’s long-time rule is “sell from your feet, not your seat.” He thinks many sales teams lost that habit when selling went virtual.

His target is at least 60% of rep time in front of customers. The weekly rule of thumb:

  • Monday and Friday: prep and admin
  • Tuesday through Thursday: on the road with customers, or more

Ron says reps who follow it are the ones who succeed.

#4. Agents Now Do the Account Research, Presentation Prep, and Proposals

Databricks has built agents, all running through Genie, for:

  • Account research and background
  • Presentation preparation
  • Exec prep docs
  • Proposals
  • Picking the right contacts on LinkedIn and customizing outreach to each one

Ron says he has seen this raise rep productivity, and the time saved is what makes the 60% customer-time target realistic.

#5. SDR Headcount Has Stayed Flat While Databricks Keeps Adding AEs and SAs

Databricks still has a large SDR team. It hasn’t grown, even as the company adds more AEs and solutions architects.

Ron attributes that to productivity. Outbound, prospect and contact signals, and campaigns are automated, with personalization down to the individual person. He also notes Databricks sells into one of the hottest markets ever in data and AI, so inbound interest helps.

If he were starting a company today, Ron would build a demand gen team and the tools behind it, and keep that team small.

#6. Outbound Reply Rates Went From 1-2% to 6-10%

Ron described the old outbound model as loading 5,000 contacts into “the automated spammer,” sending to all of them, and hoping for 1-2% response rates.

With outreach customized to each prospect, Databricks now sees 6-10% response rates.

His point is that this doesn’t make reps less necessary. As long as companies buy software, he says, they’ll need people to sell it, because the sale still depends on relationships, trust, and teaching customers how to get value from the product. Reps now spend more of their time on that.

#7. Ron Keeps the SDR Team Because That’s Where His Future AEs Come From

Many Databricks SDRs move up to AE. Ron’s question for companies cutting SDRs to zero: who teaches new sellers how to sell your product?

He expects the SDR team may shrink over time, but he wants to keep some form of academy for younger sellers, with a path into AE or management. Without one, every AE has to be hired from outside, and no one mentors the next generation. He sees that as a gap.

Some of Ron’s best sellers today came up this way. They grew up with AI, embrace new technology, and write their own programs and apps using Genie and LLMs.

#8. The AE Owns the Whole Account, and the Buyer Is Now the CFO and CMO Too

Ron expects AEs to reach new departments, people, and stakeholders themselves. His line: “You’re the CEO of your account.” Covering every part of the account is the AE’s job, not just the SDR’s.

The buyers have also changed. Databricks used to sell mostly into IT. Now AI is a CEO-level initiative, business leaders want to build with it, and Databricks sells to CFOs, CMOs, CIOs, and CEOs. Ron says getting into a company’s most strategic initiatives is where his team spends more time now, and the automation is what freed up the time to cover those buyers.

#9. Show Up With a Working Build on Industry Data Instead of a PowerPoint

Ron says the forward deployed engineer model has taken off and customers now expect to see what you’ll deliver. In his view, showing up with a PowerPoint no longer works.

The build may not run on the customer’s production data, but it should run on dummy data that looks like their industry and company. Databricks closes by showing a customer what it built for a specific use case, such as supply chain predictions or stockout prevention, and then deploying it. It has done this with large retailers and pharma companies.

This matters more when selling to business buyers, who need to see the outcome. Ron also thinks most vendors’ messaging sounds identical, so buyers decide on what you can solve for them, how fast, and whether they trust you.

Databricks has always been consumption based, so this is the core motion: pick the top use cases for an industry, sell them to business users, and implement them as fast as possible with FDEs.

#10. Databricks Charged $1,000 Per User. Ron Made Users Free and Consumption Went Way Up.

Ron calls consumption pricing one of the smartest decisions Databricks made. As customers’ data and queries grow, Databricks grows. AI agents add to that: Ron expects millions of agents querying data alongside people, and says Databricks has more data under management than any company in the world.

He told several AI coding companies early on they would never get huge on per-user pricing. They have since moved to usage pricing on tokens.

His framework:

  • Find your base unit. It should scale over time and track customer value. LLMs use tokens. Databricks uses DBUs.
  • Price added value as multipliers or add-ons on that unit. Security, accelerators, and premium support are examples.
  • Match price to value. Overprice and no one buys. Underprice and you leave money on the table.

The mistake: early on, Databricks added per-user pricing and a platform fee on top of consumption. When Ron asked customers why they weren’t ramping faster, they said every user cost them $1,000. He asked if they’d open it to everyone if users were free. They said sure. Consumption went way up after the change.

Ron’s other pricing advice:

  • Don’t require a commit before customers can use the product. Keep the entry point as low as possible with free tiers, trials, PLG, or a credit card. Once customers like it, usage spreads from one or two users to a department, then multiple departments, and then you ask for a commit.
  • Don’t push for a big deal on day one. Early-stage companies need logos and new customers.
  • You can fix the wrong model later. Ron thinks companies that started with the wrong pricing can adjust. The bigger mistake is not capturing value from customers at all.
  • Set pricing early. Switching from per-user to usage pricing later is very hard.

issues.title: Looking Back on a Few Investments I Shouldn’t Have Made, One Sign Stands Out: The Founders Didn’t Know Their Space 10,000% Cold
issues.summary: One clear sign, looking back, on a few investments I shouldn't have made: When they literally didn't know their space 10,000% cold Every competitor, every market dynamic, every player Yes, even at pre-seed. The best founders always do. — Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) November 4, 2026 Years ago a founder building a software testing company... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
One clear sign, looking back, on a few investments I shouldn't have made:

When they literally didn't know their space 10,000% cold

Every competitor, every market dynamic, every player

Yes, even at pre-seed. The best founders always do.

— Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) November 4, 2026

Years ago a founder building a software testing company came in to pitch me. Partway through, he explained how Salesforce ran testing internally and why his product fit right into that process.

I had just spent time with a VP of Engineering at Salesforce, and that wasn’t how they did it. It wasn’t close. So I told him.

He argued with me. He didn’t ask what I’d heard or say he’d go check. He told me the Salesforce VP of Engineering was wrong about how Salesforce worked.

The company’s growth was strong, so I invested anyway.

I lost all my money on that one.

I’ve been writing venture checks for 13 years now, across two funds. Most of the time, when I look back at the investments that didn’t work, I can find the reason. Sometimes it was a founder who wasn’t better than me. Sometimes it was a CTO who was good but not great. Sometimes it was numbers that got fudged.

But when I go back through the handful I really shouldn’t have made, one more sign shows up again and again. It’s the one I underweighted for too long, and it’s the one I saw in that pitch:

The founder didn’t know their space 10,000% cold.

They didn’t know every competitor, every market dynamic, every player, who was winning which deals, and why. And when they hit something they didn’t know, they filled the gap with a confident guess and then defended it.

And yes, that applies even at pre-seed. The best founders always know their space cold. In fact, it’s often why they started the company.

The short version:

  • The best founders know every competitor, including the ones that launched last month, plus pricing, positioning, who wins which deals, and why.
  • They have deep respect for the leaders in their space. They can tell you exactly what the incumbents are strong at, beyond where they look weak.
  • At pre-seed there’s very little else to diligence. What the founder knows about the space is most of the signal you get.
  • The founders who didn’t know their space got surprised later by competitive moves they should have seen coming 12 months out, and they reacted instead of planning.
  • In 2026 the bar is higher. AI categories turn over in months, and an agent can map a whole market in an afternoon, so not knowing your space is now a choice.

It’s the crispness and nuance of the answers that stand out. Why a competitor failed. What another gets right. What’s changed in the market.

You leave thinking that same attention to detail probably shows up everywhere in the business. https://t.co/6Cq8KdI4Go

— Chris Saum (@christophersaum) November 4, 2026

1. What “Cold” Actually Means: Every Competitor, Every Price, Every Lost Deal

Most founders can name their top three competitors. That’s table stakes, and it’s not what I mean.

Founders who know their space 10,000% cold can tell you, without opening a laptop:

  • Every competitor, including the seed-stage one that launched six weeks ago, the incumbent’s new agent product, and the adjacent company that’s two quarters away from moving into their lane.
  • Where each one is genuinely strong, meaning which customers it wins and why those customers are right to pick it.
  • What everyone charges, and how each one prices: seats, consumption, outcomes. They know list price, and they know what deals actually close at.
  • Who the buyer is, and whose budget it comes out of. Is it the CIO’s software line, a headcount budget, or a services budget?
  • Which deals they lose, and to whom. At pre-seed that might mean design partners who picked something else. They know the name and the reason.
  • Where the market goes in 2-3 years. They don’t need to know about 10 years out. They do need a specific view of what changes over the next 24 months, and who that change helps.

None of this is trivia. Every item on that list feeds a decision the founder will make in the next year: pricing, which segment to attack first, which feature makes them 10x better at one thing, and which deals to walk away from.

2. The Best Founders Can Tell You What the Incumbent Does Better Than Anyone

Lots of founders can list where the incumbent looks weak: the old UI, slow releases, AI bolted onto a product built in 2012, a sales cycle customers hate. Everyone in the market already knows those things. Being able to list them doesn’t show insight.

The founders I’ve done best with go further. They have real respect for the leaders in their space, and they can tell you exactly what those leaders are strong at:

  • Distribution. The incumbent already sells to the buyer, already sits on the approved vendor list, and already has a rep with a standing QBR on the calendar.
  • Trust. It has passed every security review, has had the SOC 2 for a decade, and the customer’s legal team has already signed its paper. For a large enterprise, that alone can be worth a year of sales cycle.
  • The installed base and the data inside it. Years of customer records, workflows and integrations that nobody wants to touch. Moving a database is now just annoying. Moving ten years of context is still hard.
  • The boring features. Permissions, audit logs, admin controls, compliance, and support in 40 countries. Nobody demos these, but they’re what renewals come down to.
  • Bundling power. The incumbent can give your core feature away free inside a contract the customer is already paying for.
  • The ecosystem. Partners, SIs, consultants and admins whose careers are built on the incumbent’s platform.

The best founders can explain why a smart customer rationally stays with the incumbent. They can explain it so well it almost sounds like a pitch for the incumbent. Then they tell you about the one narrow wedge where none of those strengths matter, and why they win there anyway.

In the investments I regret, the founders could only tell me why the incumbent was “old.” Every one of those incumbents was still growing, still had the relationships, and still closed the deals my founders assumed were theirs. Being old doesn’t mean being slow, and it definitely doesn’t mean being dead. Some of the biggest names in B2B are still growing current RPO in double digits at tens of billions of dollars in revenue.

Respect also changes what founders do. Founders who respect the leaders get to know the competitor CEOs. They study how the incumbent actually wins deals instead of mocking its website. They don’t start fights they can’t win in year one, like head-to-head bake-offs in the incumbent’s strongest segment, and they choose the ground where the incumbent’s strengths don’t help it.

3. At Pre-Seed, What the Founder Knows Is Most of What You Can Diligence

People push back on this one. “It’s pre-seed. They have no customers. How deep can they really be?”

That’s exactly backwards. At pre-seed there’s no NRR to look at, no cohort data, no pipeline. You have the founder, the product (if there is one), and what the founder knows.

The best pre-seed founders I’ve backed already knew the space better than anyone I could call for a reference check. Usually they’d lived inside the problem for years. They’d sold the incumbent product, or bought it, or built the internal workaround that everyone at their old company used. Knowing the market cold wasn’t homework they did for the pitch. It was the reason the company existed.

In the investments I regret, the founders had mostly picked the space. They found a market that looked big and hot and then learned it on the way. Some of those founders were smart and hardworking. But they were always one step behind people who’d been in the market for years, and that gap never really closed.

4. The Founders Who Didn’t Know Their Space Got Blindsided 12 Months Later

The way this showed up in outcomes was very consistent.

Something would happen in the market:

  • an incumbent bundled the core feature for free,
  • a better-funded competitor launched into the same segment,
  • the category moved from seats to consumption pricing,
  • or a big platform shut off API access.

The founders who knew their space cold had already seen it coming. They’d talked about it at the board meeting two quarters earlier and had a plan. Maybe they’d already moved upmarket, or already repriced, or already built the integration that made them harder to rip out.

The founders who didn’t know their space were surprised every time. Every board meeting became a story about a “new” competitive dynamic that wasn’t new at all. They reacted. They copied features. They cut prices. They burned quarters chasing a market that had already moved.

There’s a second problem too. When a founder doesn’t know the market cold, they fill the gaps with confident guesses, like the testing founder who told me how Salesforce worked. The guess is a problem. Defending it against someone who knows better is a bigger one.

So not knowing the space is a sign of more than one thing. It tells you how curious the founder is, and how honest they are when they hit something they don’t know.

5. In 2026, AI Categories Turn Over in Months, and an Agent Can Map a Market in an Afternoon

Two things changed, and both of them raise the bar.

First, spaces move much faster now. In almost every agentic B2B category I look at, there’s a new well-funded entrant every month or two. The incumbents are finally shipping their own agents. Pricing models are changing under everyone’s feet. A competitive map from six months ago is already out of date. A founder who knew the space cold in the spring and stopped paying attention can be behind by Q4.

Second, there’s no excuse anymore. At SaaStr we run 20+ agents in production, and some of them do nothing but research. You can point an agent at a category and get back every competitor, every pricing page, every recent funding round, every relevant job posting, every product launch, and every G2 complaint in an afternoon. Ten years ago, building that picture took months of calls. Today it takes an afternoon and some judgment.

So in 2026, a founder who doesn’t know their space cold isn’t short on information. They’ve chosen not to do the work, or they don’t think it matters. Either one tells me what I need to know.

6. My 2x Deal Size Test Depends on Knowing What Competitors Charge

Right now I won’t invest in an agentic B2B company unless it unlocks budget beyond the software budget. The proof I look for is deal sizes at least 2x what the pre-AI competitors get.

You can’t answer that question if you don’t know your space cold.

I ask, “What does the leading pre-AI tool charge a customer like this one?” The founders who know their market give me a number, a range, and the caveats: “List is $X a seat, they usually close around 30% off, but the real comparison is the two contractors this replaces.” Then they show me their own deal sizes against it.

The founders who don’t know their market give me a guess, or a TAM slide, or “we’re not really comparable to them.”

The founders who can’t answer this lose the deal with me. They’re also the ones most likely to underprice their product for its whole life, because they don’t know what the customer was paying before.

7. How I Test It in the First Meeting

I don’t need a competition slide. Most competition slides are a 2×2 where the founder is in the upper right, and they tell me nothing. Here’s what I actually ask:

  • “Who did you lose your last deal to, and why?” If it’s pre-revenue: “Which design partner almost went with something else?”
  • “Rank your top five competitors, and tell me where each one beats you.” This is the most revealing question I ask. Strong founders answer right away and get specific. Weaker founders start to struggle at number three.
  • “What does the incumbent do better than you, and better than you’ll do in two years?” If the founder can’t name three real strengths, they haven’t studied the incumbent. They’ve only reacted to its weaknesses.
  • “What will the incumbent ship in the next 12 months, and what does that do to you?”
  • I name a competitor that launched in the last 60 days and ask what they think of it. The best founders have already tried the product.
  • “What was this customer paying, and who were they paying, before you?”

And the red flags, which haven’t changed in a decade:

  • “We don’t really have competition.”
  • Calling the incumbents “old,” “legacy” or “dinosaurs” without being able to explain why customers keep renewing with them. Every founder can see the incumbent’s weaknesses. The best ones also understand its strengths.
  • Being vague on pricing. If they don’t know what competitors charge, they don’t know what they’re replacing.
  • Not knowing the incumbent’s AI roadmap. In 2026, every incumbent has one.
  • Arguing when they’re corrected on a fact about their own market, instead of asking what you know.

8. Knowing Your Space Cold Is Different From Worrying About Competitors

This doesn’t mean founders should obsess about competitors or build to the competitor’s roadmap. Some of my best founders barely talk about competition in board meetings.

Those founders know it all cold, and then they put it away. They know exactly where they’re 10x better and where they aren’t. They know which deals to chase and which to skip. When a competitor raises a big round, they know what it does and doesn’t change, so they don’t panic.

Competitors rarely kill a top-tier team. But a team that doesn’t understand its market can lose quarter after quarter without ever seeing who’s beating it.

What I’d Do This Week if I Were Raising

  1. Write a one-page brief on every competitor: pricing, positioning, recent launches, funding, top customers, and where they beat you. Have an agent build the first draft, then fix it yourself. The fixing is where you actually learn the market.
  2. Write down the incumbent’s five real strengths, and explain why a smart customer stays with it. If you can’t argue its side, you aren’t ready to beat it.
  3. Call three customers who almost picked someone else, and ask why.
  4. Try the product of every competitor that launched in the last 90 days, and write down one thing each one does better than you.
  5. Put the incumbent’s AI roadmap on one slide, with what you’ll do when it ships.
  6. Know your deal size against the pre-AI alternative. Get the real numbers, not list prices.
  7. Do it again every quarter. In 2026, a competitive map goes stale in about 90 days.

The founders I’ve done best with never needed this list. They’d have done all of it before the first meeting.

issues.title: Don’t Brainstorm What Your AI Agent Should Do. How Owner Had Its Support Queue Write the Spec

issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Owner is at nine figures in revenue, growing triple digits, selling agentic software to manage restaurants. To small SMBs, in essence. So how did they build the Owner Agent? Off their hundreds of thousands of support tickets, to start.

Owner Agent went GA about two months ago, has handled tens of thousands of conversations, and usage is growing about 30% week over week.

Daniel Ternyak, Owner’s Head of AI Agents, wrote up how they built it: Building a self-improving agent: Owner Agent.

(Disclosure: SaaStr Fund is an investor in Owner.)

What Owner did

Owner had hundreds of thousands of historical support cases. Each one showed what the restaurant owner asked for, how support handled it, and how long it took.

They built an internal tool called Eval Dash to explore those cases and ranked them by how much support time each type took to resolve. When they grouped similar requests together, the hundreds of thousands of tickets came down to about 2,000 distinct operations, things like changing hours, issuing a refund, or updating a menu price.

Those 2,000 operations did two jobs. They became the roadmap, in priority order by support time saved. And they became the evals the agent is tested against.

Nobody had to guess what restaurant owners wanted the agent to do. Years of support tickets already said so.

Why it works

A support ticket is about the strongest demand signal a company has. A customer stopped what they were doing and asked for help with something they couldn’t do on their own. That beats a survey or a feature vote.

Ranking by time to resolve, rather than by ticket count, matters too. It puts the work that costs your support team the most hours at the top of the list, so the agent starts paying for itself early.

The evals come almost for free. Knowing whether an agent works, and whether it still works after the next model upgrade, is one of the hardest parts of building one. Most teams write test cases after the fact. Owner’s came from real requests where a person had already produced the right answer.

Grouping also shows you how big the job really is. Hundreds of thousands of tickets sounds unmanageable. About 2,000 operations is something a team can plan around and finish.

And customers use it right away, because the first version handles the things they ask for most often. A restaurant owner can change Sunday hours with one sentence between lunch and dinner and approve it on one card.

The loop after launch

Owner kept using the same idea after launch.

An internal system called Owner Agent Insights scores production conversations for capability, completeness, speed and feedback, and tracks how often owners approve or reject each tool. When owners keep asking for something the agent can’t do yet, Insights writes it up as a recommended tool and alerts the team that owns that area in Slack.

When a conversation fails, Forge, Owner’s internal platform for background coding agents, turns it into an offline eval case, works on a fix, and runs the full test suite. The new case has to pass and stays in the suite.

The support history gave them the first spec. Real usage keeps adding to it.

How they built so much so quickly

Owner treats the agent as another client of its platform, alongside the dashboard and mobile app. Each product team ships its own capabilities into the agent rather than waiting on a central AI team.

As of October 2026, Owner Agent has 241 tools across 27 product areas, from 829 merged pull requests in 25 weeks. The ranked list of operations told each team what to build and in what order.

Other things Owner got right

The agent gets the same permissions as the user it’s acting for. If someone can’t change special hours in the dashboard, the agent can’t change them either.

Every tool is labeled with how costly a mistake would be. Looking up today’s sales is harmless. Closing a store on the wrong day costs a day of revenue, so those actions get an extra confirmation.

Every change is shown before it happens. If an owner asks to remove a taco at one location and raise the price of guac at another, the approval screen lists each change on its own line with the before and after, and the owner can approve or reject each one.

Quality dropped once they passed about 200 tools, because loading every tool on every request filled up the model’s context. Now the agent loads only what a request needs. Raising the price of guac loads 3 menu tools instead of 241.

When the agent can’t finish a job, a support rep takes over with the full conversation.

How to do this at your company

You don’t need Owner’s scale to try this.

  1. Export your support history from Zendesk, Intercom, Gorgias or whatever you use, going back as far as the data is clean.
  2. Use an LLM to group tickets into distinct operations, such as “change billing date,” “add a user” or “export a report.” Expect hundreds to low thousands.
  3. Rank them by total support time: how often each comes up multiplied by how long it takes to resolve.
  4. Build the top 20 first.
  5. Turn the resolved tickets for those 20 into test cases. You already know what the right outcome looks like.
  6. After launch, score real conversations, send unmet requests to the team that owns that area, and add every failure to the tests.

Most AI agent roadmaps start from guesses. Owner started from what customers had already asked for, ranked by what it cost to help them. If you’re about to plan your own agent, start with your support tickets.

Read the full write-up from the Owner team: building.owner.com/self-improving-agent

issues.title: Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
issues.summary: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket […] The post Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apne
issues.author: melissa
issues.content_html:
• How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?
  • Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?
  • Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
  • How to Check Your Insurance Coverage
  • Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic
  • Frequently Asked Questions
Key Takeaways
  • Most insurance plans don’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but some partially cover costs of another GLP-1, Zepbound, that’s prescribed for sleep apnea.
  • In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity. Currently, Ozempic is only approved to treat type 2 diabetes.
  • You can find out if your insurance covers weight loss medications for sleep apnea by checking their online directory or calling your insurer directly.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket costs often reach several hundred dollars, and some plans require you to try CPAP or a weight-loss program before approving the medication.

So, will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea? The short answer is no, but some insurance plans may cover other GLP-1s for sleep apnea, especially if you also have other health conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.

Even if your insurance won’t cover a GLP-1, you still have options. Your provider can document medical necessity, which strengthens insurance approval attempts for weight loss medications. Below, learn how weight loss drugs may improve sleep apnea, how to check your insurance coverage, and what other options exist.

Get a Home Sleep Study for as Low as $0

Based on claims data, eligible insured patients may pay as little as $0 for the home sleep study and related consultations. Actual out-of-pocket costs vary by insurance plan, deductible, coinsurance, and coverage. We will provide your out-of-pocket cost prior to your first consultation. Cost does not include any post-diagnosis medication or treatment, if and when prescribed.

Take a one-night sleep study in your own bed, review results with a certified sleep expert, and get a personalized treatment plan for as low $0 with most major insurance plans.

Check Your Coverage 4.8 60,000+ patients

How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) happens when your airway gets blocked during sleep, causing a pause in breathing. These episodes can happen many times throughout the night and last anywhere from 10 to 30 seconds.

Carrying extra weight around the neck is a major risk factor for OSA, as excess tissue can crowd your airway while you sleep Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source . About 31% of people with obstructive sleep apnea have obesity while 44% are overweight Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . Because of this connection, experts have started researching to see if GLP-1s like Ozempic can also improve symptoms of OSA Trusted Source Journal of Translational Medicine View Source .

A clear relationship exists between weight loss and better sleep apnea outcomes. A study review found that a 20% decrease in BMI led to a 57% reduction in sleep apnea symptoms Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Other research confirms GLP-1s may improve sleep apnea symptoms through weight loss, a lower BMI (body mass index), and a smaller waist size. But not all GLP-1s offer the same benefits. For example, another study review found that tirzepatide (Zepbound) improved OSA symptoms more than liraglutide (Saxenda). Trials also show that tirzepatide improves daytime sleepiness and blood pressure, two issues that often accompany sleep apnea.

Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?

Currently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved Ozempic to treat sleep apnea or weight loss. Ozempic is only approved by the FDA to treat type 2 diabetes. The only FDA-approved GLP-1s for weight loss are semaglutide (Wegovy), liraglutide (Saxenda), and tirzepatide (Zepbound).

Among these, only Zepbound has FDA approval for sleep apnea. In 2024, the FDA approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity Trusted Source U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) The FDA is responsible for protecting the public health by ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of human and veterinary drugs, biological products, and medical devices; and by ensuring the safety of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, and products that emit radiation. View Source . This approval was based on a large clinical trial showing significant reductions in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) or sleep apnea severity after weight loss.

Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?

Insurance typically won’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea since the FDA hasn’t approved its use for that condition. Sometimes, providers will prescribe medications “off-label,” meaning they offer them because they may help with a condition not listed in the approved indications. But insurers typically won’t cover a drug for off-label use.

However, if you have another health condition alongside OSA, you may still be eligible for GLP-1 coverage. For example, Ozempic is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, so if you have this condition, your insurance may pay for it. Weight loss and improved sleep apnea become added benefits. Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source .

Some insurance plans also cover GLP-1s for obesity-related health conditions like high cholesterol or high blood pressure, but each company sets its own criteria. If you have one of these health conditions plus a high BMI and obstructive sleep apnea, you may get insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that Zepbound has been approved to treat OSA, more insurers may cover this medication. Many payers are adding Zepbound to formularies, although prior authorization is common. Requirements often include a BMI threshold, documentation of CPAP intolerance or failure, and proof of structured weight loss attempts.

How to Check Your Insurance Coverage

Every insurance company has a range of coverage plans and each covers different drugs. The first place you can look is your insurance provider’s website. Most insurers have a formulary listed under each of their plans, so you can see exactly what’s covered and how much you can expect to pay.

Medicare and Medicaid have a similar list available online. If your insurance company’s online formulary is confusing or difficult to use, you can call the customer service number on the back of your insurance card to ask for copay information on any medication.

You can also submit an appeal if your provider submits a GLP-1 request for approval and insurance says they won’t pay. Appeals can push insurers a little harder if they have denied payment for your weight loss drug or if it’s not on their list of approved medications. You may be able to get it covered with an appeal if your provider can prove it’s medically necessary.

For most plans, you have six months to file an internal appeal with your insurer. If that appeal is denied, you can request an external review for a third-party to weigh in. Typically, appeals are submitted through your insurer’s website, but you may also request more information through their customer service.

Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic

If your insurance plan won’t pay for Ozempic, you can ask about Zepbound or another GLP-1 medication. If no weight loss medication is covered, you still have options. Exercise and diet changes are encouraged for people on GLP-1s, and these changes improve sleep apnea symptoms on their own Trusted Source UpToDate More than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights. View Source .

To lose weight through diet, create a calorie deficit: take in fewer calories than you use daily. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Cutting foods like sweet and alcoholic beverages, may also help you lose weight faster. However, everyone responds differently to diets, so you may need to try more than one approach. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . You should also talk to your doctor before making any big lifestyle changes, especially because they may be able to make medically-sound suggestions based on your history or refer you to a nutritionist.

You can also boost your calorie deficit by exercising.. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommends getting 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous exercise each week. They also suggest you include muscle strengthening exercises at least two days per week . Adding resistance training is especially helpful because increased muscle mass improves metabolic rate.

Beyond lifestyle changes, your provider can recommend sleep apnea treatments like Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source :

  • CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) therapy, which keeps your airways open while you sleep.
  • Oral appliances that reposition or retrain your tongue to stay clear of your airway and prevent blockage.
  • Surgical options like nerve stimulation, tonsil removal, and excess tissue removal to improve OSA symptoms through a variety of methods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicare cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

Medicare does not cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but partially covers another GLP-1, Zepbound, for this diagnosis. Under Medicare, patients are expected to pay $50 per month for Zepbound.

How much is Ozempic without insurance?

Ozempic costs $499 per month without insurance. Some pharmacies offer discount programs, but costs still remain high.

How much is Ozempic with insurance?

The cost of Ozempic with insurance depends on your plan, but you may pay as little as $25 per month on some plans. To get a better idea of how much Ozempic can cost with your insurance plan, you can contact a representative from your insurance network to talk through any out-of-pocket costs.

How long will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

The length of Ozempic coverage depends on your plan and health history. Typically, an initial authorization lasts for six months, but some plans cover this medication for 12 months at a time [/ocm_reference] . Renewals often require documented weight loss progress or updated provider notes.

Medical Disclaimer: The content on this page should not be taken as medical advice or used as a recommendation for any specific treatment or medication. Always consult your doctor before taking a new medication or changing your current treatment.
